15080-godey-s-lady-s-book-vol-42-january:
Godey's Lady's Book for January 1851 opens with New Year's Day in France and a model cottage in the style of Heriot's Hospital, Edinburgh. Elevation and ground plan show porch, lobby, living room, kitchen, back kitchen, pantry, dairy, bed closet, store closet, fuel, cow house, pig sty, yard and dust hole.

Scots admire the style, belonging to a favourite public building said to have been designed by Inigo Jones. Around the cottage, the monthly number keeps Godey's blend of fashion, fiction, household advice and engravings for American women readers. The issue is a window on mid-century domestic life: what a good cottage should hold, and how a magazine taught taste to its subscribers.
15638-notes-and-queries-number-62-januar:
Number 62 of Notes and Queries, for Saturday, January 4, 1851, cost threepence, or fourpence stamped. Its subtitle calls it a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. The motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: When found, make a note of it. The issue is a small weekly forum for questions that no single reader could answer alone.

Notes cover old ballads on The Winter's Tale, crossing rivers on skins, and folk lore of south Northamptonshire. Queries ask about the Penny Postage, the Red Book of the Irish Exchequer, and minor points from chapels to Cranmer's descendants. Replies settle God speed the Plough, Defender of the Faith, and Beatrix Lady Talbot. The number shows Victorian scholarship as a shared, public conversation, carried on in short notes.
15639-notes-and-queries-number-63-januar:
Number 63 of Notes and Queries, for Saturday, January 11, 1851, cost threepence, or fourpence stamped. Its subtitle calls it a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, with Captain Cuttle's motto: When found, make a note of it. The issue keeps the weekly pattern of notes, queries, and replies, in short pieces from many hands.

Notes cover the Breeches, or Geneva Bible, poems found among Sir Kenelm Digby's papers, and the works of Camoens. Folk lore, Elizabeth Walker and Shakespeare, and old English actors in Germany follow. Minor notes treat the curse of Scotland, George Herbert, and errors in the dates of printed books. Queries ask about Dousa's poem on Sidney, an old Dutch song book, and minor points from Sir Cloudesley Shovel to lynch law. Replies settle Pagnini's Bible, the frozen horn, and dominicals.
15640-notes-and-queries-number-64-januar:
Number 64 of Notes and Queries, for Saturday, January 18, 1851, sold with an index to volume two for ninepence, or tenpence stamped. It calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, and keeps Captain Cuttle's motto: When found, make a note of it. The format stays the same: notes, queries, and replies, in short, signed pieces.

Notes here cover the authorship of Henry VIII, the Cavalier's Farewell, Gray's Elegy, and Nineveh monuments beside Milton's Nativity Ode. Queries ask about a sonnet on the Cambridge library, burial in church walls, and minor points from Erasmus and Farel to Darby and Joan. Replies follow on later pages. The issue shows how a learned weekly turned scattered readers into a working community of fact-checkers.
15641-notes-and-queries-number-65-januar:
Number 65 of Notes and Queries, for Saturday, January 25, 1851, cost sixpence, or sevenpence stamped, dearer than usual for a longer issue. Its subtitle calls it a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, with Captain Cuttle's motto: When found, make a note of it. Notes, queries, and replies fill the pages, from ballads to Bibles.

Notes cover traditional English ballads, the father of Philip Massinger, Touchstone's dial, and discrepancies in Dugdale's account of Sir Ralph de Cobham. Henry Chettle, Coverdale's Bible, an answer to Cowley, and folk lore of Lancashire follow. Minor notes treat Langholme Fair, seats in churches, and a specimen of foreign English. Queries ask about the tale of the wardstaff, a ballad ascribed to Sir C. Hanbury Williams, and minor points from William Wallace in London to Lady Bingham.
16032-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, number fifty-one, dated October 28, 1897, under the Great Round World Publishing Company. News, science, and stories fill the paper in words young readers could follow. This number leads with Cuba, where General Weyler's efforts to remain have failed. The paper kept children abreast of a war near America's shores.

Despite letters, petitions, and soldiers' demonstrations for Weyler, Spanish Prime Minister Sagasta recalls him and sends General Ramon Blanco instead. Many who disapprove of Weyler's cruel conduct greet the news with surprise and delight. Seen now, the issue shows 1897 children learning of Cuba's war: a cruel general recalled, and hope for a gentler rule.
22694-the-international-magazine-volume-:
The International Magazine of Literature, Art, and Science offers its issue of January 1851, volume 2, number 2. The catalog record names no editor. New York's International Magazine gathered British and American writing for a growing middle-class audience, reprinting much from London journals alongside fresh work.

This number reprints Mrs. Hall's account of a pilgrimage to the homes and grave of Edmund Burke, from her series on English shrines in the London Art Journal, illustrations included. Literary biography, essays, and tales fill the rest of the pages. Magazines like this one were the internet of their day: fast, miscellaneous, and shameless about borrowing. The issue preserves the reading diet of 1851 in a single helping.
24902-the-international-monthly-volume-2:
The International Monthly for March 1851 leads with Austen Henry Layard, the digger of Nineveh. The sketch recalls his letter in the Knickerbocker Magazine, sent by his friend Minor K. Kellogg, announcing the Nimroud finds, and notes Layard's move to Bagdad to hunt for Babylon's remains.

Kellogg praises Layard as young, hardy, fluent in Persian and Turkish, and tireless in his work. Later pages turn to fiction, where Emily Hastings walks with Mr. Marlow through a world of decorum and scandal. The issue mixes archaeology, art, and letters in the style of a mid-century magazine for educated readers.
25093-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-vol-:
Harper's New Monthly Magazine for July 1851, volume 3, number 14, opens with Benson J. Lossing's account of the national anniversary and the men who framed the Declaration of Independence. The issue then ranges widely, as Harper's did, mixing history, science, fiction, and poetry for a growing American middle-class readership.

Readers find pieces on the solar system, natural history, and the arts alongside stories and verse, all illustrated in the magazine's popular style. The number is a useful time capsule of what educated Americans read in mid-century, from patriotic history to plain explanations of astronomy.
25325-the-international-monthly-volume-3:
The April 1851 number of the International Monthly Magazine, volume three, number one, shows a New York journal one year old and growing. Its preface boasts London advance sheets of important English books and correspondents in Paris, Berlin, and other cities.

This text holds only the first number, though its contents list the whole volume. Fiction samples include a courtship scene in which Sir Philip consents to a suitor, while calling his daughter too young to marry yet. The magazine mixes literature, science, art, wit, humor, and romance from the best foreign publications.
26196-the-international-magazine-volume-:
The International Magazine for February 1, 1851, volume two, number three, opens with a long profile of Thomas Chatterton, the marvellous boy of English letters. It quotes Shelley, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Keats, and Byron laying flowers on his tomb, and it weighs his Rowley poems against charges of mere old phrasing. Campbell's praise for Sir Charles Bawdin gets a full hearing.

Later pages survey Goethe, from his youth and lyrics to Gotz von Berlichingen, Werther, Egmont, and Wilhelm Meister, with his ties to Schiller and the French Revolution. The issue mixes biography, criticism, and literary news, and it shows a New York magazine keeping American readers close to European letters.
29246-the-international-monthly-volume-3:
The International Magazine of Literature, Art, and Science published this number in New York on May 1, 1851. It is volume three, number two. Its opening portrait honors George Wilkins Kendall, editor of the New Orleans Picayune. Kendall, a Vermonter, was famous as editor, author, traveler, and good companion. The magazine calls him a new Chevalier Bayard with a steel pen instead of a Damascus blade.

Other contents include pieces on William Hogarth and Nathaniel Hawthorne. There is Yeast: A Problem, The Littleness of a Great People, and Policarpa La Salvarietta, the heroine of Colombia. Readers get a mid-century American magazine at full stretch, mixing biography, criticism, and foreign heroism for a curious, well-read audience.
30943-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-volu:
Held here is number twelve, volume two, of Harper's New Monthly Magazine, dated May 1851. It opens with Jacob Abbott's piece on the Novelty Works, with some description of the machinery and processes used in building marine steam-engines of the largest class. A picture shows a general view of the Novelty Iron Works in New York, as seen from the East River.

Abbott frames steam power as a contest for dominion of the seas. Two struggles run at once: human ingenuity against ocean storms, and a keen but friendly rivalry between the two great commercial nations to conquer that common foe. The armories for that warfare, he says, are vast iron works, plain outside but huge in capacity. The issue offers a vivid view of American industry at mid-century, when steam was reshaping travel and trade.
31455-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-vol-:
Number eight of Harper's New Monthly Magazine, for January 1851, volume two, opens with the personal appearance and habits of Robert Southey, by his son. The younger Southey, youngest of all his children, recalls a father whose natural buoyancy had been subdued by labor, anxiety, and sorrows, yet who remained a striking figure. Mr. Cottle's description of Southey at twenty-two, quoted in the piece, calls him tall, dignified, and possessed of great suavity of manners, with an eye piercing and a countenance full of genius.

The rest of the number follows Harper's early miscellany pattern, mixing biography, fiction, and information for American readers. Southey's portrait gives the issue its center: a poet laureate remembered by his own child. For readers of literary biography, the number preserves a son's intimate view of a famous father in decline.
33965-the-international-monthly-volume-3:
The International Magazine of Literature, Art, and Science for July 1, 1851, opens with a life of Fitz-Greene Halleck. Halleck was born at Guilford, Connecticut, in August 1795, and moved to New York at eighteen. He wrote early satires as Croaker with Dr. Drake, then Fanny in 1819 and Marco Bozzaris in a small 1827 volume.

The issue, like the magazine as a whole, mixes lives of writers with art, science, and letters from abroad. Readers of 1851 found here a survey of the literary world of their day. The volume now serves as a window on mid-century taste and talk.
33983-godey-s-lady-s-book-vol-42-may-185:
Godey's Lady's Book for May 1851, volume forty-two, gathers the month's reading for American women. Its pages hold a Hindoo belle, a spring carol, cottage furniture, a lady's work-box design, Etruscan lace cuffs, and the month's fashions. Stories, poems, and garden notes sit beside an editor's table and a book table.

Incidents in the life of Audubon, moral courage, and a tale of city and country round out the issue. Godey's was the leading women's magazine of its day, shaping taste in dress, home, and letters. The issue offers a full picture of American women's reading in 1851.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: Taylor, Fillmore, Pierce, and Buchanan fill this fifth volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. The volume spans twelve years down to March 1861, the eve of the war between the States. It prints the official utterances of executives in an eventful epoch before the war. Richardson presents the record as Congress ordered it published.
affair-in-araby-pg10551: Talbot Mundy spins an adventure of intrigue in Araby, where a letter from Damascus draws the hero into plots, desert travel, and shifting loyalties. The tale moves between towns, camps, and the open desert, mixing suspense with vivid scenes of Arab life as seen by a Western storyteller of its time. Fast dialogue and sudden turns keep the focus on daring, honour, and survival.
agrippa-three-books-occult-philosophy-16:
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa sums up all magic in Three Books of Occult Philosophy, here in the first English text of 1651. Agrippa was a sage, healer, and rogue of the age of print's dawn. His three books take in the magic of the earth world, of the stars and sums, and of rites and the names of God and souls in one vast scheme.

J. F. turned the Latin to English for the London press. Adepts since then have kept the book as their base. Its range has no peer in its age. It is the craft's great store.
anzus-treaty-1951:
Australia, New Zealand, and the United States signed the ANZUS security treaty at San Francisco in 1951. The pact was sealed while the Korean War raged and fear of communist expansion ran high across the Pacific. Australia and New Zealand also wanted an American promise of protection as they accepted a lenient peace with Japan.

Under the terms, each party must act to meet a common danger if another party is attacked in the Pacific area. The three also promise to consult whenever one of them feels threatened. The treaty anchored the American alliance system in the South Pacific. Ties between the United States and New Zealand later frayed over nuclear ship visits, but the pact still frames regional security.
arxiv-2509-00051:
Faria Binte Kader and Santu Karmaker survey how generated music is judged in 2025. Music generation has leapt ahead, yet ways to score its output lag behind. Music is hard to grade: structure, coherence, creativity, and feeling all matter, and they resist a single number.

The survey builds a taxonomy, a sorted map of metrics, for both audio and symbolic music, where symbolic means notes written as data. It flags deep flaws in current practice: scores match human taste poorly, cultural bias creeps in, and no shared standard exists, so models cannot be compared fairly. The authors sketch paths toward a full framework that joins numbers with human judgment. Fair grades are needed before claims of progress can be trusted.
arxiv-2509-00151:
Valentina Vaulato leads a team of sixty authors who characterize the ultra-hot Jupiter WASP-121b in 2025 with three spectrographs. Ultra-hot Jupiters are giant gas planets baked by their stars, which makes them fine labs for air chemistry under extremes. Nine transits, when the planet crosses its star, were watched with HARPS, NIRPS, and CRIRES+ at high resolution.

Signals of iron, carbon monoxide, and vanadium are detected by cross-correlation, a method that stacks many faint lines. Retrieval fits bound the water content, though a hydrogen continuum may mute its signal. Ratios of volatile to refractory elements, which trace how a planet formed, match solar values in chemical balance. Extra light curves and orbit data sharpen the whole picture.
arxiv-2509-00251:
Rimom Costa, working alone, proposes Instruction-Level Weight Shaping in 2025, a framework for AI agents that improve after each session. Language models are fluent but largely static after pre-training. Retrieval adds facts at a cost in latency and fit, prompt tweaks are brittle, and fine-tuning is costly and risks forgetting.

Curated system instructions act as external, auditable pseudo-parameters. A Reflection Engine reads conversation traces, diagnoses successes and failures, and proposes typed edits to instructions, user preferences, and tools. Edits are version-controlled, scored by a sliding window of user star ratings, auto-repaired on first failure, and rolled back on repeated failure. An edit budget triggers deeper consolidation when crossed.
arxiv-2509-00551:
Kalyan Banerjee, with two co-authors, links three areas of number theory. The areas are elliptic surfaces, class groups, and Selmer groups. An elliptic surface is a family of elliptic curves over a base. Its Picard group collects divisor classes. Those classes are formal sums used to study curves on the surface.

The team links the n-torsion of the Picard group to class groups. The n-torsion is the part wiped out when scaled by a fixed integer n. They ask when the class group of torsion fields can be divided by n. Class groups measure how far number fields are from unique factorization. A parallel link is made for Selmer groups. Selmer groups help bound rational points on curves.
arxiv-2509-00851:
Hao Zhang leads a team of three authors who review spectrum cognition. Spectrum cognition aims to optimize how radio spectrum gets used. Future wireless networks grow more complex and demanding. Better spectrum use is thus an essential goal. The review frames the field through a three-step lens.

The steps run from data processing to signal analysis to semantic situation. Semantic situation is the highest level of the three. It extracts meaningful information from raw spectrum data. Such information can support intelligent network decisions. The authors formally define spectrum cognition in the review. They distinguish it clearly from traditional spectrum sensing. They survey both traditional and intelligent frameworks in depth. Concrete technical solutions are proposed for key challenges.
arxiv-2509-00951:
Natalie LeBaron leads a team of forty-eight authors on AT 2024wpp, a fast blue optical transient. It is the most luminous such event known to date. The team ran a photometric and spectroscopic campaign on it. Coverage ran from ultraviolet to near-infrared light. Monitoring covered roughly the first one hundred days.

The event radiated huge energy in its first weeks. It surpassed the prototypical AT 2018cow by an order of magnitude. Radioactive nickel decay cannot power such output alone. Its spectrum stays a persistently blue thermal continuum. Temperatures stay very high with no sign of cooling. The team reads this as continuous energy injection from a central source. Later faint hydrogen and helium features imply asymmetry. A near-infrared excess suggests a dust echo or extended emission.
arxiv-2509-01051:
Matte Lim leads a team of five authors on Chronotome, a tool for topic modeling in streaming embedding spaces. Many datasets show semantic changes over time. An artist's body of work is one example. A person's social media history is another. Existing dimensionality reduction methods capture such change poorly.

Chronotome combines force-based projection with streaming clustering methods. It builds a spatial-temporal map of embeddings. Users can explore evolving themes in time-based data interactively. The exploration happens in real time as data arrive. Use cases on text and image data demonstrate the approach. It offers a new lens for the aesthetics and semantics of temporal datasets. The tool targets analysts who need to track change as it unfolds.
arxiv-2509-01151:
Fractional programming seeks the best value of a ratio, and its nonsmooth forms arise when the functions involved have sharp corners. Mootta Prangprakhon and Nimit Nimana study a class where the top part is convex, curving one way, and the bottom part is concave. The problems also carry fixed-point constraints, rules that a solution must leave unchanged.

The pair proposes splitting methods that take subgradient steps, steps based on rough slope data, for the top and bottom parts apart. No subproblem must be solved at each round, which keeps the method simple. They prove the methods converge under stated assumptions. They also add a version for large sums of ratios and test the approach against existing methods in numerical trials.
arxiv-2509-01251:
Robots that move among people need fair tests for how socially well they navigate, yet shared measures are scarce. Pilar Bachiller-Burgos, with ten co-authors, leads a joint effort toward a data-driven metric for social robot navigation. The group sets out how rated trajectory data sets should be formatted and stored for reuse.

Their first data set holds over four thousand trajectories, mostly simulated with a small real share, and human raters scored nearly all of them after quality checks. From these ratings they trained a learned metric, called SN26, presented as the first all-encompassing one of its kind. Results include test loss, comparisons with hand-crafted metrics, and ablation tests. All data, software, and model weights are public.
arxiv-2509-01351:
Statistical conclusions often rest on a Gaussian limit, and when that limit fails, the answers can mislead. Giuseppe Cavaliere, Luca Fanelli, and Iliyan Georgiev show that the bootstrap, a resampling method, can itself detect such failures. Their diagnostic tests compare the bootstrap statistic's distribution with the Gaussian shape a valid setup would imply.

The tests carry three traits: they cause no pre-testing bias, they use the same critical values across applications, and they consistently spot departures from the Gaussian limit. The method is computationally simple, needing only repeated draws of the bootstrap statistic. The authors derive conditions that let data randomness and bootstrap randomness mix correctly. Several scenarios where the Gaussian approximation may break show the tests' practical reach for honest inference.
arxiv-2509-01851:
Jef Pauwels, Cyril Branciard, Alejandro Pozas-Kerstjens, and Nicolas Gisin build symmetric entangled measurements from orbits of Pauli group actions. Entangled measurements remain far less charted than entangled states, above all for many parties. Their construction spins one starting state under products of Pauli operations, the basic flips of quantum bits, to fill a full measurement basis. Symmetry and local running cost guide the design.

The known elegant joint measurement for two qubits appears as one special case. The method extends to more parties and higher dimensions as well. Costs are judged through a ladder of operation classes, letting the team sort which bases run locally with ease. Symmetry makes that sorting tractable where brute force would fail.
arxiv-2509-02151:
Amit Haldar leads eleven co-authors in creating dual transparency windows in a terahertz metamaterial coupled to a perovskite film. Electromagnetically induced transparency makes a narrow clear window inside an opaque band, slowing light. Strong coupling between light and matter phonons, lattice vibrations, creates polaritonic states with new control options. Their micron scale metamaterial couples to a lead halide perovskite phonon mode.

The system switches reversibly between single and dual transparency behavior without structural changes. Field maps and slow light effects confirm the dual window nature. Structural symmetry further allows switching between dual transparency and conventional strong coupling responses. Such tunability suits terahertz switches, filters, and slow light devices. The work links metamaterial design with phonon engineering.
arxiv-2509-02351:
Alireza Sedighi Moghaddam and Mohammad Reza Mohammadi wrote a 2025 computer vision paper on wrong labels in ordered image tasks, such as grading disease severity or estimating age. Neighbouring grades blur together, so human labels often land in the wrong class.

Their ORDAC method corrects labels during training instead of throwing suspect images away. It uses label distribution learning, which spreads a label across nearby grades to reflect doubt. For each sample, the method shifts the centre and width of that spread as training proceeds. Tests on age and diabetic eye disease data, under several noise patterns, showed clear gains in error and recall. Extended versions improved results further, including on noise already present in the data.
arxiv-2509-02451:
Rangel Daroya and sixteen co-authors present a 2025 dataset paper, RiverScope, built to map rivers in fine detail from satellite images. Narrow or muddy rivers vanish in coarse imagery, yet tracking them matters for climate, farming, and flood planning.

The set holds over a thousand high-resolution images covering a large total area, with expert-drawn river masks that took more than a hundred hours to label. Each image aligns with Sentinel-2, SWOT, and a global river database, so cost and accuracy can be compared across sensors. The team also sets a global benchmark for river width, reaching a median error of a few metres. Tests across network types show transfer learning plus full multispectral input works best.
arxiv-2509-02651:
Alissa A. Valentine and five co-authors wrote a 2025 health informatics paper on bias in emergency psychiatry notes. Black patients in the United States receive a first schizophrenia diagnosis in an emergency department more often than other groups, in a setting where stress and bias run high.

The team measured clinician bias exposure as the share of negative sentences in psychiatric notes, labelled by a language model. Records covered nearly thirty thousand patients with several diagnoses at a large medical centre. Regression models linked a high negative sentence ratio to higher odds of a schizophrenia diagnosis, even after demographic and risk controls. That link also weakened the direct effect of race. Black men with high ratios faced the highest odds. The authors propose sentiment metrics as a practical bias monitor.
arxiv-2509-04351:
Dror Aiger and three co-authors flip the usual order of image search in a 2025 research paper. Finding a known picture in a huge database usually starts with global features, a whole-image summary, then re-ranks finalists by local detail matching. That order existed because local matching was too costly at scale. Faster local search now allows the reverse: detailed local retrieval first, then re-ranking with global features computed fresh from the local match pattern.

Their re-ranking embeds images so that distances respect the local similarity scores, using multidimensional scaling, a layout technique. Results on the Revisited Oxford and Paris benchmarks set new best marks for retrieval accuracy. Partial matches that global search tends to miss become findable at scale.
arxiv-2509-04451:
Nicole Fronda and four co-authors design drone controllers that keep flight risk under a chosen limit in a 2025 research paper. Judging drone risk usually needs incident probabilities that scarce data cannot supply, and older frameworks offered no way to steer risk down. Their approach, PRReach, instead studies reachability: the full set of trajectories a drone could feasibly fly under its dynamics. Hazards are mapped from open spatial data, and risk is assessed over that whole trajectory set.

A control optimization then nudges the existing control law as little as possible while respecting the accepted risk threshold. Simulations on real-world data cut risk by up to about a quarter before flight and over half during flight.
arxiv-2509-04551:
Ore Gottlieb, writing alone, maps the outflows of collapsing massive stars to explain a new family of cosmic flashes in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The Einstein Probe satellite keeps finding X-ray transients tied to a stripped, broad-lined supernova type, with bright early optical light and sudden afterglow rebrightening within days. Jet, cocoon, and refreshed-shock models each fail some feature. Three-dimensional relativistic simulations of collapsars, stars collapsing into black holes, supply Gottlieb's alternative picture.

Episodic, wobbling jets with flat-topped cores sit inside a smoother cocoon and disk debris. Wobble changes radiative efficiency, explaining swings between X-ray and gamma-ray dominance. When a jet core swings into view, the sudden rebrightening follows naturally. The structure likely typifies this supernova class.
arxiv-2509-04651:
Costly physics runs can make aircraft flight path design far too slow. Jonathan R. Cangelosi and one co-author tackle that bottleneck in a 2025 paper on adaptive surrogate modelling, where the stand-in adapts as it learns. A surrogate is a fast stand-in for a costly function. One example is an airflow coefficient that would normally need a fluid dynamics run.

Their approach refines the stand-in only where needed. Clues from a current solution show how it responds to change. Those clues are combined with pointwise error estimates to choose new test points. The stand-in is then updated and the run repeated. The goal is accurate results without testing the true functions everywhere.
arxiv-2509-04951:
Eye blinks in brain recordings are usually discarded as noise, yet their rate carries useful information. Artem Lensky and one co-author evaluate deep learning models for detecting blinks in brain wave recordings in a 2025 paper. Blink patterns can signal cognitive load, attention, and possible nerve disorders.

Their pipeline segments signals from one, three, or five frontal electrodes into blinks and non-blinks. They test recurrent, convolutional, temporal convolutional, transformer, and hybrid designs on data from healthy people and Parkinson's patients. A convolutional-recurrent hybrid performs best in their tests. Including Parkinson's data also checks robustness against tremor.
arxiv-2509-05051:
Designing new drug-like molecules means searching a vast chemical space for a rare balance of properties. Aaron Mark Thomas, lead author with four co-authors, present QCA-MolGAN in a 2025 paper. Their generative adversarial network uses a quantum circuit Born machine as a learnable prior for making molecules.

The quantum prior is trained associatively. That aligns its latent space with high-level features from the discriminator. A multi-agent reinforcement learning system then guides generation toward several target properties at once, including drug-likeness, partition behaviour, and how easily a molecule can be made. Experiments show better property alignment for the molecules it makes in their tests.
arxiv-2509-05151:
Brain diseases that spread misfolded proteins also disrupt the circuits those proteins travel through. Christoffer G. Alexandersen, lead author with five co-authors, review network models of neurodegeneration in a 2025 paper. The review covers both of the main modelling camps. Modelling has traditionally split into two camps. One covers neuronal dynamics, the other biological progression, each studied in isolation.

One tradition simulates oscillations, connectivity, and network stability. It treats the brain as a circuit in motion. The other tracks prion-like protein spread through the connectome, plus glial and vascular responses. Evidence shows the two interact: activity affects protein release and clearance, while protein burden disrupts circuits. The authors argue integrated frameworks are necessary. Only they can explain where disease emerges and how it might be altered.
arxiv-2509-05251:
Neutron beams reveal how atomic magnets move inside a mineral called aegirine in a 2025 study led by Oleksandr Prokhnenko with ten co-authors. The mineral belongs to the pyroxene family and can hold electric and magnetic order at once, which makes it a natural multiferroic material.

Measurements between very low temperatures found two magnetic changes in sequence, then waves of spin motion rising from the ordered pattern. A simple spin wave model fits the cold phase using three main exchange couplings, the forces between neighbouring spins, plus a small directional preference. No single coupling dominates, so the magnetism is three-dimensional, not confined to chains as earlier suggested.
arxiv-2509-05451:
Computing inside memory chips, rather than shuttling data to a processor, is benchmarked on real hardware by Niansong Zhang and six co-authors in a 2025 computer architecture paper. Compute-in-SRAM designs promise speed and energy gains, but most earlier evidence came from simulators or small prototypes.

The team measures a commercial device against ordinary processors and graphics cards under realistic workloads. An analytical framework exposes the main performance trade-offs, and three optimisations follow, covering how reductions are mapped, how transfers are merged, and how data are laid out. On retrieval tasks over huge corpora the system beat an optimised processor baseline several times over and matched a strong graphics card while using far less energy.
arxiv-2509-05551:
Fuzzy dark matter, made of extremely light particles, is tested against early universe data by Bahareh Soleimanpour Salmasi and S. Mobina Hosseini in a 2025 cosmology paper. The share of neutral hydrogen over cosmic time, measured from Webb telescope data, carries a fingerprint of when the first stars ionised the universe.

The authors simulate the hydrogen fraction across ranges of particle mass and fuzzy share, and build full probability distributions for the observations with a Bayesian sampler. A hybrid neural framework learns both values and their linked uncertainties, then compares simulations with the observed trend. A small fuzzy share with one favoured mass range matched best, while lighter masses were strongly constrained.
arxiv-2509-05651:
Teams of language model agents working on long tasks coordinate better with a dedicated overseer, Lukas Beckenbauer and three co-authors propose in a 2025 multi-agent systems paper. Partial observability and weak coordination drag such systems down on complex, non-linear jobs.

Their framework, Orchestrator, adds a monitoring mechanism that tracks how agents interact with each other and with the environment. Reflective benchmarking inspired by active inference, the idea that agents minimise surprise, then steers the whole system toward global performance. Tests use maze puzzles of rising complexity in dynamic settings. The authors report clearer gains in coordination and task performance over long horizons than without the overseer.
arxiv-2509-05751:
Finding the object a sentence names, in every frame of a video, is done without any training by Bingrui Zhao and seven co-authors in a 2025 computer vision paper. Referring video segmentation struggles when look-alike objects move and pose differently across frames, and simple fusion of text and video blurs compositional descriptions.

Their framework first parses the query into structured semantic commands with a large language model. A grounding module then builds candidate trajectories for possible targets. A two-stage identification step reasons coarsely about motion, then verifies pose in fine detail only if doubt remains. The system reached leading scores on three major benchmarks while remaining training-free.
arxiv-2509-06651:
Running many-antenna wireless computations on very low voltage is explored by Mikael Rinkinen and four co-authors in a 2025 electronics paper. Massive MIMO systems promise far better use of radio spectrum, but the signal processing behind them burns power. Near-threshold computing cuts voltage to save energy, yet makes chips error-prone.

The authors add algorithm-based fault tolerance, a software check that inspects the final result of matrix calculations for errors, to a Newton-iteration MIMO algorithm. No circuit changes are needed. A MIMO accelerator built on reconfigurable hardware was tested, and the checking overhead depends mainly on how many users the system serves. For large enough problems, the method saved about a third of power with only a few percent extra computation, pointing to efficient and dependable massive MIMO processors.
arxiv-2509-06851:
Choosing the best treatment for each person, among several options and with risk attitudes included, is packaged as Stata software by Giovanni Cerulli in a solo 2025 econometrics paper. Optimal policy learning estimates the assignment rule that maximizes welfare from observed outcomes, treatments, and personal features. Multi-action treatments, with more than two arms, complicate the task.

Two community-distributed commands implement the first-best version of the algorithm. Users can pick risk-neutral, linear risk-averse, or quadratic risk-averse preferences, reflecting how much decision makers dislike uncertain outcomes. The output includes a picture of the optimal policy and an estimate of the best achievable welfare. That estimate is computed three ways: regression adjustment, inverse-probability weighting, and a doubly robust formula that stays valid if either of two models is right. The paper is a software note aimed at applied researchers.
arxiv-2509-07151:
Amogh Anakru's 2025 paper, with 6 co-authors, studies metals made of composite fermions. A composite fermion is an electron bound to magnetic flux, and in strong magnetic fields these particles can form a sea much like electrons in a normal metal. Theory predicts that a shared gauge field, a kind of internal force field, should leave a clear mark on how the particles arrange themselves.

Using a new quaternion method to build accurate wave functions for up to 900 composite fermions, the team computes the static structure factor, which tracks particle spacing patterns. Field theory predicted a term with a logarithm, but the large-scale results show a plain cubic term instead. A simpler model of non-interacting dipolar particles matches both the shape and the size of the effect. The result corrects how scientists should picture these strange metals.
arxiv-2509-07551:
Sean Bocirnea and 1 co-author revisit micros in 2025 as a faster route to extensible language embeddings. An embedding implements one language inside another. Macro embedding, the popular approach in Scheme-like hosts such as Racket, rewrites source syntax into source syntax and can support extensible typed languages, but compile-time performance suffers as macros stack up.

Micros instead translate syntax into an intermediate representation, an efficient internal form, and stop there, producing a deep embedding that compile-time functions can process quickly. The IR is then shallowly embedded back into source syntax. Design patterns make both the IR and its functions extensible, recovering the flexibility of macros. The authors report significantly improved compile times for extensible statically typed languages and propose new abstractions that package the patterns. The work targets language builders who need both extensibility and speed.
arxiv-2509-08051:
Joseph R. Farah and colleagues argue that a wobbling magnetar powers the brightest exploding stars, in a 2025 astronomy paper. Type I superluminous supernovae shine at least ten times as bright as normal ones. Their light curves often rise and fall in bumps. A plain magnetar model, a fast-spinning magnetic neutron star feeding the debris, cannot make those bumps.

A tilted magnetar does not spin cleanly. Space itself drags its axis around, an effect called Lense-Thirring precession. The energy it beams out then swings with time. Those swings print bumps on the light curve in a natural way. Past surveys have not settled the cause. The wobble model gives clear patterns to hunt in the next bright events.
arxiv-2509-08251:
Jizhou Li and 2 co-authors use paper folding as a language for chaos in higher dimensions in a 2025 maths paper. Hénon maps in three and four dimensions make horseshoes. A horseshoe is a set that has been stretched and folded many times. Such sets organise chaotic motion. Past two dimensions, they are hard to draw or sort.

Folded paper shows the same acts of fold and stack. The team matches fold patterns to the horseshoes these maps make. That match gives a clear, visual way to sort chaotic sets in high dimensions. Two systems with the same fold pattern share deep traits. That holds even when their equations look nothing alike. Classification by template is the prize.
arxiv-2509-09351:
Harshini Sri Ramulu and 5 co-authors assess ethics in computer security research in a 2025 paper. Ethical questions are discussed regularly in the field, yet researchers lack clear guidance when the right choice is not clear cut. Reporting practice in current papers is the starting point.

All top tier security papers from 2024, over eleven hundred, are reviewed for ethics discussion. Reporting is inconsistent, focusing on board approval, human subjects, and disclosure, with little weighing of harms and benefits. Interviews with twenty-four researchers, reviewers, and committee members show desire for ethical research but inconsistent values and frameworks. Suggestions to improve practice are contributed.
arxiv-2509-09551:
Tom Fraysse and 3 co-authors use catastrophe theory to classify bright patterns called caustics in a 2025 optics paper. Caustics appear inside instruments built to steer beams of charged particles, from electron microscopes to ion devices, where rays bunch into sharp shapes. Rather than model one device at a time, the authors define a control space cleverly enough that the behaviour follows from geometry alone.

That universal treatment reproduces the conduct of many caustic forms on paper. Better still, it exposes hidden links among aberration coefficients across optical systems, links normally buried under complicated ray paths. The authors see future value for designing corrected instruments, with ion-based devices a particular target for improvement.
arxiv-2509-09751:
Junqiao Wang and 9 co-authors present Meta-RL-Crypto in a 2025 paper, a system meant to predict cryptocurrency returns and trade on those predictions. Crypto prices shift fast, driven by on-chain activity, news, and social sentiment, while labeled training data are scarce. Their design joins meta-learning with reinforcement learning inside one transformer-based agent that needs no extra human supervision.

The agent rotates through three roles, acting, judging its own actions, then judging the judging, in a closed loop. Market inputs in several forms feed the loop, and the agent keeps refining both its trading policy and its scoring rules. Across varied market conditions the authors report stronger results on real market indicators than other language model based trading baselines.
arxiv-2509-10351:
Leonardo Baggiani, Martin Herdegen, and Nazem Khan revisit a basic investing problem in this 2025 finance paper. An investor picks a portfolio to maximize utility, with risk kept under a cap. Their setup is broadly drawn. It allows the odd-shaped utility curves that prospect theory describes. It also allows risk gauges that are not convex. Value at Risk is one of those gauges.

Their main result says exactly when such a problem is well-posed. Well-posed means the problem has a sensible answer at all. Under mild conditions, all hinges on a simple either-or test. Either the utility side or the risk side must react strongly to large losses. Many known pairs can then be sorted at a glance. For plain expected-utility investing, the test shrinks to one ratio. It weighs how the investor treats large losses against large gains, in the limit.
arxiv-2509-10451:
Linling Shuai and seven co-authors calibrate the CHARA Array in this 2025 paper. The array links several telescopes into one interferometer. Polarized infrared light carries clues about young stars' inner disks. It also traces dust forming around aging giants. The array's long mirrored beam path is the problem. It bends polarization in time-varying ways, and that corrupts measurements.

The team uses Jones matrix mathematics. Each combiner's distortions get a model. An unpolarized calibrator star supplies the fit for the instrumental parameters. The modeling exposes real hardware stories. One telescope's oversized phase shift traces to a plain mirror, standing in for a deformable one. Compensator plates on two telescopes sit misaligned. Nightly corrections then bring calibration to a useful level. Genuine polarization from targets like AGB stars now stands clearly above the instrument's own noise.
arxiv-2509-10851:
Primordial black holes could have condensed from the infant universe's densest specks. Owais Farooq, Romana Zahoor, and Balungi Francis compute how cosmic non-Gaussianity would change their numbers, in this 2025 paper. How many form hinges on the extreme tail of the distribution of primordial curvature fluctuations. Black holes are thus a sensitive probe. They reveal how non-Gaussian that distribution was.

The authors work through the curvaton scenario exactly. They derive the full probability distribution from the sudden-decay relation. No perturbative shortcuts are taken. Gaussian and quadratic benchmarks supply comparisons. A self-consistent model then fixes the fluctuation spectrum once. From the same ingredients, it produces two outputs. One is the black hole mass function. The other is the induced gravitational wave background. Both are checked against current observational limits. The sensitivity windows of detectors, from pulsar timing arrays to LISA, supply the second check.
arxiv-2509-11051:
Wu Xiong and 4 co-authors show how stretching two silver compounds can make them far better thermoelectrics in this 2025 paper. Thermoelectric materials turn heat into electricity, but their key traits fight each other: raising electrical performance usually raises heat leakage too. The compounds studied, ScAgSe2 and TmAgTe2, share a layered crystal structure with promising band features.

First-principles calculations show that a small two-direction stretch realigns the valence bands and raises the power factor several-fold along one axis. The same stretch weakens silver bonds, slowing heat-carrying vibrations and increasing their scattering, which cuts lattice heat flow. Combined, the figure of merit rose two to four times at room temperature in the calculations, an unusually large gain.
arxiv-2509-11351:
Chen Wang, Eric Goetz, and Robin Shelton use simulations to explain puzzlingly narrow spectral lines in this 2025 astrophysics paper. The lines come from five-times-ionized oxygen in gas where fast-moving clouds mix with the Milky Way's surrounding medium, and many observed lines are thinner than equilibrium physics predicts.

The team ran ten hydrodynamic simulations of cloud mixing, tracking the ions out of equilibrium, and produced synthetic spectra for the simulated sight lines. The broadening values they found span a wide range, and both the total and the thermal parts can fall well below the equilibrium figures. The reason is a lag: oxygen ions recombining from the higher state linger, leaving plenty of the ion present at temperatures where equilibrium says it should be gone. Non-equilibrium mixing, they conclude, naturally makes the narrow lines astronomers see.
arxiv-2509-11451:
Ahaan Dabholkar and three co-authors expose a privacy hole in federated transfer learning in this 2025 machine learning security paper. In this popular setup, a server pre-trains a model centrally, then clients fine-tune only the final classification layers on their private data, supposedly keeping raw data safe.

Their attack, MAUI, reconstructs clients' private inputs using only the gradients of that classification head, the one part that is shared. Earlier attacks faltered here because the most input-rich gradients never leave the client, and attacks that visibly tamper with the model are easy to spot; MAUI makes no overt changes at all. It first extracts robust feature representations of a batch from the head's gradients, then inverts them back into images. Across image datasets and many architectures, including transformers, the reconstructions were sharp and beat prior attacks by wide margins.
arxiv-2509-11651:
Jan Nordström asks a plain question about boundary conditions in this 2025 paper. What truly differs between the linear and nonlinear versions? His past work derived open boundary conditions for initial boundary value problems. Those are stable in energy and entropy. Solution estimates rest on external data alone.

Here he sets those procedures beside the classical ones. The classical characteristic conditions serve linear problems. The new ones extend them to the nonlinear setting. Both are laid out side by side, with gains noted. The new conditions bound problems of both kinds alike. They can be imposed in a strong or a weak way. That choice is one the classical approach lacks.
arxiv-2509-11751:
Gregor Zens and Mark F. J. Steel make Bayesian model choice fast enough for big data. This 2025 statistics paper treats latent regression models. Unobserved variables hide behind the data. Their marginal likelihoods are intractable. Their model spaces grow exponentially. Variable selection and model averaging face a triple bind.

The authors build an integrated likelihood approximation. Mean-field variational posteriors supply it. It selects models consistently under broad conditions, they prove. Their scheme fixes the latent outcomes once, at a baseline null model's estimates. Every candidate model shares those fixed values. Selection behavior matches the full method to first order. The cost is a fraction. Across probit, tobit, count, and Poisson log-normal models, runtimes fell from days to hours.
arxiv-2509-12451:
A language model shown a few examples learns the task from them, so picking the right examples is half the battle. Wonbin Kweon and five co-authors propose TopicK in 2025, a retrieval method that chooses demonstrations to cover the fine-grained topics a test question needs.

Instead of grabbing the nearest examples by embedding similarity, TopicK first estimates which topics the input requires and how well the model already knows each one. It then adds examples one by one, each covering a needed topic where the model is weak. Experiments across datasets and both open and closed models favor the coverage approach.
arxiv-2509-12651:
Topologically protected light paths are robust because they hug the border between regions of different topology, but that also freezes the route at fabrication time. Stephan Wong and three co-authors propose a way to redraw the border on demand in 2025, in driven polariton lattices.

Pumping the system off-resonance feeds an exciton reservoir whose nonlinear interaction with the polaritons can flip the local topology, moving the interface and rerouting the protected channel. A continuous model based on the driven-dissipative Gross-Pitaevskii equation, read through the spectral localizer, confirms the flip with a local Chern marker. The authors foresee a new class of reconfigurable photonic devices.
arxiv-2509-12751:
Chenyu Hu, Ben Wang and five co-authors use quantum theory in 2025 to ask how close two stars of unequal brightness can be and still be told apart. Bright glare makes faint partners hard to resolve, a core limit for telescopes that combine light from far apart.

They show the best limit for the gap stays fixed even when brightness differs, so super-sharp views remain possible in theory. They compare two ways to combine light and find that blocking the bright star is best when no light is lost. When loss is high, the second way competes well. The results guide future large telescope arrays.
arxiv-2509-12951:
Shilian Chen, Jie Zhou and ten co-authors merge large language models through their service ports alone in 2025. Merging joins strengths of many models into one. Most ways need raw weights, but top models are sold as black-box services with no weight access.

Their Evo-Merging frame uses only port queries and a search that needs no slopes. One part cleans noise across models by sparsity. A second part sets mix weights by sign and score. Formal grounds back the sparse step. Wide tests beat strong baselines on many tasks. The work opens merging to closed models.
arxiv-2509-13051:
Mete Akcay, Siddharth Rao and two co-authors study in 2025 how single objects shift the felt privacy of a photo. Photos fill online media, yet they leak cues past user intent. Past work grades whole images and skips the role of each object.

A mixed study with ninety-two users maps how people judge multi-object photos. Thought models and fine patterns emerge. Shoot context and the mix of co-present objects sway scores much. Such detail can guide personal, context-wise guards on social nets. Future tech can warn on the risky object, not just the frame.
arxiv-2509-13451:
Arijit Chatterjee, Sakil Khan and two co-authors observe in 2025 the quantum Mpemba effect with no bath engineering, in nuclear spin thermalization. Far-from-balance states can relax faster than near states, a counterintuitive act. Dipolar relaxation dominates decoherence in the test system.

Conditions for the effect are derived for nuclear spins first. States prepared to those conditions then thermalize with no external control. Both the standard and genuine quantum forms appear in runs. Effects prove natural in thermalization, not lab artifacts. Spin baths may show Mpemba acts in daily settings once conditions align by chance or design.
arxiv-2509-13651:
Yongkang Du and 3 co-authors propose controllable trade-offs between fairness and accuracy in natural language processing in a 2025 paper. A language system can be fairer, or more accurate, and pushing one goal often costs the other. Most work in this area hunts for a single best answer, one point where the two goals balance. It is called the Pareto front: the set of choices where neither goal can improve unless the other gets worse.

The authors want the whole menu, not one dish. A user's preference, written as a reference vector, sets the target trade-off. Multi-objective optimization can reach many spots on the front. Steering it precisely is the hard part. Their approach calms the fairness update down, averaging recent stochastic gradients with a moving average. It also trims the gradients, keeping only those tied to the parameters that matter most.
arxiv-2509-14051:
Suhang You and eight co-authors predict prostate cancer recurrence from fused medical data in a 2025 paper. Nearly a third of patients who have the prostate surgically removed later suffer biochemical recurrence. A rising marker in the blood signals returning cancer and higher mortality. Flagging those patients at surgery time would let doctors adapt treatment early.

Their model, PROFUSEme, learns embeddings from clinical records, radiology, and pathology together. It fuses the modes midway so they can inform each other. The result feeds a survival model of the Cox proportional hazards family. Against late-fusion alternatives, it performed clearly better. It reached a strong concordance score in internal cross-validation. It also took a solid score on the held-out validation leaderboard of the CHIMERA 2025 challenge.
arxiv-2509-14451:
Yuya Kawamata, Kosuke Mitarai and Keisuke Fujii put forward a quasi Monte Carlo method in 2025 for a quantum trick called linear combination of unitaries with classic post work. The trick builds non unitary steps from an integral over unitary ones, which cuts circuit depth.

On a quantum device, a Hadamard test rates each part of the integral, and classic maths adds the parts up. Past work used plain Monte Carlo sampling or the trapezoid rule for that sum. Quasi Monte Carlo, with sample points spread by design, gave lower errors in the tests here. Two numeric tests cover ground state traits and Green function work. Cheaper, sharper sums cut the quantum runs a target needs.
arxiv-2509-14751:
Zhenfei Qin and Hayato Shimabukuro test in 2025 whether twenty one centimetre radio stats can bound early isocurvature perturbations, extra ripples from multi field inflation models of the early universe. Such ripples are weakly bounded, most of all at small scales. The radio signal from early hydrogen gives a fresh window.

Semi numeric runs with the 21cmFAST code model cosmic dawn and the epoch of reionisation under both adiabatic and cold dark matter isocurvature modes. One point stats, the variance and skewness of brightness heat, react to the isocurvature share and its spectral shape. Structure timing and neutral hydrogen history shift as well. Radio arrays now being built could thus test inflation physics that galaxy surveys leave loose.
arxiv-2509-15051:
Marius Cizauskas leads a team of seven authors measuring how stacking quantum dot layers changes spin behavior, in a 2025 semiconductor physics paper. Their dots, grown layer by layer, emit at telecom wavelengths used in fiber networks. Spin coherence in such dots matters for quantum communication hardware, where spins can store and process information.

Time-resolved pump-probe measurements of Faraday ellipticity compared single, double, and four-layer stacks. Adding a second layer flipped the resident charge from electrons to holes, consistent with electrons tunneling down into lower-energy dots. The four-layer sample gained an extra decaying signal component, which the authors link to strain changes reducing the mixing of hole states. With four or more layers, hole spin behavior changes character again. The layer count thus acts as a design knob for spin properties.
arxiv-2509-15151:
Stelios Katsis and four co-authors probe how audio effects change the emotions music carries, using foundation models, in a 2025 audio research paper. Reverb, distortion, modulation, and dynamics processing are the everyday tools of music production, and producers know they steer feeling. Systematic evidence on how each effect moves emotion has lagged behind studio practice.

Large pre-trained models encode rich links between musical structure, timbre, and affective meaning. The team applies probing methods to the internal embeddings of such models, asking how effect choices shift estimated emotion. The relationships come out complex and nonlinear, with patterns tied to specific effects. Testing the robustness of the foundation models themselves is part of the work. Results aim to give producers and researchers a firmer map from sound design decisions to listener feeling.
arxiv-2509-15351:
Marco Barbieri, Urban Jezernik, and Matevž Miščič prove bounds on growth inside finite simple Lie algebras. A Lie algebra is a space where a special kind of product is defined. Starting from a small set of items, repeated products can build the whole space. The diameter is the worst case count of steps that takes. A famed guess makes a like claim for finite simple groups.

The trio prove a strong, explicit bound that holds for any starting set. For a key class of these algebras, with random starting items and a fixed type, the bound is far sharper. Their work moves a group theory idea into a new setting. It is aimed at readers in algebra and growth theory.
arxiv-2509-15451:
Ankit Kulshrestha leads a team that automates the design of quantum circuits. Hand design takes much expert effort and can bake in bias. As quantum tasks grow, that hand work cannot keep up. The team borrow a trick from classical computing, where a search process picks the layout of a neural network. They adapt that trick to quantum circuits.

They build two search methods and test them on data squeezing tasks. The found circuits beat hand made base lines on three tasks: cleaning noisy quantum data, squeezing classical data, and squeezing pure quantum data. The results suggest search can cut the hand effort in circuit design. It also keeps the found circuits lean and fit for their task.
arxiv-2509-15551:
Sepehr Dehdashtian leads a team that attacks detectors of fake images. Such detectors guard against ever more real looking images made from text. Red team tests find their weak spots by feeding them images they misjudge. Past attacks needed inside access to the detector, or costly work per image. Both limits block tests of top private detectors.

Their method, PolyJuice, needs only black box access and works for all images at once. It finds a shift in the maker's inner space between images the detector gets right and wrong. Steering all new images along that shift fools detectors far more often. The shift can be learned at low resolution and moved across detectors.
arxiv-2509-15651:
Yuchen Zhang and Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri speed up a tool that grades each training point's sway on a model. The influence function gives that grade in theory. In practice it is costly: the slopes it needs are as large as the model itself. Even with shortcuts, big models strain compute and memory.

Their trick uses dropout, the random silencing of parts during training, as a squeeze on those slopes. The squeeze cuts cost both in the influence math and in the squeezing step itself. Theory and tests show the method keeps the key parts of each point's sway. That makes influence grades usable on modern large models.
arxiv-2509-15851:
Tomonori Ikeda leads a team that reports the first direct gamma ray detection from the center of our galaxy in a low energy band. Their camera tracks the electrons that gamma rays knock loose, giving both images and spectra over a wide view. A one day balloon flight over Australia gathered the data. The image map shows a clear excess from the galactic center region.

Three models of the glow all fit the data: a single point source, a multi part structure, and a smooth spread. One part of the multi part model matches the flux reported by an earlier satellite. The team stress the method is simple and direct. It sets up sharper MeV band surveys to come.
arxiv-2509-16151:
Programs that learn to defend a computer network often fail when the network layout changes even a little. Isaiah J. King, Benjamin Bowman, and H. Howie Huang frame defense as a two-player game played on a graph of hosts and their links. Their agents read the network as a graph and act by editing that graph, which builds in a sense of how hosts relate.

Such agents learn rules that carry over to networks they have never seen. In tests they beat prior leading methods by a wide margin. They held up against varied attackers in complex, multi-agent settings, a step toward defense tools that adapt on their own.
arxiv-2509-16451:
Robust plans that adapt as uncertainty unfolds beat static plans inside the guessed range, but they can break badly just outside it. Karl Zhu and Dimitris Bertsimas liken this brittleness to overfitting in machine learning: the adaptive parts lean too hard on the assumed range. Their fix sizes the safety range per constraint, with tougher guarantees for the constraints that hurt most when breached.

Read as regularization, the tighter guarantees shrink risky adaptive moves while looser ones keep useful freedom. The view gives a principled way to design uncertainty sets that balance toughness with flexibility.
arxiv-2509-16651:
Sayantan Chanda, Chandeshwar Misra, and Ranjini Bandyopadhyay study soft gel particles in thick suspensions in a 2025 physics paper. The particles shrink when warmed past a set point, as water leaves them. Past work saw the thick mix shift from one solid-like state to another. A fluid-like stage sat in between.

The team test how water-liking traits and electric forces shape that shift. Common salts and sugar are used to tune the particle surface. With sugar, the key surface trait stays the same across the shift point. Such easy tuning could help design new soft materials. The work links tiny particle traits to bulk flow.
arxiv-2509-16751:
Son-Hsien Chen, Seng Ghee Tan, and Ching-Ray Chang steer entanglement over time in a 2025 quantum paper. Two spin qubits link through a central unit that polarizes electrons around it. That link is the RKKY exchange, named for its finders. The team map paths that entanglement can take: snaking, bouncing, resting at edges, and pulsing.

A damping trick can freeze a chosen path in place. Frozen paths hold their entanglement level over time. The frame gives a planned way to shape entanglement rather than just watch it. Uses could span computing, secure links, and fine measurement, where steady entanglement is prized.
arxiv-2509-16851:
Ming Chen, Jie Han, and Donglei Yang settle a graph question in a 2025 math paper. A factor made of cliques tiles a graph with tight clusters of a set size. Past work asked when such a tiling must exist. Conditions hinge on how connected each vertex is and how few large independent sets appear.

The team prove the tiling exists for large graphs under those conditions. Their case covers clique sizes of at least four. It settles the first still-open case in a question posed by earlier authors. Tiling results like this guide network design, where tight clusters must cover every node with no overlap.
arxiv-2509-17351:
Slava Kitaeff leads a team of thirteen co-authors on a 2025 arXiv report about research computing in Australia. The report surveys what universities and research groups run on their own sites. These local systems sit between laptops and national supercomputers, and the report argues they play a vital role in the national research ecosystem.

The survey counts well over a hundred thousand CPU cores and a few thousand GPUs serving thousands of researchers. The kit would cost a large sum to replace at current prices. Local systems support heavy data work, train students, host prototypes, and meet data sovereignty rules that national sites cannot. The authors find clear patterns in how the kit is deployed and used. Their case is that smart local investment multiplies the value of national facilities rather than duplicating them.
arxiv-2509-17551:
Yuxiang Yao, writing alone, proves a patching theorem for tame fundamental groups in a 2025 arXiv paper. The stage is the projective line over a finite field with a set of points removed. That punctured line carries a short exact sequence of tame fundamental groups, and fixing a rational point turns it into an action of the Galois group on the geometric group.

Using Harbater's formal patching, Yao proves a Seifert-van Kampen style theorem for this tame setting. The theorem yields a purely algebraic account of how the Galois group acts on the generators tied to each removed point. From that action, he computes the geometric tame fundamental group by algebra alone. The paper closes with an explicit description of the full tame group of the punctured line, a basic object in arithmetic geometry.
arxiv-2509-17651:
Filippo Botti and five co-authors generate face images from semantic masks with a leaner architecture. Their 2025 arXiv paper works on semantic image synthesis, where a labeled mask of face parts guides the picture. Diffusion models lead this field but cost heavily, since their attention layers grow quadratically with image size.

Their design, SISMA, swaps the transformer core for Mamba, a state space architecture built for long sequences at linear cost. A mask sets the shape of the face, and the model fills in a high-quality sample that honors it. On the CelebAMask-HQ benchmark, SISMA beat leading rivals on the standard FID quality score. It also ran about three times faster than the best-known designs. The authors pitch it as a viable, lightweight substitute for transformer-based face synthesis in tools that must respond quickly.
arxiv-2509-17751:
Silvia Salvatore and five co-authors model two galaxies that may glow in neutrinos. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns Seyfert-starburst composites, which pair an active nucleus with a burst of star birth. IceCube has seen high-energy neutrinos from the direction of one such galaxy, NGC 1068, and hints point to a second, NGC 7469, at even higher energies.

Theory fingers the nucleus's corona as the likely neutrino source, since it can hide the gamma rays that would otherwise give the game away. The team updates its 2022 model with a proper treatment of stochastic acceleration in the corona and of secondary electrons and positrons. A Markov chain Monte Carlo study then scans the parameter space under prior knowledge. For NGC 1068, the model explains the observed non-thermal traits, with both corona and starburst playing parts. The fits sharpen where future neutrino telescopes should look.
arxiv-2509-18051:
Tiziano Arnone Cardinale, Thomas Bland, and Stephanie M Reimann study a strange phase where a gas is both solid-like and free-flowing. Their 2025 paper uses ultracold polar molecules, shielded by a microwave field. Such molecules pull on each other in strong, angled ways that open rich phases.

A broadened theory frame is checked against exact Monte Carlo sims. For a wide range, it nails the fluid, supersolid, and droplet phases. Tilting the shield makes flow depend on direction, a trait round setups lack. The shift into the supersolid phase can be sharp or smooth, set by that tilt.
arxiv-2509-18151:
Jindi Lv and 5 co-authors guess a neural net's score from its shape, to speed up shape search. Their 2025 method, HyperNAS, deals with a slow step in architecture search: each new shape used to need a full costly run. Surrogate guessers learn from past runs, but often travel poorly to new shapes.

A global code scheme holds the whole shape's macro form. A shared hypernetwork, trained as a side task, brings out links between shapes. A joint loss that adapts per task steadies training. Across five search spaces, the guesser set top marks with far fewer samples, a plus in few-shot cases.
arxiv-2509-18351:
The center of the Milky Way shines in gamma rays, and that glow is still not fully explained. Isabel S. Sands and five co-authors model it with galaxy simulations that track cosmic rays in detail. Their 2025 paper uses the FIRE simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxies. Unlike most past work, the cosmic rays evolve over time with full energy spectra for many particle types.

The team computed the diffuse gamma ray glow made when cosmic rays hit gas and light. The glow's strength varied by about tenfold between runs and times. Its slope at high energies shifted by about ten percent. Star birth bursts and the shifting, turbulent gas between stars drove the changes. Some parts of the glow, from electron processes, flickered on million-year scales. The authors argue that parts of the real Milky Way spectrum may be short-lived effects, not steady traits.
arxiv-2509-18451:
A racquetball moves fast, bounces in wild ways, and shows as a tiny mark on screen. Prithvi Raj Singh, Raju Gottumukkala, and Anthony Maida test how well classic trackers follow such an object in this 2025 paper. Tracking leans on Kalman filters, which predict motion step by step. Those filters do well on tame targets but strain here.

The team scored five top tracker variants on a custom set of 10,000 labeled racquetball frames. They weighed two factors: processing speed and update rate. One variant, DeepOCSORT, had the lowest tracking error by a wide margin. Another, ByteTrack, was a hair faster per frame. Yet all trackers drifted badly, with errors three to four times higher than on standard tests. The authors say fast, tiny targets need new methods built for them. Sports robots stand to gain from that work.
arxiv-2509-18951:
Amiya Chowdhury and five co-authors ask how best to feed material data into machine learning models. Their test case is the thermal conductivity of rare-earth oxides used in heat-shield coatings for engines. Predicting such traits with data models can cut years off lab work. But a model's skill depends on how each material is described to it: as a list of hand-picked traits, or as a graph of atoms and bonds.

The team compares two classic models fed hand-made trait lists with a graph neural network that reads the crystal structure itself. They also test two ways to stretch their small dataset. The graph model wins by a wide margin over both classic models. The result supports graph-based descriptions for this kind of materials search.
arxiv-2509-19051:
Layered composite panels bend and crack in ways that depend on how they fail, and a single damage law often misses that. Shubham Rai and Badri Prasad Patel propose a damage model for laminated composites that changes with the failure mode. Their model stays consistent with thermodynamics and uses polynomial curves to describe how damage hardens as it grows. All of its parameters are fit from lab stress-strain curves, both straight pulls and shear tests.

An optimization routine adjusts the parameters until the model's curves match the lab curves closely. The fitted model is then applied to a curved composite beam of moderate thickness, using finite element analysis. Compared with older models, theirs captures the softening bend of the load-deflection curve as stiffness decays. It also treats damage in tension and compression differently, in line with the lab data.
arxiv-2509-19251:
How galaxy groups grow old is still debated, especially fossil groups, where one giant galaxy dominates after its companions merged away. Kethelin Parra Ramos and twelve co-authors observed galaxies in four groups and ten fossil candidates from a large sky survey. They hunted for substructures with a dendrogram method that reveals a group's dynamical family tree. Stellar population tools then dated and characterized the stars in each region.

Properties varied smoothly from a group still assembling, through a well-formed massive group, to a complex non-fossil system and a near-fossil one. Two fossil groups were confirmed optically, though their X-ray brightness is still unknown. Smaller substructures held younger stars, and metal-poor systems lacked massive substructures. The pattern fits a picture where galaxies exchange energy with the group's gravity well as they interact. Fossil status may also depend on the group's place in the cosmic web.
arxiv-2509-19751:
The faint radio glow of early hydrogen can reveal when the first stars lit the universe. E. Jong, C. Trott, C. D. Nunhokee, and Q. Zheng scout which sky fields suit that hunt with the coming SKA-Low telescope. They reuse archived observations from the Murchison Widefield Array in Australia. Image and calibration measures were pulled for each candidate field.

Gain errors tied to calibrator positions inside the beam were traced into the final power spectra. Comparing fields on equal footing shows which measures truly predict clean results. Picking the right patch of sky is cheap insurance for a flagship experiment. Contamination from bright sources or sloppy calibration can swamp the faint signal. The study helps the SKA team aim its deepest looks with confidence.
arxiv-2509-19951:
Layered semiconductor wells steer infrared light for emitters and detectors, but design software must predict their absorption colors precisely. Konstantinos Pantzas and seven co-authors rebuild the model of one such structure from atomic-scale images. Z-contrast microscopy and strain maps reveal how the alloy grades across each interface. That graded profile replaces the usual square-well guess with nominal mixes.

Fed into absorption calculations, the honest profile lands within a few milli-electron-volts of the measured spectrum. The naive model missed by nearly ten times as much. Growth by vapor phase epitaxy blurs interfaces in ways designers ignore at their peril. Predictive accuracy at this level lets engineers design mid-infrared devices on screen before growing them. The method generalizes to other layered heterostructures.
arxiv-2509-20651:
Counts of galaxies across the sky show a dipole, a lopsided pattern that should match the motion seen in the cosmic microwave background. Vasudev Mittal, Oliver Oayda, and Geraint Lewis compare ways to measure that pattern in a 2025 paper, the second in a series on cosmic multipoles.

The authors test a fitting tool from the healpy software and find it unbiased at varied noise levels and sky coverage. With little sky covered, though, its answers scatter widely and become unreliable. They then compare the tool against Bayesian methods. Bayesian results look steadier when coverage is low. The study helps clarify whether the dipole mismatch is real or a measurement artifact.
arxiv-2509-20751:
Vision models and language models learn from entirely different data, yet their inner representations partly line up. Zoe Wanying He, Sean Trott, and Meenakshi Khosla map that alignment in a 2025 paper accepted at EMNLP 2025. They ask where the match appears, what cues support it, and whether it tracks human choices.

Alignment peaks in the middle-to-late layers of both model types, where features shift from surface form toward shared concepts. The match survives changes in appearance but collapses when meaning changes, such as removing an object. Grouping several examples of one concept also affects the strength of the match. The findings suggest that separate training paths can still converge on similar concept structures.
arxiv-2509-20951:
Elastic constants describe how a material springs back, but heat makes them hard to compute because thermal noise swamps the signal. Debashish Mukherji, Marcus Muller, and Martin Muser present a noise-cancellation method for that computation in a 2025 paper. They generalize a trick first developed for piezoelectric coefficients.

A slight strain is applied to a solid that has been equilibrated. Simulations of the strained system and an unstrained reference run with identical thermostatting. Subtracting the paired runs cancels much of the thermal noise. The authors demonstrate the method theoretically and on model systems, for ordered and disordered solids alike. Anharmonic effects, which spoil simpler methods, are handled more gracefully. The approach could make finite-temperature elastic constants routine in materials simulation.
arxiv-2509-21051:
Real requests rarely give a language model just one instruction; they stack several at once. Keno Harada and six co-authors measure how well models cope in a 2025 paper accepted at EMNLP 2025. They introduce two benchmarks for following many instructions simultaneously.

One benchmark tests text generation with up to ten instructions. The other tests code generation with up to six style and content constraints. Across ten models, performance consistently degrades as instructions multiply. Checking every combination of instructions is infeasible, so the authors also develop ways to estimate capability from partial testing. The work quantifies a gap between laboratory demos and real-world use, where instructions almost always come in bundles.
arxiv-2509-21351:
Auto written radiology reports still fall short of clinical quality, despite rapid progress elsewhere. Behind the work are Valentin Samokhin and 7 co-authors. Auto report tools could ease the growing workload of radiologists. Past methods still fall short of clinical quality. Large vision language models improved with preference based training methods from language models. The authors adapt one such method for radiography reports.

Their framework uses Direct Preference Optimization, which trains on pairs of better and worse outputs. Random contrastive sampling builds those pairs, so no reward model or human labels are needed. The method is model agnostic and was added to three state of the art models. Tests showed gains on clinical performance metrics. The work aims at reports accurate enough for real clinical settings.
arxiv-2509-21451:
