The authors say it tops OlmOCR-Bench while being nine times smaller and much faster than past best models.
arxiv-2601-14751:
Steven Vander Eeckt and Hugo Van hamme fight forgetting in speech models in this 2026 paper. Catastrophic forgetting remains a major challenge for continual learning in automatic speech recognition. A model must adapt to new domains without losing performance on previously learned conditions. Several past methods try to penalize changes to important weights.

The team's method uses inverse-Hessian regularization. The Hessian captures how sharply the loss curves around each weight. Its inverse marks which weights can move safely. Regularization then steers learning toward those safe directions. Readers get a continual learning scheme for speech recognizers that must pick up new accents and settings without unlearning old ones.
arxiv-2601-14951:
Carolin Holtermann, Nina Krebs, and Anne Lauscher test whether image generators grasp time. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with text-to-image models. Time changes how things look, from objects and places to animals.

A model that ignores time can draw the wrong scene. A landscape in spring should not match the same landscape in winter. The authors present TempViz, a way to gauge temporal knowledge in these models. The study asks how well these models use time cues, such as seasons or ages, when they build an image from a written prompt.
arxiv-2601-15151:
Jean Bruant, Pierre-Henri Horrein, Olivier Muller, and Frédéric Pétrot speed up network hardware design. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with FPGAs, chips that cloud providers use for fast packet work. These chips promise low delay and high throughput.

The snag is the slow hardware design process. It keeps FPGAs out of fast-moving infrastructure, from incident response to long-term change. The authors build a pipeline automation framework. It aims to make high-throughput network applications on FPGAs reusable, so a design can be rebuilt quickly and often rather than by hand each time.
arxiv-2601-15251:
Varshini Reddy, Craig W. Schmidt, and co-authors test whether language models can still do math when the numbers look strange. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with LLM numeracy. The models rival humans on basic arithmetic in the usual format.

But training data favors a few prevailing conventions for writing numbers. The authors probe numerical reasoning across many numeral scripts and formats. A number in Latin digits is set against the same number in Devanagari digits, among other forms. The study asks how much of the skill is real and how much is format habit.
arxiv-2601-15351:
Md Khairul Islam and Judy Fox build a foundation model for the spectra of stars and galaxies. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents OmniSpectra. Spectra are the spread of light by wavelength, and surveys now gather them in huge numbers.

Older foundation models take only fixed-length inputs in a fixed wavelength range. OmniSpectra is the first to work at native resolution. It takes spectra of any length at their original size, with no resampling or interpolation. That freedom lets one model serve data from many instruments and many large modern sky surveys.
arxiv-2601-15451:
Emily Heath, Coy Schwieder, and Shira Zerbib count colors in a coloring game on the hypercube. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with generalized Ramsey numbers. The board is the hypercube, the graph of corners of a many-dimensional cube joined by edges.

The question asks for the minimum number of colors for the edges. The coloring must give every copy of a fixed cycle at least a set number of colors. No cycle may be too plain. The authors study how that minimum grows with the cube's dimension and the cycle's length.
arxiv-2601-15551:
Bismack Tokoli, Luis Jaimes, and Ayesha S. Dina present a tutoring system design in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is called ALIGNAgent. Personalized learning tools tailor content, pacing, and feedback to each student. Most current systems stay fragmented, the authors note. One tool traces knowledge, another diagnoses gaps, a third recommends resources. Few join these parts into one adaptive cycle.

ALIGNAgent is built to close that loop. Its name expands to adaptive learner intelligence for gap identification and next-step guidance. The design links diagnosis to the guidance a student gets next. A record note in the abstract lists the venue as Nuclear Physics B, an odd fit for the topic. Readers should treat that line with care. The core idea is a single agent that finds gaps and steers study.
arxiv-2601-15751:
Xinda Chen and four co-authors study how software should reason over growing tables in a 2026 arXiv paper. Tabular data is a fundamental form of data structure. Table tools trace a long arc of progress in data handling. Tables do not sit still, though. Their columns change as technology and needs shift. Data integration also merges tables with mismatched shapes. A system that reasons step by step must cope with that churn.

The title names the task: tabular incremental inference. Incremental means conclusions update as the table grows or changes. Old answers should not silently rot when a column appears. The work targets tools that analyze tables in real workflows. For data platforms, steady inference over shifting tables is a daily need, not a luxury.
arxiv-2601-15851:
A. Herle and five co-authors measure a survey contaminant in cosmic simulations in a 2026 arXiv paper. Intrinsic alignments are a major astrophysical nuisance. They affect next-generation sky surveys like Euclid and LSST. Galaxies tend to align with their surroundings, faking part of the lensing signal. Large hydrodynamic simulations help model that effect. The team uses the FLAMINGO simulation suite for the task.

They measure two-point statistics for a luminous red galaxy sample. Position-position and position-shape correlations carry the alignment signal. The record cuts off mid-claim, but the aim is clear. Survey teams must subtract alignment effects to read dark matter maps. Simulation-based estimates of the signal guide that subtraction. Better models mean cleaner cosmology from the coming surveys.
arxiv-2601-16251:
The RES-NOVA group tests a cold probe for dark matter hits. Their 2026 preprint reports work with a test build of the probe. The full probe will watch for rare hits from dark matter grains. Cold probes can sense the tiny heat from one such hit. Test builds must first show they run clean and quiet.

The group reports what the test probe saw in its first runs. Noise, base line and hit marks are all checked with care. Clean runs would clear the way to a full scale probe. That probe would join the hunt for dark matter mass. The work is a step in a long build chain.
arxiv-2601-16551:
Ergash Tursunov and Daniel Baye split the M1 part of a key nucleus build act. Their 2026 preprint deals with alpha plus deuteron to lithium six. That act makes lithium six with a gamma ray shed. Its M1 part is a small but key part of the rate. A trick form of the M1 step is shown to match the long wave form.

Match holds in all rate sums the team checks. The trick form lets them split the M1 part with care. Parts can then be weighed by their true weight in the rate. True rates guide star and early space maths. The work is a fine sum study of one act.
arxiv-2601-16651:
Lukas Hinterleitner, Loris Schoenegger, and Benjamin Roth ask a plain question about large language models. When a model gives an answer, which training texts shaped that answer? Their 2026 preprint tests ways to trace such links. The usual tools rely on model gradients, which are huge in size.

To cut the cost, most teams use only part of the model. That part is often picked with no clear reason. The authors check two routes in a strict way. One route picks a small set of weights. The other presses the full signal into fewer numbers. Their tests help teams pick a route with proof, not habit.
arxiv-2601-16851:
Albert Zhu, Daniel Bennett, Daniel Larson, Mohammed Al Ezzi, Efstratios Manousakis, and Efthimios Kaxiras map twisted graphene from first rules. Two sheets of carbon, turned by a hair, form new patterns. Those patterns shift how electrons move and pair. Their 2026 preprint spans a wide range of twist turns. It uses dense first-rule math with a lean base set.

The team let each twist form relax to its true shape. Turns as low as one degree come in reach. Maps of form and electron states come out. Such maps guide labs that build twist sheets by hand. They also test tales of flat-band magic in these sheets.
arxiv-2601-17151:
Qianchu Liu, Sheng Zhang, and Guanghui Qin scale AI that writes scan reports for docs. Top text bots still stumble on rich health shots. Report text is a key case of that gap. Rule-tuned training lifts scores but apes stock text. It learns the boilerplate, not the scan's truth. Their 2026 preprint turns to reward-based learn steps in place of rote fits.

Such steps mix sight and text in joint training. Rewards push reports to match scan facts. Less rote text means docs can trust drafts more. The work aims at scale, not one-off wins. Care AI needs that scale with truth kept.
arxiv-2601-17251:
Yunuo Chen and five co-authors present EMPM, a way to model soft, bendable objects. Such objects include cloth, gel, and other continuum materials. Good models must look right and act right. They must also learn from little data and work on new cases. Many past methods fail on at least one of those needs. They smooth out rich motion or need huge training sets.

EMPM aims to keep rich dynamics while staying data-light. The work sits where vision, graphics, and robotics meet. Robots need such models to handle soft goods with care. Film and game teams need them for real motion. A broad, light model could serve all three fields at once.
arxiv-2601-17451:
Nikos Georgiou, Brendan Guilfoyle, and Morgan Robson study families of oriented lines in space. They view such families as submanifolds of the tangent bundle of the sphere. One key family is lines normal to a surface. The authors show those families match ones that are isotropic for a natural structure. Isotropic here means the family sits in a null way in that structure.

That match gives a clean test for line families. Line families model light rays, robot paths, and sight lines. A firm test helps geometers sort them fast. It also links surface theory to line geometry. The focal sets of such families add more shape data. The work builds a bridge both fields can use.
arxiv-2601-17651:
Reese Lance derives higher order double point formulas with SSM-Thom polynomials. Double point loci mark where a map between complex manifolds hits one point twice. Classical formulas give the class of that locus from global data. Lance uses Segre-Schwartz-MacPherson classes to extend the story. Those classes refine older Chern class tools.

Higher order formulas capture finer overlap patterns. Maps with self-intersections arise in geometry and robotics paths. Exact classes save long local computations. Thom polynomials give universal forms for singularities. Lance's work links those universals to double points. Geometers gain formulas they can apply by substitution. The result enriches singularity theory's core toolkit.
arxiv-2601-17751:
Hong-Bae Jeon and Chan-Byoung Chae design a new kind of aerial relay for 6G wireless networks. Their 2026 preprint puts an active reflecting surface on a high platform in the sky. The surface can boost a signal as it reflects it, not just bounce it on. The goal is full three-dimensional coverage for drone base stations and for users on the ground.

Older designs of this kind covered only flat, two-dimensional areas. They also served ground users only, or worked in a passive mode with no boost. A boosted signal helps beat the fading that hits a signal twice on its path. The design aims to do all this while using energy with care.
arxiv-2601-17851:
Hua Yue, Lin Nie, Yiqing Guo, and Hongbo Hu revisit a long-standing puzzle in cosmic ray physics. Their 2026 preprint is about the knee, a bend in the cosmic ray energy spectrum. No one yet knows for sure what makes the bend. Guesses point to how the rays are sped up, how they hit other matter, or how they spread through the Galaxy.

New data give the team fresh leverage. The LHAASO observatory has measured the proton spectrum with fine care, along with total and composition spectra and the rays' direction spread. By testing models against all of these at once, the authors narrow where the knee's cause can sit. Joint use of spectrum and direction is the key move.
arxiv-2601-17951:
Yuhan Wen and co-authors look for signs that black holes starve their own galaxies. Their 2026 preprint studies quasars with moderate radio output. An active galactic nucleus pours out energy that can heat cold gas or push it out of the galaxy. Cold gas is the raw stuff of new stars, so losing it can shut star birth down. The team asks how radio activity links to the size of those gas stores.

They compare quasars across levels of radio strength. If stronger radio output pairs with thinner gas, that is a clue that feedback is at work. The title reports evidence of gas depletion in these quasars. Such clues help piece together how black holes shape the growth of galaxies over time.
arxiv-2601-18051:
Mia Kumamoto and Catherine Welch compute how neutrinos interact inside merging neutron stars when strong magnetic fields are present. Their 2026 preprint deals with neutrino opacities, which set how far neutrinos travel before they scatter. Neutrinos shape both transport and flavor change in the debris of a merger. Simulations hint that mergers can build fields as strong as 10^17 gauss. Yet computing field effects on interaction rates has been too hard to include.

The authors take on that computation directly. Better rates change how merger models predict heat, composition, and the light we see. Those predictions feed the study of how heavy elements form. The work removes a known gap in merger physics.
arxiv-2601-18251:
Kesha Ou and co-authors model how a user's interests shift over time, for better click prediction. Their 2026 preprint presents GenCI. Click-through rate prediction is pivotal in online ads and recommenders. Most models match a candidate item against the user's history. That matching can overfit to the traits that dominated the past. It then fails when interests move fast. The authors instead model interest shift in a generative way, learning intent through cohorts of similar users.

Cohort views let the model borrow strength from people with like patterns. A user whose taste is turning can be read against a cohort that already turned. Fresher intent reads should lift both ads and feeds.
arxiv-2601-18551:
Paloma Thevenet and four colleagues watch the jet of a far bright galaxy core twist and swing over time. The core, named 3C 66A, shoots a thin jet of stuff at near light speed. Shots from a world web of dishes can read the jet at fine scale, close to its root. More and more such jets are seen to change their aim with time.

That change of aim can hint at a wobble in the disc that feeds the core, or at shakes in the jet it-self. The team track the jet across many dates to chart its twist and swing. A clean chart helps sort which cause fits the moves. It also feeds the tale of how cores and their discs dance as one. Such work needs long, calm watch over years.
arxiv-2601-18751:
Seyed Amir Hosseini and six colleagues tackle a flaw in a way to teach agents from side-by-side picks. In that path, a judge says which of two runs was best, and the agent learns from the pick. Real judges are a mixed lot. Some are sharp, some are sloppy, and some pick the worst run on aim. Past tools treat all picks the same, or try to drop the bad judges out.

Both paths fail when a judge is sly: their picks look like help but push the agent wrong. The team build a tool that can trust, doubt, or flip each judge's picks as it learns. A flipped pick from a sly judge turns from harm to help. Such care could make pick-based training safe in the wild, where judges can't all be vetted.
arxiv-2601-19051:
Henry Chen and four co-authors harden language model systems by attacking them first, on purpose. Prompt based attacks are a chief risk when such systems go live, since user input is free form text with no fixed shape. Guards built once tend to age fast as attack tricks evolve.

Their system, HASTE, keeps forging fresh attack vectors and uses them to tune the defense while the system runs. It was shared at a security workshop tied to the NDSS symposium. A defense that trains against new attacks as they emerge fits a threat that never stands still.
arxiv-2601-19451:
Isha Pandey and three co-authors give speech recognition a team of projectors for many languages at once. New systems link frozen speech encoders to language models through light projector layers. In one language that works well, but a single projector strains to map the diverse sounds of many languages into meaning.

Their method uses dynamic multi expert projectors with stabilized routing, so each language leans on the experts that fit it. Speech tools that hold up across languages serve the many users whom English only systems leave behind. Stable routing keeps the team from collapsing onto a few overused experts.
arxiv-2601-19551:
Geunhyeok Yu and Hyoseok Hwang take on a flaw in deep learning models that refine their answers step by step. Many models stack layers, and each layer updates an internal state. Yet nothing forces those middle states to stay meaningful. That gap makes early stopping and adaptive computing shaky, since a half-finished state may be nonsense.

The authors set a structural rule: the internal dynamics should stay scale-consistent across rounds of refinement. From that rule they derive a method called FROST. It gives the state space a self-similar, fractal-like structure through a built-in bias. With that structure, partial results are more likely to be valid on their own. The work aims at models that can stop early and still be trusted.
arxiv-2601-19851:
Rayna Hata and four colleagues study how blind people share control with a navigation robot. Independent navigation is vital to daily life but hard without sight. Robots can guide users and build confidence. Yet a fully autonomous robot can leave the user feeling sidelined, even when they want to stay involved.

The authors ask how delegation in this partnership evolves over time. Early trips may need heavy robot guidance. As trust and skill grow, the balance may shift. Their study follows that changing relationship. Designing for delegation means respecting the user's wish for control. The findings guide robots that assist without taking over.
arxiv-2601-20051:
Gautham Vinod and four colleagues recover the true size of food from a single photograph. Diet-related chronic diseases like obesity and diabetes make accurate food monitoring valuable. AI dietary tools can name foods in a photo. Estimating how much food is present, the portion, is the pressing challenge, because a flat image hides scale.

Their method reconstructs real-scale three-dimensional models from monocular images. True scale turns a picture into a portion estimate. That answers the question diet tracking actually asks: how much did you eat? The reconstruction must work from one ordinary photo, not a lab scan. Better portion estimates could make nutrition apps trustworthy enough for clinical use.
arxiv-2601-20251:
Skyler Wu, Yash Nair, and Emmanuel J. Candès make the evaluation of large language models cheaper while keeping statistical guarantees. Testing many models on a large suite of benchmarks is expensive, since each test item costs a model call. The authors cast benchmarking as finite-population inference, like surveying a fixed set of items.

Under a fixed query budget, they seek tight confidence intervals for model accuracy with valid coverage. Smart sampling can then rank models without testing every item. This matters as benchmark suites grow: labs could spend less on evaluation and still know how sure each ranking is.
arxiv-2601-20951:
Ashwat Jain, Wojciech Jankowski, M. Mehraeen, and Robert-Jan Slager show that some topological phases can steer sound in one direction. Their 2026 paper presents the topological acoustic diode. A diode lets a signal pass one way but not back. Here the signal is sound, and the gate is a three-dimensional topological phase. The team shows such phases realize nonlinear odd acoustoelastic effects.

Two effects stand out. One is anomalous acoustic second-harmonic generation, where sound doubles its frequency. The other is rectification, where vibration yields a steady response. Both are captured by a momentum-space tensor from quantum state geometry. The work joins topology with acoustics in a fresh way. It hints at devices that route or harvest sound using quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-21151:
Carlos Pereira and a large team of co-authors give weather models a dedicated engine for moving air. Their 2026 paper presents a neural semi-Lagrangian architecture for weather forecasting. Recent machine learning forecasters often use one monolithic network. Distinct physical mechanisms are then represented only implicitly. Advection, diffusion-like mixing, thermodynamics, and forcing all blur together. Advection suffers most from that blur. It needs long-range transport across the globe.

Treating advection implicitly demands expensive global interactions or deep convolutional stacks. A semi-Lagrangian design follows air parcels along their paths instead. That matches how the atmosphere actually moves weather. The architecture builds transport in, rather than hoping a big network learns it. The paper aims for forecasts that respect physics by construction. It joins a push for hybrid models that keep the best of both traditions.
arxiv-2601-21251:
Ce Hao, Xuanran Zhai, Yaohua Liu, and Harold Soh teach robots to reuse skills across many tasks. Policies based on diffusion models do well at single manipulation tasks. Extending them to many tasks usually needs much bigger models and far more demonstrations.

Their policy mixes a small set of expert parts that share a compact skill base. A sticky routing step picks a few fitting experts for each moment of a task. Skills learned for one job can then be combined for new ones. The design aims at robots that learn broad skills without a fresh giant model for every task.
arxiv-2601-21351:
Chendong Song and seven co-authors work out the best split between two kinds of hardware in serving language models. A new serving design separates attention work from the feed-forward work after it. Attention is heavy on memory, while the other part is heavy on raw compute.

The two pools are linked at each generation step, so balance matters. Too few units on either side leaves the other side idle and slows every token. The authors derive the ratio that should work best in theory. Their result gives operators a principled way to size each pool instead of guessing.
arxiv-2601-21551:
Yang Zhou and eight co-authors improve how language models take a patient's history over several turns of talk. Good history taking is a core clinical skill, yet it is rarely tested directly. Models shine on fixed quizzes but often falter in live, turn-by-turn diagnosis.

Their method feeds the model real medical notes to guide its questions. With the notes in view, the model can refine its guesses as answers arrive. Better questioning should lead to faster, safer diagnosis support. The work treats conversation itself, not just the final answer, as the skill to train.
arxiv-2601-21651:
Savvas Panagi, Chrysovalantis Spanias, and Petros Aristidou jointly optimize heat and power in local grids filled with electric cars and heat pumps. Electrifying transport and heating gives grid operators welcome flexibility. The same devices also tie thermal and electrical behavior tightly together.

That coupling breaks the assumptions of older network management. Their framework plans both sides at once for active distribution grids. Coordinated control can shave peaks by timing charging and heating against each other. The work supports towns adding many electric vehicles and heat pumps without rebuilding the whole network.
arxiv-2601-21951:
James Matthew Young and co-authors build samplers for probability distributions that are known only up to a scaling constant. Many problems in physics and statistics have exactly that form. Diffusion-based samplers move along a path that smoothly connects a simple starting distribution to the hard target one.

The team's 2026 preprint combines that diffusion path with sequential Monte Carlo. That method carries a population of samples. It reweights them along the way. The blend aims for samples that are both accurate and efficient to draw. Better samplers feed everything from Bayesian model fitting to molecular simulation. Where the quality of conclusions is capped by the quality of the samples behind them.
arxiv-2601-22051:
Nabhanila Nandi and co-authors study thin wires where two states of matter fight. The wires join a magnet to a material that can carry power with no loss. The magnet tends to kill that loss-free state. Yet the state can live on where the pull of the magnet fades or cancels out.

Near the walls that split one magnet zone from the next, the pull drops to near zero. The loss-free state can grow there. It can also grow when many small zones mix, so that their pulls average out to near zero. The team shows how the pattern of these zones shapes where the state can live. Such wires are a test bed for new types of quantum parts.
arxiv-2601-22351:
Richard Battye and Adam Moss ask a plain question: must dark energy push the same way in all directions? Dark energy drives the late growth of the cosmos. Their 2026 preprint lets the push vary by direction and by time, in a stretched-space model.

They shape the model so a key bound from the faint early glow holds by design. That bound comes from how the glow's heat shifts as it crosses space. The work maps how much warp the data still allow. It tests a core claim of the standard cosmic story.
arxiv-2601-22551:
Meixia Lin and a large team tackle camera location across mixed devices for the CroCoDL 2025 challenge. Their 2026 preprint joins a shared retrieval encoder with two paths to a fix. One path uses classic geometry with fused features and a PnP solve; the other is a neural feed-forward model fed with geometric inputs.

Cross-device location matters when phones, drones, and robots must share one map. A hybrid that pairs classic rigor with learned speed can hold up where either alone fails. The work is a contest entry, built to a shared test.
arxiv-2601-22651:
Naoki Murata and a team assign credit for a diffusion model's output to whole groups of training data. Attribution asks which data shaped a given image. Their 2026 preprint, Guda, notes that users often need group answers — a style, a class — not one image at a time.

Group credit is a counterfactual: how would the output change if the group were gone? Their method answers by way of unlearning. Fair group credit can guide pay, consent, and data curation. The work serves artists and data holders most. It makes a vague debt concrete.
arxiv-2601-22751:
Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan and Bum Jun Kim built a physics-informed network that reads off scaling exponents as it solves. Near singularities and critical points, nature follows power laws. Their 2026 preprint notes that standard networks hide those exponents inside their weights.

Their Müntz-Szász network treats the exponents as trainable dials. It outputs both the solution and its scaling shape. Known exponents let scholars check a result against theory at a glance. The work serves physics where the exponent is the story. It makes a hidden number explicit. Clear exponents also make results easy to share.
arxiv-2601-22951:
Mayank Nautiyal and seven co-authors present OneFlowSBI, one model that answers many inference questions. Simulation-based inference learns from computer simulations when direct formulas are out of reach. Usually each question, like finding likely parameters, needs its own training run.

Their model learns the joint pattern of parameters and observations in one go. A masking trick during training lets the same model sample posteriors, estimate likelihoods, and more. One flexible model could speed up science fields that lean on heavy simulators. Query-aware masking during training is the trick that lets one trained model serve many different inference questions afterward.
arxiv-2601-23151:
Katherine Keegan and Lars Ruthotto help AI models create samples that must obey strict rules. These models work well on many tasks. But they hit a wall when each sample must meet exact equal terms, as is common in science. The sample space then forms a curved surface, and naive sampling drifts off it.

Their fix bends the samples back toward that surface in a cheap and sound way. It is built to be flexible, so it can plug into many model types. The aim is to cure known flaws of rule-bound generation. Sound samples that respect hard rules serve design, physics, and other fields where a wrong sample is useless.
arxiv-2602-00851: Hyejun Jeong and colleagues show persuasive interaction leaves a visible, task-dependent footprint on downstream agent work. In web research it raises domains visited by 16.3% and run time by 56%, while coding shows faster work with larger revisions. They ask whether off-task talk changes how AI agents act, an effect they call persuasion propagation. Agents more open to such context do not reliably predict the size of downstream shifts, prompting conduct-level evaluation of it in agents.
arxiv-2602-00951: Hector Munoz-Avila and colleagues give task planners a right to refuse unsafe or out-of-role orders. Their R-HTN agents follow built-in rules, called directives, on user-set tasks. One type halts when it finds it would break a rule. The other type rewrites its own plan to seek a new route to the same goal. Tests in two task areas found these agents never broke a rule, yet still aimed for the set goal when a route could be found.
arxiv-2602-01051: Rong Fu and co-authors build SwiftRepertoire, a fast way to read immune clues from T cell receptor sets with few marked cases. Marked data is thin, groups vary, and tuning huge nets per new job costs too much. Their plan brews small tuners from learned exemplars, keyed to light job hints from probes and pooled nets. Those tuners sit on a frozen base net, so new jobs start at once from a handful of cases, no full tune. Motif probes tie each call to real sequence signs.
arxiv-2602-01351: Poonam Sharma and Suman Banerjee build DeepPM, a deep-learning profit hunt for social nets that skips fixed spread rules. Profit hunting picks a few seed users whose spread lifts end profit for viral marketing, and past plans demand a spread model first. Real spread runs far messier than any one model's rules, so DeepPM learns seed-set latent forms and varied spread patterns from data. A novel train goal tunes cleanly under their plan, and real-net tests show its seeds earning more profit than many rivals.
arxiv-2602-01951: Shuyang Wu and colleagues propose Multi scale Pyramidal Network, a plug and play multi instance learning module for pathology. Multi scale features capture cell details and tissue layout, but existing methods use rigid or costly designs. As pretrained models trend, MSPN offers progressive whole slide analysis from one high magnification input. Grid remap groups features into coarse maps, while Coarse Guidance Network learns coarse contexts. As an add on to four frameworks on five clinical tasks, MSPN steadily improves learning, staying lightweight.
arxiv-2602-02051: Shivank Garg and colleagues offer Self-Improving Diffusion Agent, a training-free system using Qwen models. Text-to-image diffusion models enable photo images, yet use is blocked by prompt quirks, meaning mix-ups, and warped anatomy flaws. Current methods require extra training and offer limited control. SIDiffAgent manages prompt craft, corrects poor outputs, performs flaw removal, and stores past trials for prompt-based guidance. It hit a VQA score of zero point eight eight four on GenAIBench, beating open-source and closed methods.
arxiv-2602-02151: Yuli Zhou and colleagues revisit adaptive rounding for post-training quantization with VQRound, compressing the rounding matrix into a compact codebook. Dense elementwise matrices cost too much for billion-parameter models. Low-rank substitutes mishandle heavy-tailed weights. The team therefore minimizes the worst elementwise error under a norm and fits every layer codebook from a small calibration set. Across OPT, LLaMA, and Qwen3 models, VQRound converges better than classic adaptive rounding at equal step counts while training far fewer parameters.
arxiv-2602-02251: Cheng Chen and others observe weakly broken conservation laws in a dipolar Rydberg quantum spin chain. The team shows fragility leaves an experimental fingerprint in a chain of as few as fourteen Rydberg atoms. Simulations on longer chains plus a simplified standard random model reproduce the traits, establishing nonlocal observables as a probe of fragile conservation laws.
arxiv-2602-02651:
Alessandro Lella and 5 co-authors compute the gravitational waves from two state-of-the-art 3D supernova simulations, in research posted to arXiv in 2026. Most earlier models started from simpler progenitors. These two began with stars whose final hour of oxygen-shell burning was itself modeled in 3D, including a vigorous merger of oxygen and neon shells.

The teams evolved the collapses continuously in 3D for seconds after core bounce. Gravitational waves arise from prompt convection, neutrino-driven convection, the standing accretion shock instability, proto-neutron star oscillations, and lopsided ejecta. The signals showed no clear fingerprint of the violent pre-collapse activity. Real differences from published results did appear. Detection looks likely: a future Galactic supernova should register in current and next-generation interferometers across a broad frequency band.
arxiv-2602-02751:
Lisa Alazraki and 3 co-authors scale small language-model agents by auctioning each task to the agent with the best plan, in a 2026 paper. Small agents match large ones on simple tasks but fall behind as complexity grows, and running the largest model for everything is wasteful. Their framework borrows from freelancer marketplaces.

Agents bid on each task with short strategic plans. A systematic cost-value mechanism scores the bids, and a shared auction memory refines bidding over time, enabling per-task routing and self-improvement without training a separate router. Across deep search and coding tasks, reliance on the largest agent fell by about half and overall cost by about a third. Performance actually exceeded the largest agent alone, with negligible overhead. Conventional routers based on task descriptions either underperformed or failed to save money, underscoring the fit problem.
arxiv-2602-02851:
A single spectral line from calcium anchors a 2026 solar study by P. A. Ondratschek and 4 co-authors. The line, at 854.2 nanometers, helps probe the Sun's chromosphere, the layer above its visible surface. Observed profiles show a red asymmetry, meaning the red side is stronger, and a shifted center.

The team simulates the line with an advanced Sun model and solves how light travels through it. They test three ways of treating calcium atoms, including splitting among six isotopes. Only the isotope treatment reproduces the red asymmetry. Matching the line width also needs a suitably restless simulated atmosphere. Together, the model matches average quiet-Sun observations well.
arxiv-2602-02951:
Pruning image tokens from vision-language models can wreck spatial understanding, and Yihong Huang and 6 co-authors fix that problem in a 2026 paper. Pruning speeds up these models by dropping tokens. It preserves question answering well, but visual grounding, locating what words refer to, degrades sharply because pruning loses the global spatial frame.

Their framework, named Nüwa, works in two stages. After vision encoding, it separates, aligns, and aggregates tokens to keep information-rich spatial anchors, borrowing ideas from swarm algorithms. Inside the language model, text-guided pruning then keeps task-relevant tokens. Experiments show top question-answering scores. Grounding accuracy rose dramatically, from very low levels to nearly half of cases correct.
arxiv-2602-03051:
Compressing large language models layer by layer ignores how errors pile up, and Xing Hu and 4 co-authors address that blind spot in a 2026 paper. Low-rank shrinking shrinks each layer on its own. Reconstruction error from early layers then propagates and accumulates through the network, amplifying the final deviation from the full-precision model users expected at deployment time.

Their system, SAES-SVD, jointly handles rebuilding within layers and compensation between them. One part uses second-order activation statistics to align each layer's output with the original, explicitly offsetting accumulated error. Another adapts a weighting coefficient to use the rank budget effectively. Tests across architectures and tasks showed consistent gains after shrinking, without fine-tuning or mixed-rank strategies.
arxiv-2602-03351:
A tiny transformer that makes moral decisions is built for inspection by Mayank Goel, with 2 co-authors. Their custom model processes trolley-style dilemmas as ordered scenarios. Embeddings encode who is affected, how many people are involved, and which outcome each person belongs to. That lets the authors trace how those factors drive a choice. They need not read free text loosely for moral cues.

The two-layer architecture reaches solid score on Moral Machine data while staying small enough for detailed analysis. Interpretability techniques then uncover how moral thinking distributes across the network. Among other findings, biases localize to distinct computational stages. Keeping the model deliberately small is the point, trading raw results for a system whose moral decision process can actually be examined.
arxiv-2602-03551:
Translation quality varies hugely across languages, and data scarcity is only part of the story. Vitalii Hirak and 2 co-authors ask whether a language's typology, its grammatical structure, itself makes translation harder. Their 2026 paper analyzes two large pretrained systems, NLLB-200 and Tower+, representing the encoder-decoder and decoder-only designs.

Across a broad set of languages, the target language's typology drives translation quality for both models. The effect survives controls for training resources and writing script. Some typological profiles also gain more from searching the output space wider, hinting that nonstandard decoding could help them. The authors release fine-grained typological features for 212 languages to support further work.
arxiv-2602-03851:
Learning the Arabic Hijaiyah letters by rote bores the young students who need them to read the Quran. Wisnu Uriawan and 5 co-authors turn the drills into a game in a 2026 paper, developing their method through the ADDIE instructional design framework. The resulting application is built with Unity 2D and Firebase.

Points, badges, leaderboards, and progressive levels structure the play. Visual animations, authentic tajwid-based pronunciation audio, and letter tracing exercises build recognition and fine motor skills together. In a trial with fifty elementary students, mean scores more than doubled, from about forty-three to about eighty-nine. Engagement and motivation ratings ran high, and the authors note gains in perseverance, responsibility, and disciplined practice.
arxiv-2602-04351:
Classical probability cannot describe quantum randomness in its own terms, so Antonio Falcó and 1 co-author survey an algebraic alternative. Their 2026 paper presents algebraic probability, where one starts from an algebra of random variables plus a state, a linear rule that assigns expected values.

Kolmogorov's measure-based framework remains standard, yet quantum and quantum-like effects strain it. The algebraic view contains classical probability as a special case, and quantum probability too. Its roots reach back to early probability ideas, though physics developed its modern form. The authors argue that counting uncertainty in classical settings also gains from the broader language, which makes hidden structure clear.
arxiv-2602-05151:
Optical frequency combs are rulers made of light, vital for precise measurement, navigation, and clocks. Grégory Moille and 13 co-authors show a new chip-scale comb design in this 2026 optics paper. Chip combs have stayed in the lab partly because copying tabletop designs does not yield the strong octave-spaced output needed to pin down the comb's offset. Tabletop designs cascade outward from one pump laser.

Their design flips the layout: two lasers, an octave apart, pump a tiny resonator, and the comb fills the spectrum between them. A parametrically driven soliton forms and lines itself up to both pumps, robustly, across several foundry-made devices. The single comb spans from telecom to visible wavelengths, and its offset is set by the pumps, so it can be detected and stabilized reliably. With the same comb, the team showed frequency synthesis, low-noise millimeter-wave generation, and optical clock readout.
arxiv-2602-05851:
Quasi hereditary algebras were created to mirror the highest weight representation theory of Lie algebras inside finite dimensional algebra, and Claus Michael Ringel shaped much of their theory. Changchang Xi surveys Ringel contributions to the subject, including joint work with his collaborators. The algebras, introduced by Cline, Parshall, and Scott, now appear across many branches of mathematics.

The survey traces homological, structural, and categorical properties that grew out of that work. It also mentions related research and recent developments, placing Ringel results in the current landscape. The note runs to twenty four pages. Such a survey serves researchers entering representation theory who need a map of one founder results. It also records which questions the Ringel school opened for others. The paper is a work of mathematical exposition rather than new theorems, and it says so plainly in its framing.
arxiv-2602-05951:
Flow matching generators start from a source distribution and flow toward data. Nearly all of them inherit the standard Gaussian source from diffusion models, without asking whether it is a good start. Junwan Kim, Jiho Park, Seonghu Jeon, and Seungryong Kim propose learning a condition dependent source distribution instead. In text to image systems, rich conditioning signals are available before generation even begins.

Directly wiring conditioning into the source causes failure modes, including collapse and instability. The authors show that variance regularization and directional alignment between source and target are the critical stabilizers. They also analyze how the choice of target representation space changes where structured sources help most. Across text to image benchmarks, the method improved results consistently and converged far faster on image quality metrics. The work reframes the source distribution as a design choice, not a fixed default.
arxiv-2602-06351:
Software agents that operate computer interfaces must first find the right button or field from a spoken instruction, a task called GUI grounding. Longhui Ma and 4 co-authors present Trifuse, a framework that locates interface elements without task-specific training. It leans on the attention patterns inside a multimodal model, which alone prove unreliable.

Trifuse adds two anchors: text read from the screen by optical character recognition, and captions describing icons. A fusion rule demands agreement across these sources while keeping the location peak sharp. On four grounding benchmarks, the method performed strongly with no fine-tuning on the target task. Removing the added cues hurt scores, confirming each source helps.
arxiv-2602-06451:
Multimodal models usually learn by binding data types, like images and text, inside one data set. Zhuo Huang and 5 co-authors argue that this binding breaks when a new data type appears that the original set never held. Collecting fresh multimodal sets for every combination is costly.

Their framework, BrokenBind, binds two modalities that live in different data sets, joined through one shared modality present in both. Even though the sets do not correspond sample by sample, their relationship through the shared type lets the method hallucinate the missing embeddings for each side. That fills the gaps and frees pairing from single-set limits. Harder scenarios with more missing pieces test how far the trick stretches.
arxiv-2602-06551:
Protoplanetary disks set the chemical starting point for planets, including the carbon-to-oxygen ratio that shapes atmospheres. Pablo Rivière-Marichalar and 7 co-authors study the disk around the young star AB Aur, often called a Rosetta stone for planet formation. New interferometric observations of carbon monosulfide join earlier sulfur monoxide data.

From the ratio of the two molecules, the team finds only models with carbon richer than oxygen can reproduce the observations. The comparison also points to strong sulfur depletion in the disk gas. No single model fits every observed species at once, so the chemistry remains partly unresolved. The work links disk chemistry to the atmospheres planets will eventually inherit.
arxiv-2602-06651:
Dominique Bourn writes on category theory, the branch of mathematics that studies algebraic structures through their relationships. The paper takes up the semi-direct product, a standard way of building a group from two smaller pieces, and develops an outside, or extrinsic, account of it for the category of groups. Two related structures, called hypersubtraction and the hyper-Slominski setting, carry the main work.

By characterizing the semi-direct product from the outside, the paper gives algebraists a new handle on a construction that appears across group theory. The two named settings are presented as the tools that make the characterization possible.
arxiv-2602-06951:
Mikhail M. Ivanov and three co-authors build a systematic toolkit for gravitational Raman scattering, where massless fields bounce off compact objects and lose or gain energy. In the low-frequency regime tied to tidal effects during binary inspirals, their setup dodges the coordinate, gauge, and field-redefinition ambiguities that muddied past work. Worldline effective theory, background-field methods, and modern amplitude tools combine in the framework.

The team computes phase shifts for spin-zero, spin-one, and spin-two fields off generic compact objects at third post-Minkowskian order, and shows that the object's recoil is essential for a consistent result. For black holes, leading static Love numbers vanish exactly, while dynamical ones are nonzero and run with scale in a logarithmic way, settling past off-shell matching disputes. Results also reach higher dimensions, where spin-two Love numbers run at second order.
arxiv-2602-07151:
Quantum computers store information in qubits, but electrons are fermions, and translating between the two is a long-standing problem.  Riley W.  Chien and ten co-authors review methods for coding fermionic degrees of freedom into qubits, aimed at simulating real materials and molecules.

The perspective pushes back on a persistent belief: that fermionic systems beyond one dimension are somehow fundamentally harder to handle.  Walking through the coding choices and their costs, it gives newcomers a map of the field and specialists a clear statement of what is difficult.  Readers planning quantum simulations will find the useful guidance here.
arxiv-2602-07651:
Cosmology usually extracts values from groups of galaxies, but single bound systems may retain cosmological information in their baryonic content. Kito Liao and three co-authors present the first analytic, interpretable tracer linking the matter density parameter to galaxy-scale observables.

Found with symbolic regression on CAMELS hydrodynamical simulations, a compact functional form recovers the matter density well across the IllustrisTNG, ASTRID, SIMBA, and Swift-EAGLE suites. The result suggests one galaxy, properly read, can constrain the cosmos. Space experts get a new kind of tracer that couples galaxy formation and cosmos inference instead of splitting them.
arxiv-2602-07751:
The no-three-in-line problem asks how many points can sit on a square grid with no three lying on a straight line. Thomas Prellberg attacks it with constraint satisfaction programming, a search method that treats the placement rules as a system of constraints to be satisfied at once.

He exhibits arrangements of 2n points on the n-by-n grid for every n up to 60, with no three collinear. As a result, the smallest grid size where it remains unknown whether 2n points are achievable jumps from 47 to 61. The paper gives combinatorialists concrete extremal configurations and a sharper frontier for a classic puzzle.
arxiv-2602-07851:
Control systems sometimes face impossible constraints, and then the best one can do is get as close as possible. Regina S. Burachik and three co-authors study an infeasible double integrator, a basic model of motion with bounded acceleration, where the control limits are too tight to satisfy.

They characterize infeasibility through a gap function measuring the separation between constraint sets. Then they give an analytical bang-bang solution with at most one switch, reducing the problem to two algebraic equations for the switching time and gap. They also describe a relaxed Douglas-Rachford recipe with numeric tests. Control theorists and users get both exact insight and a workable recipe for best-guess control.
arxiv-2602-08051:
The abc conjecture concerns triples of coprime numbers where one is the sum of the other two. Approximation gain measures how unusually large the biggest member is relative to the smallest. Benne de Weger generalizes a concept introduced by Müller and Taktikos for special triples related to convergents of surds, extending it to all abc-triples in several variants.

Extensive numeric computations illustrate the generalized notion and its behavior across many examples. The short note gives number theorists a broader, computationally grounded tool for studying the extremal structure of abc-triples, where large gaps between members signal the most interesting cases.
arxiv-2602-08151:
Prediction with expert advice is easiest when the sequence is easy, yet most regret bounds ignore that easiness. Yoav Freund and four co-authors show a variant of the NormalHedge algorithm enjoys a second-order quantile regret bound. It scales with the square root of cumulative second-moment regret times a log factor, when that variance-like quantity exceeds log of the expert count.

The recipe draws on a continuous-time limit using stochastic differential equations, while the discrete analysis leans on self-concordance methods. Online-learning theorists gain a bound that adapts to easy sequences: when experts' regrets vary little, the guarantee tightens automatically, matching the intuition that predictable problems should cost less to learn.
arxiv-2602-08351:
Training a language model means choosing both the data mix and the model setup, but each choice depends on the other. Zhiliang Chen and eight co-authors call this a chicken-and-egg problem and offer JoBS, a method that optimizes both sides together. Their arXiv paper argues that tuning data and model in isolation misses their interaction.

JoBS spends part of its budget learning a predictor that guesses a setup's promise from a few training steps. The rest of the budget then runs Bayesian search using only that predictor, avoiding many costly full runs. The authors also work out the best split of the budget and show JoBS beating data-only, model-only, and multi-fidelity baselines. Readers get a cheaper way to co-design training recipes.
arxiv-2602-08751:
Biology demands models whose insides can be read, not just good models that resist inspection. Nobuyuki Ota builds Central Dogma Transformer II, a design mirroring DNA-to-RNA flow with its own focus for DNA, for RNA, and across DNA-to-RNA. His arXiv paper asks whether such a mirror recovers known control structure in readable form.

On K562 CRISPR tests with five genes fully held out, the model predicts knockdown effects with mean match score 0.84 and recovers the GFI1B network at 6.6-fold boost. Its focus sits mostly on ENCODE control sites including CTCF sites. For a drug antibody target, scores point to genes matching medical anemia and ferroptosis reports, without medical data as input. Readers get an AI lens for cell control.
arxiv-2602-08951:
Of more than 7,000 spoken languages, commercial identifiers reliably recognize only a few hundred in writing. Rasul Dent and three co-authors argue this gap is largely self-inflicted. The field treats language identification as context-free text classification, hiding the central role of prior probabilities, and institutions reward global models with fixed priors.

This position paper reframes identification as a routing problem: given where and how text appears, which languages are locally plausible? It calls for principled ways to fold environmental cues into the decision, so tail languages get a fair chance. Better priors, not just bigger classifiers, are the path to wider coverage.
arxiv-2602-09051:
Optimizing Pandas code by hand is slow, and asking a language model to do it per program is unreliable and expensive. Avaljot Singh and four co-authors propose RuleFlow, a three-stage hybrid. First, it discovers optimizations per program. Second, they are converted into reusable rewrite rules. Third, those rules are installed in a compiler that applies them anywhere, ending repeated model calls. Discovery, bridge, and deployment are thus decoupled.

On PandasBench, a demanding notebook benchmark, RuleFlow sets a new state of the art: up to 4.3 times faster than Dias, the previous compiler-based leader, and 1,914.9 times faster than Modin, the previous systems leader. The approach turns one-off model cleverness into durable, automatic speedups, and code is public.
arxiv-2602-09151:
Philippe Bouafia surveys integrals that converge without full convergence, including the Henstock-Kurzweil and Pfeffer integrals, and applies their ideas to multi-way Young summing. The focus is Young shape-based summing: summing broad differential forms over m-way subsets of Euclidean space, in the spirit of Whitney's shape-based summing theory.

To make that work, the paper brings suitable notions of chains and cochains adapted to the Young setting. The survey collects spread results into one place while pushing the shape theory itself. For analysts working with rough paths and broad forms, it offers both a map of non-full summing and new tools for summing over rough domains.
arxiv-2602-09251:
Kunihiko Tanaka and two co-authors image the Milky Way's circumnuclear disk in atomic carbon emission with ALMA, covering the central about 7 by 4 parsecs. The data reveal low-density molecular gas, near a thousand hydrogen molecules per cubic centimeter, flowing inward both inside and outside the disk. The carbon-to-CS intensity difference fades inward from 4 parsecs to under 2 and along the disk's rotation, tracing inflow paths.

Projecting the data into orbital coordinates reveals four features: outer spiral streamers feeding the disk and inner streamers reaching within half a parsec of Sagittarius A-star. The other two are an outer disk at 3 to 6 parsecs and the rotating ring at 2 parsecs. Total inflowing mass reaches 15,000 suns, nearly twice the ring's mass, and inflow along the western-arc flow runs roughly a tenth to a sixth of a solar mass per year. That supports the disk's transient nature.
arxiv-2602-09451:
Future road systems need vehicles to both sense nearby traffic and talk, yet separate radars and radios split spectrum and hardware. Integrated sensing and communication shares one waveform, hardware set, and spectrum for both jobs. Akanksha Sneh and three co-authors compare candidate signals for that dual role in their 2026 paper, testing traditional radar waves against a communication protocol's signal on single-point and extended targets.

Frequency-modulated continuous waves respond more poorly to moving targets than phase-modulated continuous waves. The communication protocol's signal, from the IEEE 802.11ad standard, outperforms both radar waves. Radar processing steps were also built on a Zynq system-on-chip through hardware-software co-design with fixed-point analysis, letting the authors weigh computational load for real deployments. The study guides signal choice for roadside dual-use systems.
arxiv-2602-09651:
Spread models do not recover meaning structure evenly over time: samples shift from meaning doubt to class choice within a narrow regime. Florian Handke and four co-authors note that theory links the shift to moving wobbles along class-splitting ways, but usable ways to find and use these windows remain limited. Their 2026 paper tracks the class-given entropy of a latent meaning variable given the noisy state as a reliable mark of these shifts.

Cutting entropy to meaning groups further settles meaning choices at varied levels. Work in many-dim Gaussian mixture models shows the entropy rate bunching on the same log time scale as the splitting mirror wobble before found in variance-keeping spread. Tests on two trained models show class-given entropy picking out the noise regimes key for meaning structure building, and the design measures how guidance shifts meaning information over time.
arxiv-2602-09751:
Kejie Lin and Weixu Su confirm a conjecture about the Carathéodory metric on Teichmüller space in their 2026 paper. Teichmüller space parametrizes Riemann surfaces of a given genus with marked points. According to the conjecture, coincidence of the Teichmüller and Carathéodory metrics on a Teichmüller disk happens precisely for linked holomorphic quadratic differentials. Their zeros, apart from those at marked points, are all of even order.

Gekhtman and Markovic had verified the conjecture for one pair of identified spaces. Lin and Su now confirm it for the genus-two case, the space of genus-zero surfaces with six marked points identified with genus-two surfaces with none. A conjecture linking metric coincidence to even-order zeros thus gains its genus-two confirmation, extending the known cases.
arxiv-2602-09851:
Feature craft is pivotal in auto learning but stays a choke for old methods working in rigid spaces without domain sense. Beicheng Xu and four co-authors note large language models offer a hopeful swap making open ops with meaning. Yet current methods focus on solo subtasks like feature making, short of free chains. Rarely coupled with downstream tuning, they yield greedy feature-then-tuning workflows missing strong links. Their 2026 paper presents CoFEH, a joint frame mixing language-model feature craft and Bayesian tuning for auto learning.

CoFEH uses a language-model feature tuner powered by Tree of Thought to explore chains. A Bayesian tuning module handles tuning, and a tuner picker mixes step types on the fly. A mutual tuning gear shares context between language model and Bayesian tuner for both-ways calls. Tests show CoFEH beating old and language-model rivals in solo feature craft and settings.
arxiv-2602-10151:
Correlation functions of non-Gaussian fields usually rely on local expansions, which fail when the mapping from Gaussian to non-Gaussian fields turns non-analytic. A 2026 paper by Hardi Veermäe presents a non-perturbative route to correlations and polyspectra of locally non-Gaussian fields, plus a semi-perturbative framework that needs no local expansion. The method computes N-point functions even for non-analytic mappings.

As an example, the paper treats exponentially tailed distributions, which can arise in ultra-slow-roll models of inflation. Exact analytic results follow in the strongly non-Gaussian regime, showing the framework reaches cases where expansion methods cannot go.
arxiv-2602-10351:
Superconductivity in strongly correlated systems remains a central question in condensed matter. A 2026 paper led by Humberto M. Silva, with six co-authors, uses a standard Hubbard model with local repulsive forces to describe a two-dimensional system. The equations are solved by Green's functions within a Hubbard-I mean field approximation that handles the strong interaction limit. Both attractive and repulsive cases are covered, giving the zero temperature phase diagram.

In the repulsive case, a superconducting ground state emerges via motion energy and a non-local order parameter. Some minimum repulsive interaction strength is required to create a pairing state, while at finite temperatures with strong interactions the critical temperature levels off like Bose-Einstein condensation seen for strong attractive interactions.
arxiv-2602-10451:
Jinkyo Han and Bahador Bahmani model systems that can behave in several distinct ways at once in a 2026 paper. Many real and building systems switch between regimes, so their outcomes form multiple modes rather than one tidy spread. Standard machine learning captures the modes but can violate physics; physics models stay consistent but struggle with limited data.

Their system uses mixture density networks, which represent a full conditional spread as a mix of parts, and embeds real knowledge through part-exact regularization. Each part can carry its own real constraints, keeping the result clear. The approach suits settings where data are scarce and real consistency matters, from building design to scientific prediction under regime switching.
arxiv-2602-10551:
Guanting Ye and six co-authors fix a positional encoding flaw in solid mixed models in a 2026 paper. Current models align 3D visual traits with language-model models, but they inherit a straight-line rotary encoding. Flattening images into a sequence breaks spatial flow along columns and lets focus decay, so earlier visual tokens fade as strings grow.

Their replacement, C2ROPE, models local spatial flow and spatial causal links explicitly for visual processing. Nearby visual content keeps its neighborhood structure instead of dissolving into a time order, and long-range focus no longer starves early tokens. The paper presents the encoding as a targeted repair. It keeps the language backbone, but gives vision a shape that matches how images sit in space.
arxiv-2602-10751:
Bas Maat and Peter Bloem study how to predict whole numbers from steady inputs in a 2026 paper. Labels like up-vote counts or ready rental bicycles are integers, yet standard practice models them as steady values. That switch quietly changes the label spread from discrete to steady, discarding structure.

The authors ask whether integer labels can be modeled directly by a discrete spread whose settings are predicted from instance traits. For neural network outputs, the settings must stay steady so backpropagation can learn the weights. The paper develops that direct discrete approach, keeping the count nature of the labels while keeping slope-based training intact. The work matters wherever predictions must be counts, not approximations of counts.
arxiv-2602-10851:
Frederik Glitzner studies stable matchings that bend capacities slightly in a 2026 paper. Near-fit modifies agent capacities a little to promise desirable outcomes when no stable matching exists or some agents stay unmatched. But prior work left open whether such matchings behave well in the first instance, and whether room changes create deviation incentives.

Working in the stable fixtures model, which transfers older models through non-bipartite preferences and capacitated agents, the author develops a formal system for both questions. The analysis addresses steadiness of near-feasible matchings in the unmodified instance and the incentives agents face when a central authority adjusts capacities. The paper matters for clearinghouses in school choice and job markets, where small room tweaks must not invite gaming.
arxiv-2602-11051:
How far does a random walk roam on a graph? Itai Benjamini and Justin Salez study the range, the count of distinct vertices visited, for walks on infinite graphs. Their main result needs only positive vertex expansion: with no degree cap, the expected range grows linearly with time.

The proof moves from expansion to a Dirichlet inequality, then to a uniform chance of escape from each vertex. A finite version says a random target in a vertex expander is hit in straight expected time. A lollipop chain example shows range can instead grow like a cube root, and a final mixing note ties unmixed starts to commute times. The paper is a revised note, short and direct.
arxiv-2602-11451:
Looped models reason by iterating, but fixed loop counts waste or starve compute. Ahmadreza Jeddi and two co-authors offer LoopFormer, a looped model trained on factor-length paths for budget-conditioned thinking. A shortcut-consistency training scheme aligns paths of other lengths.

Shorter loops thus yield informative forms while longer loops keep refining them. Each loop is conditioned on current time and step size, so forms evolve steadily rather than drifting or stagnating. LoopFormer holds up on language-model and thinking benchmarks under aggressive compute limits and scales gracefully with extra budget. The work opens a path toward controllable, budget-aware language models.
arxiv-2602-12251:
Translators and language workers now face AI tools daily, yet few courses teach how those tools work under the hood. Ralph Krüger works alone here, presenting a technical curriculum on language-oriented AI for translation and specialised communication. The aim is domain-specific AI literacy, built through clear exposure to concepts and algorithms rather than hype.

Four blocks form the core: vector embeddings, neural network basics, tokenisation, and transformer networks. Together they build computational thinking, awareness of how algorithms steer work, and agency to use them well, feeding digital resilience at work. A trial in a Cologne MA course found the teaching effective, though students needed lecturer support and wider scaffolding for best learning.
arxiv-2602-12451:
Slow-fast neuronal models can produce elliptic bursting, and a stable torus near a saddle-focus equilibrium may explain its onset. Andrey L. Shilnikov led this work with one co-author, Leonid P. Shilnikov, proposing a conceptual model for that torus onset. That kind of shift is common in slow-fast setups where elliptic bursting shows up in many nerve-cell models studied in mathematical neuroscience.

Other versions of the model also pick up different patterns that keep reappearing close to the saddle-focus, so its use is not limited to one example. The paper also discusses homoclinic bifurcations for which the model assumptions hold. Readers get a compact conceptual frame for torus onset and nearby dynamics in slow-fast neuronal systems, with the homoclinic cases marked where the assumptions remain feasible.
arxiv-2602-12651:
Cell identity and function are linked to both inner gene makeup and outer spatial context within the tissue setting. Rui Yan led this work with five co-authors, noting that spatial transcriptomics offers in situ gene expression views at single-cell detail. Yet data are noisy, large, and complex in structure, limiting old methods' ability to capture interplay between spatial links and inner gene ties.

Their method uses cross-scale profiling of cell and gene links to uncover spatial tissue zones and cell types in spatial omics. By jointly modelling local cell neighbourhoods and global gene patterns, it recovers tissue zones and cell types more accurately than prior methods on benchmark spatial transcriptomics data sets. Uses reveal meaningful zones and cell-type layout in tissue samples.
arxiv-2602-12851:
Running rich learning models straight on network switches offers line-rate traffic study, but hardware limits and the need for checkable conduct stand in the way. Rong Fu and ten co-authors present Chimera, a system that maps focus-style neural math plus logic limits onto data plane building blocks inside the match-action pipeline. A kernel-style, linear-style focus stand-in pairs with a two-stage key-pick scheme and a fusion cascade.

That fusion locks in hard logic pledges while keeping neural richness, and a hardware-aware map plus a two-time-scale update scheme keep running stable at line rate within off-the-shelf switch budgets. Tests show close-to-exact calls inside the resource budget of tunable switches. The result is a sound path to trusted, in-network smarts that staff can both run and audit.
arxiv-2602-13051:
Debris disk appearance is set by colliding dust grains, but how tough those grains are at micrometre to millimetre sizes is poorly known. Tobias Stein and two co-authors test fragmentation-energy prescriptions spanning three orders of magnitude in collisional evolution models. Above a threshold strength, evolution becomes dominated by rebounding collisions, where both impactors survive, slightly eroded, shedding only a small mass fraction.

Disks dominated by rebounding would show brightness rising outward beyond the parent belt, a pattern not observed. That absence caps how hard debris dust can be. The limit is approximately one eighth of the square of the local Keplerian speed for grains near blowout size. For micrometre grains in typical disks, that means at most ten to the ninth to tenth power erg per gram. Rebounding collisions, though minor for evolution, turn out far more frequent than disruptive or cratering ones in all disks.
arxiv-2602-13151:
Removing knowledge from a language model is hard enough, and quantising the model for deployment can undo the removal, reviving forgotten behaviour. João Vitor Boer Abitante and six co-authors show full-parameter fine-tuning usually makes changes too small to survive 4-bit quantisation. Their fix concentrates unlearning into low-rank adapters while freezing the base model, so the effective update persists after quantisation.

On Llama-2-7B with the MUSE dataset, low-rank unlearning lifts 4-bit utility by up to 7.93 points on BOOKS and improves NEWS utility too, while cutting privacy leakage sharply: for one method on BOOKS, PrivLeak moves from minus 25.68 to minus 5.86, near the ideal zero, with forgetting measures staying near zero. For deployed unlearning, the lesson is to unlearn where quantisation cannot erase it.
arxiv-2602-13451:
Can rival AI providers, each chasing its own goals, still leave diverse users well served? This paper models that question as a Stackelberg game: providers commit to conversational policies as leaders, and users follow by choosing a model, how to talk to it, and how to act. Providers pursue their own objectives over user actions, and users differ in preferences while making downstream choices.

With user-specific personalization, a weak market alignment condition suffices for every equilibrium to give each user outcomes comparable to a perfectly aligned shared model. Without personalization, when providers must use one anonymous policy, some equilibria turn uninformative under the same condition. A stronger condition then guarantees each user their best outcome even anonymously. Natalie Collina leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13551:
Reward models grade language model outputs, but the dominant judge paradigm needs large models with strong reasoning, while alternatives need reference answers or explicit rubrics. FLIP sidesteps both: it infers, by backward inference, the instruction that would most plausibly produce a given response, then uses the similarity between inferred and original instructions as the reward signal. No reference response or rubric is required.

Across four domains with 13 small language models, FLIP beat judge baselines by an average of 79.6 percent, and it improved downstream results under test-time scaling via parallel sampling and GRPO training. It worked best on longer outputs and resisted common reward hacking, exploiting the gap between validating and generating. Yike Wang leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13651:
Joint learning clients join unevenly, and that unevenness often tracks data traits or resource limits. Yet fairness work usually equalizes loss or accuracy given joining, assuming comparable chances to contribute over time. That assumption can steadily sideline rarely available clients even when per-round performance looks fair. This paper proposes total benefit parity: clients should receive comparable long-term benefit per joining chance, not per training round.

Joining-adjusted total benefit puts the idea to work, separating fixed physical limits from avoidable code bias in scheduling and pooling. Tests on time-skewed, non-IID joint benchmarks show much improved long-term representation parity while keeping near-perfect performance, a fairness gain that does not sacrifice benefit. Stefan Behfar leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13851:
Arshad Beg and two co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv study of machine-written formal specs for C code. Exact specs in the ACSL language help prove software correct, but writing them by hand for real programs is slow. The team asked whether language models can do it.

They compared a rule-based script, the Frama-C RTE tool, and three large models: DeepSeek-V3.2, GPT-5.2, and OLMo 3.1 32B. On a filtered slice of the CASP benchmark, checked with Frama-C and several solvers, the rule-based route proved most reliable. Model output varied more, so the authors cast models as helpers, not replacements, for spec writing.
arxiv-2602-14251:
Pinqiao Wang and one co-author propose a 2026 arXiv debate framework for tabular anomaly detection. Single detectors and static ensembles struggle when heterogeneous model families disagree under distribution shift, missing data, and rare anomalies. The MAD framework treats that disagreement as a signal to resolve, not noise to average away.

Each agent is a machine-learning detector reporting a normalized anomaly score, confidence, and structured evidence, plus a language-model critic. A coordinator turns messages into capped per-agent losses and shifts agent weight by an exponentiated-gradient rule. The output is a debated anomaly score with an auditable debate trace, and the framework recovers mixture-of-experts and expert-advice methods as special cases.
arxiv-2602-14351:
Mehran Aghabozorgi and three co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv world model for lean continuous control. Model-based reinforcement learning promises thrift but often trips on piling model error, one-peak world models that average over multi-peak motion, and over-bold guesses that skew learning. WIMLE widens Implicit Max Likelihood Guessing to model-based reward learning.

The method learns random, multi-peak world models with no loop sampling, and gauges guess doubt via groups and latent sampling. During training, each fake step is weighed by guessed trust, keeping useful fake runs while damping skew from unsure guesses. Across 40 continuous-control tasks, WIMLE beat strong baselines on sample thrift, lifting Humanoid-run thrift by over 50 percent versus the strongest rival, with matching or better final scores.
arxiv-2602-14451:
Qianyue Wang and seven co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv method to curb overthinking in large reasoning models. Long thought chains with repeat self-search inflate compute costs and can even drop scores. Spurred by humans, who crack new problems by drawing on past like cases, Past-Case Guided Thought shifts the plan from full self-search to guided learning from past cases.

Two tasks anchor the design: which past cases to take, and how to use them. Past-Case Pick builds a tight, meaning-tied and telling past-case set per question and model, ranking cases by meaning likeness and model surprise, then tuning past-case count to max surprise drop. Test-time Past-Case Uptake then updates light adapters on past-case-tuned instruction, taking past lore in at test time.
arxiv-2602-14651:
Curved sheets that obey a fixed curvature law can run far out in neat shapes. Aires E. M. Barbieri, with three co-authors, studies the far ends of such sheets in three-space. The sheets in view have finite total bend and meet a strict elliptic law.

The authors work out the far shape of these ends and prove a max rule that holds far out. They also solve the Dirichlet task for the same law in two-space on strictly convex bounded plots. The pair of results links far shape to edge-fixed shape. It gives a full view of how such sheets end and bend.
arxiv-2602-15151:
Nickel and colleagues revisit the classical Hitchcock-Koopmans transportation problem under Monge costs. When the cost matrix obeys the Monge property, they derive compact formulas for optimal dual solutions from the northwest-corner rule. The results offer structural insight and computational gains at once.

As a use, the team turns to a broad class of facility location problems. Within a Benders decomposition framework, those expressions yield fresh formulations in mixed-integer linear programming for the Discrete Ordered Median Problem, where weights do not increase. Numerical tests show the new forms reach state-of-the-art performance and stay strongly robust over many different instances.
arxiv-2602-15551:
Ahmed and colleagues probe a black hole that carries a quantum correction, asking what an observer could actually measure. Their object is a Reissner-Nordström black hole set by mass, charge, and a quantum correction parameter. They first work out orbital and epicyclic frequencies for neutral test particles. Those frequencies then model quasi-periodic oscillations, fitted to observed data from stellar, middleweight, and supermassive black hole candidates.

The quantum correction shifts where oscillations arise and how far their orbit sits from the innermost stable orbit. The team also derives scalar perturbations, greybody factors, and emission rates, and it finds logarithmic corrections to black hole entropy that matter most for small holes. Together, the results show the correction leaving marks on both motion and thermodynamics that oscillation data can constrain.
arxiv-2602-15751:
Govorkova and colleagues demonstrate ultra-fast, radiation-hard machine learning on FPGAs for future high-energy physics experiments, using the PicoCal calorimeter planned for LHCb Upgrade II as a test case. Their work has three parts. First, a lightweight autoencoder compresses a 32-sample timing readout into a two-dimensional latent space. Second, a hardware-aware quantisation strategy cuts the model to 10-bit weights with minimal performance loss.

Third, the team adds a new backend to hls4ml, the community standard synthesis tool, which previously lacked support for hardened FPGAs. That backend translates models automatically into high-level synthesis projects for Microchip PolarFire FPGAs, among the few commercially available hardened options.
