Synthesis on a target PolarFire device reaches 25 nanosecond latency with low resource use, fitting within inherently protected FPGA logic and opening broader adoption of on-detector machine learning in harsh settings.
arxiv-2602-16251:
Hyoungwook Jin and coauthors introduce RelianceScope, a framework for examining how students rely on generative AI chatbots while solving problems. Good progress depends on learners managing their own choices when asking for aid and when handling chatbot replies. Engagement can differ across those two actions: a student may seek help actively, yet use responses passively by copying outputs, or vice versa. So far, no study has supplied a steady method tracking engagement in help seeking and response use together.

RelianceScope operationalizes reliance into nine patterns from combinations of engagement modes in help-seeking and response-use. Those patterns sit within a knowledge-context lens that accounts for prior knowledge and instructional significance. Applied to chat and code-edit logs from seventy-nine college students in a web programming course, active help-seeking associates with active response-use. Large language models can reliably detect reliance in both actions.
arxiv-2602-16451:
Zamin Mamiyev leads five coauthors on confinement epitaxy of large-area tin at the graphene-silicon carbide boundary. Confinement epitaxy beneath graphene stabilizes exotic phases by restricting vertical growth and altering lateral flow. Yet achieving long-range interfacial order while keeping graphene high-quality remains challenging.

The team demonstrates large-area graphene through a tin layer. While the tin layer shows a robust metal band structure, the free graphene layer keeps charge neutrality. Using Raman images, the authors distinguish direct entry from spread-driven expansion, the critical pathway to superior quality. Temperature-dependent analysis reveals dynamical coupling between free graphene and the tin layer, a novel degree of freedom for strain work. Beyond uncovering the spread mechanism, the work establishes metal layers as a strategy for tailoring durable graphene-metal heterostructures with tunable properties.
arxiv-2602-17151:
Peter Koepernik led a three-author team replacing random sampling with exact deterministic paths for stochastic differential equations. Monte Carlo estimation is standard for such equations, but accurate answers demand huge sample sizes. Lyons and Victoir proposed cubature formulae, weighted sets of paths that match Brownian signature moments to some degree, yet explicit constructions had stalled at low degree, too small for practical use.

The paper presents ARCANE, an algorithm that builds cubature formulae of arbitrary degree automatically and fast, reproducing prior best results in seconds and reaching far higher degrees within hours on modest hardware. Across varied equations and error measures, the formulae beat Monte Carlo by orders of magnitude in error for the same path count. Deterministic paths thus offer a practical escape from sampling noise.
arxiv-2602-17351:
Peter Elbau led a three-author paper stretching diffraction tomography to focused-beam scanning systems. Standard imaging of this kind assumes single-color plane wave illumination, a shortcut that fails for real systems like medical sound scans, where focused beams scan a region of the human body. Setups pairing focused beams with scanning had not yet entered the imaging theory.

To bridge the gap, the authors model incoming fields as Herglotz waves, bringing focused beams into the theory. Within that setting they derive a new Fourier link, the basis for measured imaging rebuild from scanning data. Using that result, they carefully analyze how varied scan shapes influence the rebuild, giving focused-beam imaging a firm imaging footing.
arxiv-2602-17651:
Suvradip Chakraborty and team link zero-knowledge proofs to one-way functions in a high-error regime. A recent breakthrough showed that zero-knowledge with negligible errors for NP implies one-way functions, given a standard hardness assumption. This paper asks what follows when errors are large rather than tiny.

A zero-knowledge argument counts as non-trivial when the sum of its completeness, soundness and zero-knowledge errors stays bounded away from one. Under the same hardness assumption, non-trivial non-interactive arguments for NP imply one-way functions, and the same holds for constant-round public-coin interactive arguments. The interactive case yields standard four-message arguments as well. The work closes a gap left by prior results and sharpens the bridge from worst-case hardness to cryptography.
arxiv-2602-17751:
Nina Brolich and team study how the number of target classes affects neural network compressibility for energy-autonomous bird monitoring. Biodiversity loss makes wildlife monitoring vital, and birds suit the task since their songs identify them well. Manual counting is costly, while passive acoustic monitoring records soundscapes over long spans for later analysis.

Machine learning speeds that analysis, yet standard models demand heavy compute. The team instead runs models on cheap microcontroller units in the field, under tight hardware and energy limits. They trained and compressed models for varied numbers of target classes to test multi-species detection on edge devices. Results show strong compression rates with minimal performance loss, plus benchmarks across hardware platforms and a feasibility check for energy-autonomous deployment.
arxiv-2602-17851:
Krishna Neupane and team show causal effects of financial report mood on bank profits, moving beyond link-only analysis. A causal forest method controls for many mixing factors, enabling orderly analysis of spread and curves often overlooked. A pre-trained FinancialBERT model makes mood scores from quarter reports, treated as causal shocks on profit moves such as returns and swings.

Data span NEPSE, NRB and individual banks, with SHAP tests identifying key profit drivers. A two-pronged causal analysis explores how mood impact is shaped by loan holdings mix and by balance sheet strength and debt. Average treatment effect tests, joined with SHAP insights, reveal real causal links between certain balance sheet and expense handling factors and profits. The causal method frame extends past work, giving a more robust account of how financial mood truly shapes firm performance.
arxiv-2602-18351:
Jordan Robinson and three co-authors validate political stance predictions for arguments on two scales at once. Their 2026 paper tackles a mismatch: real knowledge work needs subjective, continuous traits like political position, but pairwise checks are the accepted gold standard for human evaluation. The team builds a dual-scale frame for stance prediction in argumentative discourse.

Using twenty-two language models, they build a knowledge base of position predictions for over twenty-three thousand arguments from thirty debates on the UK program Question Time. Pointwise scoring shows moderate human-model agreement, reflecting genuine subjectivity, while pairwise rankings align far more strongly, up to zero point eight six for the best model. The work delivers a practical validation method, a validated argumentation base for graph reasoning and retrieval, and evidence that ordinal structure can be pulled from pointwise predictions.
arxiv-2602-18451:
Yaxuan Yang and three co-authors automate the creation of science assessments aligned with modern standards. Their 2026 paper starts from the Next Generation Science Standards, which demand assessments of students' ability to apply science knowledge to problems and design solutions. Performance-based assessments elicit that ability, but Evidence-Centered Design, the framework safeguarding their validity, needs diverse expertise and is costly and labor-intensive.

The team integrates Evidence-Centered Design into a multi-agent system that ensembles several large language models with varying expertise, automating multi-stage item generation workflows once done by human experts. AI-generated items match human-developed items in overall quality on alignment with three-dimensional standards and cognitive demands. They show distinct strength in inclusivity but lag in clarity, brevity, and multimodal design, while both AI and human items share weak spots in evidence collectability and student interest alignment. Human expertise remains essential.
arxiv-2602-18551:
Shuquan Ye and four co-authors forecast battery chemistry from a single spectrum. Their 2026 paper notes the solid electrolyte interphase matters for lithium-ion performance, yet operando infrared spectroscopy is complex and costly, limiting access for small labs. The team defines a new task, Operando IR Prediction: forecasting spectral fingerprints from one static spectrum.

They present OpIRSpec-7K, the first operando dataset at large scale with seven thousand one hundred eighteen samples across ten systems, plus OpIRBench, a benchmark with set rules. Their ABCC framework changes MeanFlow, adds a Chemical Flow modeling reactions, splits solvent from interphase, and enforces physics rules like mass conservation. ABCC beats static and generative baselines, works on unseen systems, and enables recovery of formation, aiding AI-driven discovery.
arxiv-2602-19051:
Quadratic reformulation can make hard solvers much faster. Cheng Lu, with four co-authors, develops new reformulations in 2026 for zero-one quadratic programming. The convex version, QCR, already speeds up solvers like CPLEX and Gurobi. A newer nonconvex version, QNR, offers an alternative route.

QNR adds flexibility. Nonconvex quadratic constraints can enter the formulation directly. Valid inequalities, such as triangle inequalities, then tighten the lower bound. The authors analyse how the new forms affect solver lower bounds. They also propose methods to maximise McCormick relaxation bounds. Numerical tests compare the new forms against convex reformulations. Results show clear effectiveness on zero-one quadratic problems. Reformulation choice thus matters for solver speed.
arxiv-2602-19351:
Travelers benefit from accurate travel time forecasts, yet most studies predict single roads rather than a whole network. Yufei Ai and four co-authors propose a machine learning framework for predicting the network-level travel time index. A case study uses more than 50,000 index records from the Washington, DC area collected over six years, giving the models a long, varied history to learn from.

The approach also identifies the effects of weather and seasonality on network travel times. Several machine learning models were assessed and compared, and ridge regression outperformed the others in both short-term and long-term prediction. Readers get a tested framework for network-wide forecasting that accounts for conditions drivers actually face.
arxiv-2602-19551:
David S. Jerison and Carlos E. Kenig revisit the Dirichlet problem, homogeneous and inhomogeneous, for the Laplacian on Lipschitz domains. Recent postings by Amrouche and Moussaoui purport to contradict Dahlberg's known area integral estimates and Sobolev space estimates of Jerison and Kenig. The paper explains the fatal gap in those postings' reasoning.

A self-contained proof covers a special case of Dahlberg's results, and it suffices to disprove the postings' central conclusions. Two further proofs of Dahlberg's results are provided, adapted from Kenig and from Dahlberg-Kenig-Pipher-Verchota. Other proofs live in Dahlberg's original paper and in work by Fabes, Mendez, and Mitrea, placing the dispute in its literature.
arxiv-2602-20351:
Aleksandr Gushchin and two co-authors present BiRQA, a compact full-reference image quality metric built for speed and adversarial robustness. Current neural quality metrics remain slow and vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, a problem for compression, restoration, and generative modeling. BiRQA processes four fast complementary features in a bidirectional multiscale pyramid, with bottom-up attention feeding fine-scale cues upward through an uncertainty-aware gate and top-down cross-gating returning semantic context.

Anchored Adversarial Training strengthens robustness by pairing clean anchor samples with a ranking loss that bounds prediction error under attack. On five public benchmarks, BiRQA matches or beats the previous state of the art while running about three times faster. Under unseen white-box attacks, its correlation scores rise substantially on KADID-10k. To the authors' knowledge, BiRQA is the only full-reference metric combining competitive accuracy with real-time throughput and strong adversarial resilience.
arxiv-2602-20451:
Three groups of mathematicians found genus-2 fibrations of type four-three, and all of them live on the same total space. Evan Huang shows in this short note that the Lefschetz fibration structures are the same. The fibrations in question come from Baykur-Korkmaz, Hamada, and Xiao, whose constructions share one underlying space.

The note's claim is one of identity, not mere resemblance: the fibration structures coincide. Readers thus get a single structure where the literature offered three separate constructions. The result tidies the picture for genus-2 fibrations of this type, showing that different routes to the same space yield the same fibration.
arxiv-2602-20551:
Word-prompted segmentation hits a wall with objects that words cannot pin down, a common case in factories and 3D printing shops. Zhenran Tang and two co-authors note that image examples also fall short, since they encode looks like color and texture rather than a part's shape. One part may come in many materials, finishes, or colors, so look-based prompts mislead. Yet such parts are usually defined by exact CAD models that hold their true shape. The paper builds a CAD-prompted method on SAM3.

The method feeds multi-view renders of a CAD model as prompts, giving shape-based guidance that ignores surface looks. Training uses synthetic data made from mesh renders in simulation across varied views and scene settings. The result is single-stage, CAD-prompted mask prediction, stretching promptable segmentation to objects that neither words nor looks alone can robustly describe.
arxiv-2602-20851:
Image fusion blends complementary sources, like infrared and visible light, into one stronger picture. Ran Zhang, Xuanhua He, and Liu Liu propose a hybrid method in this 2026 arXiv paper that trains in about a minute. A learnable U-Net produces a dynamic guidance map, which then steers a fixed Laplacian pyramid fusion kernel.

Separating policy learning from pixel synthesis removes the gap between patch-based training and full-resolution use, and the fused output is built linearly from source information alone, keeping it faithful. The model needs no external model and generalizes without further training across tasks from infrared-visible to medical fusion. Training takes about a minute on a high-end graphics card, or about two minutes on a laptop card.
arxiv-2602-21151:
Fusion reactors must guess where plasma heat lands on wall faces. Zhichen Feng and seven co-authors model divertor heat flux in this 2026 arXiv paper via a theory-based blobby transport model. The Coherent Structure Transport model joins with gyro-motion churn runs and rest-state answers for the background charge field with drifts and true-to-life X-point shape.

The fast model can study any rest-state answer quickly, layering blobby churn told by blob width, strength, and rate. Results recover the known inverse ring-field scaling of the heat-load width. Adding blobby churn gives a second heat-flux peak shifted outward from the strike point, growing with start blob density. The paper details the model and its scaling conduct.
arxiv-2602-21251:
Legacy JavaScript systems lack type safety, and adding types by hand is pricey. Clemens Pohle does the whole job by machine in this 2026 arXiv paper with AgenticTyper, a language-model agentic system for typing legacy projects. Prior work centered on type guessing, rarely spanning checking setup, meaning making, bug spotting, or conduct rightness at code-store scale.

Round-by-round error fixing plus conduct keeping through code-translation match-up closes those gaps. Trials on two closed code stores adding to eighty-one thousand lines of code clears all six hundred thirty-three first type errors in twenty minutes, cutting manual effort from a full working day. Keepers get a route to type safety with no manual slog.
arxiv-2602-21351:
Earth science stores hold vast data, much of it idle, and finding the right data sets is itself a research problem. Dmitrii Pantiukhin, Ivan Kuznetsov, Boris Shapkin, Antonia Anna Jost, Thomas Jung, and Nikolay Koldunov present a layered multi-agent setup for self-run finding in this 2026 arXiv paper: PANGAEA-GPT. A hub-based boss-worker layout routes by data type, runs code in boxed fixed-rule boxes, and self-corrects from run feedback.

Unlike simple language-model wrappers, the system spots and fixes run-time errors while running hard multi-step workflows with least human hand. Use cases spanning real sea study and ecology show finding and study across mixed store data. Workers get a method for querying stores through teamed agent workflows, not just chat over data.
arxiv-2602-21551:
Zhihao Li and three co-authors offer a Gaussian particle form for PDE operators that can be read. Learning fluid motion now leans on neural operators and Transformer models. But those tools often hide how they work, struggle with small, fast-changing patterns, and cost grows with sample counts squared.

Their design uses a Gaussian basis. Learned atoms carry clear geometry: centers, directional scales, and weights. The result is a compact state that needs no mesh and can be drawn directly. A Gaussian Particle Operator then acts in modal space. Gaussian modal windows take a Petrov-Galerkin measurement, and PG Gaussian Attention links scales across the whole field. The basis-to-basis design works at any resolution and costs near-linear time for a fixed modal budget. It handles rough geometries and extends smoothly from 2D to 3D, with leading accuracy on PDE tests and real data.
arxiv-2602-21851:
Matteo D'Achille and two co-authors prove tight bounds for random Euclidean problems with p-costs, covering matching between two sets and the traveling salesperson problem in dimension 3 and above. For a range of exponents, the optimal cost stays close to its typical value at the natural energy scale. Their method pairs a functional inequality with a robust geometric argument giving uniform bounds on the edges of optimal routes.

The team also states a conjectural transfer principle for optimal matching. If true, it would extend the bounds to all exponents at or above 1. The work thus pins down the bounds for matching and route problems in higher dimensions while pointing to a route for widening the range.
arxiv-2602-22051:
Data visualization is now a mature field with its own tools, textbooks, and design rules, but the values baked into those rules are rarely questioned. Shehryar Saharan and three co-authors step back and examine the values beneath classic works by Bertin, Tukey, Wilkinson, Ware, and Munzner. They name three dominant values: universality, objectivity, and efficiency.

The paper traces how those values seep into tools, courses, and research habits, and sets them against critiques calling for more diverse priorities and viewpoints. It is a short position paper, not a new tool, and its ask is plain: let the field embrace a wider range of values when shaping future tools and guidelines. Readers get a compact challenge to habits the field usually takes for granted.
arxiv-2602-22451:
How electrons push and pull drives magnetism, loss-free current, and topology, but their full landscape remains unmapped in layered van der Waals materials. Gal Tuvia and sixteen co-authors show that heavy-fermion physics can rival charge order, not just magnetic order, in a five-f-electron van der Waals material. They exploit the wide-spread five-f orbitals of beta-UTe3 to boost Kondo hybridization beyond its rare-earth cousins.

Scanning tunneling spectroscopy reveals Fano resonances typical of the heavy-fermion state. The work extends the classic Kondo-versus-magnetism rivalry into charge-ordered territory, using a material whose wide orbitals strengthen hybridization. For correlated-electron physicists, it opens a new arena where heavy fermions and charge density waves fight for the ground state.
arxiv-2602-22651:
Ryotaro Honma and one co-author extend a fundamental precision limit to quantum systems under feedback. The thermodynamic uncertainty relation ties current fluctuations to entropy production, setting how precise a tiny nonequilibrium machine can be. Feedback should calm fluctuations further, but its place in that relation was unclear for quantum control, which runs on information.

The team studies open quantum systems weakly tied to a heat bath, with quantum jumps watched continuously and Markovian feedback applied. Using quantum mutual information to price the feedback's information, they derive a finite-time uncertainty relation for any time-integrated current. A quantum clock model shows the payoff: feedback sharpens clock precision even with a single heat reservoir.
arxiv-2602-22851:
Sebastian Schmitt and three co-authors test a feared quantum failure mode on real hardware. Variational quantum algorithms can stall on barren plateaus, where gradients fade exponentially and optimization dies. Noise-induced plateaus were predicted to arise generically from noise buildup, regardless of size, circuit shape, or observable locality.

Using information content landscape analysis on IBM machines, the team estimated gradient norms for circuits from 8 to 102 qubits, with hundreds of parameters and runtimes of hundreds of microseconds. Against expectations, gradient sizes levelled off past a characteristic runtime instead of decaying exponentially. Classical simulations of the 8-qubit case under four noise models agreed, and theory points to T1-dominated non-unital noise as the plateau blocker. Average calibration scores, they warn, may mislead.
arxiv-2602-23051:
Aihong Wang and three co-authors propose a general blind-spot-risk metric for linked and self-driving cars. Blind spots hide key road users from sensing systems, and risk metrics miss the piling nature of threats over time. The Risk of Tracking Loss adds up momentary risk strength across occluded periods, covering both high-strength threats and long exposure.

Large-scale number crunching on varied, true-to-life datasets maps blind-spot risk and validates the value of the metric for evaluating vehicle-to-everything rollout strategies. Full V2X uptake in theory eliminates the risk, but gains are highly uneven: a gain needs seventy-five to ninety percent uptake. A one-sided message framework lets non-linked cars receive warnings, so the approach at twenty-five percent uptake beats the usual two-sided model at seventy-five percent, with gains topping out at fifty percent.
arxiv-2602-23251:
Li Wang and three co-authors measure tidal synchronization among binaries in the Pleiades, a 125-million-year-old open cluster. Tides in close binaries shape their long-term spin and orbital evolution, and circularization patterns across clusters already constrain tidal dissipation. Direct evidence on synchronization itself, however, has stayed limited.

Combining Gaia Data Release 3 membership, K2 rotation periods, and orbital solutions from a long spectroscopic survey, the team studies 42 binaries with reliable periods. Seven systems with orbital periods under 8.6 days are tidally synchronized, including one early-type and six late-type systems. Longer-period primaries are generally super-synchronized and most systems are eccentric. The synchronization transition near 8.6 to 14 days resembles the known 7.2-day circularization period, synchronization tracks mass ratio more than primary mass, and most synchronized systems, with high mass ratios, will likely evolve into double white dwarfs.
arxiv-2602-23351:
Amita Kamath and five co-authors argue that scale alone cannot fix vision-language models' reasoning gaps, because the gaps come from reporting bias in training data. People describing visual content by default leave out tacit information: saying 'at the game today!' is far more likely than 'a photo of 37 people standing behind a field.' The team examines data behind OpenCLIP, LLaVA-1.5, and Molmo through theories from pragmatics.

Reporting bias leaves four reasoning skills thinly represented: spatial, temporal, negation, and counting, despite web-scale and synthetic corpora. On curated benchmarks, models perform poorly on exactly those skills. Contrary to popular belief, scaling data size, model size, and language count does not make the skills emerge by default. But annotations collected specifically to capture tacit information do help, pointing to intentional data curation rather than scale as the remedy.
arxiv-2602-23551:
Axel Larsson and six co-authors compare shrinking methods for speeding up non-linear finite element runs, with open source code and shared benchmarks. Shrinking can accelerate reduced order models for non-linear systems, yet side-by-side scores and speed are poorly known.

The team tests fill-in methods based on gappy proper orthogonal splits plus the empirical quadrature procedure, on non-linear spread, non-linear stretch, and Lagrangian flow, using the libROM, Laghos, and MFEM codes. Findings show side-by-side scores depend on both the problem and the time stepping method. EQP generally gives lower errors than fill-in methods and uses points more efficiently, with lower wall time for spread and stretch problems. Its online cost runs high for Lagrangian flow problems. Fill-in methods show wider spread.
arxiv-2602-23651:
Rethna Pulikkoonattu explains how to compute the distance spectrum of IEEE 802.11 binary convolutional codes. Binary convolutional coding has anchored IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN since its inception, staying relevant from legacy 802.11a/g through Wi-Fi 6 to forthcoming Wi-Fi 8.

Though low-density parity-check codes now dominate high-throughput uses, binary convolutional coding stays mandatory for backward compatibility. It serves as the default forward-error-correction scheme where bandwidth is tight and costs matter: 20 MHz-only devices, Internet-of-Things nodes, and settings where LDPC decoding is too complex. Rate one-half coding is used throughout the packet preamble in every compliant frame. The new Enhanced Long Range format in 802.11bn mandates rate one-half coding for the data portion. Under Viterbi decoding, performance is governed by the distance spectrum. The note computes it exactly for the mother code, rate one-half, constraint length 7, generators 133 and 171, plus three punctured derivatives.
arxiv-2602-23751:
Morteza Zarei and Mohammad Hossein Zarei study a quantum error-correcting code built from rotating units, known as a toric-rotor code, under phase noise. The 2026 paper links the code to a classic model of flat spins, the XY model, through its partition function.

The link turns a known phase change in the spin model into a resilience change for the code. Below a critical noise width, the stored state keeps part of its strength, measured by a value between zero and one. At the critical width that value drops sharply to zero. The work also looks at higher dimensions, and it offers a strict math frame for judging how continuous-variable codes survive noise when no error signal is seen.
arxiv-2602-23951:
Xiaozhen Qiao and six co-authors present AHAP, a feed-forward framework for rebuilding three-dimensional humans from images taken at arbitrary camera angles, without calibration. The 2026 paper notes that multi-view reconstruction usually demands checkerboards or multi-view stereo calibration, which limits scale and use in varied real scenes.

AHAP fuses multi-view geometry into association, reconstruction, and localization. A cross-view identity module matches people across views with learnable queries and soft assignment, trained by contrastive learning. A human head fuses cross-view features and scene context to predict body models, guided by reprojection losses that enforce pose consistency. Multi-view triangulation then resolves depth ambiguity that plagues single-view methods. Tests on two egocentric datasets show competitive reconstruction and camera pose accuracy at far greater speed than optimization-based rivals.
arxiv-2603-00151: Zoppellari and colleagues present a multi-view architecture for predicting the progress of robot manipulation actions, so robots can assist in time and decide safely beside humans. A single camera often falls short, since self-occlusion hides the robot's own actions from view. Their approach fuses several viewpoints to track how far an ongoing action has advanced. Experiments on the Mobile ALOHA platform confirm the approach works.
arxiv-2603-00351: Weber and colleagues present acoustic sensing for jamming grippers, whose soft bodies grasp objects but lose compliance with tactile sensors. A speaker and microphone inside the cavity, away from the membrane, turn the soft body into the sensor. Sound through gripper and object encodes traits for machine learning, with compliance intact. Size comes within under three millimetres and orientation within under one degree. It resists 80 dBA noise, tells materials apart with up to 100 percent accuracy, and names 16 objects with 85.6 percent accuracy. Sorting runs 53 minutes of uninterrupted grasping and sensing.
arxiv-2603-00651: Zhao and three colleagues study data set pruning for three dimensional data, largely unexplored next to pruning for flat images. Long tailed classes make overall and mean scores pull in opposite directions, complicating pruning choices. They frame pruning as matching full data risk with a weighted subset, exposing coverage gaps and prior mismatch bias. Careful selection with per class keep quotas protects long tail coverage, while prior free teacher guidance with calibrated soft labels and embedding geometry distillation steadies training. Tests show both scores improve across settings.
arxiv-2603-00751: Strunk and Assam generalise Bayesian Flow Networks into General Proximal Flow Networks, widening belief update rules. Where Bayesian updates equal proximal steps under Kullback-Leibler divergence, the new system accepts any such measure, such as Wasserstein distance, for step by step generative modelling. Training and sampling follow, linking the method to proximal optimisation and recovering standard updates as a special case. Tuning the measure to data geometry improves output quality.
arxiv-2603-00951: Steier investigates why contrastive Forward-Forward training wobbles with random seed, focusing on margin clamping in the contrastive loss. On CIFAR-10, clamping multiplies test-accuracy variance nearly sixfold with no change in mean accuracy, driven by saturation cutting gradients in early layers. The effect fades on other datasets, and a gradient-neutral subtraction alternative removes the inflation where it applies, with a simple layer-zero check to spot it.
arxiv-2603-01051: Atif and ten colleagues build CelloAI, a repeatable test suite for AI coding help in high-energy physics and high-performance computing. Existing tests ignore science limits and huge performance-critical codebases. Three tracks cover doc comments, GPU kernel code, and graphical data study with vision models. With repeatability, auto scoring, and domain-realistic failure modes, the suite lets teams compare models fairly and improve reliability for science software.
arxiv-2603-01151: Lou and eleven colleagues close the simulation-to-reality gap for dexterous grasping with D-REX, a differentiable real-to-sim-to-real engine. Gaussian splat representations let it infer an object's mass from camera views and robot control signals. The engine builds faithful digital twins while learning grasp policies at the same time. Human demos transferred into simulation teach force-aware grasping from little data, with accurate mass estimates across shapes and masses and stronger grasping results.
arxiv-2603-01251: Greer and Tayou survey special cycles and the generating series built from their classes, asking how modularity behaves for them. Their central focus is a conjecture of Kudla, examined for orthogonal Shimura varieties and for unitary ones under toroidal compactification. The pair also put forward new conjectures covering more general quotients of period domains, and related phenomena for special cycles in other Shimura variety types.
arxiv-2603-01451:
When epoxy resin hardens, tiny filler grains inside it can clump, and that clumping shapes how strong the final solid is. Yujiro Furuta and Rei Kurita study that change in this 2026 lab work. They ask if hardening by itself pulls grains together, even when no strong pull should exist.

The pair placed small glowing plastic beads in epoxy resin and set off hardening with a curing agent. A fine microscope let them map bead spots in three dimensions before and after the resin set. Clumping grew during curing, and the growth tracked the mean gap between beads, not just how full the mix was. That rule gives makers a way to guess the final spread of filler in paints, glues, and similar goods.
arxiv-2603-01651:
Anka Chandrahas Tummepalli and Preethu Rose Anish pull event timelines out of Indian Supreme Court judgments in this 2026 work. Court texts are long and unstructured, which limits how well AI tools can sum them up or predict outcomes. A clear timeline of who did what, and when, gives those tools firm ground.

Their frame, LexChronos, pairs two agents in a loop driven by confidence scores. One tuned agent drafts candidate events, while a second agent scores and refines them round by round. Since no large Indian legal event set existed, they built a synthetic gold set of two thousand cases. The pipeline scores well against that set on a text-match measure. In later tests, a top model preferred timeline-based summaries over plain text in most cases.
arxiv-2603-02051:
Dang-Khoa Le, Hoang-Viet Le, Dai-Nam Le, and colleagues split the motion of a magnetoexciton with no shortcuts at all. Their 2026 work studies excitons, bound pairs of an electron and a hole, in flat materials with a magnetic field. In such materials, mass shifts with direction, so pair motion splits in an uneven way.

Most past work fakes that split with a fixed-form wave, which can skew the pair energy a lot. The team starts from the full energy rule and uses a saved quantity, the pseudomomentum, to split the motion in exact form. New terms that shift with direction show up, which shortcut models miss in full. They then solve the pair rule with a method that homes in step by step. Tests on black phosphorus and titanium trisulfide give pair energies for the ten lowest states.
arxiv-2603-02151:
Darij Grinberg and Benjamin Liber prove a counting claim in this 2026 graph paper. Take a split graph, where nodes fall into two groups with links only across groups. Count its forests, which are link sets with no cycles. Then count the degree lists of all its subgraphs, where each list records links per node.

Shteiner and Shteyner guessed those two counts are always equal for split graphs. Grinberg and Liber prove the guess in full. Along the way, they give several ways to read a key graph score at one point. Those readings use degree lists drawn from directed versions of the graph. The proof ties a pure count of trees to a count of degree patterns.
arxiv-2603-02251:
Carl Mazzanti studies algebraic cycles on a special four-dimensional shape in this 2026 mathematics paper. The shape is the double EPW quartic, a hyperkähler variety first built by Iliev and colleagues. A typical one can also be seen as a moduli space of bundles on a K3 surface. It carries a symmetry that flips its core form, and it links to conic curves in related fourfolds.

Mazzanti uses that rich geometry to test broad conjectures about algebraic cycles. Such conjectures predict how curves and surfaces inside a variety relate to its cycle ring. Hyperkähler varieties are a key test ground, since their cycle behavior is partly mysterious. Double EPW quartics offer enough structure to settle the conjectures in this case.
arxiv-2603-02351:
Leo Kaixuan Cheng, Abdus Shaikh, Ruofan Liang, and colleagues scale up 3D reconstruction in this 2026 paper. New neural models rebuild scenes from photos with high accuracy. Their full attention design, though, eats GPU memory and caps collection size. Large, unordered photo sets simply do not fit.

Their framework, MERG3R, splits the job without any retraining. Photos are reordered and cut into overlapping, varied subsets that fit in memory. Each subset is rebuilt on its own by an existing model. A global alignment step then merges the pieces, weighted by confidence. Across four large benchmarks, accuracy, memory use, and scale all improved. Even a thousand mixed photos yielded solid camera poses and point clouds.
arxiv-2603-02451:
Sheng Sun and Sarah Evans present a framework for trust in distributed AI systems in this 2026 paper. Attestation proves that a system part is what it claims to be. Traditional checks verify a whole system at once, which scales poorly. Systems also change constantly, so one-time checks go stale fast.

Composable attestation verifies parts separately, then combines their proofs. The authors define core properties: proofs must compose, ignore order, and stay deterministic. Merkle trees anchor one construction, with accumulator and multi-signature options also explored. Each option trades speed, security, and features differently. New parts can join through inclusion, without rechecking the whole system. Uses include AI model integrity, federated learning, and live trust assurance.
arxiv-2603-03151:
Qianfeng Li and Emil Wiedemann prove a uniqueness claim for a rigid body in a squeezed, frictionless fluid. Fluid-body problems are hard even for smooth flows. The squeezed, no-friction case had no math results at all before this 2026 paper. Their route lets the fluid's thickness shrink toward zero.

That limit yields a short-time solution of a broad kind, one that can track wiggles and shocks. The main claim is weak-strong uniqueness: when a smooth classic solution exists, the broad one must match it. The proof needs a new trick, since the test shapes used in the no-friction form shift as thickness changes. The result anchors future work on such coupled systems.
arxiv-2603-03251:
Tanishq Kumar, Tri Dao, and Avner May make AI text decoding speculate about its own speculations. Speculative decoding speeds up text output: a fast draft model guesses the next tokens, and a slow target model checks the guesses in one pass. One chain of waiting remains, since drafting waits on checking.

Their new scheme preps drafts for the likely check outcomes while the check still runs. When the real outcome matches a prepped one, that draft returns at once, and drafting costs nothing. The paper names three hurdles this creates and gives principled fixes for each. Their tuned system, Saguaro, ran about thirty percent faster than the best past schemes. Against plain step-by-step decoding, gains reached fivefold.
arxiv-2603-03451:
Luca Previdi and three colleagues push quantum sensing toward measuring several things at once. Near a phase transition, a quantum system becomes hypersensitive, which helps precision, but estimating multiple parameters together usually collapses. The information matrix turns singular, a flaw called sloppiness. Their 2026 paper shows the collapse can be beaten, at a price.

Working with the ground state of the Dicke model, light coupled to atoms in one cavity, they estimate two parameters simultaneously with only mildly reduced precision scaling. A doubled version with photon hopping adds a triple point where two excitation gaps close together. That restores the ideal scaling for chosen parameter pairs. Even with photon loss, steady states keep diverging precision. Preparation time is folded into the comparison of strategies.
arxiv-2603-03551:
Teruki Matsuzaki and three others compute the X-ray fingerprint of a rhenium oxide from first principles. Predicting spectra of correlated quantum substances is hard because spin-orbit coupling, lattice vibration, and electron correlation all tangle jointly. Their 2026 paper applies the formula-of-motion coupled-cluster method, a high-accuracy quantum chemistry tool, to the compound Ba2MgReO6, deriving its spin-orbit-lattice entangled states directly.

The computed interaction parameters land within a few percent of values extracted from real resonant inelastic X-ray scattering spectra. The method also pins down a weak coupling to one vibration family that tests struggle to reach. Simulations show that family creates a shoulder on the elastic peak. Both vibration families prove necessary to reproduce the spectrum's fine structure. The authors present coupled-cluster as a strong predictive tool for such substances.
arxiv-2603-03951: Rowntree and colleagues study how supermassive black hole growth, galaxy mergers, and gas processes shape the stellar mass-gas metallicity relation in the Horizon Run 5 simulation. Minor mergers produce the largest metallicity differential, with every environment peaking over non-merging galaxies, while major mergers show little influence. The node population also shows a consistent negative offset in residuals across all redshifts, with filament and void galaxies showing a smaller offset. High black hole growth and low gas also shift metallicity across environments.
arxiv-2603-04051: Ma and colleagues define localization operators for weighted Bergman and Fock spaces. With symbols and windows scaled naturally, Bergman-space operators converge weakly to Fock-space operators as radius grows without bound. Applications follow, including sharp Toeplitz-operator norm bounds on Fock spaces, windowed Berezin transforms on Bergman spaces, and Szegö-type results for Bergman-space localization operators.
arxiv-2603-04251: Liu and others predict oscillations in complex networks with delayed feedback. Oscillatory motion are common in complex networks, often playing key roles in regulating function. From gene networks to ecosystems, delayed feedback steps mainly drive system-scale oscillations. Analyzing and predicting such motion is highly challenging given high-dimensionality, non-linearity, and delay.
arxiv-2603-05151: David Rogerson and colleagues simulate lattice gauge theories with a virtual rishon representation that enforces gauge symmetry at intermediate steps. Gauge and matter degrees of freedom become dynamical variables encoded in qubits, covering theories in any number of space dimensions plus time. Tests on a U(1) theory with and without matter capture conformal signatures in the one-dimensional multi-flavor Schwinger model and recover the confining string tension in two dimensions. The framework suits both classical tensor networks and near-term quantum hardware.
arxiv-2603-05651: Van Nuenen and Sachdeva introduce a perturbation framework testing language model moral judgments with the moral conflict held constant. From 2,939 dilemmas from r/AmItheAsshole, they generate surface edits, point-of-view shifts, and persuasion cues. Surface perturbations produce low flip rates within the self-consistency noise floor, whereas point-of-view shifts induce 24.3% instability. A large subset withstands surface noise yet flips under perspective changes, showing conditioning on narrative voice. Protocol choices dominate, with low structured-protocol agreement and only about a third matching across all three.
arxiv-2603-05751: Ngo and team present a privacy-keeping framework for medical go-between robots spotting speech acts and making gestures. Talk is vital in healthcare across language walls, where gestures matter. Built on local open-source models, it uses few-shot prompting for intent finding. The authors present a data set of clinic talks tagged for speech acts and gesture clips. Their naming module hits 0.90 score with sharpness and F1-score. The approach improves speed and, in user studies, beats the speech-gesture base on human-likeness while keeping similar fitness.
arxiv-2603-06151: Das and colleagues compute precise ZH production cross sections and invariant mass distributions at the LHC, accounting for leading and subleading soft gluons. Threshold resummation in the QCD framework sharpens both subprocess families, whether quark driven or gluon driven. The paper offers refined predictions for ZH production where soft gluon effects matter most, near threshold.
arxiv-2603-06451: Ovalle and colleagues examine whether a Schwarzschild black hole can arise as the continuous endpoint of non-singular collapse. Using an extension of the regular Schwarzschild metric in time, they track collapse and find continuity cannot hold. The metric function breaks at the origin: Minkowski breaking. Before Schwarzschild point source forms centrally, curvature singularities appear and the Cauchy horizon vanishes. Spacetime seems not to evolve smoothly toward Schwarzschild; formation instead appears to involve a discrete change, pointing to a noncontinuous, possibly quantized, framework for singularities.
arxiv-2603-06651: Hu and colleagues propose geodesic gradient descent, a learning-rate-free Riemannian algorithm for hypersurface geometry beyond single-manifold descent. Each iteration approximates a neighborhood of the hypersurface with an n-dimensional sphere. A tangent vector from the Euclidean gradient is mapped onto the sphere to form a geodesic, with parameters updating at its endpoint. The maximum step equals a quarter of the sphere's arc length, eliminating the learning rate. Against Adam, GGD cuts test MSE by up to 48.76% on Burgers' data and cross-entropy loss on MNIST.
arxiv-2603-06751: Nixson and colleagues study whether cell-cycle model parameters stay identifiable when only sparse, literature-collated data are available. Treatment response hinges on cell-cycle position, yet modellers often lack resolved time-series data for fitting. Synced populations drift out of sync over cycles toward balanced exponential growth, whose phase shares come from FACS data, while FUCCI reporters add finer phase timing. Their age-structured PDE model lets phase progress follow a delayed gamma distribution, with analytic expressions for the growth phase.
arxiv-2603-06851: Zhao studies context trade with feedback, where the price does not change which values are seen. There, action-free feedback removes the polynomial penalty from heavy-tailed games. Parameter-free methods reach best rates up to log factors, with no knowledge of moment order, scale, or smoothness, nonparametrically. The measure is a squared-loss gap whose noise-square term drops out, leaving noise damped by the gap. Values have bounded curves and heavy tails with infinite variance, and an epoch-based method with trimmed means hits regret.
arxiv-2603-06951: Goswami and colleagues present Space-Control, a process shielding design for shared CXL memory. CXL memory splitting lets hosts share assets, yet sharing sets only coarse host rules and leaves shielding to the OS. Virtual memory shields tasks on one host, while CXL shields only hosts, so shared split memory lacks process shielding, a key security gap. Space-Control adds cross-host ID to enforce secrecy and soundness. It splits control from the outside OS with a hardware-rooted check engine and a checker at the memory egress point.
arxiv-2603-07151: Luo and colleagues propose FDTO, a solver for part rules that tunes step losses built from finite gaps with time stepping. Physics-aware neural networks often suffer ill-set goals and costly auto math. Earlier step solvers also struggle on body-fitted grids and time-tied problems. FDTO pairs curved transforms with body-fitted set grids and splits long runs into in-steps, well-set sub-tasks, aiming for true, fast flow answers.
arxiv-2603-07251: Paul and Paul pin down weighted zero-sum constants for sequences over cyclic groups when the weights are plus or minus one. A sequence counts as weighted zero-sum when two weighted sums both vanish. The constants mark the shortest length that forces such a subsequence to appear. They settle the main constant and two related ones for the case where one weight set is plus or minus one and the other is just one.
arxiv-2603-07651: Zhuravlev derives an exact exponent from information geometry for Fisher curvature scaling at critical points. On periodic grids the Fisher manifold's scalar bend grows as a power of system size, with power built from correlation-length and anomalous-dimension exponents. The formula is backed for flat Ising by exact transfer-matrix math and simulation, and matches 3D Ising runs. Potts cases show wobbling powers with log fixes, as said.
arxiv-2603-08451: Kuperberg and colleagues study left prime truncations, inspired by a prime that stays prime as its left digit is stripped away again and again until nothing remains. They map the distributions of how many left prime truncations integers admit. A parallel count covers irreducible truncations for polynomials over a finite field. The focus is the share of all numbers or polynomials with a given digit length that reach each count, how much that share varies, and the largest share attainable.
arxiv-2603-08651: Andrzej Cichocki and Piergiulio Tempesta build a wide family of mirror descent updates from group entropies. Their group-based maps swap cleanly with their inverses, a trick they call mirror duality, and tuning the map parameters fits the update to the data shape. Tests on large simplex-bound programs back the updates' validity, toughness, and performance.
arxiv-2603-08951: Neil Ernst and Christoph Treude warn that generative AI is no silver bullet for qualitative software research. Qualitative work spans field studies to deductive coding, and claims that AI could automate its analysis overgeneralize from narrow wins. Their paper maps qualitative work, reviews emerging evidence, weighs AI-mediated practice, and revisits quality factors to inform researchers about promises and pitfalls.
arxiv-2603-09151: Junnan Dong and colleagues frame hard questions over messy tables as Deep Tabular Research, a task needing many linked steps across table regions. Such tables often carry two-way headers and non-standard layouts that trip up language models. Their agent framework treats the work as a closed loop, joining query and table reading to pick each next move. Past outcomes feed a paired memory of parameter updates and summary texts, so the system keeps refining its path.
arxiv-2603-09951: Maximilian Beck and coauthors train language models to act as interactive debuggers for Python code. Models trained on execution traces can predict a program line by line, yet real developers jump to breakpoints and inspect variables. Their neural debuggers support stepping into, over and out of functions, plus setting breakpoints. The models predict both future states and, in reverse, earlier states, scoring well on CruxEval.
arxiv-2603-10051: Sizhe Huang, Zitong Li and Shujie Yang argue that encrypted traffic classification fails when traffic is flattened into raw byte strings. Masked pre training on bytes treats random header fields as learnable and merges fields with distinct meanings. Their protocol native paradigm instead builds on field semantics as design priors. FlowSem-MAE, a tabular masked autoencoder over flow semantic units, filters to learnable units and embeds each field type separately.
arxiv-2603-10251: Bouvel and coauthors develop decomposition methods for chirotopes, a combinatorial abstraction of planar point sets. Their aim is counting how many triangulations a given point set supports in total. They generalise the convex and concave sum operations known for a special family called chains. With the kernel method and a functional equation, they get a tight asymptotic count for triangulations of the double circle configuration.
arxiv-2603-10351: Hongbin Zhang and co-authors tackle translationese bias, where models used as multilingual judges favor machine translated text over human writing, most in low resource languages. They trace the bias to spurious links with English shaped latent structure and cross lingual predictability. Their DIBJudge framework fine tunes a model to keep only judgment critical features, pushing spurious factors into a separate bias branch, with a penalty keeping the two apart. On reward benchmarks and a dedicated bias suite, DIBJudge beats strong baselines and cuts the bias a lot.
arxiv-2603-10551: Longan Wang, Yuang Shi, and Wei Tsang Ooi present P-GSVC, a layered progressive 2D Gaussian splatting framework for scalable image and video representation. Splats are organized into a base layer plus successive enhancement layers, giving coarse-to-fine reconstructions from one representation. A joint training strategy updates all layers together, aligning their paths so layers stay compatible and progression stays stable. The system scales in both quality and resolution. Against sequential layer-wise training, joint training gained clear PSNR improvements for both video and image cases.
arxiv-2603-10651: Elisa Tosello and co-authors tackle scheduling and motion planning together for multi-object navigation in shared workspaces, as in automated warehouses. There the tasks are given, and the hard part is deciding if, when, and how to run them safely under time and motion limits. Their framework interleaves standard schedulers and motion planners in a learning loop: the scheduler proposes plans, the planner checks them and returns symbolic feedback. On logistics and job-shop benchmarks with motion tasks added, the loop produced valid plans under complex constraints.
arxiv-2603-10751: Federico Gerbino and co-authors study how monitored quantum systems lose their quantum information over time, a process called purification. The systems here are not unitary, and the work spans random-matrix symmetry classes. Away from the measurement-induced transition, the loss follows universal laws. Two toy models reach that limit from two sides: discrete steps with Gaussian matrices, and weak monitoring that moves eigenvalues like a Brownian motion. Both yield explicit forms for how the Rényi entropies fall, and simulations agree.
arxiv-2603-10851: Luis Boza tightens the known upper bounds for three classical Ramsey numbers, improving on results that mostly came from one long-used recursive inequality. He shows that R(4,4,4) is at most 229, R(3,4,5) at most 157, and R(3,3,6) at most 91. The paper exploits the fact that the standard inequality becomes strict when its right-hand side and one term in the sum are both even.
arxiv-2603-10951: Pedro Araújo, Giovanne Santos, and Maya Stein pin down the semidegree threshold that forces an oriented graph to contain every possible spanning tree of bounded degree. They show that a minimum semidegree of three-eighths of the vertex count, plus any fixed slack, guarantees a copy of every such bounded-degree oriented tree. The bound is asymptotically best possible.
arxiv-2603-11051: Chandler Smith and coauthors release OpenSanctions Pairs, the first large-scale public benchmark for matching entities across sanctions and open-source intelligence data. It holds 755,540 expert-labeled pairs drawn from 293 source datasets across 45 jurisdictions, spanning many languages and writing systems with messy, time-varying records. Baselines show a production rule-based matcher over-matching while language models stumble on cross-script transliteration, with GPT-4o reaching 99.0 percent F1, suggesting pairwise matching nears its practical ceiling.
arxiv-2603-11251: Martin Dindoš and coauthors study the Green function for second-order elliptic systems with constant coefficients in the upper half-space. They pin down both its qualitative nature and quantitative bounds. Starting from a minimal base that picks out the object uniquely, they prove two results. These are optimal nontangential maximal estimates and regularity results right up to the boundary. The proof leans on the Agmon-Douglis-Nirenberg Poisson kernel construction and boundary regularity estimates. It uses a divergence theorem that takes boundary traces in the nontangential pointwise sense.
arxiv-2603-11451: Ghosh and Meyer show that some directed graphs share one key total despite having different arc sets. For a fixed root vertex, each graph's total adds the weights of all its arborescences. Two graphs with the same vertex set can land on the same sum. The pair tie their result to the Matrix-Tree Theorem. They also show how it gives a graph-based route to factoring matrix determinants.
arxiv-2603-11551: Okamoto and co-authors build a projection mapping system that leaves no shadows on tabletop workspaces. It layers content onto real objects, yet users block light and cast shadows. Multi-projector fixes exist, though their compute adds lag. Their synthetic aperture system packs far more projectors around the space. With so many angles covered, shadows vanish, no live compute needed. An offline blur fix counters softness from misaligned overlaps. They also define a sense of projection and give design rules from user studies to shrink it.
arxiv-2603-11651: Bisht, Rani, and Tantubay compute automorphism groups and derivation algebras for the Hamiltonian Lie algebra H_N and its derived subalgebra, for even N. For both algebras, the automorphism group comes out as GSp_N(Z) times a power of the nonzero scalars. All derivations of H itself prove to be inner. The team also works out the derived subalgebra's full derivation space. A second cohomology computation closes the work.
arxiv-2603-11751: Loukojärvi and co-authors introduce PhiPlot, a web tool for exploring data on molecules that matter for the atmosphere. Chemistry data sets in this field grow too high-dimensional to read raw. PhiPlot joins visualization, clustering, and guided embedding work in one interactive space. Users can hunt for patterns and shape new questions as they explore. The tool links to a growing set of molecular databases for air chemistry research.
arxiv-2603-12051: The ATLAS Collaboration searches for long-lived particles in proton collision events with missing transverse momentum. The hunt needs at least one displaced vertex, a sign of a particle that traveled before it decayed. It uses Run 2 data taken from 2016 to 2018 at 13 TeV. Two vertexing methods run side by side, one of them a new fuzzy algorithm tuned for heavy quarks. Neither search found an excess over background. The team sets 95 percent confidence limits for four new-physics models.
arxiv-2603-12151: Cheng and a large team of co-authors map how to split sampling compute in LLM reinforcement learning. Three resources compete: parallel rollouts per problem, problems per batch, and update steps. The best rollout count per problem grows in a steady way with budget, then levels off. Easy problems gain through sharper solutions, while hard ones gain through wider coverage. Extra rollouts also cut interference across problems in a batch. Batch size mainly steers stability and can sit in a broad range, a rule teams can apply directly.
arxiv-2603-12951: Riccardo Raciti and co-authors modernize SIENA, a trusted tool that measures brain volume change from MRI scans. Its classic steps for skull stripping and tissue segmentation can fail and bias atrophy scores. The team swaps in deep learning tools, SynthStrip and SynthSeg, at those weak points. Three pipeline variants were tested on ADNI and PPMI cohorts. Skull stripping swaps gave the most steady gains in disease links and scan-order robustness. GPU variants also cut runtime by up to 46%.
arxiv-2603-13051: Michael Scholkemper and Sach Mukherjee propose a light framework that predicts how unseen cell perturbations will act. Big foundation models can do this task, but they need huge data and compute. Many labs and clinics lack both. Their causal transfer method leans on the structure of interventions and built-in invariances. It needs only common bulk molecular data to learn. Tests against large interventional datasets matched top foundation models with far smaller size and time.
arxiv-2603-13251: Nabin Oli introduces ManiBench, a benchmark for Manim code generation by language models. Code that must produce dynamic teaching visuals needs more than plain logic and syntax checks. ManiBench targets syntactic hallucinations, where valid Python calls Manim APIs that do not exist or are deprecated. It also targets visual-logic drift, where visuals diverge from the intended math through timing errors. The set spans five difficulty levels across calculus, linear algebra, probability, topology, and AI. Scoring covers executability, version conflicts, alignment, and coverage.
arxiv-2603-13351: Heejin Jo tests whether the STAR reasoning method still works inside a long production prompt. STAR had raised car wash problem accuracy from zero to near perfect in a prior study. Inside InterviewMate's 60-plus line production prompt, scores fell to 0 and 30 percent in two runs. The STAR-only prompt scored a full 100 percent in the same tests. Jo argues that style rules like lead with specifics force conclusion-first output, which breaks the reason-then-conclude order. Structured methods may not transfer from lone tests to complex prompt setups.
arxiv-2603-13651: Yurui Zhu, Giovanni Colavizza, and Matteo Romanello benchmark LLMs on reference extraction and parsing in the humanities and social sciences. Citations there are often in many languages, set in footnotes, and shaped by old conventions. Their benchmark spans three datasets with English, German, and humanities material. Tasks run from extraction to parsing to full document parsing, all in a set schema. GROBID, a supervised pipeline, is compared with several LLMs. Lightweight LoRA tuning gave steady gains, they find.
arxiv-2603-14651: Amega presents EARCP, a self-regulating ensemble for sequential decision making. Fixed ensemble weights age badly when conditions shift. EARCP reweights varied expert models online as data arrives. Weights track both solo performance and agreement among models. A multiplicative update rule with a coherence term drives the balance. The design proves sublinear regret bounds under standard assumptions. Tests cover time series forecasts, activity recognition and finance tasks. An open-source package ships with the study.
arxiv-2603-15051: Sheshanarayana and co-authors present AdaAnchor, a way for language models to reason silently in latent space. Instead of writing long chains of thought, the model refines a set of latent anchor vectors tied to the input. A halting rule watches the anchors settle and stops early on easy problems. Hard problems get more steps under a shared budget. On three math word-problem benchmarks, accuracy rose by up to 5 percent. Average refinement steps fell by about half, and output tokens by over 90 percent.
arxiv-2603-15851: Lewis and Summers sort which prime character degree graphs can arise from groups. The graphs encode prime divisors of character degrees for solvable groups. Their project targets graphs with eight vertices. A general algorithm grows from known results and constructions. Of 12,346 such graphs, the 1,229 disconnected ones are fully sorted. Among connected graphs, 37 are shown to occur. Most join from smaller graphs, and three have diameter three. Some 58 graphs are ruled out, while 204 stay open.
arxiv-2603-16351: Pinheiro and co-authors identify parasitoid wasps from photos with a YOLO-based system. Naming species by hand is slow and needs rare expertise. Their dataset holds 3,556 high-resolution images of hymenoptera specimens. The model sorts wasps by family, led by Ichneumonidae and Braconidae. Accuracy passed 96% across varied body forms. HiResCAM maps show the model reads wing veins and antennae segments. Such visual proof builds trust for biodiversity work.
arxiv-2603-16451: Bonazzi and co-authors shrink an anomaly detector to run inside the sensor itself. Factories must spot defects with few labeled fault examples. The GLASS method learns normal patterns from clean data only. TinyGLASS swaps in a small ResNet-18 backbone and quantizes the model. It runs on Sony's IMX500 sensor chip. The model reached 94.2% image-level AUROC on MVTec-AD. It runs at 20 frames per second on 4.0 millijoules per inference.
arxiv-2603-16551: Ibrahim and co-authors generate medical images for demographic groups missing from training. Generators trained on skewed data fail at unseen intersections. Their CompDiff encodes age, sex, and race as separate tokens. Those tokens compose with clinical text during diffusion. Across chest X-rays and fundus images, fidelity beat rival methods. Zero-shot tests covered 16 unseen chest X-ray intersections. Blind readers picked CompDiff images as most realistic most often. Pretraining on its images also helped downstream classifiers.
arxiv-2603-16651: Alcaraz asks what Pinocchio teaches about building rule-following AI agents. His thesis builds an end-to-end pipeline for norm-compliant agents. It builds on the AJAR, Jiminy, and NGRL architectures. In the hybrid model, learning agents answer to argumentation-based advisors. The advisors act as normative supervisors. A new algorithm extracts the arguments behind advisor decisions. The thesis also defines norm avoidance in learning agents. It offers a strategy to reduce that failure mode.
arxiv-2603-17151: Lin studies how option prices encode the market's outlook, through implied density and implied volatility. An explicit link connects the two, turning risk neutrality of the density into conditions on volatility that rule out static arbitrage. He revisits this link with a minimalist lens: volatility acts as a pointwise corrector mapping the Black-Scholes quasi density into the true risk neutral density. He then builds neural representations that respect arbitrage limits. In synthetic tests, a shallow network with one hidden layer worked best.
arxiv-2603-17351: Liu and co-authors present OmniVLN, a navigation system for air and ground robots that follow language orders. It joins rotating LiDAR with panoramic vision to build a five-layer scene graph. A compact octant view then guides a language model to pick rooms, aim, and move. Spatial referring accuracy rose from about 77 to 93 percent in their tests. Prompt tokens fell by up to 61.7 percent, and success rose as well.
arxiv-2603-17451: Pan and co-authors study magnetotransport in overdoped infinite-layer nickelate films. They ran pulsed fields up to 62 tesla on crystals with high order. Resistance grows in a straight line with field at high field-to-temperature ratios, they find. Below 30 kelvin, resistance follows a clean T-squared law across the doping range. Both traits coexist in this unconventional superconductor family. The results constrain theories of its normal state.
arxiv-2603-18251: Adcock, Can, and Wang add Christoffel adaptive sampling to sparse random feature expansions. Random feature models fit multivariate functions and solve PDEs with low cost. Sparse versions help when data is scarce, but sample choice still matters. The Christoffel function guides picks toward points that inform the current basis most. Tests show adaptive sampling keeps high accuracy with fewer samples across approximation tasks.
arxiv-2603-18351: Juliao and co-authors show Nb3Sn films carrying continuous supercurrent across a diffusion bonded seam. Bronze pairs were joined, then coated with niobium by sputtering near 715 degrees Celsius. Conversion to Nb3Sn and diffusion bonding happened in the same heating step. Magneto-optical imaging at 9 K shows supercurrent flows freely across seams in several samples. A pre-coating variant gave weaker seam coverage than the hot bronze approach.
arxiv-2603-18451: Chen and co-authors study a mass trap for dark-state polaritons in atomic media. In a two-dimensional electromagnetically induced transparency system, a trap can arise from spatially varied effective mass. That mass pattern is set by tuning the control fields of the medium. Bound polariton motion, spatial profile, and coherence can then be tailored by design. The scheme offers spatial control of optical information and a path toward polariton condensation.
arxiv-2603-18751: Bhardwaj, Das, and Sawant settle when two powers of certain graph ideals agree. They study Alexander duals of connected ideals of graphs. The question is when ordinary powers match symbolic powers. The authors give a complete classification of all graphs where the two coincide. They also prove the Conforti-Cornuéjols conjecture for this class of ideals. The result closes both the equality question and a packing conjecture in one sweep for this ideal family.
arxiv-2603-18851: Huang and co-authors design waveforms for systems that send data and power at once. The peak-to-average power ratio pulls design both ways. Low ratios help amplifier efficiency, while high ratios exploit rectifier nonlinearity to harvest more energy. A unified framework ties waveform statistics to both device behaviors. Frequency segments are then split to balance data rate against harvested energy. The approach extends to MIMO-OFDM setups with many antennas and subcarriers. Simulations show gains in amplifier efficiency, rectifier output, and total energy transfer.
arxiv-2603-19151: Özdem studies the magnetic traits of hidden-charm pentaquarks, exotic particles made of five quarks. He uses QCD light-cone sum rules with four ways to build the states in a diquark model. The sums cover light and charm quark parts and higher terms, with checks that the math settles. He finds that the magnetic moments shift a lot with the inner quark layout and spin. Some layouts give values far apart in size and sign. Such traits could help tell rival models apart.
arxiv-2603-19251: Maniyar and co-authors make small legal language models safer and better grounded in long documents. Such models often invent clauses or cite false precedents. The team traces errors to poor search in repetitive legal text and to answers given with too little context. Their fix enriches search with metadata and mixes sources. A preference tuning step then teaches the model to refuse when context is thin. The pair of changes lifts grounding and trust in local legal use.
arxiv-2603-19851: Hebballi and co-authors design runtime monitors that can be reprogrammed while a system runs in the field. Many monitors sit on FPGAs, which can lag fast processors. Their monitor is built from standard cells on the same chip as the system. Small programmable units combine to check bounded metric temporal logic rules. Simulations show the design can be reset through its pins after deployment. A fairly large version takes only 0.55 square millimeters and runs at 1.25 gigahertz.
arxiv-2603-20051: Štefanič and Hribar-Lee study how water hydrates seven alpha-amino acids, using Kirkwood-Buff theory. Amino acids serve as small models for protein behavior in water. The team measured solution densities from about 278 to 308 kelvin. From these they derived apparent and standard molar volumes. Side-chain contributions were read off against glycine as a baseline. Volumes rose with temperature, pointing to weaker water tightening around the molecules. An integral equation model with a coarse bead picture reproduced the measured volumes very well.
arxiv-2603-20551: Lu studies when Lagrangian systems and their geodesics split into new solution branches. This is part one of a two part series. Morse theory supplies the main tools for the study. Three setups get full treatment in the paper. One covers paths that join two submanifolds. One ties path ends by an isometry, and one covers brake orbits. For each, Lu gives sharp terms for when bifurcation must occur. The tests rest on Morse index and nullity counts. Focal points in the geometry link to branching in the solutions.
arxiv-2603-20851: Wang and co-authors test whether ChatGPT truly understands modern Chinese poetry. They worked with professional poets to judge the model's readings of poems by different poets. The readings were scored on several dimensions. The authors report that the model's readings matched the poets' own intent in over 73 percent of cases. Its grasp of poetic quality was weaker. They present their framework as a base for later work on language models and poetry tasks.
arxiv-2603-21051: Zhang and co-authors present Cortical Policy, a dual-stream view transformer for robotic manipulation. View transformers read multi-view images to pick actions, but often reason weakly about 3D space. One stream aligns features of stable keypoints from a pretrained 3D model. The other stream models gaze, inspired by the brain's dorsal pathway, and adapts as scenes change. The two streams merge to choose final actions under language commands. On RLBench, COLOSSEUM, and real robot tasks, the method beats leading baselines.
arxiv-2603-21151: Tan and co-authors solve functional renormalization group equations with neural networks. The renormalization group tracks how an effective potential changes with scale, a core tool in nonperturbative field theory. They train networks to represent the potential's field derivative, with the flow equations built into the loss. No precomputed training data is needed. For the O(N) scalar theory, the method captures symmetric, broken, and critical regimes. Results match finite-difference and Galerkin methods well.
arxiv-2603-21351: Aleksandrov and Peller study functions of pairs of commuting self-adjoint operators under relatively bounded perturbations. They extend their earlier results for functions of a single self-adjoint operator to the two operator case. The main tool is double operator integrals. The work shows how such functions behave when the operators are perturbed by relatively bounded terms. It gives a parallel set of results for pairs, where the single operator theory does not apply directly.
arxiv-2603-21851: Zhan and co-authors check whether two implementations of the same model compute the same thing. Rewrites across frameworks change operator splits, tensor layouts, and fused kernels, so manual rules are brittle. Their Emerge framework places both versions in an e-graph, guesses relations from run values, and builds new rewrite rules when old ones fall short. Each rule is verified by solver checks or randomized tests. On HuggingFace and vLLM graphs, Emerge confirmed correct pairs and caught 10 of 13 known bugs, plus eight new issues that developers later confirmed.
arxiv-2603-22251: Badwaik and co-authors present exaCB, a framework for continuous benchmarking of high-performance computing systems. Software teams already use continuous integration to check correctness. Performance and energy checks usually sit outside that flow. exaCB brings benchmarking into the same pipelines, with shared parts and one reporting protocol. Teams can adopt it step by step, from basic run checks to full instrumentation. The framework was built for the JUPITER exascale system. Its early-access program ran continuous benchmarks for over 70 applications. The runs support regression tracking and energy-aware studies.
arxiv-2603-22551: Desai and co-authors report lab tests of dimpled scalar vortex coronagraph masks. The masks need broadband starlight suppression near ten orders of magnitude, plus high planet throughput. Scalar designs avoid the polarization split of vector masks but struggle across wide bands. The new prototypes add radial phase dimples to a sawtooth pattern to fix that. On an in-air testbed the team reached near bench-limited contrast in narrow and broad bands alike. Measured contrast matched predictions within a factor of two at three bandwidths.
arxiv-2603-22751: Huang and co-authors present a shared way to measure privacy leakage in language model agent pipelines. Most studies inspect one part at a time, such as memory or retrieval. Their tool, CIPL, maps a target through stages from source to extraction. They apply it to memory, retrieval, and tool-based systems. Memory proves a near-saturated high-risk case. Retrieval targets leak often but partly. Tool targets depend on what the attacker can observe. Cleaned weak controls sharply cut leakage, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-22851: Peng and co-authors present UniQueR, a feedforward system for 3D reconstruction from unposed images. Older feedforward models predict per-pixel maps tied to visible surfaces only. UniQueR instead treats reconstruction as a sparse 3D query problem. A compact set of anchor points acts as geometric queries in global space. Each query spawns 3D Gaussians for rendering, including in hidden regions. Cross-attention across views gives strong geometry at lower memory and compute cost. Tests on Mip-NeRF 360 and VR-NeRF beat prior methods on rendering and geometry.
arxiv-2603-23151: Yevgenieva and co-authors study a reactor model that is steered from its boundary. The model is a nonlinear parabolic equation for a tube-shaped reactor with flow spread along its axis. The edge rules are of Robin type, and feedback acts at the boundary. The team finds conditions under which the steady state is stable in an exponential sense. They also give a clear estimate of how fast states decay toward it. Computer runs test how sharp that rate is for distinct feedback gains.
arxiv-2603-23451: Coppens studies smoothness in refined Brill-Noether schemes on a general k-gonal curve. The curve maps to the projective line with degree k. Degeneracy schemes refine the classic loci by tracking how sections vanish along that map. Inside each closure sits a known smooth open part. Coppens finds larger natural open sets where the closure stays smooth. He applies this to list all line bundles with an injective Petri map. Where these sets form components, the Brill-Noether scheme is smooth at such points, bar overlaps.
arxiv-2603-23651: Spitzer and Nechita make quantum graphs concrete with a family of worked examples. Quantum graphs describe the zero-error behavior of quantum channels. Unlike plain graphs, they are not discrete objects, so examples stay scarce. Their examples come from classical matrix groups shrinking step by step. Each graph rests on three matrices with split roles. Two parts form a classical weighted strange graph, while the third is purely quantum. That split yields exact counts or bounds for components, coloring, and clique numbers.
arxiv-2603-23851: Hao and co-authors study how a phase change affects heat flow in the material CaSnF6. They combine first-principles calculations with a machine-learned potential for large simulations across many temperatures. The runs capture a first-order structural phase transition. Negative thermal expansion comes from low-energy rigid unit modes that rotate linked octahedra and shrink the volume. Strong anharmonicity, led by four-phonon scattering, keeps heat conduction low. Near the transition, conductivity shows a clear non-monotonic anomaly.
arxiv-2603-24151: Burda and co-authors study how the leaders of a Brownian particle gas reshuffle over time. The gas has N particles moving in one dimension in a growing potential.
