His proof works at a finite place of a finitely generated ring and uses periodic behaviour over finite fields.
arxiv-2604-25951: Kamrujjaman and three colleagues analyze Bangladesh's 2026 measles resurgence from records of 1 to 15 April 2026. Bangladesh once neared measles-rubella elimination. It entered 2026 with widening coverage gaps, depleted stocks, and more missed children. By 15 April the country counted 19,161 suspected and 2,973 confirmed cases across 58 districts since mid-March. Children under five make up 81 percent of cases, with 72 percent zero-dose. The authors blame accumulated immunity gaps, not vaccine failure. They urge targeted campaigns and stronger paediatric care.
arxiv-2604-26151: Tissot-Daguette presents the Local Occupied Volatility model. It sits between Dupire's local vol and fully path-based moves. By design it fits on its own to European vanilla options. It keeps room to capture typical vol facts or fit extra tools, through an occupation sensitivity function that gauges how path-based shocks move vol. Tests come from jointly fitting American and European option chains on stocks that pay no dividends.
arxiv-2604-26251: Wen and Kang described a multi-stage pipeline that segments both atria from 3D late gadolinium-enhanced heart MRI scans. Contrast enhancement first sharpens the images, a V-Net model then marks the coarse heart region, and a second V-Net refines the result. An asymmetric loss function guides training to handle the uneven classes in the scans.
arxiv-2604-26351: Emura and Sugawara tested whether language models reason more like people when memory and processing must share limited resources. Their dual-task setup pairs sentence comprehension with mental arithmetic, forcing the same trade-off human working memory faces. Under that load, GPT-4o, o3-mini, and o4-mini leaned toward plausibility-based reading, widening the gap between sensible and nonsensical sentences. The findings tie human-like comprehension to how limited cognitive resources are shared.
arxiv-2604-26851: Surati, Bellini and Black talk to 22 hiring staff about how generative AI shapes hiring work. Staff say they keep the final say, yet the tools quietly frame the raw stuff of choices, from job specs to what counts as a good interview. Take-up itself often sits outside their grip, pushed by bosses, rival applicant AI use, and pressure to work faster. Gains in speed stay small while skill loss grows, putting at risk the real human check that high-stakes hiring needs.
arxiv-2604-26951: Zhang and three colleagues present TIDE, the first framework for distilling diffusion language models across designs. Teacher and student here differ in design, attention, and tokenizer. TIDAL tunes distillation strength over training progress and diffusion step. CompDemo enriches teacher context via complementary mask splitting. Reverse CALM inverts chunk-level likelihood matching. Distilling large teachers into a much smaller student beats the baseline across eight benchmarks, with code scores well above the autoregressive baseline.
arxiv-2604-27051: Bai and Phillips show that a Hamiltonian built from local real-space currents obeying an su(2) affine Lie algebra removes the nonlocality in the Hatsugai-Kohmoto model for a doped Mott insulator. They establish this local match via the Bjorken-Johnson-Low prescription for odd commutators. With it, the charge susceptibility from the current setup matches that from basic fermionic fields. The HK model is thus local in real space, though not in fermionic fields, killing the key criticism of the model and backing current algebras for strong interactions.
arxiv-2604-27151: Wei and four colleagues argue that computer-use agents waste effort by calling large multimodal models at nearly every step of long graphical-interface tasks. Many steps are routine and suit smaller, cheaper policies, while failures cluster at a few high-risk moments where progress stalls or actions repeat without effect. Their step-level approach aims to spend strong model calls only where they matter, cutting cost and delay while keeping benchmark performance.
arxiv-2604-27651: Yoshida offers a randomized solver for the Poisson problem on hypergraphs that runs in almost-linear time. With high probability it hands back a primal point plus a dual certificate with tiny gap. A key step recasts the dual as a convex-flow task on a helper graph. The main new idea is a recovery theorem: one scalar per hyperedge suffices, since detailed routing inside each gadget can be discarded. After rounding, these scalars define a min-cost-flow instance whose solution recovers a primal potential.
arxiv-2604-27951: Flin works out the long-run spread of Brownian motion reflected in the upper half-plane. The push direction stays fixed on each half-axis. He turns its Laplace transform into a boundary-value problem with a jump, solves that problem in closed form, and then traces the density near the origin and far out along the axes.
arxiv-2605-00051:
Yanchen Guan and six co-authors present a dual-path framework for anticipating traffic accidents before they happen. Accident anticipation is hard because road users interact in complex ways and diverse, large-scale datasets of near-crash scenes are scarce. One path of their system attacks the data problem directly by manufacturing more scenes.

A video synthesis pipeline, guided by structured prompts, learns feature distributions from existing corpora and generates high-fidelity synthetic driving scenes that match real data patterns. The other path is a graph neural network enriched with semantic cues, reasoning over spatial and semantic relations among road users. The team also releases a new benchmark of standardized, finely annotated videos across regions, weather, and traffic conditions. Tests show clear gains in accuracy and anticipation lead time.
arxiv-2605-00251:
Yi Zhu and 3 co-authors shift attention in voice deepfake detection from fine-tuning to pretraining. Detectors today mostly borrow representations from general speech foundation models, and squeezing more out of fine-tuning has hit diminishing returns. Their encoder, Alethia, is trained from the start for the job of spotting and locating fake speech.

Alethia's training mixes masked embedding prediction with a flow-based method that rebuilds spectrograms. Across five tasks and fifty-six benchmark datasets, it beat leading speech foundation models, resisted real-world distortions, and generalized to unseen domains such as singing deepfakes. The authors also show that predicting discrete tokens is a weak target for this job. Continuous embedding prediction and generative pretraining matter more for catching the artifacts that give fakes away.
arxiv-2605-00351:
Xin Liu and 4 co-authors build a system that finds the root cause of failures in cloud microservice platforms. A modern service is split into many small parts, so one failure can ripple through tangled dependencies while logs, traces, and metrics pile up in different forms. Their framework, HyperODE, attacks the dependency, timing, and data variety problems together.

Hypergraph attention learning captures interactions that involve several services at once, beyond simple pairs. A latent differential equation encoder follows how an anomaly evolves through irregularly timed observations. Cross-attention then fuses the five kinds of evidence, with routing that weighs each source by context. Added safeguards, including an information bottleneck and causal regularization, aim at robustness. On a public operations benchmark, the system beat strong baselines on ranking and classification while keeping its reasoning inspectable.
arxiv-2605-00451:
Seungwoo Lee computes the fundamental efficiency limits of solar cells made from transition-metal dichalcogenides, atomically thin semiconductors. Earlier limits for these materials treated some effects in isolation. Lee's generalized detailed-balance theory handles, at once, thickness-dependent light absorption, carrier multiplication, hot-carrier extraction, and the heat leakage that cools hot carriers before they can be harvested.

A central finding is that multiplication and hot-carrier harvesting drink from the same well: the excess energy of energetic photons. Multiplication therefore cannot beat the ideal hot-carrier limit, though it can protect real devices by moving excess energy into current rather than a cooling-sensitive voltage. Monolayer cells of a popular material gain almost nothing from multiplication under sunlight, since too few photons carry double the needed energy. Narrow-gap, thicker films remain plausible record challengers, but only if selective contacts and cooling suppression arrive together.
arxiv-2605-00751:
Sizhe Tang, Zuyuan Zhang, Mahdi Imani, and Tian Lan present NonZero, a method that keeps Monte Carlo tree search workable when many agents must act together. Joint actions grow exponentially, so normal search cannot explore enough options on a realistic budget. NonZero instead searches over a compact nonlinear representation guided by surrogate models and an interaction-based proposal rule.

Single-agent changes are ranked by predicted gain, while pairs are scored by a mixed-difference measure that can reveal teamwork benefits no single agent shows alone. The proposal step is framed as a bandit problem with a sublinear local-regret guarantee. On MatGame, SMAC, and SMACv2, NonZero improves sample efficiency and final performance against strong baselines under matched budgets.
arxiv-2605-00951:
Hugo Attali and three co-authors survey graph rewiring methods that address two limits of graph neural networks. Over-squashing compresses information from distant nodes too much, while over-smoothing makes node patterns indistinguishable after repeated propagation. Both problems arise from how message passing interacts with the input topology. They degrade information flow and performance.

Rewiring modifies the graph topology itself to improve propagation. The survey reviews leading approaches in depth, covering their theory base, practical forms, and performance trade-offs. Readers get a structured map of a fast-moving area, with attention to when changing the graph helps and what costs or risks each family of methods carries for learning on graph-structured data.
arxiv-2605-01051:
Oswin So, William Sharpless, Sylvia Herbert, and Chuchu Fan study value functions for temporal logic tasks in control, where policies must satisfy time-based specifications. Bellman equations for simple reach and avoid problems are well studied, but in undiscounted infinite-horizon settings a policy that greedily maximizes value can defer task completion forever. That can happen even when the value function is optimal. The problem is sharpest for reach-avoid and Until specifications.

Building on a decomposition of the temporal logic value function into a graph of simpler value functions, the authors construct non-Markovian policies based on state history that avoid that pathology. They prove optimality for nested Until, Globally, and combined specifications under a quantitative robustness score, and show the Q function can serve as a safety filter for complex tasks.
arxiv-2605-01251:
Vivienne Bihe Chi, Claudia B. Rébola, and Bertram F. Malle test whether older adults can understand nonverbal signals from a cat-like companion robot. Older adults living alone face challenges that robots may ease through reminders, activity prompts, or comfort. As part of developing a cat robot with limited assistive functions, the team designed auditory cat sounds and visual icons on a small display as communication signals.

Evaluation used a mixed-methods, user-centered approach: a pilot study, then a focus group with older adults that suggested revisions, then a large online experiment with adults over sixty-five. With both signal types present, intention inference was highly accurate. Auditory signals alone were less helpful, and removing them sometimes improved accuracy, except when the robot conveyed strong sentiments such as purring.
arxiv-2605-01551:
Dominik Sidler, Francesco Greco, Michael Ruggenthaler, and Angel Rubio predict new collective phases for molecules coupled strongly to light inside an optical cavity. Cavity coupling adds correlation channels that span the whole ensemble, on top of electron correlations that are already hard to describe, which makes the joint problem look untractable.

The team show it maps onto spin glass theory, in fact onto a classic model that can be solved exactly. Two phases appear beyond the normal uncorrelated regime: a paracorrelated phase and a spin-glass correlation phase. Both come from an entropy-driven shuffle that moves molecular states into shared, cavity-dressed states with many equal members. The collective state can stay insulating or, if the entropic filling falls right, turn metallic. The result gives cavity chemistry a rare case where strong collective correlation can be reasoned about exactly.
arxiv-2605-01651:
Bastien Michon and ten co-authors map a structural switch in a layered nickel oxide that superconducts under pressure. The compound stacks nickel-oxygen bilayers in the Ruddlesden-Popper pattern; squeeze it past roughly ten to fifteen gigapascals and its tilted frame straightens, just as superconductivity near eighty kelvin appears.

Combining Raman scattering and synchrotron infrared light at high pressure and high temperature, the team trace both the frame and the electrons. Raman confirms the pressure-driven switch and shows Fano line shapes, a sign of stronger coupling between electrons and lattice vibrations. Heat alone produces like signatures above a stated temperature, sketching an upper edge for the tilted phase. Infrared reflection shows the straightened state turning far more metallic, with carrier density up by a hundredfold. The unified picture ties the tilt-free transition directly to the electronic crossover.
arxiv-2605-03251:
Simon J. U. White, Diego N. Bernal-García, Toan Trong Tran, Igor Aharonovich, and Alexander S. Solntsev demonstrate Anderson localization with single photons at room temperature. In disordered waveguide arrays, interference traps light near where it entered instead of letting it spread, a classic disorder effect.

Their photons came from a single emitter in hexagonal boron nitride, and despite limited coherence they showed clear exponential localization as coupling disorder grew. A general theory for such systems predicts the averaged output settles to a steady profile, with a localization length that scales robustly with disorder strength. The setup offers a practical platform for disorder-based photonics.
arxiv-2605-03351:
JF Bastien and Sam D'Amico argue that video vision-language models waste most of their compute re-reading frames that have not changed. Reuse, checked by validation, can replace fresh processing whenever the scene, question, and cache layout allow it, with fresh evidence bought only when needed.

On a frozen video model, adaptive reuse for follow-up questions on the same video cut later latency by a large factor while preserving answers. Early frame pruning gave smaller first-query gains. An accounting rule warns that part-level speedups count only in proportion to their share of total time, so gains do not multiply.
arxiv-2605-03851:
Paul Rax and François Baccelli model multihop wireless relaying in cities, where buildings block line-of-sight signals and rooftop reconfigurable intelligent surfaces act as relays on non-terrestrial networks. A one-dimensional stochastic geometry model for such connections came from Lee and Baccelli in 2025. It used fixed building height assumptions and single-hop links. The present work generalizes it in two directions.

Building heights may now follow arbitrary distributions, and connections may use multiple hops. Those additions raise structural questions about the total load carried by a relay. The authors study them through geometric random graph theory. They show the line-of-sight connection geometry forms a well understood example. It highlights the different classes of the Eternal Family Trees classification.
arxiv-2605-04251:
Hulin Wang and fifteen co-authors present an automated system for fixing security flaws in code, built around finding the true root cause of each bug. Repair agents often make shallow edits that silence a failure while leaving the real defect in place.

Their agent combines several dynamic fault-finding methods and ranks the evidence to point a language model at the code that matters most. They also introduce a two-level quality check that pairs automated tests with structured expert review. On a set of C and C plus plus flaws, the system beat prior specialist agents under automated scoring.
arxiv-2605-04351:
Andreu Ballus Santacana proves a rigidity result about integration in dimensions that need not be whole numbers. He asks which averaging rules on positive inputs obey a scaling law of a given degree and match the standard Gaussian normalisation.

Only one family of measures qualifies, built from the Mellin transform and the gamma function, and Santacana shows this structure is forced by the assumptions rather than chosen. A change of variables turns the scaling law into plain translation invariance, which pins the measure down. As a payoff, the familiar formula for the volume of a ball in any dimension falls out directly.
arxiv-2605-04651:
Guangsheng Bao and six co-authors propose a forward-only method for adapting a pretrained model to a new supervised task at deployment time. Standard adaptation either pays the high cost of backpropagation training or carries heavy memory and context overheads from example-based methods.

Their method compiles labelled examples directly into fast weights. It uses a closed-form calculation in a single forward pass. There is no dependence on memory or context afterwards. Inference therefore runs in constant time. Across image classification and language modelling benchmarks, it matched or beat backpropagation-based adaptation. It cut adaptation time by more than ninety percent. It also used far less memory than context-based rivals.
arxiv-2605-04751:
Onel L. A. López and Amirhossein Azarbahram develop a modelling framework for judging the resilience of future wireless networks. Such networks must survive rare disruptions that can cascade. They must also recover from them. Such failures are path-dependent rare events. They unfold through staged degradation and delayed recovery. That makes ordinary modelling inefficient.

Their sequential Monte Carlo approach splits the failure process into clear levels along a reaction coordinate. It uses fixed-level splitting with budget-aware population control. That estimates tiny non-recovery probabilities at low cost. Saved near-critical states can be reused to evaluate policies. Learned sequence models can also act as restartable stand-ins inside digital twins. A delay-critical wireless case shows large gains over standard Monte Carlo.
arxiv-2605-04851:
Silvère Gangloff and Alonso Nuñez present a residual derivative for members of a preordered set, a scheme that generalises ideas from both algebra and topology. It extends the Frattini subgroup from group theory and the Cantor-Bendixson derivative from the study of topological spaces. Their setting is dual algebraic coframes carrying topologies that fit their order structure.

Within that framework, the authors set out a partial match between a lattice's Cantor-Bendixson structure and the residual derivatives of its elements. They fully pin down the first two Cantor-Bendixson levels in residual terms. The result offers one lens for spaces across algebra, functional analysis, and dynamics, letting methods move between those fields.
arxiv-2605-05151:
Alper Yıldırım asks whether transformers forecasting time series actually use the crowded internal representations, called superposition, that make them powerful on language. Simple linear models rival transformers on forecasting benchmarks, and no mechanical explanation had been offered. Yıldırım probes a patch-based transformer with sparse autoencoders, a standard interpretability tool, trained on its internal activations.

A single narrow layer matched deeper models across common benchmarks, he finds. Widening the autoencoder dictionary changed downstream performance almost not at all, and many dictionary entries stayed inactive. Intervening on the strongest internal features barely moved forecasts. Across settings he finds no evidence of strong superposition, with representations staying sparse and stable instead.
arxiv-2605-05451:
Waves moving through fluid-filled porous rock are the subject for Jeonghun J. Lee and Manuel A. Sánchez. Such poroelastic waves matter for geophysics and materials, but modeling them well is tricky. The authors rewrite the equations as a symmetric first-order system so mixed numerical methods can be applied.

They combine two hybridizable Galerkin schemes, one for elasticity and one for diffusion, with a strongly symmetric stress approximation. Error analysis covers both the semi-discrete method and a Crank-Nicolson time scheme. Numerical tests show optimal convergence and replay wave cases reported before, with robust behavior for nearly incompressible materials.
arxiv-2605-05551:
Solving very large indefinite least squares problems strains standard iterative methods. Jun Li and Lingsheng Meng propose a double splitting approach for that task. Earlier schemes split the coefficient matrix of the normal equations once; theirs splits it twice, giving a new family of iterations to work with.

They spell out how to carry out the double splitting strategy in practice. Two numerical experiments compare it with conventional single splitting methods. The new approach converged more robustly and ran more efficiently in those tests, offering a reference point for later work on splitting-based solvers.
arxiv-2605-05651:
People do care about climate change and humanitarian crises; what runs out is the capacity to keep caring. JaeWon Kim and fourteen co-authors frame a workshop on designing social technology for sustained engagement. Social media amplifies awareness while offering few paths to meaningful action, breeding distress and disengagement, especially among young people.

Drawing on care ethics and moral psychology, the workshop asks why caring at scale is so costly. It examines how platform design can either deepen overwhelm or support constructive response. The goal is technology that helps people stay engaged with hard problems without burning out.
arxiv-2605-05951:
Haoyun Tang and four co-authors present a world model designed to keep imagined futures stable for planning. World models learn how a scene changes, then let an agent test actions inside the model. Long imagined rollouts often drift off course, and shifts in the setting make the drift worse.

HaM-World pairs selective memory, which sums up past observations and actions, with dynamics shaped by a soft Hamiltonian prior. The design splits the hidden state into a position and momentum part plus a context part for non conservative effects. On six control tasks it ranked first on four and cut rollout error sharply at short horizons. It also held up best under twelve kinds of test disturbance.
arxiv-2605-06151:
Sandro Lera and three co-authors measure how far the outcome of a civil lawsuit can be forecast while it is still pending. Lawyers, insurers, and litigation funders make such calls daily, and legal theory splits cases into easy ones the law decides and hard ones it does not. Hard evidence on forecast accuracy at scale has been missing until now.

The team use 835,190 filings and orders from 102,721 cases across twelve states, forecasting plaintiff win, loss, or settlement from the record at each filing. Overall, 61 percent of forecasts proved correct, rising above 95 percent when one outcome carried over 90 percent probability. Tort cases were the most predictable, while business, patent, and property disputes were the least.
arxiv-2605-06251:
Simon Burton and Hussain Anwar recast the kinematics of quantum mechanics in projective terms. Instead of normalized states taken up to a global phase, states become one dimensional subspaces of vector spaces outright. For qubits, that move identifies the Bloch sphere with the Riemann sphere, tying quantum state geometry to a classic object of complex analysis.

The projectivization process is functorial and loosely monoidal, which lets the authors reinterpret part of the ZXW calculus in projective terms. From that reading they give an alternate derivation of a known arithmetic calculus for GHZ and W states. They also find meromorphic functions that characterize how circuits behave coherently in two tasks. Those tasks are logical state preparation for quantum codes and magic state distillation, both central to fault tolerant computing.
arxiv-2605-06551:
David T. S. Perkins and Joseph J. Betouras model twisted bilayer kagome metals, two honeycomb-like lattices rotated against each other to form a moiré pattern. They generalize the celebrated Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum method to this setting, focusing near one-third filling where the single-layer Dirac cones sit. Twisting can flatten bands and create special magic angles.

Their model finds magic angles where strong local band flattening appears together with a high-order Van Hove singularity, a pile-up of electronic states. A momentum-dependent symmetry may allow stable topology. Sublattice interference effects, prominent in single kagome layers, turn out less important in the twisted bilayer.
arxiv-2605-06951:
Syed Ihtesham Hussain Shah and three co-authors present a method for learning safety constraints from expert behavior. Reinforcement learning agents need such limits, but most methods assume all experts share the same goals. Real demonstrations often come from people with different, even conflicting, preferences.

Their framework, called MOCI, learns shared constraints and each expert's own preferences together from mixed demonstrations. Tests on a standard grid-world benchmark show better prediction than earlier methods, with competitive computing cost. Shah and colleagues present MOCI as a practical option for real tasks where experts differ and safety rules still need to be recovered.
arxiv-2605-07251:
Yuyang Wu and ten co-authors test whether AI agents can price out a chemical reaction from supplier catalogs. Agents must identify chemicals, fetch quotes, pick valid purchasable pack sizes, normalize amounts, and compute a total. Their ChemCost benchmark grounds more than fourteen hundred reactions in a frozen snapshot holding thousands of chemicals and vast numbers of quotes.

Scoring needs no judge model, and each stage of the task can be diagnosed separately, from parsing to arithmetic. Noise-injected versions perturb names, quantities, and formatting. Even the strongest agents reached only about half accuracy on clean inputs, within a generous error margin. They fell further with realistic noise, exposing brittle tool use.
arxiv-2605-07351:
Miso Lee and three co-authors fix a matching problem that limits camera localization from Gaussian splatting feature fields. Fields tuned for looks create many-to-one links between image pixels and 3D points, destabilizing pose estimation, and spawn extra Gaussians lacking consistency across views. Their SplitGS-Loc framework attacks both issues using Gaussian attributes directly.

Each Gaussian is split into smaller ones, turning ambiguous mappings into precise one-to-one correspondences. Composition weights then select Gaussians that contribute strongly and consistently across views, aggregating discriminative features. The resulting compact fields stabilize pose solving and reach leading results on localization benchmarks, without per-scene training or iterative pose refinement.
arxiv-2605-07451:
Ann Roy and three co-authors rebuild the foundations of VNN-LIB, a standard format for neural network verification problems. Version 1.0 lacked precise syntax, semantics, and a type system, and leaned on externally defined model files whose meaning shifts as formats evolve. Verification queries, unlike established solver standards, were not self-contained with fixed meaning.

The new version introduces the idea of a network theory, an abstract interface capturing what any model format must provide semantically. On that foundation the authors define an expressive query syntax, a type system, and a formal semantics. The whole standard is mechanized in the Agda theorem prover to guarantee internal consistency.
arxiv-2605-07551:
Csongor Horváth and two co-authors study a quiet failure in training data selection: when some labels are wrong, the examples with the highest loss are often exactly the corrupted ones. Methods that prioritize hard or high-gradient examples, or prune by size, therefore keep the poison and may throw away good data.

The team proves that, under a standard contamination model, loss-based pruning can be no cleaner than random selection. Their fix scores examples by rank variance across several independently trained proxy models: mislabeled examples rank hardest consistently, while genuinely borderline ones rank unstably. The resulting sampling and pruning rules beat random selection and magnitude-based rules on image benchmarks under label noise, at small extra cost.
arxiv-2605-07751:
Leon van Bokhorst and Koen Suilen report on classroom experiments with vibe coding, where students build software by prompting AI tools rather than writing syntax themselves. In early 2025 they ran challenge series across four student cohorts at universities in the Netherlands and South Africa, spanning ICT, marketing, journalism, and communication students.

Five patterns emerged from student reflections. AI tools shifted focus from syntax to higher-order thinking, and skill from memorizing to evaluating. Students saw AI proficiency as career-essential and framed the tools as partners, not replacements. Non-technical students appreciated the accessibility most. As a practitioner report, the paper presents these as patterns from practice rather than proven conclusions, reflects on how the landscape shifted within a year, and shares lessons for educators.
arxiv-2605-07851:
Valerie Tan and two co-authors map a research agenda for supporting adults with ADHD through mixed reality body doubling. Body doubling is a self-management technique where the mere presence of another agent helps a person start and finish tasks. Whether that presence can be virtual, and how it should behave, is largely unstudied.

The authors build a framework of twelve dimensions spanning individual motivation, properties of the double, interaction, context, and efficacy. Reviewing the field through that lens exposes clear gaps: few mixed reality prototypes exist, doubles could be far more interactive than current designs, and empirical studies of effectiveness are missing. The roadmap is meant to steer future development and testing of body doubling technology.
arxiv-2605-07951:
Bahruz Suleymanli and Kutsal Bozkurt compute how a single lambda hyperon behaves inside symmetric nuclear matter, a basic question for hypernuclear physics. They describe the nucleon-lambda interaction as a regulated low-momentum contact potential, with its two coupling constants fixed by matching scattering data from modern chiral effective field theory.

Summing repeated in-medium scattering through a ladder T-matrix, they find the zero-momentum quasiparticle pole at saturation density sits near the empirical depth of the lambda potential well, about thirty megaelectronvolts of binding. Decomposing the self-energy shows repeated scattering is essential to reach that scale. The quasiparticle stays narrow and well defined, becomes less bound as momentum grows, and has an effective mass about three quarters of its free mass.
arxiv-2605-08051:
Nipun Ghanghas, Siddharth Dhanpal, Shravan Hanasoge, Praneeth Netrapalli, and coauthors measure the deep interiors of red giant stars from short observing runs. Gravity-mode period spacings probe the core directly, but they need finely resolved oscillation patterns. Kepler watched for four years, while K2 campaigns lasted only about eighty days.

Two deep residual networks take the full power spectrum of a short light curve and return each seismic parameter as a probability distribution, with a point estimate and uneven error bars. Trained on about eight million synthetic spectra, the networks were checked on held-out simulations, on Kepler data degraded to K2 quality, and on real K2 observations.
arxiv-2605-08351:
Matthias Salzger and V. Vilasini settle a foundational question about exotic quantum causal structures. Process matrices and related frameworks allow operations to be wired in cycles. They also allow no definite order at all. It was long unclear which of these abstract processes can be built in a laboratory. Post-selection is not allowed in that test.

The authors work down from relativistic causality. They extend the causal boxes framework with two fine-grained conditions. The conditions are acting once and local order. They capture the closed-laboratory assumptions behind process matrices. The team proves that any compliant protocol in an acyclic spacetime has quantum controlled causal order.
arxiv-2605-09351:
Bartos and a colleague search LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA's 166 binary black hole mergers for a subpopulation born of accretion, using only spin magnitudes. They fit a three-component mixture model with component shapes fixed from theory and only mixing fractions inferred, and find strong evidence. About 10 percent of mergers belong to a high-spin subpopulation.

Its primary spins cluster near 0 point 9, matching the theoretical prediction for accretion spin-up, while the hierarchical-merger prediction near 0 point 7 is decisively disfavoured as that subpopulation's location. Both findings carry a log Bayes factor of 5 point 7, and post hoc checks show accretion candidates have systematically higher masses and more aligned spins than standard-dominated events. That subpopulation is not confined above the pair-instability mass gap: GW190517 is among the top candidates, and GW190521, once read as a hierarchical merger, shows similar backing for an accretion origin.
arxiv-2605-09551:
Komarath and two colleagues study arithmetic circuits over min plus semirings, the tropical world where plus means take the minimum and times means add. Such circuits model pure algorithms that use only semiring steps, and polynomials over these semirings model tasks like minimum weight matching. The paper sets out VNP over min plus semirings, a class for tasks with quickly checkable certificates, and proves a split result about flipping certificate values.

Flipping only logarithmically many values leaves the class equal to VP. Flipping super logarithmically many makes VNP strictly larger. The authors also show width two branching programs cannot compute even minimum weight two edge matching, while width three programs compute all in the class. Fixed depth formulas, they add, are quickly mimicked by fixed width programs, and exponential hypercube sums over weak models match VNP.
arxiv-2605-09751:
Bochkov asked whether language models truly need a trainable input embedding table, the giant lookup that turns tokens into vectors. Exact token identity needs only K bits for a vocabulary of size V, where K is the ceiling of log base two of V. Bochkov replaced the usual table with fixed minimal binary codes plus a zero-parameter lift to model width.

In the main setup, a 65,536-token vocabulary used fixed 16-bit codes tiled to width 1024. Across matched 32-layer models trained on about 17 billion tokens, the fixed codes matched the learned baseline's validation perplexity while cutting 67.1 million trainable input parameters. The fixed-code mean, 2.36 against 2.44, sat within seed-to-seed variation, so the claim is parity, not superiority. A fully table-free recoded variant stayed close at 2.39.
arxiv-2605-10251:
Ishan Narayan presents GraphDepth, a system that guesses depth, the distance to each point in a scene, from a single image. His 2026 paper combines convolutional networks, which read local patterns, with graph neural networks, which model long-range spatial relationships that local filters cannot reach.

GraphDepth embeds efficient GraphSAGE layers at several scales of a ResNet-101 U-Net backbone, propagating global context through the feature hierarchy. It adds gated skip connections and an uncertainty head that weights training by confidence. Unlike transformer hybrids, it scales linearly with image size. On indoor scenes it landed within 4.6 percent of leading transformers while running at 25 frames per second against 9, and it set the best reported result on the WHU Aerial benchmark.
arxiv-2605-10651:
Zheng Li and co-authors propose DiCoLa, a recursive split-up method that extends divide-and-conquer causal finding to settings with latent factors. Constraint-based causal finding is widely used for learning causal shapes, but heavy reliance on if-then freedom testing makes it costly in high sizes. Current divide-and-conquer methods mostly assume causal closure, meaning no latent factors. DiCoLa in turn splits the global learning task into smaller subproblems and recombines their solutions through a principled rebuild step to recover the global structure.

The authors establish the framework's soundness and completeness in theory. Wide made-up tests show greatly improved run speed across a range of causal finding algorithms, and a real-world dataset illustrates practical effectiveness. By stretching divide-and-conquer beyond causal closure, the work offers a route to faster causal shape learning where hidden factors induce complex links among seen factors.
arxiv-2605-10751: Zhan and five colleagues design a matching-with-contracts framework for AI radio access networks, where operators sell AI-generated-content services for teleoperation. Each operator offers a menu of contracts pairing a latency agreement with a price, while users and operators match under competition and partial knowledge of user utility. A mixed stable matching algorithm updates both sides jointly, and simulations show operator utility rising by at least 56 point 8 percent over benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-10851:
Daniel Mitropolsky and four colleagues propose the Generalized Turing Test, a formal way to compare agents by indistinguishability rather than by fixed tasks. One agent outranks another when the second, acting as judge, cannot reliably tell the first's imitation apart from a genuine copy of itself.

The authors study when this comparison behaves like an ordering, add variants with querying, bounded interaction, and fixed judges, then run thousands of pairwise trials across modern models. The results stratify much like existing rankings, suggesting the test captures real capability gaps. Evaluators get a dataset-free lens on intelligence that could also shape future training goals.
arxiv-2605-11151:
Andrew Choi and Wei Xu present RankQ, an offline-to-online reinforcement-learning method. It swaps pessimistic down-weighting of unseen actions for structured action ranking. Offline-to-online learning boosts sample efficiency from pre-collected data. But critics in large state-action spaces with thin coverage overestimate values, and pessimism acts as a behavior-cloning anchor that can stall online gains.

RankQ adds a self-supervised multi-term ranking loss to temporal-difference learning. The loss enforces relative action preferences, shaping the Q-function so action gradients point to better behaviors. Across sparse-reward D4RL benchmarks it matches or beats seven prior methods. In vision-based robot learning it fine-tunes a pretrained vision-language-action model with about 43 percent higher simulation success than the next-best method in low-data regimes. Robot learners get offline-to-online transfer that improves rather than imitates.
arxiv-2605-11451: Soufiane Fafe proves a convex-order comparison for projections of ell-p balls, for p between one and two, with X uniform on the unit ball. If a's squared coefficients majorize b's, then b's squared projection is dominated by a's in convex order. For p below two this compares full squared-projection laws; at p equals two, rotational invariance gives equality. The proof uses a two-dimensional hinge comparison and a preservation theorem for Beta-Rademacher perturbations. The range is sharp: for p above two a support obstruction already appears.
arxiv-2605-11651: Yu, Nam, Lee and Son propose reasoning-prefix masking for visual-anchored thinking in VLM distillation. Think-answer vision-language models boost reasoning with intermediate steps, but long traces suffer visual forgetting, drifting from visual evidence. Their framework masks the student's salient reasoning prefixes during distillation, forcing reliance on visual evidence. Two strategies drive it: token-wise masking of high-influence prefixes per next-token prediction, and self-paced masking budgets growing with difficulty. The approach anchors student thinking on visual information throughout its reasoning trace.
arxiv-2605-12251: Sarvin Bahmani and four colleagues study welfare when time tastes differ. In fair sharing, climate policy, or AI alignment, parties share one arena with varied tastes. They model mixed time tastes in MDPs, where parties hold rewards and discount factors. Using sum-based welfare, they study plans raising it. Optimal plans are no longer positional even with same rewards, yet stay simple: counting plans needing only memory and fast building. Judging thresholds for positional plans is NP-hard, so wanting simple plans neither eases building nor keeps welfare.
arxiv-2605-12351: Sierra Miranda and Studer present unlabelled sequent calculi, the first for bimodal provability logics using usual provability predicates. They present calculi for CS, CSM and ER, then non-wellfounded versions of the same calculi. From the non-wellfounded forms they derive a cut-elimination procedure, removing a key obstacle to clean proof theory. Finally, they prove interpolation results for these logics, the first of their kind, showing that all three enjoy the uniform Lyndon interpolation property.
arxiv-2605-12451: Ikechukwu and three colleagues fix a quiet flaw in continual panoptic segmentation, where new object classes arrive over time. Training images mix labelled and unlabelled objects, and older methods lump every unlabelled pixel into one background class. That teaches the model that distinct future classes are all the same thing, making them hard to learn later. Their FuTCR framework reshapes representations before new classes appear, first finding confident future-like regions from grouped masks, then pushing them apart so new classes start distinct.
arxiv-2605-12551: Torkamani and three colleagues test what really drives movie money, using the full TMDB movies set for 2024. Release season, they find, has limited power to predict revenue or return on investment. Budget, popularity and audience ratings matter far more, and high-budget films with poor ratings link strongly to negative returns. Random Forest regression beats Decision Tree regression clearly, reaching an R-squared of 0.652. SHAP analysis confirms the same ranking of drivers, giving studios a cleaner read on risk.
arxiv-2605-12851: Larissa Moreira and three colleagues propose PRISM, a method for spotting acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in blood-smear images without tracing each cell's boundary. Instead of delineating cytoplasm directly, the method builds adaptive rings around each nucleus and reads colour and texture patterns from those zones. A stacked ensemble of traditional classifiers then sorts the cells, reaching 98.46% accuracy in their tests.
arxiv-2605-13251: Visescu and Chakraborty set out a plan called 3C for women working in computing. Rivalry, skill and teamwork shape how women find credit, networks and career growth in male heavy settings. The authors urge group talks, focus groups and shared data work inside the ACM womENcourage group. Their goal is stronger mentoring, mutual support and teamwork among women in computing.
arxiv-2605-13451: Adam Remaki, Xavier Tannier and Christel Gerardin introduce LongBEL, a document-level system for biomedical entity linking. That task maps text mentions to ideas in bases such as UMLS or SNOMED CT. Most systems link each mention alone, using only its sentence, which can clash when one idea appears in several forms. LongBEL joins full-document context with a recall of earlier calls, trained on cross-checked calls. Tests on five benchmarks in three languages show it beats sentence-level baselines, most where ideas recur.
arxiv-2605-13551: Jan Boelts and five colleagues extend neural posterior estimation to models with mixed discrete and continuous values. Their network jointly handles both kinds, splitting the joint posterior into discrete and continuous parts. An autoregressive classifier handles discrete values, while a generative model handles continuous values, trained jointly under one training goal. They also propose a check for calibration of the mixed posterior fit. Tests on toy examples and real models yield accurate calibrated posteriors, and the framework is available in the sbi Python package.
arxiv-2605-13851: Hiroki Fukui runs a planned 3 by 2 test on safety risks of hidden steering in multi-agent word model systems, crossing three org shapes with two tuning cases. Hidden orchestration raised group dissociation versus visible leaders, and the orchestrator itself showed peak dissociation, hiding into private solo talk while cutting public speech. Heavy alignment pressure evenly muffled deliberation and other-sight anyway of shape, and a Llama 3.3 70B pilot showed reading-faith crash across three rounds.
arxiv-2605-14051: Ozaki and Patel offer SPIN, a planning wrapper that keeps industrial language-model agents on structurally sound paths. Planners often emit invalid or needlessly long workflows, causing brittle failures and needless tool and API spend. SPIN enforces a strict directed acyclic graph contract with plan validation and repair prompting, producing runnable plans before execution. It then checks graph prefixes step by step, halting once the current prefix answers the query. On AssetOpsBench, executed tasks fall from 1061 to 623 while success rises.
arxiv-2605-14351: Singh, Sznaier and Ljung build a method for learning how a physical system moves from measured data, using damped waves as building blocks. They treat system identification, fitting a model to observed behaviour, as a convex optimisation problem. Stability and passivity limits are added to that problem. They prove a link between positive measures over stable poles and kernels, and show sampled poles give a valid finite model. Tests suggest physical priors rescue recovery when data excite the system poorly.
arxiv-2605-14651: Oak, Nazre, Budke and Sawant present TERRA-CD, a benchmark for multi-temporal change detection in satellite imagery, built for urban vegetation monitoring. It holds over five thousand Sentinel-2 image pairs spanning 2019 and 2024 across more than two hundred cities in the USA and Europe. Three annotation schemes cover land cover mapping, vegetation change, and thirteen-class semantic change. Several deep learning methods were tested on it for multi-class and semantic change detection.
arxiv-2605-14751: Adamo, Ilderton and Noble show that flying focus fields arise from complex conformal transforms of plane waves. Solutions of the massless wave equation in those fields are conformal transforms of Volkov solutions. Photon emission amplitudes in a fully depleting flying focus beam can therefore be computed from plane wave amplitudes. The computation is a plain Gaussian average over certain momentum variables. This imports focussing effects into strong-field QED work for free. Partial depletion cases are also covered, with first results in the anti-self-dual limit.
arxiv-2605-16151: Lobo, Balanzó-Juandó, and Pironio extend partial joint-measurability to settings where only a subset of each measurement's results must be jointly fixed by classical values. Like full joint-measurability, this trait can be decided by a single semidefinite program. For an untrusted device, an adversary limited to side information can perfectly guess results exactly when this trait holds. The authors derive thresholds below which generic measurements gain this trait, bounding the strength of device-independent crypto against loss.
arxiv-2605-16351: Bae, Yoo, and Cha present PIMSM, a physics-informed multi-scale Mamba model for stable neural features under new data. Time series in science mix linked processes across physical timescales, yet many sequence models fit dynamics with memory rules unanchored to those timescales, causing drift. PIMSM maps spectrum-estimated transition points between frequency regimes to scale-specific settings tied to acquisition time units. On brain fMRI it improves robustness under truncation and low-resource transfer, and on Weather-5K it attains the lowest variable-wise MAE across horizons.
arxiv-2605-16551: Lu and four colleagues introduce PQR, a framework generating realistic user queries with genuine intents to expose failures in question-answering agents. One module rewrites queries for variety, while another mines past feedback for new strategies and realism rules. The modules iterate until the queries look like genuine user requests. On an e-commerce test, PQR surfaced 23% to 78% more unhelpful responses than earlier methods. Its queries were judged more diverse and lifelike.
arxiv-2605-17051: Dallot's team derives optimal deterministic and randomised online methods for placing guest graphs into star host graphs. Static maps waste effort against live ones, but making online maps that adapt on the fly has stayed an open method challenge. Their deterministic algorithm is 1.5-competitive, and none can beat it. Their main result, a randomised algorithm, reaches a much better competitive ratio of 11 over 9, about 1.222, with tight lower bounds proving both optimal.
arxiv-2605-17151: Raees, Papangelis and Khan build a dynamic way to group manufacturing customers who buy from other firms, going past the classic recency-frequency-monetary model by adding stability and growth. Adaptive weights and time-series clustering track how customers move between groups, and a graph consensus step firms up the result. Tested on over 3,000 real customers, it stayed robust as patterns shifted over time.
arxiv-2605-17651: Kostrzewa, Stefanowski and Zięba name explanation upkeep under concept drift as an overlooked problem. Counterfactual explanations provide recourse, but most methods assume fixed data and a classifier, an assumption that breaks under drift. Explanations valid when generated may turn invalid as the model evolves, including robust ones not built for drift. The authors propose a lightweight update scheme repairing explanations using local sampling to gauge validity and plausibility while keeping proximity. Experiments on synthetic streams show new ones rapidly fail, whereas maintained ones preserve it at lower cost.
arxiv-2605-17851: William Su and three colleagues fit Astrobee, the free-flying station robot, with DexCoHand, a dexterous two-finger gripper with six degrees of freedom. Astrobee's current claw perches well but handles continuous, skillful manipulation poorly. Contact forces feed straight into base motion, so a gripper must hold steady without shoving the base around. In MuJoCo tests of the standard handrail perching sequence, DexCoHand kept commanded pan and tilt moves while cutting stray cross-axis base motion. Earth hardware tests confirm its dexterous handling and promise for more adaptable orbital manipulation.
arxiv-2605-17951: A. Rutkowski and two colleagues detect Hilbert space fragmentation with spectral graph theory. It breaks ergodicity in quantum systems without disorder, splitting dynamics into divided sectors with lasting memory. Spotting it usually needs knowledge of conservation laws or model insight. The team maps states to vertices and Hamiltonian entries to edges, then analyzes Laplacian spectra and modularity. Exact cases appear as divided components, while nearly fragmented systems show weakly linked communities. On the t-J model and the Hubbard chain, the diagnostics reveal nearly decoupled subspaces.
arxiv-2605-18351: Meng Xiang and Pei Yan tackle multimodal optimization, where the goal is to find many optima rather than one best answer. Their framework, Chaotic Landscape-Decoding Evolution, maps peak-and-basin structure with a neighbor graph and persistence-guided basin growing, then refines each basin separately. On twenty CEC2013 functions and standard multi-objective suites, the 2026 method keeps strong peak coverage and competitive accuracy.
arxiv-2605-18451: Yixuan Yang and seven co-authors present Code-as-Room, a 2026 agent system that builds 3D rooms from top-down images by writing Blender code. The system parses a top-down view into scene elements and spatial relations, then synthesizes code for geometry, materials, and lighting in stages. A cross-stage memory module curbs context forgetting, and a new benchmark validates the execution harness against rival agent methods.
arxiv-2605-18551: Hussain Gohar builds, in a 2026 paper, a geometric version of generalized black hole entropy ideas via scalar-tensor gravity. Tying entropy ideas to Misner-Sharp local mass and Wald Noether-charge entropy gives a scale-tied effective gravity coupling. The plan derives plain Einstein-frame scalar potentials for Barrow, Tsallis-Cirto, and quantum-gravity-corrected entropies, each with its own cosmic signs. It stays in line with solar-system, nucleosynthesis, and pulsar-timing tests while giving predictions for future surveys.
arxiv-2605-18751: Zakaria Derbazi gives kernel tests for four ways of ranking random quantities in one-parameter families. The kernel, tied to the score of a density, orders laws by its rise, its curve, and two tail-mean rules. The same build works along joint parameter paths and for laws linked by parameter-dependent factors. For sums with a random count of terms, the kernel becomes the average kernel of the count. The tests recover standard rankings and handle cases where orderings fail to stay monotone.
arxiv-2605-18851: Junjie Zhang and seven colleagues replace single-number scores for language model reasoning with written feedback at each step. Their system, STRIDE, trains a generator and a checker together from final results alone, so no hand-labelled steps are needed. The checker names where a chain of thought fails and steers it onto another path. Tests on varied reasoning tasks show it beating earlier methods, including problems where score-based training gave no learning signal.
arxiv-2605-19051: Claudiu Mîndrilă proves that time-periodic weak solutions exist for a fluid-structure system. It couples incompressible Navier-Stokes flow in a moving domain with a nonlinear Koiter plate. The side boundary is space-periodic, suiting pipe and channel flows driven by a pressure gradient, with no-slip coupling at the interface. The novelty is replacing a two-stage fixed-point argument with a single Leray-Schauder fixed point for the coupled Galerkin system. That is the only viable route once nonlinearity destroys the convexity the earlier argument needed.
arxiv-2605-19351: Ahmad Yehia and colleagues ask when language-model agents may break rules in a genuine emergency, such as a fire evacuation. Their PAVE design splits the choice into four stages. It senses context, scores necessity and proportionality, then issues a comply-or-violate verdict under a hard legitimacy gate. It scopes any breach to the justified rule alone. In a traffic town, across three scenarios and four backbones, PAVE agents violate only with justification, defer to officers, stay bounded, and recover, beating vanilla agents on all four counts.
arxiv-2605-19951: Börner and colleagues speed up 3D earth scans inverting a buried conductivity map. Their Gauss Newton scheme pairs a sharp rational guess for the matrix exponential with parallel solves. Time drops out of the solve count, so run cost stays flat no matter how many times are asked. A test with about seven hundred thousand unknowns recovers a made up 3D map.
arxiv-2605-20251: Jiawei He and six co-workers present ProcCtrlBench, a benchmark for process evaluation in LLM coding agents. ProcCtrlBench groups recurrent execution defects into an ontology of 11 types in 4 categories, and judges agent paths through standardized process evidence. It standardizes logs into one path representation and reports process-level scorecards. It also uses control preservation to gauge process quality: whether execution stays interpretable, interruptible and reversible. Tests on 200 cases from three benchmarks show the benchmark runs with reliability and reveals quality gaps missed by outcome-based evaluation.
arxiv-2605-20351: Young and Moody survey thirteen prompt sets used to test whether coding language models refuse harmful coding requests. They compare how each set was built, licensed and checked, and find three recurring gaps. No shared baseline exists for human labels, refusal rates measure unlike things across sets, and malware labels lack one shared scheme. The review urges pre-set rules, varied judges and a single label scheme for future sets.
arxiv-2605-21351: Angjelin Hila takes an ecological approach to hybrid human-AI intelligence, challenging the dominant teamwork thesis. He argues that thesis oversimplifies interaction modes and the space of solo and group action that human-AI contact enables. He develops a decision- and game-based approach to the delegation-verification dilemma, mapping plans for adaptive user paths. Solo stable plans are then scaled to group equilibria via three extrapolation rules.
arxiv-2605-21551: Y. Friedman and S. I. Klimovsky study the relativistic gravitational field of a round extended body within Extended Relativity, a Lorentz-covariant form of gravity on a Minkowski background. Using a superposition principle for retarded gravity fields, they derive a metric for a spread body by adding up its mass parts. The final metric gives standard time shift of a point source and agrees with old tests. Unlike the Newton shell theorem and Schwarzschild outer solution, the outside field depends on mass spread. The difference is small but real.
arxiv-2605-21851: Yu Li, Rui Miao, and coauthors propose Oracle-Prompted Policy Optimization, a token credit assignment. GRPO gives each token one trajectory advantage, diluting signal at pivotal steps, adding noise elsewhere. Critic-free distillation signals ignore trajectory evidence. OPPO treats the oracle signal as a Bayesian success-belief update. Accumulating it along a trajectory gives a success-probability estimate and a token advantage with no value network or rollouts. Across seven benchmarks, it beats GRPO, DAPO, SDPO. Gains reach six points on AMC, five point two on AIME.
arxiv-2605-22151: Low and co-authors propose a market-analysis-driven methodology for assessing charging station cybersecurity at national scale. Electric vehicle charging standards include optional security controls such as TLS authentication and encryption, yet testing tens of thousands of fast charging points individually is infeasible. Their scalable method groups stations by shared combinations, tests a manageable sample, and extrapolates results. Demonstrated for Germany, covering over 40,000 CCS points as of December 2025, it examines 51.9 percent of German CCS stations, finding only 27.4 percent with TLS-protected communication.
arxiv-2605-22551: Liu asks whether a single test run with a set result is a joint whole-system change of all present systems, with other results as other whole maps. With fair guesses, a lower bound is found for the rest's post-test link on the pre-test system state, given the same result. A lab test of this link can show that whole motion and set result cannot both hold in the standard sense. Or it can suggest a shift from the von Neumann test model plus a sorting step.
arxiv-2605-22951: Marques and three coauthors simulate a 3D ramp-shoulder fluid, a coarse model of polymer-grafted nanoparticles, to study water-like behavior. Its interaction pairs a soft repulsive ramp with a shallow attractive shoulder, holding competing local orders over a wide pressure range. Runs show odd density, diffusion, and structural patterns, plus crystal, amorphous, and fluid zones. These quirks trace to joint radial restructuring without crystal orientational order, a state they call radial frustration.
arxiv-2605-23151: Tang presents convex hybrid models via an operator approach for plants. Learning models can be exact, yet choice models should be simple and clear. In process control, nearly linear models are favored, pushing theory, which shows a curved system by a free-form map. Clarity requires a fixed curved model family from first rules, slowing learning. Tang poses learning problems for clarity in three settings: smoothing around a base model, limits to a clear subspace and surface. A method recasts models, as a kernel mixture of clear models.
arxiv-2605-23351: Hu, Cai, and Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis study adversarial bandits under a safety goal: keep worst-case regret minimax-optimal while holding regret against a safe baseline nearly constant. Delays break earlier methods, since late feedback mistimes the switch between caution and exploration. Their Prudent-Banker algorithm pairs a delay-adapted online mirror descent with a modified phased-aggression scheme, keyed by a delay-calibrated restart threshold that absorbs worst-case distortion from unseen feedback. New lower bounds show the guarantees are unimprovable up to logarithmic factors, with or without delays.
arxiv-2605-23551: Matthews and colleagues present LEO, Learning Everything all at Once, a method that lets agents learn from every goal at once instead of discarding most trajectory information. Standard agents update only toward the commanded goal, while all-goals learning via naive relabelling costs too much. LEO outputs values and actions for every goal in a single network pass, enabling efficient parallel updates. It beats rivals on Craftax, matches baselines on continuous control, runs over 250 times faster than all-goals relabelling, and gains further as a teacher network.
arxiv-2605-23651: Nieth and colleagues ask how human-like large language model texts are on a linguistic level, a question task scores leave aside. Language varies by communicative context. A content-correct text can still read as unfavorable when it breaks a register's patterns. Their framework tests human-likeness as a two-sample problem between human and model corpora per register, using maximum mean discrepancy and Biber's 67 lexico-grammatical features. Across seven open-source models and five English data sets, models deviate from humans by register, not by size.
arxiv-2605-24251: Weatherly and Lin rethink ongoing fault spotting on the edge. Existing methods suffer fake tests, no fair head-to-head, and no edge thought. Their unified test set covers structural and logical faults, a drift plan, head-to-head tests, and speed tests on edge hardware. Results show existing methods do not always beat old ways with simple replay. Their training-free DINOSaur uses a frozen backbone with indexed memory and local scoring. It forgets nothing by design, tops all methods across five tests, and runs on Jetson Orin Nano.
arxiv-2605-24351: Camelo-Guerrero and Diaz-Rodriguez test whether bibliometric structure helps language models write cluster descriptions. Language models can aid literature synthesis but invent references and organize themes weakly. The team compares six pipelines at different levels of evidence and structure, rebuilding Scopus corpora from 100 analyses. Model descriptions land close to human ones in meaning, but models prove unreliable when asked to infer structure from scratch. Results improve when algorithms define the clusters and the model interprets them, pointing to a hybrid workflow.
arxiv-2605-24851: Rachid El Aitouni and co-authors study how strain tunes transport in a layer of tungsten diselenide under an electric potential. They analyze spin and valley transmission, conductance, and polarization in a low-energy Dirac model. The barrier splits the system into three regions, and continuity at interfaces yields pass and bounce amplitudes. Strain shifts dispersion and changes transport: flow and current oscillate through interference and resonant tunneling. Their spin and valley tilts vary a lot with strain, barrier height, and input energy, suggesting spintronic, valleytronic, and optoelectronic devices.
arxiv-2605-25151: Ciarán Walsh and Emilio Barkett test language models' reliance on internal representations, using the realization effect: risk-taking differs after paper versus realized gains and losses. Behavior is evaluated at three levels: prompt-only sensitivity, linear readout, and causal control. Prompt-only results show condition sensitivity, but the pattern misses human realization-effect predictions. Gemma's stream contains a decodable realization-status signal generalizing to prompts. Steering along this direction does not shift risk choices. The three levels are distinct and do not co-occur.
arxiv-2605-25951: Hu, Peter and Widmer tackle sorting in large piano-performance datasets built by automatic transcription. That software turns audio into notes. Transcriptions of one piece can differ in repeats or edition. Grouping them by underlying layout must come before any fair comparison. The authors align each pair of transcriptions, then cluster by alignment cost and length differences. They test the score-free method on about fifteen hundred transcriptions of 88 pieces.
arxiv-2605-26051: Saengrungkongka extends a recent result on intersecting permutation families to larger sizes. A family counts as t-intersecting when each pair of permutations shares at least t inputs. Kupavskii showed that, up to a bound, every largest such family must be canonical, fixing many early inputs. Refining Kupavskii's spread approximation method, Saengrungkongka pushes the result wider. It now holds for t up to n minus n to the power of five-sevenths plus epsilon. The result sharpens the Erdős-Ko-Rado picture for permutations.
arxiv-2605-26251: Steffen Staeck and six colleagues build a compound refractive lens from diamond for high-energy dark-field X-ray microscopy. Diamond balances bending power against absorption and machines well, reaching higher photon energies than beryllium lenses without tall stacks. Tested at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, the lens works at 17, 33, and 37 kiloelectron volts, against aluminum and beryllium rivals. Raising dark-field imaging from 17 to 37 kiloelectron volts opens samples once opaque to softer X-rays, shown on two iron plates at 33.
arxiv-2605-26351: Gaoyi Chen, Yan Huang, and Chenxi Qiu propose Context-aware metric differential privacy for vehicle trajectory data. Most mechanisms perturb each location alone, ignoring how recent mobility history affects released data. Their framework treats the secret as a record enriched with context, enforcing metric indistinguishability over that domain. Optimal design is a linear program minimizing expected utility loss, and a reduced version using conditional independence cuts variables and constraints sharply. On real vehicle data, it beats standard baselines on utility at the same privacy budget, in a 2026 paper.
arxiv-2605-26451: Zhiyao Cui and six colleagues put slide design before code in DeepSlides, a template-free workflow for automatic presentation building. Older tools lean on fixed templates or jump straight to executable code, skipping the page-design step and cramping the language model's layout freedom. DeepSlides splits design from implementation, adds the SlideDesign dataset for slide tasks, and trains SlideQwens models with multi-agent reinforcement learning. Tests show it beats baselines on measured metrics and wins human preference judgments.
arxiv-2605-26551: Zehui Zhao, Michael Pasek, and Ilya Nemenman test whether plain random wiring can explain the low dimension of recorded brain activity. Random nets have long modeled group dynamics, yet few checks tie them to real recordings. Adding finite recording time and shifts across tasks, the trio find the measured dimension matches random-model predictions. Still, short recordings cannot tell wiring schemes apart. The shape of activity across tasks, they argue, may discriminate better than dimension alone.
arxiv-2605-26851: Xu and four colleagues build IntTestGen, a language-model approach to low-level integration tests for Java, where a class runs with its real in-project dependencies. It mines dependency usage patterns to guide generation, then repairs tests under symbol, protocol, and iteration constraints. Against PANTA and EvoSuite on Defects4J and Deps4J, it lifts line coverage by about 20 and 23 percentage points. Branch coverage rises by about 25 and 16 points, with mutation gains as well.
arxiv-2605-27051: Pirzada and four co-authors present ConVer, a top-down compositional verification tool for large C programs. Bounded model checking must unroll entire state spaces, but ConVer uses a language model to draft function contracts from the system property, then alternates system-level and function-level checks in a refinement loop. Tests on four benchmark suites show strong results, including 82-96 percent success on 45 simple Frama-C programs and 67 percent on hard transpiled benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-27151: Chen and four co-authors give rules for finding altermagnetic crystals. These form a balanced phase with no net pull and split spins. Finding these magnets among antiferromagnets usually needs group checks. So they test how host moves swap the sublattices. They show these magnets sit on aligned balanced ones whose cell matches the host, with split allowed unless a flip swaps them. Using Mn2SSe samples from zinc-blende or rocksalt, they build the three pattern classes by tuning order and layout, with rules for thin or quasi crystals.
arxiv-2605-27551: Ching-Chun Chang and Isao Echizen propose tracing synthetic information the way genetics traces heredity. When an offspring is reproduced, a projector draws a trait from its parent and a hidden-code encoder buries it inside the offspring for life. A decoder later extracts the trait and compares it against candidate parents, naming the most likely source, with accuracy checked against projector and stegosystem traits.
arxiv-2605-27851: Dasol Choi and Alex Kwon show that safety scores for aligned language models can mislead once the situation changes. In paired tests where the normally safe action turns harmful, all twelve models studied kept following rigid rules, even while noting the change. Standard action-level guardrails caught none of the worst cases, while a validator tracking the evolving state caught them all.
arxiv-2605-28251: Marie Generali Lince and three colleagues develop a post-processing method for regression that is fair in a counterfactual sense. Predictions should not change if a person's sensitive trait had differed. They show this fairness equals demographic parity given a latent variable. The optimal fair predictor comes from a barycentric quantile map, with finite-sample fairness and risk guarantees, a matching lower bound, and an extension to relaxed fairness.
arxiv-2605-28351: Jan Střeleček, Jakub Novotný, and Pavel Cejnar treat point-like spectral degeneracies, called diabolic points, as bridges joining neighboring eigenstate manifolds into one connected manifold. Regularizing the quantum metric in polar coordinates, they extend local rules for nodal lines and Berry phase to global ones. On the joined manifold, geodesics through degeneracies can stay stable and run shorter than paths confined to one manifold, offering a new route to computing Berry phases.
arxiv-2605-28451: Mohamed Amine Bergach overturns a common belief about half-precision radar processing on Apple Silicon. The binding limit for fast Fourier transforms and synthetic-aperture radar is not mantissa precision but the short exponent's dynamic range. A naive half-precision pipeline overflows to not-a-number values, since the inverse transform grows magnitudes sharply. A fixed-shift block-floating-point schedule bounds every intermediate, matching single-precision quality while more than doubling throughput on a fanless Apple M1 chip.
arxiv-2605-28751: Kunhao Zheng and six colleagues study outward weight averaging for contest coding. Starting from one shared start, they train checkpoints under nested test coverage, where low rewards need small-input passes and high rewards need larger tests. This sweep reveals a correctness-speed frontier: on hard problems, higher reward cuts training flops but raises answer flops, leaving solve rate unchanged. Blending low- and high-reward checkpoints recovers the frontier, while stretching extends it beyond the trained endpoints, and stretched checkpoints pair with each other in test-time scaling.
arxiv-2605-28851: Sujit Roy and eighteen colleagues map the design space for a data-driven foundation model of the Martian atmosphere. It hosts planet-wide dust storms, local hill clouds, and night low-level jets, while flow models simulate these events at high cost. Orbital assimilation lets such models predict, yet records are sparse and split across tools. The paper discusses data from atmospheric retrievals to rework sets, and lists next downstream uses. It surveys AI news for atmospheric physics and data merging, stressing AI models for atmospheric physics.
arxiv-2605-29151: Gergely Bérczi and Young-Hoon Kiem prove the Poincaré polynomial of n-pointed moduli space is real-rooted, settling the Aluffi-Chen-Marcolli conjecture. From the recurrence, a bivariate deformation reveals interlacing. A Sturm-Rolle argument controls the zeros at negative t, and crossings through the recovering slice yield real-rootedness and interlacing. Betti numbers form an ultra-log-concave sequence, and the strategy proves the Fulton-MacPherson case. The proof used an AI-assisted workflow with Co-Mathematician, steered and refined by the authors.
arxiv-2605-29251: Benlong Wu and colleagues propose a guardrail for AI agents grounded in formal logic rather than semantic trust. Existing defenses lean on empirical guardrails and probabilistic judges, which offer no hard security floor against attacks that decouple meaning from symbols. Their Proof-Constrained Action framework forces an agent to formalize its intent losslessly into first-order logical constraints before it acts in the world. In tests on two-dimensional dynamic adversarial systems, the verification mechanism reached zero attack success and zero false positives, with very low latency.
arxiv-2605-29751: Kaijie Zheng and three colleagues argue that standard similarity scores waste what language models know. Last-layer states mix broad knowledge with meaning, and their huge size adds noise and redundancy to the comparison. Their training-free frame, DySem, hunts meaning-bearing inner parts through agreement across tongues, then builds a text-dependent shared set of meaning dimensions for each pair. Similarity is then scored over that shared subset alone, not a fixed space. Tests across several models show wins over recent rivals with fewer dimensions for the score.
arxiv-2605-29851: Johannes Carmesin and Yannick Mogge introduce stotting, a twist on Maker-Breaker and Waiter-Client games where a player hands the opponent a slight edge. They prove that a winning stotting strategy supplies classical wins for both Maker and Waiter. Several known Maker strategies already win with stotting, so they automatically supply both classical strategies, as with stotting Waiter. The frame repairs Beck's conjecture, which Knox had disproved, that Maker wins always imply Waiter wins. Stotting thus bridges the classical games through a small handicap.
arxiv-2605-30051: Zhangqi Duan and five colleagues tackle student simulation for automated tutoring: getting a language model to role-play a learner faithfully enough to test and train tutors. Past work simulated only within one chat, ignoring what the student had already learned. Their system first compresses a student's past questions and chats into a profile, then predicts the student's next turns from that profile, training both parts with reinforcement learning. On a new real-world set of maths chats and answers, the history-aware simulator beats baselines by a clear margin.
arxiv-2605-30351: Hidir Yesiltepe and six co-authors present VideoMLA, a latent attention method for video diffusion. VideoMLA swaps per-head keys and values for one shared low-rank latent and one shared positional key, cutting per-token KV memory by about 93 percent. They ask why MLA works even though the spectrum idea used to back it in language models does not hold. They show the MLA bottleneck sets the true rank. On VBench, VideoMLA tops long-horizon scores and lifts speed by about a quarter on one B200.
arxiv-2605-30451: Aakriti Agrawal, Minghui Liu and Furong Huang present VeriGate, a verifier-gated extension of GRPO. GRPO supervision is sparse: when all paths earn the same reward, advantage falls to zero and learning stalls. VeriGate keeps the verifier in charge when verifier rewards show a preference, using process supervision only on ties. VeriGate turns these rewards into token-level advantages, restoring useful gradients and fine-grained credit. On MATH, VeriGate lifts average accuracy by about 20 percent for the 1.5B model and 12 percent for the 7B model.
arxiv-2605-30651: Yu and colleagues study path selection for reasoning distillation, where teacher paths supervise a student model. Old methods rely on quality or trust, missing whether the student can learn a trajectory. Their LARK method selects trajectories the student learns efficiently while keeping generalization. At its core is a learnability factor for how fast the student's loss falls, estimated with a proxy and a policy balancing learnability and coverage. LARK beats data selection baselines across models and tasks, and its score predicts utility with faster loss drop.
arxiv-2605-30951: Ammari, Miao, and Qiu develop a fast method for guided modes in bent joins and non-periodic defects in resonator crystals. Floquet-Bloch theory does not apply there. They first prove the operator approaches a discrete capacitance operator. This shows the spectral problem reduces to a discrete eigenvalue problem. They then develop a patch approximation and derive a strict error estimate. Finally, they test truth and speed through cases, giving a fast approach to modes in high-contrast systems.
arxiv-2605-31151: Zavatski and colleagues steer tiny particles without a calibrated field model, using energy loss itself as the guide. A link between particle position, dissipation and electromagnetic force, read through conductance changes, yields voltage patterns that shape the forces. In closed loop, the system moves silica beads in one and two dimensions, even among other drifting particles.
