LUCID jointly uses attention scores, graph semantics, and graph structure. It extracts node and edge features from attention scores and meaning matches. A graph neural network then integrates those features with the graph's structure to judge each output. The team built manually annotated benchmark datasets for testing. Across nine datasets, LUCID reaches state-of-the-art performance against fifteen baselines. Using graph structure as evidence fits how graph reasoning actually works.
arxiv-2606-19451:
Zhang and colleagues introduce 3D-DLP in 2026, a self-supervised model that learns object-centric scene models in three dimensions. The model splits scene-level depth views into a set of three-dimensional latent particles. Each particle encodes separate attributes, a keypoint position, box dimensions, and appearance features, and stands for one distinct entity. Robotic decision-making needs such structure.

Building on the Deep Latent Particles framework, the model learns per-particle segmentation maps through a self-supervised reconstruction objective. On simulated and real datasets, the learned space proves readable and controllable. Moving particles and decoding them generates novel scene configurations. For downstream robot tasks, these compact particles beat baselines that lack explicit three-dimensional input or use memory-heavy dense inputs without object structure. A scene parsed into movable object tokens is easier to plan with than a raw point cloud, and far cheaper to store.
arxiv-2606-19651:
Max Van Puyvelde, Ibrahim Gulluk, Wim Van Criekinge, and Olivier Gevaert present BrainG3N in 2026, a tokenizer for 3D brain MRI generation. Latent diffusion for brain scans needs embeddings that keep clinical signal and rebuild anatomy faithfully. Reconstruction-driven tokenizers usually serve the second goal at the first's expense.

BrainG3N splits the jobs: a frozen 3D masked-autoencoder encoder makes the embeddings. A dedicated convolutional decoder rebuilds voxels from a linear projection of those embeddings. Pretraining uses 35,309 volumes from 18 public cohorts across four modalities and ten disease classes. On a 23-task linear probing benchmark, the encoder matches or beats leading models on 21 tasks. A conditional diffusion transformer trained on the embeddings generates scans across six variables. It also forecasts a patient's future scans over time. One embedding space thus serves both clinical prediction and controllable image generation.
arxiv-2606-20051:
Shah Faisal and Yin Li derive new upper bounds for Lagrangian capacity, a measure of how large a Lagrangian submanifold can sit inside a symplectic space. Their 2026 paper works with Liouville domains whose Gutt-Hutchings capacities are finite. A headline result computes the capacity of convex toric domains in any dimension exactly: it equals the domain's diagonal. That settles the Cieliebak-Mohnke conjecture on ellipsoids, a question that had resisted earlier approaches.

The proof uses an equivariant variant of techniques from Fukaya and Irie, built on chain-level string topology. It avoids holomorphic curves with local tangency constraints, which would have caused transversality trouble. The authors also show that any extremal Lagrangian torus in an ellipsoid must lie on its boundary. Applications include new bounds on Lagrangian width and the first capacity values for many Weinstein domains in dimensions four and six.
arxiv-2606-20251:
Yu Shen, Aiswarya Walter, and Stefanie Roos present TrustMix. It is a protocol for sending anonymous messages over mobile ad hoc networks. These are networks devices form directly with each other when the internet is shut down or missing. Mix networks normally hide who sent a message by shuffling traffic. But they assume fixed infrastructure. In TrustMix, nearby users form groups. A message is shuffled inside one group before moving to the next. An observer therefore cannot link sender and receiver.

The protocol also resists flooding attacks. Linkable ring signatures cap how many messages each party can send, without revealing identities. The authors prove security in the random oracle model. They measure anonymity of up to 8 to 10 bits in simulation. They also test an Android prototype on five phones, with acceptable throughput.
arxiv-2606-20351:
Karen Sargsyan rebuilds the foundations of Bayesian conditioning inside Cubical Agda, and finds a standard axiom wanting. Her 2026 paper shows that the convex-algebra interchange axiom, common to probability-monad formalizations since Stone, is provably too weak to support full Bayesian conditioning. Finite distributions are built as a higher inductive type, and conditioning is a total recursive function on a full-support fragment. Lifting it to the whole type exposes the flaw.

The two halves of a rearranged four-way mixture carry different Bayesian weights related by Bayes' formula, not the single shared weight the standard axiom supplies. Sargsyan exhibits the minimal generalization that repairs this and proves the standard form is its degenerate case. Around that core, she verifies bind commutativity, the semi-graphoid axioms, Pearl's do-calculus rules, and d-separation soundness on arbitrary finite graphs, all with zero postulates.
arxiv-2606-20851:
Hongzhao Zheng, Mohamed Atia, and Halim Yanikomeroglu propose a framework in 2026 for placing high-altitude platform stations to aid urban localization. Such platforms were designed for communications. They can also send structured signals that supplement satellite navigation. Dense cities block satellite signals and create non-line-of-sight errors. Simple geometric placement scores miss those effects. Their framework optimizes platform count and placement jointly.

High-fidelity three-dimensional city models and ray tracing capture blockage. Multi-objective optimization then searches a discrete, highly non-convex design space. Three metaheuristic methods, built on distinct search principles, converge fast and beat a greedy baseline. Gains are largest with few to moderate platforms. In representative dense city cases, four platforms meet an eighteen-meter average error threshold. Careful placement could extend precise positioning into urban canyons where satellite navigation alone often fails drivers and emergency services.
arxiv-2606-21051:
Lincoln Clark and eight colleagues show a multifunctional imaging device in 2026 built from an inverse-designed nonlocal metasurface, a surface thinner than a wavelength of light. Such surfaces process spatial patterns in light with optics alone. Their optimized surface switches imaging modes by polarization. No parts move, and no computing is needed to image clear samples.

For one polarization state, the surface takes a first derivative of phase. That yields pseudo-three-dimensional phase-contrast images of clear biological samples. The other state returns the identity, giving normal brightfield images. Switching is instant through polarization control. The work extends inverse design to phase-contrast microscopy. Uses span life science imaging, medical diagnosis, and materials checks, where clear specimens are hard to see in normal light and staining is not always welcome.
arxiv-2606-21251:
Zechen Tang and thirteen colleagues report a faster route to finding superconductors in 2026, built on the metallized sigma-bonding picture of how certain bonds host paired electrons. The standard test, density functional perturbation theory, is too costly for mass screening. They define a sigma-bonding density of states score, readable from a cheaper electronic structure run, and speed it further with a deep-learning Hamiltonian method.

Screening two million materials, the team flags B13Se as a candidate superconductor at normal pressure with a predicted transition above 40 kelvin. A whole family of related boron compounds scores highly as well, which supports the screening logic. By tying a physics-based score to AI acceleration, the work offers a general path for finding phonon-mediated superconductors without the usual heavy calculations.
arxiv-2606-21451:
Ramesh Krishnamurthy, Danial Chitnis, and Themis Prodromakis close the quality loop in 2026 on hardware assertions written by language models. Models can draft assertions for register-transfer-level chip designs, making formal verification easier to start. But generated assertions can pass vacuously, for trivial reasons, proof costs swing wildly by design, and failure traces baffle engineers.

Their open-source framework refines assertions with mutation testing, injecting faults to reject assertions that cannot tell faulty behavior from good. A solver-selection stage picks among SMT backends based on the design's structure, smoothing runtimes. When proofs fail, a causal narrative explains why, grounded in the counterexample trace. Across varied designs, confidence rose and runtime spread fell, arguing that quality control, not generation alone, is the missing step.
arxiv-2606-21651:
Vivian Yun Yan Tan, Adam Muzzin, and thirteen colleagues trace how the ancestors of Milky Way-like galaxies assembled from redshift 5 to today, in 2026. Using the CANUCS survey, they fit spatially resolved spectral energy distributions for 872 progenitor galaxies, extracting maps of mass-weighted age, stellar metallicity, and specific star formation rate. Mergers are separated from quiet growers using morphology statistics on the stellar mass maps.

Non-mergers show the fingerprints of inside-out growth: flat or negative age gradients and positive star-formation gradients, centers older than outskirts. Mergers at every epoch have flatter age gradients and more suppressed outer star formation, a momentary disruption rather than a rewrite. Within merging pairs, the smaller partner forms stars 0.1 to 0.4 dex more intensely, while ages and metallicities of the partners barely differ.
arxiv-2606-21851:
Dao and colleagues propose TALAS in 2026, a method for distilling large text embedding models into smaller students without the usual heavy cost. Distillation trains a compact model to copy a teacher's sentence embeddings, but forcing the student to mimic every internal feature ignores the real gap in capacity between them. TALAS, short for Teacher-Anchored Layer Alignment with sharpness-aware training, splits the copying work by depth.

Final sentence embeddings from the teacher are distilled only into the student's upper layers, which cuts cost. Lower layers instead learn from the student's own upper layers through geometric relations inside the embedding space, passed downward step by step. An adaptive sharpness-aware optimizer steers training toward flat minima so the student does not merely memorize teacher noise. On standard sentence embedding benchmarks, TALAS beat strong distillation baselines while using less compute and memory.
arxiv-2606-21951:
Kumar and colleagues investigate, in 2026, when differential privacy makes high-dimensional statistics fundamentally harder, focusing on sparse covariance estimation and principal component analysis (PCA). Without privacy, both problems need only a number of samples polynomial in the sparsity and logarithmic in the dimension. The one comparable private result, however, needed samples growing linearly with the full dimension, raising the question of whether this curse of dimensionality is unavoidable.

The answer splits by assumption. If the leading eigenvector is itself sparse, the authors show private PCA is achievable with the same mild sample complexity as the non-private problem. Without it, they prove lower bounds polynomial in the full dimension for both tasks. That establishes an exponential gap between private and non-private sample needs in the stated regime. It is the first such separation for sparse estimation problems, with stronger lower bounds even for standard private PCA.
arxiv-2606-22051:
Feng and colleagues present GeoFlow-SLAM++ in 2026, a system that lets robots track their own motion while mapping their surroundings, using several cameras plus inertial sensors. Single-camera systems suffer from narrow fields of view, sensor-specific failures, and unreliable relocalization when a place is revisited. The new system extends an earlier single-sensor design to a calibrated multi-camera rig with one shared body state.

All three run on that unified state, combining reprojection constraints, inertial pre-integration, and cross-view place recognition. Two visual front-ends can be swapped in: a conventional ORB tracker, or a neural feature tracker built on SuperPoint and LightGlue. Optional pseudo-depth predictions from ordinary images add further geometric constraints. Across five benchmarks, the neural front-end proved more robust in hard visual conditions, and cross-view relocalization reached LiDAR-comparable performance on the handheld data.
arxiv-2606-22451:
Mithil Ramteke studies exact nonnegative matrix factorization in this 2026 paper, working alone. The method splits a matrix into two nonnegative factors, with no negative entries allowed, which suits data such as counts and images. Ramteke focuses on small matrices where an exact factorization exists and asks how to find it fast.

The approach builds a polyhedral cone, a geometric object formed by the allowed factor directions, and lists its rays with the double description method. A closed-form witness matrix then either yields an exact factorization in microseconds or proves the chosen rays cannot work. Candidate ray sets are ranked by obtuseness, a measure of how close they are to perpendicular. Monte Carlo trials show a clear saturation curve: a moderate candidate budget recovers most factorizations, and larger budgets barely help. The remaining failures are structural, because the cones lack a suitable ray set on at least one side.
arxiv-2606-22551:
Milton Mondal and eight colleagues diagnose a training problem in hybrid quantum neural networks in this 2026 paper. Such classifiers read out class scores as quantum measurement values, which physics bounds between minus one and one. Feeding those squeezed scores into the usual loss leaves it barely sensitive to score differences, so gradients shrink and training turns unstable.

The authors name this measurement-induced logit contraction and propose a fix called Quantum Measurement Temperature. It is a learnable scaling parameter that stretches the outputs before the loss, acting during training, not as after-the-fact calibration. The mechanism changes neither the circuit design nor the measurement operators. Experiments on fluorescence microscopy images, the paper's protein-classification setting, and a six-class Fashion MNIST variant show consistent benefits. Score separation grew, gradients strengthened, and training stayed stable across starting points, while accuracy improved over unscaled readouts.
arxiv-2606-23151:
Fabian Dawel and colleagues report a full error budget for an aluminium ion optical clock in a 2026 metrology paper. Optical clocks tick so fast and steadily that metrologists plan to redefine the second around them. That plan demands rigorous accounting of every systematic shift in each candidate clock. The team evaluates a single-ion aluminium clock at Germany's national metrology institute. They measure its absolute frequency against two caesium fountain clocks, the current standard. They also measure its frequency ratio against a strontium lattice clock in the same institute.

Dawel and colleagues find a total systematic uncertainty of just over one part in a billion billion, in fractional terms. Atomic coefficient accuracy and collisions with background gas set the limit. Such cross-checks between independent clock types build the consistency record a redefinition requires.
arxiv-2606-23351:
Jinghua Deng and Jianfeng Hou determine density profiles for a small colored star graph in a 2026 combinatorics paper. The star has one center, one blue edge, and two red edges. A copy inside a large graph counts when the red edges land on real edges and the blue edge lands on a non-edge. The fixed-density problem asks: for each overall edge density, what are the most and fewest such copies a graph can hold? On the upper side, the authors prove the missing low-density range. Combined with earlier work, that completes the full four-branch profile.

Deng and Hou find the lower side holds a surprise. The natural candidate profile, built from quasi-star and quasi-clique constructions, turns out not to be universal. The true minimum comes from a one-parameter family of three-class complement-split graphs.
arxiv-2606-23551:
Leonardi and colleagues report catching a rare, nineteen-hour transit of a giant exoplanet, in a 2026 observational astronomy paper. HIP 41378 f orbits its star once every five hundred forty-two days and spans about nine and a half Earth radii. Such long-period planets cross their star so rarely that each crossing is precious. Timing shifts, called transit timing variations, also betray the gravitational pull of sibling planets in the system.

A coordinated campaign combined the NEOSSat space telescope with ground sites including LCOGT, MuSCAT, and NGTS to record the October 2025 event. The transit arrived about seven hours earlier than a steady schedule predicted. That offset matches earlier reported timing shifts and makes this planet the longest-period world known to show them. Fitting the timings of all three outer planets with an N-body integrator, software that simulates mutual gravity, refines future transit predictions.
arxiv-2606-23651:
Campbell and colleagues revisit a reported tension in cosmology measurements called the lensing is low problem, in a 2026 paper on observational cosmology. Galaxy galaxy lensing measures how foreground galaxies bend light from background ones, revealing the mass around them. Models fitted to galaxy clustering had predicted a lensing signal twenty to forty percent stronger than observed. That mismatch suggested flawed halo models or flawed cosmology.

New imaging from the UNIONS survey gives precise lensing measurements over a wide area of sky. The authors fit lensing and clustering together using a halo occupation model. Unlike earlier work, they find no significant lensing is low effect in this sample. The best fits prefer a slightly lower matter clustering amplitude than the standard Planck values. The authors stress that large scales, often neglected, are key to judging the effect.
arxiv-2606-24051:
Wang and colleagues aim to give self-driving language models a better sense of space. Vision-language-action models turn a pretrained vision-language system into a driving policy. Yet most ground their choices in ordinary camera views and language habits. Safe planning instead needs exact distances, a top-down scene layout, and attention to risky details. Their 2026 system, DriveStack-VLA, attacks all three gaps at once.

A bird's-eye-view representation feeds into the language model decoder through a stacked connection, giving the policy a map-like view. Render-Teacher Alignment trains the model to focus on real camera images the way it focuses on simplified rendered scenes. A self-critique head then ranks sampled driving paths and refines the best one when needed. Benchmarks on NAVSIM and the closed-loop Bench2Drive suite place the system near the top, with strong planning and driving scores.
arxiv-2606-24151:
Dai and colleagues ask how a self-improving software agent should store what it learns: as plain text notes, or as code tools it can call. Systems that evolve by reusing past experience usually pick one form at design time. The trade-offs then go unmeasured. Their 2026 study runs the first controlled comparison. The experiences stay identical; only the storage form varies.

Text memory and code memory prove complementary, not rival. They differ in construction cost, execution speed, and how well they transfer to new tasks. Neither suffices alone. Guided by that finding, the team builds Metis, an agent with a hierarchical, dual memory. Text experience is sorted into execution plans, environment facts, and common pitfalls. Recurring plans are selectively crystallised into validated callable tools. Dai's design banks the breadth of text and the precision of code in one system, choosing the form per experience, not per project.
arxiv-2606-24351:
Denis and colleagues build a tool to read the immune pattern of one of neurology's most frightening crises. Cryptogenic NORSE is a nonstop seizure state. It strikes people with no prior brain disease and no discoverable cause, despite full testing. Evidence points to immune misfires. Reported immune patterns vary wildly between patients, complicating the choice of targeted immunotherapy.

Starting from graph clustering, the Paris team separates sixty-two patients, profiled on ninety-six cytokines, into distinct immune groups. Models are tailored to assign each new patient the odds for each validated cluster. Monte-Carlo simulations and custom tests assess which model informs best. The framework is then wrapped in a doctor-friendly interface. It processes several cytokine profiles quickly, returning the likeliest cluster with its supporting evidence. Denis's 2026 goal is practical: turn an unreadable cytokine panel into a treatment-guiding classification at the bedside.
arxiv-2606-24551:
Zhou and colleagues run a controlled race between two ways for computer use agents to operate software. One clicks through graphical interfaces. The other invokes programmatic skills through a command interface. Existing evaluations confound the modality with differing tasks, starting states, verifiers, and permitted actions. Their 2026 matched benchmark removes those confounds, across hundreds of desktop tasks spanning many applications and workflow categories. Screen only GUI agents and skill mediated CLI agents get identical goals, states, and final state verifiers.

The strongest GUI agent wins the first round, its full pass rate clearly above the strongest CLI agent's. Then the race flips. Verifier guided skill augmentation lifts CLI success well past the GUI mark. Much of the gap was missing skill coverage, not modality weakness. Zhou's benchmark reframes the GUI versus CLI debate as an execution bottleneck question, and identifies where each interface actually loses its tasks.
arxiv-2606-24651:
Brown and a large DESI team report a first measurement of how non Gaussian the infant universe was. Local primordial non Gaussianity, summarised by one amplitude, would mean the early universe's ripples were not a perfect Gaussian random field. That is a clue to how inflation worked. Earlier measurements used Fourier space statistics; this one works in configuration space, through the two point correlation function of clustered galaxies and quasars.

Simulation-based models handle the statistics. A novel approach reduces imaging systematics, the survey artefacts that mimic clustering. Applied to luminous red galaxies and quasars from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument's first year data. The intervals for the amplitude straddle zero for both tracers, consistent with Gaussian initial conditions within the stated precision. Brown's 2026 result is a methods milestone as much as a cosmology one: these functions, long used for other parameters, now join the toolkit.
arxiv-2606-24851:
Jason Sulskis and Sathya Ravi ask whether neural operators should work in a real or a complex spectral basis. Fourier Neural Operators learn solution maps through convolutions in the complex Fourier domain. Their Hartley Neural Operator is the exact real mirror of the Fourier version. It swaps the Fourier transform for the purely real Hartley transform and learns one real weight per mode.

Both operators share a parameter count at equal width, so only the basis differs. Their thesis: which basis is best is a property of the equation solved. Self adjoint elliptic problems, like Poisson's equation, have real symmetric Green functions that the Hartley multiplier diagonalises exactly. Time dependent problems carry phase, through oscillation or transport, which a real diagonal multiplier cannot express. Sulskis and Ravi train both models identically, so accuracy gaps trace to the basis alone. The heat equation sits at the borderline between the two regimes.
arxiv-2606-24951:
Ali Elgindi describes the possible shapes of holomorphic hulls for compact three dimensional manifolds embedded in complex three space. At special points called complex tangents, the manifold's tangent space contains a complex line. Those points generically form a link inside the manifold. A number at each such point, the Bishop invariant, decides the local hull behaviour. The present paper reads off the hull structures that result.

Three regimes appear. At elliptic points, where the invariant is below one half, analytic discs fill a Levi flat hypersurface in the hull. At hyperbolic points, above one half, no local hull structure is added. Parabolic points, exactly at one half, are delicate: they may grow a layered onion structure of the kind Jöricke described. Explicit examples with parabolic knots and links, including mixed components, illustrate the phenomena. The classification is governed entirely by that one invariant along the link.
arxiv-2606-25251:
A kagome metal, built on a lattice of corner sharing triangles, may hide tiny circulating currents that break time reversal symmetry. Feng and colleagues test that idea in the charge ordered material CsV3Sb5 using nuclear magnetic resonance and quadrupole resonance, which sense very small internal magnetic fields. Their single crystal measurements, reported in 2026, focus on vanadium and antimony sites. Below about forty five kelvin something changes in the resonance lines.

The vanadium line broadens in a way that does not depend on the applied field, pointing to an internal field at the vanadium site. The team attributes it to a static loop current state with small orbital moments. Their analysis also finds the pattern breaks the lattice's sixfold rotation symmetry down to twofold, tying the hidden magnetism to electronic nematicity in the charge ordered phase.
arxiv-2606-25551:
Exotic particles made of four quarks would stretch the hadron catalogue, and one hidden charm strange candidate carries quantum numbers no ordinary meson can have. Bing-Dong Wan, Jun-Hao Zhang, Yan Zhang, and Ming-Yang Yuan probe its inner structure in 2026 with QCD sum rules, keeping the strange quark's mass and condensates explicit throughout. Two families of colour octet currents compete as candidate descriptions. Swapping light quarks for strange ones then acts as a controlled structural test rather than a mere mass shift.

The strange sector spectrum stayed orderly, but the induced shifts grouped by current family instead of spreading evenly. One family barely moved while the other shifted strongly, toward the threshold of a known meson pair. The authors read that contrast as a fingerprint: flavour breaking can discriminate which internal arrangement a future observed state actually uses.
arxiv-2606-25651:
A single wrong word in a clinical note can endanger a patient, and language models now write and edit such notes at scale. Congbo Ma, Hu Wang, Yichun Zhang, and Farah Shamout build MedGuards in 2026, a team of specialised model agents that police medical text without any extra training. One agent detects that an error exists, another localises it, and a third corrects it. When the agents disagree, a confidence guided arbiter weighs their reasoning traces and scores to settle the call.

A new scoring metric rewards getting the critical keywords right, not just overall similarity to a reference. Across four multilingual datasets of clinical notes, the framework improved error detection and correction over single model and heuristic baselines for several base models. The authors release their code and aim the system at safer hospital deployment of language models.
arxiv-2606-25851:
Jindong Zhao and Haiyan Zhu work in cluster algebra, a branch of algebra where structures mutate step by step between related configurations called seeds. Each cluster algebra has a group of automorphisms, symmetries that map the algebra to itself while respecting its mutation rules. Finding generators for that group is easy in small cases but explodes combinatorially as the rank grows.

Improving the marked-vertex strategy of Fu and Liang gives Zhao and Zhu an effective algorithm for the job. Their method computes all mutation paths systematically and extracts the generator elements of the automorphism group from them. Running the algorithm on cluster algebras of finite mutation type and rank four, a case that had resisted manual treatment, produces the generating sets. The result turns a previously hand-checked computation into a repeatable procedure for these algebras.
arxiv-2606-25951:
ShivaSankar, Souvik Das, Arindam Das, and Sanjoy Mandal look for shy particles at a collider that does not exist yet. The proposed Future Circular Collider would smash protons at one hundred tera-electronvolts. Its Forward Physics Facility would sit far downstream, catching long-lived particles that fly forward. The targets are heavy neutrinos and a new force carrier, the Z prime boson. Both arise in models that extend the Standard Model with an extra U(1) gauge symmetry.

Production routes through meson decays and proton bremsstrahlung anchor the study. Some Z prime bosons decay visibly. Others decay into pairs of heavy neutrinos. Still others decay promptly into single long-lived neutrinos. Event rates are computed for realistic detector layouts and decay chances. Projected limits cover heavy neutrino mass and mixing, plus Z prime mass and coupling. The forward facility would extend discovery reach well past current and planned experiments.
arxiv-2606-26251:
Wan-Zhe Feng, Zong-Huan Ye, and Zi-Hui Zhang teach a reinforcement learning agent to hunt gravitational wave signals. Early-universe first-order phase transitions can ring spacetime, and supercooled ones ring loudest. Detector-worthy signals hide in a tiny corner of each model's parameter space. Random scanning wastes nearly all its effort elsewhere. Their environment maps model parameters to phase transition and wave observables, inside a minimal dark sector model with its own U(1) force.

Reward design steers the search. Several schemes push the agent toward large amplitudes, broad frequency coverage, and detector-sensitive points. Against conventional Monte Carlo scans, the Proximal Policy Optimization agent finds the good regions far more efficiently, in both narrow and broad scan windows. Goal-directed learning beats blind sampling for this kind of phenomenology. The framework should transfer to other high-dimensional hunting grounds in particle physics and cosmology.
arxiv-2606-26351:
Siqi Wei, David Kepplinger, and Anand Vidyashankar build robust estimates of polychoric correlation for surveys with complex sampling designs. The measure captures how strongly two survey items move together when answers come in ordered categories. Ordinary fitting treats every response as equally trustworthy. Careless answers and interviewer effects can then distort the result.

Two distance measures replace the standard fit. One uses the Hellinger distance, with ridge and lasso penalties added. The other uses a negative exponential disparity. Simulations under three kinds of planted contamination show a split verdict. The penalized Hellinger methods have the smallest error when bad answers pile up in matching corners. The disparity method wins when contamination mixes corners or combines with model error. Guidelines help users choose by the pattern they expect.
arxiv-2606-26651:
Yifeng Teng and Yifan Wang study whether anonymous pricing for online resource allocation can be learned from samples. A seller receives requests over time from different agents. Supplies of several resource types are limited, and arrival order is unknown. The goal is to maximise total welfare. A well-known dynamic pricing method adapts prices per agent, raising fairness concerns, and needs the arrival order in advance.

Anonymous pricing charges everyone the same price vector. The authors show the classic dual pricing method can be learned from a modest number of samples. They also show a near-optimal anonymous algorithm can be learned from a modest number of pricing queries. Neither approach needs to know who arrives when. The results give sample-based foundations for fair, uniform pricing in online allocation.
arxiv-2606-27251:
Shi and colleagues present OmniAct, a framework for embodied agents that must keep working in messy real settings for long stretches. Earlier systems split those worlds, let context grow without bound, and ran robot policies blind to their own failures. OmniAct instead separates planning, memory, and verification inside a layered, asynchronous design. A multimodal semantic planner routes skills across one unified action space, in a framework paper published in 2026.

Layered memory compresses at event boundaries, keeping context growth sub-linear over very long interactions. An asynchronous visual preemption engine watches execution and closes the loop when physical actions go wrong. Forty real-world long-horizon tasks on two robot platforms, coordinating four smart devices, test the system. Success improves at every complexity level. Token use stays nearly flat past one hundred thousand accumulated interaction tokens. Mid-scale open models reach proprietary-level performance under the framework.
arxiv-2606-27351:
Kachkachi computes how strongly single-domain nanomagnets absorb microwave energy, a quantity called the specific absorption rate. Such particles matter for magnetic hyperthermia, where alternating fields heat tissue through the particles. Two standard tools exist: the stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, which tracks thermal noise explicitly, and linear response theory, which assumes small signals. In the 2026 nanomagnetism paper, whether the two agree, and where they part, had not been pinned down cleanly.

Both methods are proven equivalent at small field amplitude, so the cheaper linear theory is safe in that regime. Their deviation is governed by a single dimensionless product combining drive frequency and the particle's relaxation time. Below resonance, linear response overestimates the absorbed power. Above resonance the error flips sign and can reach an underestimate of up to about seventy percent in the reported analysis. Practitioners get a clear map of when each method can be trusted.
arxiv-2606-27451:
Farley and Ekim study paths that cross a graph the long way without touching each other at all. A diametral path joins two vertices at maximum possible distance, the graph's diameter. Totally disjoint such paths share no vertices, not even endpoints, modelling independent worst-case routes through a network, in a graph theory paper published in 2026. Deciding whether a graph holds a given number of them is proven NP-complete, so no efficient general algorithm is expected.

A linear-time algorithm handles a subclass of maximal outerplanar graphs called two-paths. Threshold graphs admit a polynomial-time algorithm, and proper interval graphs get a structural bound on the count. Extremal graphs achieving given numbers of disjoint diametral paths with the fewest possible edges are characterised. Hardness and tractability are mapped side by side. Network designers learn where redundant long-haul routing is computable.
arxiv-2606-28151:
Jounghun Lee reports a discovery in 2026 about dark energy and cosmic voids. Halos sitting on void surfaces tend to align perpendicular to the direction toward the void centre. Lee asks whether dark energy changes that alignment strength. Halo catalogs from the AbacusSummit suite cover ten cosmologies. They share the same initial conditions and differ only in the dark energy equation of state. Voids are found at low redshift, and halo shape axes are compared with void-centre directions.

Faster-accelerating cases show stronger perpendicular alignments. Spurious signals from differing halo mass and shape distributions are eliminated first. The net dark energy effect is then clear. A single parameter quantifies alignment strength. It is higher when dark energy's pressure is more negative and changes faster. A bilinear model captures the difference from the cosmological-constant case using two universal coefficients. The alignment thus becomes a potential dark energy probe.
arxiv-2606-28651:
Kevin O’Bryant, writing alone, measures how thick an infinite Sidon set can be. A Sidon set of nonnegative integers has the austere property that every positive difference arises from at most one pair of its elements. Allowing up to a fixed number of pairs per difference generalizes this to what he calls a gamma-Golomb ruler, named for rulers whose marks measure every distance once.

O’Bryant proves a two-sided story about density. For any ruler, he bounds the count of elements below n along a subsequence. It cannot outgrow the square root of gamma times the square root of n over log n, up to an explicit constant. In the other direction, he constructs a ruler whose count infinitely often reaches a constant times the square root of gamma times the square root of n. That shows the scale of the upper bound is truly attainable.
arxiv-2606-28851:
Putland traces the long life of the cathetus rule, an ancient claim in optics about where an image appears after reflection or refraction. The rule says the image of a point lies on the perpendicular dropped from that point to the surface. Euclid stated it for mirrors. Ptolemy extended it to refraction, and medieval writers upheld it. Valid proofs covering other lines of sight arrived only in 1585 with Benedetti. He also produced the first counterexamples.

Kepler's systematic treatise soon overshadowed Benedetti, improving the counterexamples and rescuing the rule under symmetry conditions, and Kepler took the credit until scholarship restored Benedetti's priority in 2018. Later figures kept narrowing the rule's domain: Barrow demolished it for one image type outside a narrow limit, while Newton salvaged it for another. Putland argues the rule survives inside modern first-order lens analysis. Its hidden assumption fills a real gap in tracing rays through spherical surfaces.
arxiv-2606-29251:
Lee and a large team of colleagues study how language-model summaries can quietly change financial decisions. Decision-makers cannot read everything, so models compress filings and earnings calls. The team frames the risk as information fidelity. A compressed text loses fidelity when the decision it supports differs from the one the original source supports. Fluent, plausible summaries, they find, can still do exactly that.

Two failure patterns stand out. In decontextualization, key evidence survives but loses the caveats that qualify it. In model dependency, each compressor exposes a different view of the same source. Their proposed system, Agentic Context Compression, generates several candidate compressions and audits where they disagree against the original. The authors argue financial compression should be judged not just on speed or factual accuracy, but on whether it preserves the context a decision depends on.
arxiv-2606-29651:
Tauhidi, Karmakar, Mai, and Vandierendonck present NI-ORCA, a parallel algorithm that counts the orbits of non-induced graphlets in a network. Graphlets are small subgraph patterns, and a vertex's orbit records its structural role inside those patterns. Existing algorithms handle induced graphlets efficiently, but many applications need non-induced counts, where extra edges may be present.

NI-ORCA extends the ORCA framework by reformulating a system of linear equations for the non-induced case, covering graphlets up to size four. Three stages structure the computation: triangle counting, four-clique enumeration, and orbit solving. Stage-specific parallel strategies use thread and vertex-local memory to balance workload. Experiments on eight real-world datasets and on synthetic Erdős-Rényi graphs follow. A mixed mode with dynamic scheduling delivers consistent speedup, up to thirty times faster than sequential algorithms.
arxiv-2606-29951:
Hammer and three colleagues improve Interpretable Mesomorphic Neural Networks, models that pair a deep network's predictive power with a linear model's readable explanations. In the original design nothing stops the network from dumping all explanatory weight onto one output weight, making the explanation meaningless.

The proposed Local Fidelity Regularization penalises this collapse by tying the linear output weights to local variations in the data, which structurally guarantees faithful explanations. Counter to the usual trade-off, tests across the OpenML benchmark suite show the regularised model also improves AUROC, an accuracy ranking measure, over the unregularised network and rivals leading black-box models. The authors release the code publicly.
arxiv-2606-30251:
Mingkuan Feng and seven colleagues teach tool-using AI agents to call their tools only when the tools actually help. Agentic models operate on images with code, then reason over the changed view. A crop can fix an answer, waste effort, or flip a right answer wrong. Outcome-only rewards cannot tell those cases apart. Their method, TACO, assigns credit to each tool call individually.

Two coupled channels carry the training signal in TACO. Probe tokens ask the model for predictions with and without each tool call. The difference in outcome becomes that call's own advantage score. No external judge is needed, and differencing resists probe hacking. A second, parameter-free routing rule delivers final-answer credit only to responsible segments. Calls that waste effort are quietly suppressed by the routing. Across perception, reasoning, and general benchmarks, accuracy gains are consistent.
arxiv-2606-30651:
Xinyu Qin, Vicky Ye, Ruiheng Yu and Lu Wang ask whether doctors' judgment can sharpen machine learning that flags delirium. Delirium, sudden confusion in hospital patients, is common yet often missed in routine care. The team built a user-centred interactive framework: physicians guide which features the model uses, and the model itself stays interpretable, so its reasoning can be checked.

Their data covered nearly thirty-nine hundred labelled admissions from six Toronto hospitals in the GEMINI initiative. Inputs mixed administrative records, lab results, medications and a text indicator drawn from radiology reports. SHAP values, which credit each input's role, summarised the model's reasoning. Against automated and baseline variants, the physician-guided framework discriminated better overall. It also held up more strongly over time, on both a time-separated holdout and a later validation cohort, and its explanations highlighted signals clinicians found meaningful.
arxiv-2606-30851:
Mattia Tritto and six colleagues test whether a learned verifier can pick the best SQL query a language model writes. Text-to-SQL systems often generate several candidate queries, and common selection rules rely on weak signals like whether the query runs or how often it appears. The team instead train Outcome Reward Models, scorers that judge a candidate's likely correctness from its meaning. Their GradeSQL framework generates candidates and labels them by execution, so no manual annotation is needed.

On the BIRD and Spider benchmarks, across several open model families, verifier-based selection beat execution-based selection and majority voting. Gains reached +4.33% on BIRD and +2.10% on Spider. Verifiers scaled well with larger candidate sets and helped most on complex queries.
arxiv-2606-31851:
Levchenko and Levitov propose a direct electrical signature of chiral superconductivity, a pairing state that breaks time-reversal symmetry. Probes of unconventional superconductivity are usually indirect. A superconductor also hides its own Hall response, because the condensate short-circuits quasiparticle currents in the direct-current limit.

Their setup adds a normal metal layer beside the superconductor. Coulomb drag between the layers drives quasiparticles in the superconductor, while a counterflowing supercurrent keeps its net current at zero. Berry curvature in the quasiparticle bands bends that current sideways. This gives a Hall voltage in the normal layer. The signal switches on at once below the critical temperature. Its sign reports the winding direction of the order parameter.
arxiv-2608-00451:
Peng studies when learnable latent structure can also be recovered in efficient time. An unknown support set in F_2^n has small additive doubling. It is observed through a fixed set that differs from it by a bounded share. The goal is one linear subspace whose few cosets cover every compatible support. Membership queries may change what is achievable.

For any noise share below one, polynomially many uniform samples suffice statistically. The cost grows with the doubling constant and the inverse noise gap, sharply. Under a search-LPN hardness assumption, no polynomial-time sample-only learner reaches even constant covering cost. Adding exact membership queries permits polynomial-time recovery at the same budget. A short structural list plus majority-coverage selection drives the query learner. At doubling one, a threshold at one third splits coarse from exact recovery.
belon-estranges-poissons-marins-1551:
Pierre Belon, a French naturalist, published his book on strange marine fishes in 1551. The French title promises the natural history of strange sea fishes, with true portraiture drawn from life. Belon traveled widely and drew many creatures from his own seeing, a new standard for his age.

Dolphins and whales receive careful, pictured treatment in his pages. Sea monsters appear too, but Belon tests report against the knife and the eye more than most. His pictures aim at accuracy over ornament. The book helped turn Renaissance natural history toward observation. Readers watch science learning to look closely at the wonders of the sea.
boscobel-or-the-royal-oak-a-tale-of-the-:
William Harrison Ainsworth wrote Boscobel, or The Royal Oak, a tale of the year 1651, first issued in 1872. Ainsworth takes Charles the Second's flight after Worcester as his plot. Cowley's verses on the Boscobel grove stand at the front of the tale.

Book one musters the king's army, his entry into Worcester, and the counsel of his lords. Defeat scatters the court, and Charles hides with Careless in the oak, dicing with acorn dice while hunters pass below. Jane Lane and the Penderels guide the king toward the coast in the later books. Ainsworth loads the tale with real names, places, and dates. The Royal Oak became a national symbol through retellings like his, half history and half romance.
brown-essays-on-characteristics-1751:
John Brown's Essays on the Characteristics appeared in 1751, aimed at the Earl of Shaftesbury, the most polished thinker of the age. Shaftesbury's Characteristics had taught that taste and good humor could ground morals without revealed religion. Brown, a young clergyman, judged that teaching a danger to faith and public virtue.

The essays charge that Shaftesbury's easy deism saps the roots of both religion and morals. Brown answers wit with argument, testing the earl's claims about virtue, ridicule, and human nature. The orthodox reply made its author famous almost overnight and drew him into print wars with other defenders of Shaftesbury. The book captures a key Enlightenment quarrel: whether manners and taste alone can hold a society together.
caesarius-heisterbach-dialogus-miraculor:
Caesarius of Heisterbach, a Cistercian monk, wrote his Dialogus miraculorum around 1223. Twelve Latin books hold talks between a monk and a novice, stuffed with tales. Demons, visions, and marvels crowd every chapter, told to teach the young monk how the spiritual world works.

Preachers mined the book for centuries, since each tale makes a neat sermon point. Devils tempt, saints rescue, and sinners meet fitting ends. The dialogue frame keeps the lessons lively and plain. This text follows the edition of 1851. Caesarius preserves the most quoted story-hoard of the medieval supernatural, a window on what monks believed, feared, and laughed at.
caught-in-the-net-pg2451:
Émile Gaboriau, the French founder of the detective novel, set Caught in the Net in a freezing Paris winter at the Hôtel de Pérou. The hotel shelters the shipwrecked of city life, and among its lodgers are little Rose, the old schemer Daddy Tantaine, and Paul Violaine, a young man with a past. Around such lodgers a net of blackmail, old crimes, and quiet threats begins to tighten.

Gaboriau mixes police work with melodrama: shabby rooms, coded loyalties, and a criminal association that profits from other people's secrets. The Lecoq novels made his name, and this story shares their world of patient investigation against hidden money and power. It reads as both crime puzzle and portrait of Paris poverty.
chambers-papers-for-the-people-vol-9-185:
William and Robert Chambers published the ninth volume of their Papers for the People at Edinburgh in 1851, cheap improving essays for general readers. Contents mix art, science, history, and tales: recent decorative art, alchemy and the alchemists, a tale of the forty-five, German ports and poetry, and the deserts of Africa.

The decorative art paper argues that beauty begins in useful things — a teapot or a cotton gown can be a work of art. The Africa paper maps oases along the road from Morocco to Timbuctoo, naming El-Harib and Tafilet as resting places. Electric communications and a biography round out the volume. The scan is rough, with many misread letters, but the essays stay followable.
cia-0000008651:
Death and capture struck two Americans from a US Navy plane downed in Yen Hung district, a January 1975 report records. Yen Hung lies in Quang Ninh province, in North Vietnam's northeast corner. By 1975, American combat operations had been over for two years.

Late reports like this one reached back to losses that the war's end had left unresolved. One man dead and one captured, if confirmed, split a case file into grief and continued searching. The entry shows the accounting still active in the war's final year. Its facts came through channels that kept working after the shooting stopped.
cia-0000009451:
Francis Gary Powers and the board of inquiry into his case form the subject of an untitled CIA report from January 1962. Powers piloted the U-2 spy plane shot down over the Soviet Union in May 1960. His capture and trial in Moscow caused a worldwide crisis.

A board of inquiry meant the agency examining its own man's conduct and its own decisions. Had Powers followed orders? Could the flight have been avoided? Weeks after this report, Powers came home in a prisoner swap. The file preserves the agency's self-examination at the height of the Cold War's most famous spy case.
cia-0000012251:
Bonn's course between Washington and Paris was the puzzle in a CIA paper from March 1965 on West German foreign policy. Chancellor Ludwig Erhard led a state that owed its safety to the American alliance. Yet France's de Gaulle courted Bonn toward a more independent Europe, and the pull ran both ways.

The paper weighs Erhard's compass: Atlantic loyalty against French invitations. It also judges Bonn's stance toward the Soviet bloc and the divided Germany it claimed to speak for. The study shows the Federal Republic's diplomacy at a crossroads, read closely by the ally it could not leave.
cia-0000013851: Wounded American troops had to be lifted off the battlefield, and a CIA note dated May 5, 1967, covers that work. Getting hurt men out fast was a hard, risky task in Vietnam. Rescue teams faced fire, bad weather, and rough ground. The note preserves a small piece of the war's rescue effort, seen from the files of the time.
cia-0000015251: An unidentified flying object was seen on the Iran and USSR border, in a CIA report dated July 2, 1957. Border sightings drew extra care, since no side owned the sky there. A light or craft over a tense line could mean a probe, a plane, or a mistake. The report files the sighting for the watch on Soviet skies.
cia-0000015351: Names of outside experts tapped as consultants for an advisory panel on unidentified flying objects fill a CIA item dated January 5, 1953. The panel was being formed as saucer reports pressed in from across the country. Scientists lent their names and judgment to a subject many colleagues scorned. Who agreed to serve mattered, since the panel's standing would shape how its findings were received.
cia-0000022651: Two American prisoners of war were sighted in Tan Uyen District, in Bien Hoa Province, a CIA record dated in 1972 reports. Bien Hoa, northeast of Saigon, held a major American air base in war years. A sighting so close to old friendly ground stung the men who kept the lists. It was checked like all the rest, name by name.
cia-0000023651: Allende's election is the whole subject of a CIA document dated in 1970. Salvador Allende won Chile's presidency that September, the first Marxist to do so by vote in the region. Washington watched the result with deep alarm, as other Chile files of the time show. A document titled this plainly holds the first draft of a crisis that ran for years.
cia-0000036851:
An FBIS dispatch dated September 2, 1967 notes McCain as one of many pilots downed over Hanoi. It adds that he came from the carrier Oriskany, which flew strikes off Vietnam. The dispatch places one famous loss inside the much larger air war.

Readers see the pilot's capture framed by numbers: many planes, many men, one city. That framing is itself evidence of how the air war's cost was reported. The file keeps both the man and the scale of the campaign that brought him down. Carrier pilots flew again and again over the same defended city, and the losses mounted month by month.
cia-0000037151:
Claimed sightings of American personnel still missing in action in Laos fill a CIA record dated June 4, 1982. The sightings look back to the period from 1969 onward, when the war in Laos was at its height. Laos held many missing men whose fates were never settled during the war.

The record gathers the claims so they can be weighed together rather than one by one. Grouped sightings sometimes lined up into a pattern, and sometimes fell apart under checking. Either way, the file shows the Laos cases still open and active more than a decade after the fighting there had ended.
cia-0000044451:
A Jesuit leader spoke on the killing of the priests, in a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. The leader spoke for the order that had lost six of its own. His words carried grief and authority in equal measure that autumn.

Inside, the order's public answer to the murders is preserved. The Jesuits had served El Salvador's poor and its university for years. Their leader had to mourn his brothers and answer for their work. The file holds that double task in his own words, at the moment when the order's loss was newest and its future in the country least sure.
cia-0000045251:
Further word on Rey Prendes's September 25 news conference fills a CIA record dated August 5, 1985 in the catalog. The catalog date sits oddly before the conference it names. Follow-up items chased a hard-liner's public performance that autumn.

Inside, more of the right-wing leader's case is set down. News conferences by men like Rey Prendes were aimed at Duarte. They warned him, in public, against softness toward the rebels. The file preserves the follow-up echoes of that warning, part of the pressure that hemmed the president in while he bargained for his daughter's life.
cia-0000049051: Salvadoran armed forces officers gave their views on the possible arrest of a lieutenant in a CIA item from 1983. Arresting one of their own was the test the officer corps resisted most, and their reactions map that resistance. The item survives among the records later gathered for the Truth Commission.
cia-0000049151: New developments in the investigation of the Jesuit murders fill a partly blacked-out CIA item from 1990. The case against the soldiers who killed six priests moved in public steps and private ones, and the blacked-out lines hide the private half. The item survives in the Truth Commission files.
cia-0000049251: A government investigation of killings in El Salvador is the subject of a CIA item from 1989, kept with the Truth Commission records. When the state investigated its own war's killings, the first question was always whether the probe was real. The item preserves the investigation as officials described it at the time.
cia-0000102951: Soviet bauxite mining in Severouralsk is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000102951, dated January 5, 1985. Bauxite is the ore used to make aluminum, so its output mattered for judging Soviet industry. The brief record keeps the focus narrow: one mining town, one raw material, and one dated report. It sits among many similar site reports in the files.
cia-0000107451: Turkish Interests in Syrian Territory; Impact of Communism is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000107451, dated January 2, 1949. The title pairs two topics: Turkey's interests in Syrian land, and the impact of communism there. A semicolon joins them in one short heading. The brief record is a two-topic item from the early Cold War in the Middle East.
cia-0000112351: Barbadians Report Several Ufo Sightings is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112351, dated August 3, 1987. The title reports several UFO sightings by Barbadians, people of Barbados. Several, not one, is the count word in the heading itself. The brief record is a sightings item from the Caribbean, filed in the summer of 1987 as released in the files.
cia-0000115451: Cuban Policy Toward Latin America: National Intelligence Estimate Volume Ii -- is the heading, ending with dashes, on declassified CIA document 0000115451, dated June 2, 1981. The title marks the second volume of a formal estimate on Cuban policy toward Latin America. Volume two signals a fuller treatment, in the heading itself. The brief record is an estimate volume from 1981.
cia-0000118651: Dated February 1, 1968, declassified CIA document 0000118651 lists topics tied to President Thieu: a possible coup, conditions in the Delta, and a third topic. Its heading misspells concern as Conern and breaks off at the word Sup. The first two topics are named in full in the heading itself there. The brief record preserves the misspelling and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000119751: Current as of 5 p.m. on November 6, 1956, this CIA report gives the Hungarian situation two days into the Soviet crackdown. Organized resistance was failing across the country. The report records the revolution's closing hours as the agency received them. Fighting still flared in places, but the report's hour fell after the outcome was settled, when Soviet power had plainly carried the country.
cia-0000132651:
The growth of Cuba's armed forces fills a CIA paper dated January 4, 1961. Three months before the Bay of Pigs landing, the island was arming fast. Weapons from the Soviet bloc were arriving by the shipload through that winter.

The paper measures the buildup in men, guns, and new units. Such counts shaped the plans of the exile force then training for the invasion. For readers, the entry shows the military balance as the agency saw it in the new year. Both sides were racing, and the paper records one side of that race in detail.
cia-0000132751: A same-day companion to other January 4, 1961 Cuba briefings, this CIA paper reflects the view from just after the diplomatic break. The United States had cut ties with Havana the day before, and the agency filed several papers at once to fix the new baseline. The declassified companion piece survives through the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive.
cia-0000134251: North Korea and Cuba setting up formal ties fill a CIA paper dated August 4, 1960. Pyongyang and Havana made an odd pair on the map of the Cold War. Their friendship would last for decades once the embassies opened. Two revolutions were making their bond official that summer. The short paper notes the step and the statements that went with it.
cia-0000135751: The 2506 Brigade files hold this Spanish-language document under an estimated date of 1 January 1961, flagged as estimated in the catalog title itself. The brigade was the CIA's exile force, then in winter training for Cuba. No subject is recorded for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release. Like other estimated New Year entries in this series, it is best treated as brigade paperwork placed at the year's start by the reviewers.
cia-0000136051: A CIA cable dated 1 February 1954 deals with a request to stick to plans and general conditions, the condition that follows cut off, in files since declassified. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136351: Congratulations from headquarters, received through ASCHAM, are passed down the line in this early July 1954 LINCOLN cable. A great victory has been won in the past forty-eight hours, the message says, made more notable by the extreme difficulties and the odds recognized against success from the outset. The energy and devotion of personnel at LINCOLN and the field stations were truly exceptional. Officers are told to pass the credit to the field, where it was earned.
cia-0000137451:
South Vietnamese Liberation Army Enemy Proselyting Office Handling of Prisoners, dated 1971, is a declassified CIA report from the Vietnam War. Its title names its subject in full: how the enemy's proselyting office, the unit charged with winning over captives, handled prisoners it held. Proselyting here means political persuasion work aimed at prisoners of war.

Reports of this kind served a practical purpose. Knowing how captives were treated, and how they were pressed to change sides, shaped briefings for troops and the care of men who came home. The 1971 date places the report in the war's later years, when American forces were drawing down but prisoners remained a live and painful issue.
cia-0000139451: Remote viewing, the attempt to gather intelligence by claimed psychic sight, fills document 0000139451 from Project SUN STREAK in 1988. The program ran under defense and intelligence sponsorship through the 1980s, with viewers set targets they could not see and their reports scored for hits. Nothing in this record sets it apart from the program's general run of files. Freed with the rest of the SUN STREAK archive, it helps show how far officials once went for an edge.
cia-03003751:
Korea opens a short Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 3 December 1953. Ambassador Dean believes the Communists may be planning to break off the Panmunjom talks. A mutual defence pact is reported as the fruit of talks between Presidents Rhee and Chiang. The summary gives each item a single line.

Bao Dai, in the third item, fears the French may accept Ho Chi Minh's offer. The Tudeh party in Iran reportedly plans demonstrations against Vice President Nixon. His visit to Tehran was then approaching. The file is brief, and much of its body sits behind the summary page. What survives is the day's agenda in outline: armistice talks at risk, an anti-Communist pact forming, and Indochina and Iran both unsettled.
cia-03179151:
Israel's possible course opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 4 March 1956. Ambassador Lawson predicts at minimum an emergency economy with partial mobilisation. At maximum, he allows an offensive against Egypt on a frontier incident's pretext. Even the minimum, he warns, would push Israel toward militancy on water, firing, and Aqaba transit. An approach to Moscow for arms is not excluded.

Algerian nationalists will probably refuse Mollet's cease-fire appeal, since they are winning and want independence, not promises. A Moroccan-French declaration suspends the protectorate treaty. Khrushchev's itinerary for the April visit to Britain worries the Foreign Office, which wants no triumphal tour. Danes are willing to build a merchant ship for the USSR. Indonesia plans an exile government for West Irian. A Soviet aviation mission reaches Afghanistan.
cia-06572351:
Intelligence Brief dated November 1964, from the Directorate of Intelligence's Office of Central Reference, profiles new Chilean government leaders. The brief gives short biographies of men entering office in Chile at that time. Most names and offices sit in pages whose scan is badly garbled, so only the legible entries can be grounded.

One full entry covers Bernardo Leighton Guzman. It states he was born 16 August 1909 and graduated as a lawyer from Catholic University in 1933, where he later taught philosophy of law. He had led the Conservative Youth and helped found the National Falange, forerunner of the Christian Democratic Party. The entry lists him as Minister of Labor at age 27 under Arturo Alessandri, and later as Minister of Education from 1950 to 1952 and a national deputy.
cia-06667951:
Security file on Paul Scott closes with a report of investigation dated 29 November 1961. A covering memo from the Deputy Director of Security, Investigations and Operational Support, states the case is closed. No further action would be taken unless requested, the memo says. Offices and names throughout are redacted under (b)(3) and (b)(6).

The report synopsis states that Paul James Scott was born 28 April 1921 at Greeley, Nebraska. He had worked as a reporter for Robert S. Allen since 1949. Credit files held favorable information on him, and police records showed only minor traffic violations. A 1951 mercantile agency report, compiled for a bank, gave his Washington address, his wife Jane E., three dependent children, and pay of $5,000 a year. Neighbors are reported to have held him in good regard.
ciruelo-reprobacion-supersticiones-spani:
Pedro Ciruelo, a Spanish theologian of the Salamanca school, published his Reprobación de las supersticiones y hechicerías in 1551. The Spanish work condemns popular superstitions and sorceries with strict, measured theology. It became the classic statement of Spanish demonology and shaped the country's theory of witchcraft for generations.

Ciruelo sorts spells, omens, and healers' charms, judging each against church teaching. Much folk practice fails his test, though his temper is cooler than the northern persecutors'. Churchmen quoted him for a full century after his death. The book helps explain why Spain's witch trials took their own, more legalistic course. Salamanca speaks here in its most careful voice.
curieuse-vollstandige-chymische-schrifft:
German chemical writings ascribed to Geber, king of the Arabs and adept, fill this Vienna book of 1751. Johann Paul Krauss published it, and the title says the text came from an old copy kept in the Vatican Library. Four books treat mercury, sulphur, arsenic, and the metals one by one.

Furnaces, tools, distillation, calcination, and fixing get full coverage. Salts, alum, saltpetre, vitriol, antimony, and cinnabar appear among the wares. Added tracts include a Testament and the Golden Book of the Three Words of Kallid Rachaidibi. The whole aims at the art of turning base metals into silver and gold. Pictures and an index serve the working reader.
europmc-pmc10191851:
Krishna and a large team report that glioblastoma tumors rewire human brain circuits in ways that shorten survival, in a 2023 study. Gliomas are brain tumors that grow into the networks of nerve cells around them. Past work showed that nerve activity feeds tumor growth, and that tumors in turn make nerve cells more excitable.

The team asked whether this rewiring changes how patients fare. They found that tumors which strongly reshape brain circuits are linked to worse survival and poorer thinking skills. The work names brain-tumor crosstalk as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc10248351:
Li and colleagues review inflammation and aging in a 2023 paper, covering signaling pathways and possible interventions. Aging comes with a slow, body-wide rise in inflammation, even without infection. That background inflammation travels with cell aging, immune decline, organ failure, and the diseases of old age.

The review organizes the signals that drive this inflammaging process. It then surveys interventions, from drugs that clear worn-out cells to lifestyle measures. The authors aim to turn a scattered field into a clear map. That map is meant for researchers who seek to slow the harms of aging.
europmc-pmc10477351:
Zhao and co-authors reviewed stromal cells in tumours in 2023, the support cells that frame a cancer's home ground. A tumour's zone holds cancer cells, immune cells, and stromal cells in a shared matrix. Stromal cells can be drawn from nearby healthy tissue. Tumour cells can also turn into stromal-like cells.

These cells feed tumour growth, spread, and drug resistance, Zhao reports. They release growth factors, build new vessels, and reshape the immune tone nearby. Five main kinds get close study, from fibroblasts to fat cells and vessel wall cells. In some settings, though, stromal cells hold a tumour back. That split makes them a tricky but rich drug target.
europmc-pmc10567551:
Sun led the Pharma Proteomics Project report in 2023 on blood proteins in 54,219 UK Biobank members. The project is a shared effort by drug firms and the biobank. It read 2,923 proteins in blood and searched genomes for spots that set each level. Such spots reveal how genes steer the blood's protein mix.

The search found 14,287 main gene links, and 81% were new. Sun also mapped links in people of non-European ancestry. Blood type genes showed long-range effects on gut-linked proteins. The data can test drug targets, such as the cholesterol target PCSK9, on fresh outcomes. All results sit open for any lab to use.
europmc-pmc10766651:
Appelman and co-authors studied muscle harm in long Covid in 2024, centred on crashes after effort. A hallmark of long Covid is post-exertional malaise, a worsening of fatigue and pain after body or mind effort. Its roots have stayed murky. The team ran a case-control study that provoked the crash on purpose.

Muscle build in patients tied to lower exercise capacity, Appelman reports. After the crash was induced, the harm grew worse. Muscle tissue showed strong injury signs and deposits that hold amyloid, a sticky protein. Fuel faults showed in the muscle and in the blood as well. The work maps new paths for grasping the crash state.
europmc-pmc10767851:
Schubach and co-authors released CADD v1.7 in 2024, a tool that scores gene variants for harm. CADD ranks each DNA change by how likely it is to matter for health. Clinics and labs use such ranks to sort finds. The tool has been honed since its first release years ago.

New inputs lift its calls, Schubach reports. They include protein language model scores, gene control forecasts from neural nets, and fresh conservation scores from the Zoonomia project. Tests used disease data banks and 31 deep lab scans of protein changes. Scores for the whole genome sit free on the project site. A web server lets any user score a variant on site.
europmc-pmc11217151:
Smolka and a large team present a faster, sharper tool for finding large genome changes in this 2024 paper. Structural variants are DNA changes of 50 letters or more, and they are hard to call accurately. Long reads remain the most accurate way to spot complex changes. Their tool, Sniffles2, improves the search with repeat-aware clustering and coverage-adaptive filtering.

Sniffles2 ran 11.8 times faster and 29 percent more accurate than leading callers, the authors report. Tests spanned low to high coverage and two sequencing technologies. It also calls variants jointly across families and populations, producing fully genotyped files. In 11 patients it found the causative changes near a key gene, including one allele with three overlapping changes. It even detected mosaic changes, present in only some cells, in brain tissue.
europmc-pmc11369751:
Efthimiou, Seo, Chalkou, Debray, Egger, and Salanti write a step-by-step guide to building clinical prediction models in this 2024 paper. Prediction models forecast a patient's future health from baseline traits and guide medical decisions. Many are published each year, yet evidence shows published studies often carry severe methodological flaws. Those flaws undermine the models' usefulness.

The guide walks through defining the aim and the intended users first. It then covers choosing data sources, handling missing data, and weighing modelling options. Assessing model performance closes the workflow. Steps are illustrated with an example from relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, a disease with flare-ups and remissions. Full R code accompanies the guide. The authors aim to raise the standard of a crowded literature.
europmc-pmc11701551:
Blum and a large team report the 2025 status of InterPro, a protein sequence classification resource, in this paper. InterPro sorts protein sequences into families. It merges predictive models, called signatures, from many member databases to predict domains and key sites in a sequence. Its annotations cover more than 200 million sequences.

Coverage spans UniProtKB, the main protein sequence archive, with links to the Gene Ontology, the European structure bank PDBe, and the AlphaFold structure database. Version 101.0 is detailed, with its website and software. More than 5,000 new entries were created in the past two years. Use of AlphaFold-predicted structures grew, and AI now helps write family descriptions. The site gives access to 85 member collections.
europmc-pmc1180851:
Durán and co-authors described in 2005 how a common fungus can make tiny silver particles. The fungus is Fusarium oxysporum, a microbe found in soil and plants. When silver ions in water meet the fungus, the ions change form. Solid silver particles then appear outside the fungal cells.

Those particles measured about 20 to 50 nanometers across. A nanometer is one billionth of a meter. Durán points to an enzyme and to small shuttle molecules as the drivers. The method offers a cleaner way to make silver material that can kill bacteria.
europmc-pmc1241351:
Perera and colleagues linked prenatal pollution exposure to birth outcomes in 2003. Inner-city minority families face high rates of poor birth outcomes. They also face more smoke, hydrocarbons, and pesticides. The sample held 263 nonsmoking African-American and Dominican women.

Personal air monitors tracked hydrocarbon exposure during pregnancy. Blood measures captured tobacco smoke and a common pesticide. Among African-American mothers, high hydrocarbon exposure tied to lower birth weight. It also tied to smaller head size at birth. The pesticide measure tied to lower weight and shorter length overall. Perera shows womb exposure can shrink newborns. Most women were tracked with home air samplers and blood tests. Most of the women lived in New York City. Their births took place in city hospitals. Birth weight was the main size check used in the work.
europmc-pmc1413551:
Swollen, active immune cells in the spinal cord may drive harm in two nerve diseases. Yiangou and co-authors checked human spinal cord tissue after death in 2006. They looked at multiple sclerosis, which attacks nerve insulation, and ALS, which kills motor nerve cells. They stained for three proteins tied to inflammation: COX-2, CB2, and P2X7.

Control cords showed few stained cells. Cords from both diseases held far more, with longer arms, in the hurt zones. Yiangou used scans and blots to confirm the rise. The shared pattern hints that calming these cells could help in both diseases.
europmc-pmc1636651:
A simple score can flag fatty liver without an ultrasound. Bedogni and co-authors built the Fatty Liver Index in 2006 from an Italian population study. Fatty liver is the most common liver disease in Western countries. They tested 13 candidate predictors in about 500 people.

Four measures did the job: body mass index, waist size, triglycerides, and one liver enzyme, GGT. The index runs from 0 to 100 with an accuracy of 0.84. Below 30, fatty liver is ruled out; at 60 or above, it is ruled in. Bedogni offers it to target scans and lifestyle advice.
europmc-pmc1660551:
Two gene families take up a tenth of the TB germ's genome, yet their jobs are unknown. Gey van Pittius and co-authors traced their evolution in 2006. The PE and PPE families have been tied to antigen variation and disease.

Their growth links to duplication of the ESAT-6 gene clusters, regions that export potent immune targets. Copies inside those clusters are the families' oldest members. Two repeat subfamilies arose recently, only in the TB complex and close kin. Gey van Pittius mapped all PE and PPE genes across sequenced Mycobacterium genomes, clarifying how this large, mysterious family expanded.
europmc-pmc2130951:
Theobald Smith showed that delaying a calf's first colostrum by a day can plant a lasting kidney disease. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925, from Princeton. The condition is a patchy interstitial nephritis, a spotted kidney, found in calves in their first or later months and tied to invasion by a virulent type of Bacillus coli.

Postponing colostrum feeding twenty-four to thirty-six hours, or withholding it altogether, produces the disease. Where the virulent colon bacillus is present, few calves wholly denied colostrum survive the first week. Among the survivors, the spotted kidney, the scar of colon bacillus blood invasion, is frequently found. Calves fed normally have never shown the spotted kidney, and those killed early have had uniformly sterile kidneys. A day's delay at the very start of life, Smith's calves prove, can be written into the organs months later.
europmc-pmc2131651:
Drury and Philip McMaster asked where fibrinogen comes from, in a 1929 paper at The Rockefeller Institute. Fibrinogen is the blood protein that forms clots. Rabbits had their livers removed by the method Drury reported, and their blood fibrinogen was tracked. In some, part of the fibrin was also removed to test whether the protein can be rebuilt without a liver.

In liverless rabbits the blood fibrinogen fell steadily. After partial defibrination, it fell again after a slight, brief rise. No sign of fibrinogen regeneration without the liver could be secured. The liver is thus the essential source of fibrinogen, the authors conclude, and in all probability the sole one.
europmc-pmc2147051:
Benner and colleagues reported in 2008 that immune responses to altered alpha-synuclein speed brain cell loss in a Parkinson's model. Parkinson's disease kills dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra. Their clumps contain nitrated alpha-synuclein, a protein changed by oxidative damage. The team asked whether that change creates targets for the adaptive immune system. They used mice poisoned with MPTP, a toxin that mimics the disease.

Nitrated protein appeared in neck lymph nodes, where presenting cells ramped up display machinery. MPTP-treated mice made antibodies against normal and nitrated protein.
