Immunising mice with the nitrated fragment produced strong T cell responses specific to the modified form. Mice lacking T and B cells resisted MPTP damage. Transferring those T cells accelerated dopamine neuron loss. Tolerance to the altered protein can thus break and worsen disease.
europmc-pmc2323751:
Red blood cells coated with antibody burst open when complement, a blood protein system, attacks them, and Harry Eagle and George Brewer ask what must happen first. Their 1929 study, opening a series, argues the complement must be captured by the coated cell before any bursting occurs.

Sensitization lays an invisible film of serum protein on the cell, and that film soaks up complement like a sponge. The thicker the film, the more complement is fixed. Block that capture and even abundant active complement does nothing. Salts and acidity shape bursting mainly by shaping capture: single-charge salts block it below 0.02 or above 0.35 molar, while double-charge salts block at much lower strength.
europmc-pmc2360651:
Maggi and co-authors compared two follow-up treatments for high-risk womb cancer in a 2006 randomised trial. The cancer, endometrial carcinoma, grows in the womb lining. After surgery, patients at high risk of return get either radiation or chemotherapy, and no one knew which worked better.

The trial assigned 345 patients to radiation or to a three-drug chemotherapy plan given five times. After a median follow-up of about 95 months, survival was nearly the same in both groups. At seven years, 62% of patients were alive in each group. Radiation delayed cancer returning near the pelvis, while chemotherapy delayed spread to distant sites, but neither trend was strong enough to count as proven. The authors said neither treatment won, and trials combining both were needed.
europmc-pmc2386051:
Oldfield and colleagues examined floppy protein regions as social tools in 2008. Some proteins lack a fixed shape and fold only when they grab a partner, a property called intrinsic disorder. Hub proteins, which bind many partners, may use that flexibility as a net that fits many shapes.

They studied two opposite cases in detail. The tumor guard p53 uses several floppy regions, and single regions of it can bind many different partners. The protein 14-3-3 is the reverse: rigid itself, but it binds many floppy partners. Structures of their complexes showed both tricks at work: disordered regions moulding to fit, and even firm regions reshaping slightly on contact, called induced fit. The authors said disorder gives hub proteins their binding range, with induced fit fine-tuning each grip.
europmc-pmc2429951:
Genton and co-authors followed malaria cases at two rural health centres in Papua New Guinea in 2008. Severe malaria was classically blamed on one parasite species, falciparum, while vivax was thought mild. Some hints even suggested mixed infections protect patients, and this eight-year surveillance tested those beliefs.

Of 17,201 suspected cases, 9,537 had confirmed parasites in their blood. About 6.2% of confirmed cases met the World Health Organization definition of severe malaria, most of them children under five. In that age group, severe disease struck 11.7% of falciparum cases, 8.8% of vivax cases, and 17.3% of mixed infections, so mixing gave no protection. Vivax cases showed breathing distress more often than falciparum cases, at 60% versus 41%, but anaemia less often. The authors warned that falciparum-only programs would miss much severe disease.
europmc-pmc2583951:
Müller and colleagues searched in 2008 for the enzyme that lets wild malaria mosquitoes in Ghana survive pyrethroid insecticides. Resistance threatens the spraying and bednet programmes holding malaria back in Africa. The team measured activity of over 250 detoxification genes in individual mosquitoes from a highly resistant wild population, comparing survivors of insecticide exposure with the rest.

One gene stood out: CYP6P3, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, was produced far more in the survivors. The team then made the enzyme in the lab. It breaks down pyrethroids directly, both the alpha-cyano and non-alpha-cyano types. This was the first proof of something key. A P450 found overactive in wild Anopheles gambiae can actually break down the insecticides. The finding supports simple monitoring tools that watch for this gene's activity.
europmc-pmc2592351:
Fazel, Khosla, Doll, and Geddes systematically reviewed in 2008 how common major mental disorders are among homeless people in Western countries. Over a million people are homeless across Western Europe and North America, yet pooled prevalence figures were lacking. The authors searched for interview-based surveys of unselected homeless samples and combined 29 studies covering 5,684 people in seven countries.

Alcohol dependence was the most common disorder, ranging from 8.1 percent to 58.5 percent across studies, followed by drug dependence at 4.5 percent to 54.2 percent in the samples. Psychotic illness ranged from 2.8 percent to 42.3 percent, with major depression showing similar spread. Estimates varied far more than chance allows, and alcohol dependence had grown more common in recent decades. The authors conclude homeless people carry far higher rates than the general population.
europmc-pmc2621351:
Hastings, Ira, and Lupski proposed in 2009 a mechanism explaining how the genome gains and loses chunks of DNA, creating copy number variation behind many genomic disorders. Their clue came from duplications in Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease. Those events showed three odd features. Most were complex mixtures of duplications, deletions, and inversions. The junctions shared tiny 2 to 5 letter matches, called microhomology. The endpoints clustered near repeated DNA stretches.

Their model, named microhomology-mediated break-induced replication, starts when a DNA copying fork breaks in a stressed cell. The loose strand end latches onto any nearby single strand sharing a few matching letters and restarts copying sloppily, switching templates repeatedly. The result is exactly the complex, scrambled rearrangements observed, and over time this process may even build the repeats themselves.
europmc-pmc2643051:
Yu-Wai-Man and colleagues reviewed in 2009 two inherited eye diseases that damage the optic nerve, the cable carrying signals from eye to brain. Both strike mainly young adults. One, called LHON, follows faults in the DNA of mitochondria, the cell's energy makers. The other, called DOA, usually follows faults in a gene named OPA1, which helps mitochondria work.

In both diseases the cells that die are retinal ganglion cells, whose fibers form the optic nerve. Why these cells suffer most, when the gene faults sit in every cell, remains a key puzzle. The review covers what is known about family patterns, why some carriers stay healthy, and how the damage unfolds. Knowing the weak points, the authors argue, is the first step toward treatments, which are still lacking.
europmc-pmc2656551:
Gaillard and co-authors recorded brain signals in 2009 from inside the skulls of ten patients to find what marks a word becoming conscious. Some words were flashed and then masked, so patients never noticed them. Others were shown clearly. Electrodes placed for medical care let the team watch both kinds of processing directly.

Masked words still stirred activity in several brain areas, but only briefly and locally, like a wave that dies out. Words seen on purpose looked very different. Four signs converged on the same moments. Lasting voltage shifts appeared, strong in the front of the brain. Fast gamma waves rose sharply. Distant areas pulsed in step, and far-apart regions clearly influenced each other. The authors argue these are four windows on a single state: a brain-wide pattern that holds the word in awareness.
europmc-pmc2699551:
Abbas and colleagues used in 2009 a mathematical unmixing technique to read the cell traffic inside blood samples from lupus patients. Lupus is an autoimmune disease with a shifting cast of blood cell changes, which ordinary gene readings blur together. Their method, expression deconvolution, teases a mixed sample's signal apart into the voices of its cell types.

First the team proved the method on real blood and on lab-made mixtures, where it recovered the true proportions. Applied to lupus, it found a broad activation pattern: monocytes, natural killer cells, and helper T cells all expanded and switched on together. These shifts partly explain the disease's famous interferon signature, a gene pattern long observed but unassigned. The patterns tracked how sick patients were and what treatment they received. Cell-level bookkeeping of this kind, the authors argue, turns a blood sample into a census of the disease.
europmc-pmc2703651:
Androutsopoulos, Tsatsakis, and Spandidos reviewed in 2009 the wider roles of CYP1A1, an enzyme that breaks down foreign chemicals in the body. The enzyme sits mostly outside the liver and is switched on by smoke and other pollutants through a sensor called AhR. For years it was known chiefly for turning some chemicals into forms that can cause cancer.

Their review weighs newer proof that CYP1A1 can also clear harmful chemicals and unlock helpful compounds in food that may guard against cancer. AhR also affects cell growth and death, not just chemical breakdown. Whether CYP1A1 helps or harms, they argue, depends on which of these jobs wins out in a given tissue.
europmc-pmc2705351:
Hofvander and co-authors described in 2009 the mental health and daily life of adults with autism spectrum disorders who have normal intelligence. Autism affects social contact and speech and nonverbal cues. Most outcome studies had focused on children or on people with added learning disability, leaving this adult group less known.

They assessed 122 adults seen in clinic, most with Asperger disorder or a related form. Core autism traits were common in all groups, and lifetime mood and anxiety problems were very common too. Few led an independent life, and very few had held a long-term relationship, which shows high support needs in adult life.
europmc-pmc2778451:
Alvarez and Ashraf reviewed in 2010 the role of vitamin D in insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity, the two processes that govern blood sugar. Vitamin D is known for bone health, but evidence hints it also protects the cells that make insulin and the tissues that answer it. They gathered cross-sectional, prospective, and intervention studies on vitamin D and glucose control.

Blood levels of the vitamin D marker ran inversely with insulin resistance in snapshot studies, though direct sensitivity measures are still needed. Reports on insulin secretion conflicted with each other. Prospective studies supported a protective effect of high levels against type 2 diabetes. Trial results were inconsistent overall, likely due to differing populations, study lengths, and supplement forms. They call for trials in people at high risk of both vitamin D deficiency and diabetes.
europmc-pmc2813751:
Liu, Fowler, Smith, and Dalgleish tested in 2010 whether standard chemotherapy can make tumors easier for the immune system to attack. Chemo drugs were long assumed to clash with immune therapy because they also harm immune cells. The team treated tumor cells with three common drugs and watched a display protein called HLA class 1, which flags cells for killing.

The drugs raised HLA display on tumor cells, even where it started low, and killer T cells then destroyed more of them. Blocking HLA erased that gain. Liquid from drug-treated tumors also matured dendritic cells, the scouts that train T cells, and T-cell growth rose. The findings suggest some chemo restores a slice of immune surveillance.
europmc-pmc2876151:
Enserink and Kolodner reviewed in 2010 the targets of Cdk1, the master enzyme that drives cells through division in budding yeast. Cdk1 is a cyclin-dependent kinase, an enzyme switched on by partner proteins called cyclins. A decade of work had pinned down roughly seventy-five proteins it modifies to run the division cycle.

Those targets control copying the DNA, separating the copied chromosomes, switching gene programs, and shaping the dividing cell. Several also guard genome stability, repairing damage and checking that copying finished before division starts. By modifying each target at the right moment, one enzyme sequences the whole cycle in order. The review organizes the target list by job and flags where human cell division uses the same logic.
europmc-pmc2893951:
Kilkenny, Browne, Cuthill, Emerson, and Altman introduced in 2010 the ARRIVE guidelines for reporting animal research, modeled on the checklists that cleaned up clinical trial reports. Reviews had shown that papers routinely omit basic facts, such as how animals were assigned to groups, whether assessors were blinded, and how group sizes were chosen. Without those facts, readers cannot judge a study and funders' money is wasted.

The guidelines list the essential items every animal study report should state, from design and animal details to full statistical methods. They were built with input from scientists, journal editors, and funders, and journals began requiring the checklist at submission. The aim is simple: an animal experiment should be reported completely enough for others to repeat and trust it.
europmc-pmc2910551:
Balistreri, Caruso, and Candore reviewed in 2010 how body fat acts as an endocrine organ whose signals fan chronic inflammation across the body. Fat tissue releases adipokines, hormone-like messengers that reach the liver, vessels, and immune system. In obesity, over a billion people are overweight worldwide and more than three hundred million are obese, the balance of those messengers tips toward inflammation.

The review traces how the pro-inflammatory tilt feeds the diseases that travel with obesity, including insulin resistance, fatty liver, vessel disease, and some cancers. Individual adipokines get full treatment: leptin and adiponectin, the best-known pair, plus newer names from fat-resident immune cells. Understanding fat as a signaling organ reframes obesity treatment from calorie bookkeeping toward calming a body-wide inflammatory state.
europmc-pmc2920551:
Wiese and colleagues reviewed in 2010 saxitoxin and its fifty-seven chemical cousins, the paralytic shellfish toxins that close beaches and poison seafood eaters. The toxins are made by ocean dinoflagellates and by freshwater cyanobacteria during blooms. They block nerve signals, so poisoning can paralyze breathing muscles within hours of a contaminated meal.

The analogs sort into structural classes, from unsulfated to doubly sulfated and greasy variants, each with its own potency. Shellfish, bacteria, and even the human body convert one analog into another, sometimes softening and sometimes sharpening toxicity. Tracing those conversions matters twice over. It predicts how long a harvest stays dangerous. It also hints at detox methods for contaminated shellfish and drinking water. The review maps both active goals.
europmc-pmc2923151:
Dumas and co-authors recorded in 2010 two brains at once to catch the neural signature of people falling into sync during social interaction. Nine pairs of participants took turns imitating each other's hand movements spontaneously, switching leader and follower freely, while dual EEG headsets captured both brains. Interactional synchrony, the smooth mutual adaptation of partners, is the bedrock of conversation and joint play.

When behavioral synchrony peaked, a synchronizing network emerged between the two brains in the alpha-mu rhythm band, linking right centroparietal regions on both sides. The coupling rose and fell with the quality of the interaction rather than with movement alone. Brains literally tune to each other during real exchange, the authors argue, giving social neuroscience a measurable inter-brain phenomenon to study.
europmc-pmc2930851:
Studerus, Gamma, and Vollenweider tested a long-used questionnaire for altered states of consciousness in a 2010 psychometric study. The OAV scale had served researchers for over twenty years, yet its factor structure had never faced strict statistical testing.

Pooling data from forty-three experiments, they covered several hundred sessions involving psilocybin, ketamine, or MDMA. Modern modelling showed the original factor plan fit poorly, and two broad factors could merge at a higher level. The team instead drew out eleven narrower factors and checked how drug type and other causes shaped scores, giving future studies a firmer scale.
europmc-pmc2973851:
Jombart, Devillard, and Balloux introduced a method for uncovering genetic clusters in populations in a 2010 article, designed for the flood of data from fast sequencing. Popular model-based clustering tools strain under huge datasets because they lean on heavy assumptions and computing.

Their method first compresses genetic data into principal components, then seeks the grouping that best separates clusters while keeping members tight. When groups are unknown, a repeated grouping routine proposes them. Tested on simulated data against a leading program, it recovered structure well and also supplies membership scores, visual separation, and which gene variants drive the split.
europmc-pmc2976751:
Liu, Yu, and Edwards developed a statistical shortcut for estimating species family trees from many gene trees in a 2010 article. Gene histories legitimately differ inside a species tree, and the exact best-fit calculation for the standard model turns out not to exist.

Their substitute scores candidate trees with a pseudo-likelihood, an approximation they prove settles on the truth as gene counts grow. Simulations confirm the approach even in a tricky zone where gene trees commonly mislead. Applied to mammals, it recovered the same four major groupings as a rival method, with stronger support values in places.
europmc-pmc2990751:
Hoshida presented nearest template prediction, a method for classifying a single patient's gene activity profile, in a 2010 article. Gene signature tests had stalled before reaching clinics because measurements vary between labs and platforms, and most methods judge batches rather than individuals.

Given only a list of signature genes and one sample, the method assigns a class and computes a confidence score for that call. Tests showed it working across platforms, across species, and with several classes at once, without tuning settings for each dataset. That flexibility targets the practical barriers holding back bedside use.
europmc-pmc3004851:
Charlson and colleagues sequenced airway bacteria from healthy smokers and non-smokers in a 2010 study, asking how smoking reshapes whole microbial communities rather than single species. Smokers suffer more airway infections, for reasons only partly explained.

Samples from both sides of the nose and throat in sixty-two adults yielded hundreds of thousands of gene reads. Community makeup depended mainly on airway site, yet smokers' communities were more diverse and grouped apart from non-smokers'. Several bacterial groups shifted consistently with smoking, and the throat gained anaerobic types tied to gum disease. The work gives a baseline map of the smoker's airway.
europmc-pmc3069751:
Murshudov and coauthors explained in 2011 the principles behind REFMAC5, the program most CCP4 users rely on to refine crystal structures. Refinement adjusts an atomic model until it best matches the measured diffraction data while staying chemically sensible. The program has been a suite staple for years, and this paper gathers its design in one place.

It covers how the program balances data fit against prior knowledge of bond lengths and angles. It also covers handling of disorder and partial occupancy, and treatment of low resolution and twinned data. Restraints drawn from known small molecule chemistry keep models plausible where data are weak. The authors also describe validation checks that flag overfitting. For practicing crystallographers, the paper is the reference for what the program is doing during its many cycles, and why its settings matter.
europmc-pmc3082551:
Braidy, Guillemin, Mansour, Chan-Ling, Poljak, and Grant tracked in 2011 how aging drains a key metabolic cofactor in rat organs, with knock on effects for stress defense. The cofactor, NAD in its charged form, fuels energy chemistry and also feeds enzymes that guard DNA and control aging programs. The team measured it and related markers in heart, lung, liver, and kidney from young and middle aged female rats.

By middle age, cofactor levels and balance had fallen significantly in every organ. Damage markers from oxidation rose in step, total antioxidant capacity fell, and DNA damage tags accumulated. The activity of a longevity linked enzyme that depends on the cofactor dropped, while the power stations of the cells ran weaker across the board. The tight match between DNA damage and cofactor loss suggests keeping levels up may be one key to healthy aging.
europmc-pmc3094351:
O'Donovan and colleagues reported in 2011 on older adults carrying a heavy combined load of two inflammatory signals. Those adults were more likely to have short chromosome caps in their white blood cells. Short caps, called telomeres, mark biological aging, and chronic inflammation is suspected of wearing them down. The team studied nearly two thousand well functioning adults in their seventies in a long running aging study.

People high on either of two inflammation markers had higher odds of short caps. People high on both had higher odds still, beyond either alone, after accounting for many other risk factors. A third common marker, C reactive protein, showed no such link. The authors call this the first large scale evidence tying cumulative inflammation to telomere shortening in older adults. It supports the idea that quiet, long running inflammation helps drive the aging of immune cells.
europmc-pmc3118151:
Jorma Panula and colleagues tracked deaths after hip fracture surgery in older Finns in a 2011 study in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. Hip fractures are the gravest result of falls in old age, and death rates after them are known to be high. The team followed more than four hundred patients aged sixty-five and over and compared them with the general older population.

About a quarter of patients died within a year of surgery, and most had died by the end of follow-up. Death rates ran about three times higher than in the general population, across every major cause, with heart and circulation diseases first, then dementia. Men fared worse than women, notably for chest and cancer deaths. The study shows the fracture marks lasting risk, not a brief crisis.
europmc-pmc3121651:
Jane Achan and colleagues reviewed the place of quinine in malaria care in a 2011 paper in Malaria Journal. The drug, drawn from tree bark used in South America in the sixteen hundreds, was the first chemical cure for an infectious disease. Nearly four centuries on, it remains in use, though newer drugs beat it in several settings.

For severe malaria, injected artesunate should now come first, with quinine as a backup. In pregnancy, especially early on, quinine still plays a central role until safer options exist. For mild illness, combined artemisinin treatments work better, but supply gaps in poor regions make dropping quinine risky. The authors advise fixing supply chains and watching for clashes with HIV and tuberculosis drugs.
europmc-pmc3127851:
Marianne Sinka and colleagues mapped the main malaria-carrying mosquitoes of the Asia-Pacific region in a 2011 paper in Malaria Journal. The region hosts many such species at once, often in look-alike groups with flexible behaviour, which makes control unusually hard. This paper closed a three-part world survey of dominant malaria vectors.

The team combined expert range maps with records gathered from published sources, covering more than ten thousand places across thirty-one countries. Modelled maps were produced for each of nineteen dominant species, alongside plain-language summaries of each species' habits and ecology. The result is a reference intended to sharpen species-specific control and guide further study of mosquito biology in the region where malaria control faces its most tangled vector problem.
europmc-pmc3138751:
Marc Jeschke and colleagues followed severely burned children for three years in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Deep burns trigger sweeping metabolic upheaval, but how long the body stays in that crisis state was unknown. Nearly a thousand children burned over almost a third of their bodies were tracked at a specialist centre and compared with uninjured children.

Resting energy burn, body composition, heart and organ function, and blood markers all stayed clearly abnormal for the full three years. Stress hormones and inflammatory signals also stayed high, showing a prolonged overdrive state rather than a brief reaction. The authors argue care and nutrition support for severe burns must extend far beyond hospital discharge, reshaping follow-up plans for young patients.
europmc-pmc3141051:
Erik Gullberg and colleagues showed that vanishingly weak antibiotics still breed resistant bacteria in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Drug resistance is usually blamed on treatment doses, yet bacteria also meet faint traces of drugs in soil, water, and waste. Using sensitive head-to-head growth contests, the team asked how faint a drug level can still favour resistant strains.

For three major antibiotics, levels hundreds of times below those needed to stop normal bacteria still let resistant ones take over, even when they started rare. Brand-new resistant mutants also arose and were picked out at these low levels. A mathematical model predicts how fast such mutants would sweep a normal population. The results argue that faint environmental drug pollution matters for the resistance crisis.
europmc-pmc3203851:
Jacob Durrant and J. Andrew McCammon reviewed molecular dynamics simulations in drug discovery in this 2011 article in BMC Biology. These simulations track the atoms of a protein and a candidate drug molecule as they move over time. The authors survey the many points in a drug project where such simulations can help.

Simulations can reveal hidden binding pockets that static structures miss, including sites away from the main active site. They can sharpen virtual screening, the computer sifting of huge compound libraries, and they can directly estimate how tightly a molecule will bind. The authors are candid about limits: the calculations are expensive and rely on approximations of physical forces. Even so, with faster computers and better algorithms, they expect simulations to matter more and more.
europmc-pmc3237351:
Shannon Levesque and colleagues examined how diesel exhaust inflames the brain in this 2011 study in Environmental Health Perspectives. Air pollution is linked to brain disease, but the mechanism was unclear. The team exposed rats to diesel exhaust and tested exhaust particles on cell cultures, looking for effects on microglia, the brain's immune cells, and on dopamine neurons.

Inhaled exhaust raised inflammatory markers across most brain regions, with the midbrain responding most strongly, and particles injected into the airway activated microglia near dopamine pathways. In culture, particles alone caused little cytokine output, but they primed microglia so a later bacterial stimulus triggered an exaggerated response that harmed dopamine neurons. A protective signal, fractalkine, softened some of that damage. The findings outline how pollution could stoke neuroinflammation.
europmc-pmc3257651:
Philip Calder reviewed omega-3 fatty acids and inflammation in this 2010 article in Nutrients. The long-chain fats in oily fish influence inflammation through several routes, most of them running through the fatty makeup of cell membranes. Changing that makeup alters membrane fluidity, cell signaling and gene activity, and which lipid messengers a cell produces.

Inflammatory cells are normally rich in the omega-6 fat arachidonic acid, whose messenger products promote inflammation. Eating the omega-3 fats EPA and DHA displaces some of it, and the messengers made from them often act differently, some actively resolving inflammation; these resolvins were a recent discovery. Membrane changes also affect peptide signals such as cytokines and adhesion molecules. Calder concludes the marine omega-3s may serve as treatments for disorders with an inflammatory component.
europmc-pmc3369951:
Schwartz and colleagues reported in 2012 that Staphylococcus aureus, a germ that colonizes skin, builds fibers to hold its biofilms together. Biofilms are sticky surface communities behind many stubborn infections. The fibers turned out to be made of small peptides called phenol soluble modulins.

Lab tests showed the peptides clump into amyloid-like fibers with classic amyloid traits. Mutant germs unable to make them fell apart when enzymes or physical stress attacked the biofilm. Loose peptides scattered biofilms, while the clumped form did the opposite. The switch helps explain how the germ balances holding on and spreading.
europmc-pmc3404651:
Dodson and a team tested hundreds of consumer products in 2012 for chemicals that disrupt hormones or aggravate asthma. Lab and human studies had raised concern, but labels rarely reveal what is inside. They bought more than two hundred products across fifty types, from cosmetics and cleaners to sunscreens and vinyl goods.

Fifty-five target compounds turned up across the samples. Vinyl products held heavy loads of one plastic softener, while fragranced goods and sunscreens carried the widest chemical mixes. Some products swapped well-known problem chemicals for less-studied cousins with similar effects. Many detected chemicals never appeared on labels at all. Smarter shopping can dodge some, the authors say, but fuller labeling is needed.
europmc-pmc3525951:
Microbe communities get knocked around constantly, and Ashley Shade leads a thirteen-author team laying out how to think about their stability in 2012. Their overview defines resistance, how little a community changes under disturbance, and resilience, how fast it recovers, borrowing hard-won lessons from general ecology.

The team reviews studies of short pulse disturbances and long press disturbances across habitats, hunting for general response patterns. Traits of individual microbes, populations, and whole communities that might govern stability come next. They close with systems views powered by meta-omics data. For anyone predicting how soil, gut, or water communities answer drought, antibiotics, or pollution, this is a framework paper.
europmc-pmc3539351:
Short protein chains called peptides are becoming cancer drugs, and Jyothi Thundimadathil surveys the field in this solo 2012 review. The paper covers approved peptide medicines and those in clinical trials, organized by how they attack tumors.

Some peptides kill cancer cells directly. Others act as guided carriers, hauling poisons or radioisotopes to cancer cells while sparing healthy ones. Hormonal peptide therapy is well established in breast and prostate cancers, and peptide vaccines bring extensive clinical data. Combining peptide approaches with each other or with standard treatment is emerging as the route to stronger effects. The review weighs prospects for this targeted strategy against conventional chemotherapy.
europmc-pmc3564751:
Ewout Steyerberg and colleagues wrote the third paper in the PROGRESS series in PLoS Medicine in 2013, on prognostic models. Such models combine several patient measures to predict the risk of a future outcome for one person. Good predictions can guide treatment choices and counseling, yet many published models are built or tested poorly and never reach practice.

Chapters work through the full life of a model: building it, checking how well it performs in new patients, and testing whether using it changes care or outcomes. Worked examples from several disease areas show each stage. The authors press for honest reporting of limits, outside checks before use, and impact studies rather than more untested models. Clinicians and researchers get a shared standard for what a trustworthy prediction tool must prove.
europmc-pmc3574151:
Quentin Geissmann presented a free counting program, OpenCFU, in PLoS ONE in 2013. Biologists often count round objects in photos: cell colonies on agar plates, seeds, eggs, or pollen. Done by hand, the counting is slow and depends on who counts, even though cameras and image software are now cheap. Existing automatic tools had not won wide use, so colonies were still tallied by eye in most labs.

OpenCFU detects circles in still images and video streams and counts them. Its maker reports the program as fast, accurate, and robust, including where colonies touch the background or overlap, with settings the user can tune and a modern, simple interface. The software runs on common systems and costs nothing, with source code open to inspection. For routine colony counting, it offers labs a way to swap tedious manual tallies for repeatable machine counts.
europmc-pmc3660251:
Colon cancer splits into six gene-based kinds, Marisa and a large team report in a 2013 PLoS Medicine study. Stage alone foretells return of the disease poorly, and no gene signature had proven sound. The team profiled gene activity in fresh tumour samples from 750 patients at seven centres, treated between 1987 and 2007. They logged common DNA faults in each tumour.

Six kinds emerged from the patterns. One had broken DNA repair, one a KRAS gene fault, one stem-cell traits, and three unstable chromosomes split by immune and growth signals. The scheme held in a held-back set of 123 samples and in a separate set of 1,058 cases. Outlook differed by kind. The authors offer the six-way sort as a base for sharper outlook models.
europmc-pmc3665851:
Violence at home and mental illness around birth travel together, Howard, Oram, Galley, Trevillion and Feder find in a 2013 systematic review and meta-analysis in PLoS Medicine. The team pooled studies of women in pregnancy and the year after birth, asking how often women with mental disorders had faced domestic violence. Its overlap with illness at this life stage was less clearly sized.

Women with likely depression before birth showed about triple the odds of having faced partner violence over their lives, and about five times the odds of violence during pregnancy itself. Raised odds appeared after birth as well, across depression, anxiety and stress disorders. The pattern ran in cross-section and long-run studies alike. Care around birth should ask about violence and treat the two harms as linked.
europmc-pmc3676851:
Obesity is a state of chronic oxidative stress, Savini, Catani, Evangelista, Gasperi and Avigliano argue in a 2013 review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Oxidative stress, the rust-like strain from reactive oxygen forms, may be the link between obesity and its many complications. Obese patients show lower antioxidant defences than lean peers, and defence levels fall as belly fat rises. Reactive forms run high at the same time, a double tilt of the balance.

Why defences sag is weighed next: poor diets, faster use of defence molecules, and too little activity. The review then sets out plans to restore balance, centred on food choices rich in plant chemicals and vitamins, and on regular physical activity. Each plan is judged by its effect on the body's redox state, the balance point between strain and defence.
europmc-pmc3721551:
Rémi Lemoine and a large group of co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2013 on how sugar moves through a plant. Sugars made in leaves travel through tubes called the phloem to roots, fruits, and other parts that need them. This source-to-sink flow is a major driver of plant growth and crop yield.

The review sums up how the phloem loading and transport system works, then surveys what can disturb it. Dry or salty soil, lack of minerals, heat, cold, and pollution can all shift where sugar goes or damage the tubes themselves. Living threats, from aphids and fungi to viruses and parasitic plants, also divert or block the flow. Recent work has found some of the sugar transport proteins used by both the plant and its attackers.
europmc-pmc3722151:
Jeffery Pettis and co-authors reported a field study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on honey bees hired to pollinate crops. The team collected pollen from hives placed in seven major crops. They asked which pesticides the bees met, and how those chemical mixes affect their odds of catching a gut parasite called Nosema ceranae.

The pollen held 35 different pesticides, with heavy loads of fungicides, which are usually thought to be fairly safe for bees. In most crops the bees had gathered pollen mostly from weeds and wildflowers, not the crop itself. Bees that ate pollen with a higher fungicide load were more likely to be infected with Nosema. Two insecticides also turned up at levels above their known lethal dose in at least one sample.
europmc-pmc3753751:
Bo Wang and Yanli Du wrote a review in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2013 on the neurotoxic effects of cadmium. Cadmium is a heavy metal of concern at work and in the environment. The body clears it slowly, so it builds up over time in the kidneys, liver, and nervous system.

Cadmium can reach the brain through the nose and smell pathways, and it can loosen the blood-brain barrier that normally guards the brain. How it harms nerve cells is not fully settled. The review weighs candidate mechanisms, including effects on nerve signal chemicals, oxidative damage, interplay with metals such as zinc and cobalt, hormone-like action, and epigenetic changes. The authors conclude that lab and animal evidence links cadmium to both chemical and functional changes in the central nervous system.
europmc-pmc3762851:
Souhaila Bouatra and a large group of co-authors reported a full chemical census of human urine in PLoS ONE in 2013. Urine is easy to collect in large amounts and rich in breakdown products from food, drugs, and the body itself, but that richness made it hard to catalog. The team combined a literature search with direct measurement on several platforms.

Their experiments identified 445 urine metabolites and measured 378 of them. Nuclear magnetic resonance alone found 209, and each other platform added its own share. The literature review added 2,206 more compounds, giving a database of 2,651 confirmed urine metabolite species with structures, concentration ranges, and disease links. The free online database is meant as a reference for the field.
europmc-pmc3812051:
Geir Kjetil Sandve, Anton Nekrutenko, James Taylor, Eivind Hovig, and Philip E. Bourne wrote a short guide in PLoS Computational Biology in 2013. It gives ten plain rules for computer-based research that other scientists can repeat and check. The rules speak to anyone who runs code on data.

The rules cover habits such as tracking each result by hand, saving exact code and data versions, and keeping a clear record of each step. The point is simple. A result that no one can redo has weak value. Careful records let others repeat the work, find errors, and build on solid ground. The guide stays short and direct, so labs can adopt it fast.
europmc-pmc3826651:
Wei Ma, Hua Kuang, Liguang Xu, Li Ding, Chuanlai Xu, Libing Wang, and Nicholas A. Kotov report a DNA sensor in Nature Communications in 2013. Gold nanorods, tiny gold bars, are linked by DNA into twisted pairs. The twist bends light in a way that can be read as a signal.

When target DNA is present, a chain reaction builds more twisted pairs. The light signal grows in a straight line with the amount of target, letting the team read tiny traces. Their limit ranks among the lowest reported for DNA tests, in the attomolar range. The method suits targets too large for older hot-spot tricks. Uses could span early disease checks, crime labs, and water testing.
europmc-pmc3828151:
In PLoS Genetics in 2013, Andrés Moreno-Estrada and a large team trace Caribbean population history from gene data. The Caribbean holds some of the most tangled human mixing in recent centuries. Native peoples, Europeans, and Africans met there after long apart, and the team trace that mix in DNA.

Gene data came from island and mainland groups, set next to a large reference set from three continents. New methods split each genome stretch by its root source and read the length of those stretches. The native share in islanders traces most likely to South American roots shared with inland Amazon groups, hinting at wide sea travel before Columbus. Later mixing waves also left clear marks. The work rebuilds the region's past from living DNA.
europmc-pmc3898251:
Douglas B. Craig and Alan A. Dombkowski present a protein design tool in BMC Bioinformatics in 2013. Adding a disulfide bond, a sulfur link between two protein spots, can make a protein sturdier or tune its action. Software that forecasts which spot pairs would form such a bond makes the craft far surer.

Their first tool for that task ran only on one system and had grown dated. Version 2.0 runs on the web for any system and adds sharper pictures and analysis. A key gain is a heat-flex score for the regions involved, which flags bonds likely to add real heat stability, not just form. The free server aims at labs that build proteins for research or industry.
europmc-pmc3921251:
Kristy Deiner and Florian Altermatt test how far DNA shed by river creatures travels downstream, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Environmental DNA testing can reveal species from a water sample, but in flowing water a positive result may come from animals living far upstream. The pair tracked two lake-dwelling invertebrates, a water flea and a freshwater mussel, in the river flowing out of their lake.

Water was sampled at eleven sites up to 12.3 kilometers below the lake, in July and again in October. The water flea's DNA appeared at every site at both times. The mussel's DNA faded with distance and was gone beyond 9.1 kilometers. The results warn river surveyors that detection distance differs by species, so a DNA hit does not pin an animal to the sampling spot.
europmc-pmc3922951:
Daniel Baylis, David B. Bartlett, Harnish P. Patel, and Helen C. Roberts explain the idea of inflammaging in Longevity and Healthspan in 2013. The term names the slow rise of the body's inflammatory response with advancing age. It is thought to grow out of a lifelong remodeling of both the fast, innate immune system and the targeted, acquired one, ending in steady production of inflammatory signals.

Genes, environment, worn-down cell cleanup, and rising body fat all shape who is most affected. The body pushes back through stress hormones such as cortisol, though that pushback itself may add to frailty, while a protective adrenal steroid fades with age. The review links this push and pull to chronic illness, loss of function, and death in old age.
europmc-pmc3963851:
Jaroslav Flegr and three colleagues test a common parasite against disease burdens by country. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. The parasite is Toxoplasma. It infects an estimated 30 to 50 percent of all humans. It then sits quietly in tissue for life. The team gathered infection rates for women of childbearing age. The rates covered 88 countries. They set those rates beside national death and disability data. Wealth, latitude, and humidity were held in check.

Infection rates explained about 23 percent of the gaps in disease burden across Europe. Of 128 disease groups tested, 23 tracked with infection rates. Most links were positive, and five were negative. A dozen more groups trended positive. The authors stress one point. Country-level links are not proof of cause. Still, they argue the pattern earns this parasite far more study.
europmc-pmc4013551:
Saskia Haegens, Helena Cousijn, George Wallis, Paul J. Harrison, and Anna C. Nobre measure how the brain's alpha rhythm speed varies, in NeuroImage in 2014. The alpha rhythm is a steady wave at the back of the head, long dismissed as idling. Fresh work gives it an active part in thought.

The team recorded brain fields in fifty-one healthy people at rest, during plain viewing, and during a memory task with two load levels. The rhythm's peak speed rose as task demand grew, in both the side and back head areas studied. The harder memory step showed a higher peak than the easy step. Across people, peak speed spread widely, well beyond the narrow band many studies assume. A fixed, narrow band could thus bias results against some people and tasks. The authors urge wider bands and care with each person's own peak when the rhythm is studied.
europmc-pmc4053751:
David B. Neale and eleven colleagues report the draft genome of the loblolly pine, in Genome Biology in 2014. Conifer genomes are giants, tens of billions of letters, which long blocked full sequencing. Loblolly pine matters to forestry and breeding, making it the natural first target.

The team's trick was to start from haploid tissue: the seed's nutritive part carries one copy of each chromosome, halving the assembly puzzle. Shotgun reads from a single breeding tree built a draft spanning over twenty-three billion letters. Long scaffolds let them call more than fifty thousand gene models. Pine genes sprawl, with spacer stretches inside them sometimes longer than whole genes elsewhere. Repeats make up about four fifths of the genome, explaining its bulk. Some gene families look unique to conifers.
europmc-pmc4109851:
Keith H. Turner, Marvin Whiteley, and colleagues hunted the genes Pseudomonas aeruginosa needs to run acute and chronic wound infections. Their study appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2014. The same bacterium can spread fast and kill, or persist for years despite treatment, without much genetic difference between strains.

Using mouse burn wounds for acute infection and chronic surgical wounds for the persistent kind, the team combined gene activity profiling with a mutant fitness screen across the genome. Surprisingly, a gene's activity in the wound rarely matched its importance, except for metabolic genes. Joining expression-based metabolic models with mutant data revealed what the bacteria must eat to settle and persist. The findings expose separate requirement sets for the two infection styles.
europmc-pmc4119351:
Eva van Rooij and Sakari Kauppinen reviewed the maturing field of microRNA therapeutics. Their review appeared in EMBO Molecular Medicine in 2014. MicroRNAs are short RNAs that tune gene activity, and they are frequently disordered in human disease, making them promising drug targets.

Two broad strategies dominate: blocking a harmful microRNA with an anti-miR, or replacing a lost one with a mimic. The authors describe how these molecules are designed and delivered, and update progress by disease area. Cancer, cardiovascular disease, and hepatitis C infection lead the pipeline. Tens of thousands of mature microRNAs are known across hundreds of species, so choosing the right target matters. The review argues the field is coming of age, moving from concept toward clinic.
europmc-pmc4135351:
Weiwei Wang, Matthew R. Whorton, and Roderick MacKinnon measured exactly how three signals control the GIRK2 channel, a potassium gate in heart pacemaker and nerve cells. Their study appeared in eLife in 2014. The channel answers to G proteins, a membrane lipid called PIP2, and sodium, placing it under several pathways at once.

The team purified the mammalian channel and rebuilt it in flat artificial membranes. Both the G protein piece G-beta-gamma and PIP2 had to be present together for the channel to open. Sodium was not essential but tuned the response across normal levels. Another G protein form closed the channel by removing its partner. The dual requirement helps explain why only certain receptor families can switch GIRK2 on.
europmc-pmc4141851:
Janneke H. H. M. van de Wijgert and a team of peers reviewed ten years of work on the germs that live in the vagina, read by their DNA. Their review came out in PLoS ONE in 2014. They searched for work from 2008 to late 2013 that used DNA tools such as gene reads or probes.

Sixty-three studies passed their tests. As one, they show that sets of germs led by the lactobacillus group mark a sound state. The ill state long called bacterial vaginosis is in truth a mixed shift of many germs, and its depth tracks lab scores and acid strength well. One kind, Lactobacillus crispatus, guards health more than a close kin. Sets led by it tend to shift to mild forms, not to full ill states. The team also weighs how acts, age, and place move these sets.
europmc-pmc4163751:
Susan Lagdon, Cherie Armour, and Maurice Stringer systematically reviewed the mental health outcomes adults suffer after intimate partner violence. Their review appeared in the European Journal of Psychotraumatology in 2014. Research had centred on physical violence, leaving other forms understudied.

Searching eleven databases for 2004 to 2014, they found fifty-eight papers. Victims showed worse mental health than people never exposed, and often worse than survivors of other traumas. Depression, posttraumatic stress disorder, and anxiety linked most strongly. More severe and more varied abuse brought heavier symptoms. Psychological violence, they conclude, is more damaging than once thought and should count as a serious form of abuse. They call for one shared definition and measure of partner violence.
europmc-pmc4181351:
Rita V. Krishnamurthi, Valery L. Feigin, and a large Global Burden of Disease team measured world stroke burden in The Lancet Global Health in 2013. Stroke splits into two kinds: ischaemic, from a blocked vessel, and haemorrhagic, from a burst one. Planners need to know how each kind is shifting by region.

Drawing on 119 studies, the team estimated first-ever stroke counts, deaths, and lost healthy years for 1990, 2005, and 2010. The raw number of people struck rose sharply, up 37 percent for ischaemic and 47 percent for haemorrhagic stroke, mostly in poorer countries. Most of the burden fell on people under 75 in those regions. The authors argue prevention plans must fit each region's stroke mix rather than copy rich-country models.
europmc-pmc4190351:
Zachary Munn, Alan Pearson, and three co-authors proposed a confidence rating for qualitative research summaries in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2014. Health decisions increasingly draw on syntheses of interview and observation studies, not just trials. Readers of such syntheses had no standard way to judge how much trust a finding deserves.

Their approach, named ConQual, rates each finding on two grounds. Dependability asks whether the studies behind it were done soundly, judged by a set of appraisal questions. Credibility asks how closely the summary's claims fit the original data, from clearly supported to unsupported. The two ratings combine into one overall confidence grade, presented in a summary table. The authors offer ConQual as a practical aid for clinicians and policy makers weighing qualitative evidence.
europmc-pmc4203351:
Nahid A. Khan, Anu Suomalainen, and nine co-authors tested a vitamin treatment for mitochondrial muscle disease in EMBO Molecular Medicine in 2014. Mitochondrial myopathy weakens muscles because faulty power stations cannot make enough energy. A form of vitamin B3 called nicotinamide riboside raises NAD levels and had boosted mitochondria in healthy mice.

Given to mice with mitochondrial myopathy, the vitamin delayed both early and late stages of the disease. Muscles and brown fat built fresh mitochondria, the abnormal structures inside existing ones were prevented, and harmful DNA deletions did not form. The treatment also switched on a protective stress program inside mitochondria. The authors propose NAD-boosting strategies as a promising line for these diseases, which currently have no effective treatment.
europmc-pmc4212551:
Trishnee Bhurosy and Rajesh Jeewon asked what drives obesity in developing countries in The Scientific World Journal in 2014. More than half a billion people worldwide live with obesity, and the rise is now fastest outside rich nations. Diet, inactivity, and wealth all shift at once during development, making the cause hard to assign.

Comparing body mass index trends across World Health Organization regions from 1980 to 2008, they found the steepest climb after 1999, with women's averages above men's throughout. Poorer countries may soon pass richer ones in mean body mass. Within countries, rising income first buys more food and less physical work, so obesity follows money upward before the pattern flips. The authors urge action on food policy, media, schools, and neighbourhoods, not just on individual willpower.
europmc-pmc4236651:
Dominica A. Gidrewicz and Tanis R. Fenton pooled studies of breast milk composition in BMC Pediatrics in 2014. Milk from mothers who deliver early differs from full-term milk, and both change over the weeks after birth. Feeding guidelines for fragile preterm babies depend on knowing those numbers well.

Their meta-analysis covered 41 studies, 26 of preterm milk from 843 mothers and 30 of term milk from 2,299 mothers. Preterm milk carried more true protein, with the gap widest in colostrum at up to 35 percent, then narrowing to near nothing by ten to twelve weeks. Colostrum beat mature milk on protein but trailed on energy, fat, and lactose. Composition held fairly steady from week 2 to week 12. The authors warn that how protein and energy are measured shifts the numbers by wide margins.
europmc-pmc4270451:
Kirsty M Rhodes, Rebecca M Turner, and Julian PT Higgins study how much results tend to differ between studies in a meta-analysis. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2015. In small meta-analyses this spread, called heterogeneity, is hard to estimate, yet it shapes how much trust a pooled result deserves.

The team modeled thousands of meta-analyses drawn from the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. They built predictive distributions for the spread a new meta-analysis is likely to show, split by outcome type, treatment comparison, and medical area. These distributions can serve as informed starting values in Bayesian analyses, so small reviews need not guess the spread from a handful of studies alone.
europmc-pmc4283151:
Suchismita Sarker and six co-authors tracked tiny vesicles shed by the placenta into a mother's blood during early pregnancy. Their study appeared in the Journal of Translational Medicine in 2014. The placenta releases these packets, called exosomes, but their course across the first weeks of pregnancy had not been charted.

Blood samples were drawn from ten healthy women each week from week six to week twelve. Vesicles marked as coming from the placenta rose steadily over that span, and their protein and RNA cargo stayed stable through freezing and thawing. The work lays ground for blood tests that could watch placental health without any procedure on the womb.
europmc-pmc4287451:
Irina Makarevitch and seven co-authors test whether jumping genes help maize switch on stress defenses. Their study appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2015. Transposable elements, DNA pieces that copy and move, fill much of the maize genome and were long treated as junk or parasites.

Seedlings were exposed to stresses such as heat, cold, salt, and ultraviolet light, and both gene and element activity were measured. Many elements sitting near genes woke up under stress, and nearby genes often changed activity with them. The pattern suggests these elements act as stress sensitive switches that add variety to how maize responds. The work recasts a class of DNA once dismissed as mere clutter.
europmc-pmc4296151:
Nicholas J. Loman and Aaron R. Quinlan introduce poretools, a software toolkit for data from nanopore sequencers. Their paper appeared in Bioinformatics in 2014. The MinION is a portable sequencer the size of a USB stick. It reads single DNA molecules as they pass through tiny pores. Early users had no standard way to handle its output files.

Poretools works directly on the device's native file format. It checks data quality, pulls out the sequences, and supports the first steps of downstream analysis while data still stream in. The toolkit gave the early nanopore community a shared set of basic operations, at a moment when the technology was moving from promise to practice.
europmc-pmc4359051:
Anthony Gershlick and colleagues ran the CvLPRIT trial, reported in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology in 2015, on heart attack care. Patients having emergency artery opening for a major heart attack often show other narrowed arteries too. Doctors were unsure whether to fix all of them during the same hospital stay or only the artery that caused the attack. The UK trial assigned 296 patients in seven centers by chance to one of the two plans.

Within 12 months, the combined rate of death, repeat heart attack, heart failure, and further artery work was 10.0 percent with complete treatment, against 21.2 percent with culprit-only treatment. No single part of that mix drove the gap on its own, and no part clashed with the trend. The benefit seemed to start early after treatment.
europmc-pmc4416251:
Ty Ferguson, Alex Rowlands, Tim Olds, and Carol Maher tested consumer activity trackers against research devices, in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity in 2015. Wrist and clip-on monitors were booming, but their accuracy in daily life was unproven. Twenty-one healthy adults wore seven consumer monitors, from Fitbit, Jawbone, Misfit, Nike, Striiv, and Withings, plus two research-grade devices, for 48 hours of normal free living, and the readings were compared.

All consumer devices tracked research devices strongly for step count and sleep time. Agreement was weaker for energy expenditure and only moderate for vigorous activity, where typical errors ran from 26 to 298 percent. Two Fitbit models ranked among the most accurate overall. Steps and sleep can be trusted from the wrist; calorie and intensity numbers deserve caution.
europmc-pmc4474551:
Xue Gong and eight co-authors, including Irina Kerkis, built a scaffold for growing tumor balls in PLoS ONE in 2015. Multicellular tumor spheroids, small balls of cancer cells grown in three dimensions, predict drug effects in the body better than flat cell layers. Older ways to make them are slow, laborious, and give uneven sizes, which spoils repeatability and blocks large drug screens.

Their method casts agarose, a seaweed gel, over a template of uniform tiny wells in standard culture plates. Cells settle into the wells and form spheroids whose size can be tuned by the template, in large numbers at once. The clear gel lets researchers watch the balls form and grow under a microscope. Using a breast cancer cell line, they charted growth and roundness by well size and showed drug testing on the platform, offering a robust tool for screening.
europmc-pmc4502551:
Helen Fones and Sarah Gurr assessed Septoria tritici blotch, a major wheat disease, from a European Union perspective in Fungal Genetics and Biology in 2015. The disease, caused by the fungus Zymoseptoria tritici, threatens wheat across temperate climates, and solid peer-reviewed figures for its yield and financial damage are surprisingly hard to find. Old loss estimates from single regions have been borrowed worldwide without warrant, the authors note.

The review weighs the value of wheat in the three main European producer countries and the cost and return of fungicide treatment against the disease. The fungus's flexible genome raises the threat level, as it can adapt to resistant varieties and fungicides, and climate change may shift the risk further. The authors estimate spore production per infection cycle to ground the discussion, and call for control strategies planned on real numbers rather than inherited ones.
europmc-pmc4529251:
Marina Marcet-Houben and Toni Gabaldón rethink how baker's yeast doubled its genome, in PLoS Biology in 2015. Whole-genome duplication, copying every gene at once, reshaped many lineages. For the yeast behind bread and beer, when the doubling happened is known, but how it began was not.

Comparing gene trees across yeasts, the pair found strong signs of a mating between two species at the same era. A hybrid carries two full gene sets from the start, so the doubling may be the direct result of that cross rather than an error within one species. The extra copy then stabilized the fragile hybrid. The scenario, they argue, offers a general origin story for genome doublings elsewhere.
europmc-pmc4560751:
Masao Nagasaki leads a twelve-author team sequencing over a thousand Japanese genomes, in Nature Communications in 2015. Most reference gene panels lean on European ancestry, which can mislead studies of other populations. The Tohoku Medical Megabank sequenced 1,070 healthy Japanese people at deep coverage, about 32 times over, to build a panel of their own.

The effort found 21.2 million single-letter variants, 12 million of them new, plus millions of insertions, deletions, and copy-number changes. The panel covers 99% of variants found in at least one in a thousand Japanese people, and it sharply improves genotype guessing for the wider population. Such population-specific panels, the team argues, are key to finding rare disease variants.
europmc-pmc4568951:
Lian Zhao leads a ten-author team showing that the retina's own immune cells eat living sight cells, in EMBO Molecular Medicine in 2015. Retinitis pigmentosa, an inherited blinding disease, kills rod photoreceptors through mutations in the rods themselves. No broad treatment exists. The team asked whether microglia, the retina's resident immune cells, share the blame.

In rd10 mice, a model of the disease, microglia moved in early as rods began to die, armed with engulfing machinery, while sick rods displayed 'eat-me' signals. Live imaging caught microglia swallowing rods that were not yet dead. Removing microglia genetically, or blocking their engulfing receptor with a drug-like molecule, preserved rods and vision measures, marking this eating behavior as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc4598751:
Michael Schuliga wrote a solo 2015 review of NF-kappaB signalling in long-term airway disease. Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD, differ in cause but share airway inflammation. A protein complex called NF-kappaB switches on many inflammation genes, and oxidative stress activates it. The review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences.

Steroid drugs calm asthma partly by blocking NF-kappaB, yet in severe asthma and COPD that block fails after chemical changes to the steroid receptor and its partners. Drugs that block the enzymes which activate NF-kappaB are candidate treatments. Restoring the steroid block is another route the review weighs. Readers get a clear map of one central inflammation pathway and the treatment ideas built around it.
europmc-pmc4786551:
Kenneth Michael Pollard, writing alone in Frontiers in Immunology in 2016, reviews the link between silica dust and autoimmune disease. Breathing crystalline silica is a known job hazard for miners and stone workers, and population studies tie it to lupus, scleroderma, and rheumatoid arthritis. The dust also scars lungs in the disease silicosis, whose long record may hold clues to the immune turn.

In the lung, dust grains swallowed by immune cells spark swelling, then scar tissue that walls the grains in nodules. Pollard sets out a likely chain: that early alarm wakes the wider immune system, tolerance to the body's own tissue breaks, and self-attacking antibodies follow. Genes clearly sway who falls ill after exposure. Many steps in the chain, he notes, still lack direct proof.
europmc-pmc4831151:
Amy Langdon, Nathan Crook, and Gautam Dantas review antibiotics' collateral damage in Genome Medicine in 2016. Eighty years of antibiotic use saved millions of lives and also killed uncountable friendly microbes. The gut community those drugs reshape helps run immunity, infection defense, and food processing, so the reshaping has costs that surface across a life.

The review follows the evidence from infancy to adulthood, tying early antibiotic exposure and repeated courses to malnutrition, obesity, diabetes, and severe gut infection. It then tours the escape routes: drugs that disarm germs without killing them, blunting resistance pressure; probiotics; and stool transplants that rebuild a wrecked community. The authors press for a working grasp of gut ecology to guide both new drugs and restraint with old ones.
europmc-pmc4866051:
Xiaoming Wang and a large team studied mice fully lacking Shank3, a gene tied to autism, in work from 2016. Brain scans in people suggest faulty wiring underlies autism traits, but the circuit steps were unclear. The knockout mice lacked a large Shank3 segment. In their striatum, a hub for habits, a receptor scaffold pairing called mGluR5-Homer was selectively altered.

Synapses in the striatum worked oddly, brain shape and wiring shifted, and mice showed autism-like behavior. A cortex-striatum-thalamus loop ran too hot at rest and too cold during social acts. Tuning mGluR5 eased excess grooming and fixed faulty synapse learning. The chain links one gene fault to circuit failure and behavior.
europmc-pmc4869251:
Ambarish Biswas and co-authors released CRISPRDetect in 2016, a flexible program that finds CRISPR arrays in microbe genomes. CRISPR arrays are DNA stretches of repeated blocks split by unique spacers, the memory bank of a bacterial immune system. Older finder tools miss newer known traits of these loci. CRISPRDetect spots likely arrays and refines them step by step.

The tool extends arrays by catching variant repeats, fixes their direction, and trims repeat and spacer edges. It runs as a web program or a command line tool. Better array maps help track how microbes store invader records, which feeds work on immunity, editing tools, and microbe family history.
europmc-pmc4888851:
Dennis J. Selkoe and John Hardy marked 25 years of the amyloid hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease in 2016. The idea holds that a build-up imbalance of the amyloid beta protein, above all its Aβ42 form, starts the disease early. All known dominant mutations for early-onset Alzheimer's sit in the protein's source or in presenilin, the cutter that frees it.

Extra copies of the source gene in Down syndrome seed deposits in the teens, with full disease marks later. A common risk gene, APOE4, slows amyloid clearing. Soluble amyloid clumps from patient brains shrink synapses and block memory wiring in tests. Drug failures keep debate hot, yet the pair judge the core case stronger than ever.
europmc-pmc4941051:
Mingxi Yao and eight co-authors measure how talin, a force bearing linker protein in cells, unfolds and refolds under pull. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Talin joins the actin skeleton to adhesion sites where cells grip their surroundings. Its tail end holds 13 helical bundles that sense force as a cell spreads or moves. How those bundles share and buffer force was poorly known, so the team pulled on each one and timed its opening and closing.

All 13 bundles opened and shut at set force levels, each with its own kinetics. Together they act as a shock absorber. The cycle keeps the force passed along the talin path within a narrow band of a few piconewtons, even as outside pulls vary. The authors argue this buffering explains how adhesion sites read steady force signals. It also shows how one protein can tune force for many cell tasks.
europmc-pmc4947151:
Marco Todesco leads a team surveying when cross breeding between species or forms pushes rare ones toward extinction. Their review appeared in Evolutionary Applications in 2016. Hybridization can swamp a rare form genetically, replacing it with hybrids. It can also waste births on unfit hybrids, shrinking the population. In the other direction, it can rescue small inbred groups by adding fresh genes. The team reviewed the literature to find which factors decide the outcome.

Genetic swamping proved far more common in the record than demographic swamping. Human involvement raised the risk, while strong reproductive isolation lowered it. Climate change is often predicted to raise hybridization driven extinction, but the authors found little direct evidence yet. Genetic rescue looked as likely as harm in theory and experiments. They conclude risk is highly situation dependent, so managers must judge each case on its ecology and genetics.
europmc-pmc5036151:
Gabrielle Fredman and eleven co-authors report in Nature Communications in 2016 that clogged arteries suffer from a failed cleanup signal. Plaques grow dangerous when inflammation inside them never resolves. Special lipid mediators called SPMs switch inflammation off, while leukotrienes fan it. The team measured both kinds of lipids in human neck artery plaques, comparing stable regions with the weak, rupture-prone regions of the same plaques.

The weak regions held far less of the resolving mediator resolvin D1, and the balance of resolvers to the inflammatory leukotriene B4 was badly tipped. Mice bred for artery disease showed the same slide as their plaques advanced. Giving those mice resolvin D1 restored the balance and steadied the plaques: less cell death and oxidative stress, better clearing of dead cells, and thicker protective caps. The results back a therapy idea built on restoring resolution rather than only blocking inflammation.
europmc-pmc5052651:
Shu G. Chen and a large co-author group test a gut-brain link in Scientific Reports in 2016. Parkinson's-type diseases involve clumps of alpha-synuclein, a protein that can seed further clumping like a prion. What starts the first clump is unknown. Gut bacteria make amyloid, called curli, so the team fed curli-producing E. coli to aged rats and to worms engineered to make human alpha-synuclein.

Rats exposed to curli producers built up more alpha-synuclein deposits in gut and brain than rats given bacteria unable to make curli. Their brains also showed more activated immune cells and higher inflammatory signals. The worms on curli bacteria likewise formed more clumps. The groups did not differ in survival, weight, or body-wide inflammation. The authors propose that bacterial amyloid can cross-seed the human protein and prime the brain's immune system, a possible trigger worth testing.
europmc-pmc5059451:
Corey J. A. Bradshaw and nine co-authors compile the world cost of invasive insects in Nature Communications in 2016. Invasive insects spread disease, eat crops, and damage forests and buildings, yet their bills had been counted only in scattered studies. The team built a database of every reported goods-and-services and health cost estimate they could find and summed the floor it sets.

The minimum comes to seventy billion US dollars a year for goods and services, plus over 6.9 billion in health costs. Totals keep rising as more estimates are added, and the worst harms are already counted, above all in health. Many costs have never been studied properly, so the authors call the sum a gross underestimate. Warming, denser populations, and growing trade will spread these insects further, while sharper surveillance and containment could save large sums.
europmc-pmc5109551:
Line S. Reinert and a large group of co-authors studied defense against herpes simplex virus in the brain, reporting in Nature Communications in 2016. Herpes simplex encephalitis is the most common acute viral brain inflammation in rich countries, and interferons, the cell's alarm proteins, are key to control. The team asked which brain cells sound that alarm.

They found that microglia, the brain's immune cells, are the main source of interferon after infection, switched on through a DNA-sensing path called cGAS-STING. Mice lacking that path fell badly ill. Infected microglia also helped neurons resist the virus and primed star-shaped astrocytes to make their own interferon through a second sensing path. The work casts microglia as conductors of the brain's antiviral response.
europmc-pmc5129251:
Philip Haaf, Pankaj Garg, Daniel R. Messroghli, David A. Broadbent, John P. Greenwood, and Sven Plein reviewed a heart imaging method in the Journal of Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance in 2016. Magnetic resonance scans can already show heart scars, but widespread fine scarring across the muscle can slip past the standard technique.

Their subject is T1 mapping, which measures heart tissue directly, before and after contrast dye, and a derived value for the space outside cells. These measures can reveal both patchy and diffuse tissue change, help sort out which disease is weakening the heart, and track change over time without radiation or tissue samples. The review weighs the evidence across heart muscle diseases and sudden chest pain cases and judges the method ready to support diagnosis and prognosis.
europmc-pmc5129651:
Maria Fiorentino and eight co-authors studied leaky barriers in autism in Molecular Autism in 2016. One theory holds that stray material crossing a weak gut wall, then a weak blood-brain barrier, helps trigger autism spectrum disorders. The team tested that idea in postmortem brain tissue and gut samples.

In the brains of people with autism, several genes that seal the blood-brain barrier were turned up, alongside signs of nerve inflammation, and one sealing protein was more abundant. The pattern differed from schizophrenia samples in most measures. In gut biopsies, three quarters of autism samples had lower levels of wall-sealing parts while two thirds had more of the pore-forming parts. The authors read this as evidence of altered barriers in autism, specific enough to set it apart from schizophrenia.
europmc-pmc5161751:
Matthew P. Swaffer, Andrew W. Jones, Helen R. Flynn, Ambrosius P. Snijders, and Paul Nurse asked how one enzyme times the cell cycle, reporting in Cell in 2016. Cells must copy DNA first and divide second, in strict order. Several cyclin-CDK complexes drive these steps, and the textbook view credits each complex with choosing its own targets.

In fission yeast, their protein-wide phosphorylation survey showed a single cyclin-CDK can order events by itself. As its activity climbs through the cycle, targets with low thresholds react early and insensitive ones late, and fast phosphate removal sharpens the steps. In normal cells carrying several complexes, target choice and these thresholds work together to fine-tune the pattern. The study shifts weight from which enzyme acts to how much activity has built up.
europmc-pmc5167251:
Karl Friston, Thomas FitzGerald, Francesco Rigoli, Philipp Schwartenbeck, John O'Doherty, and Giovanni Pezzulo set out a theory of behavior and learning in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews in 2016. Their frame, active inference, treats action as driven by beliefs about hidden states of the world, not by the states themselves.

Agents choose actions that score well on expected free energy, a measure blending two pulls: reaching preferred outcomes and gaining information that resolves uncertainty. That second pull makes curiosity and exploration fall out of the theory naturally. Habits, they argue, are learned by watching one's own goal-directed behavior and are then selected quickly during later action. The paper contrasts this belief-based picture with model-free learning from rewards and model-based planning.
europmc-pmc5181151:
Frank Milton asked whether bilharzia, or schistosomiasis, exists in India, in The Indian Medical Gazette in January 1914. A curious surgical case reported the previous October, a urinary fistula with a bladder stone, raised the possibility that the blood fluke Bilharzia haematobia was at work in an Indian patient.

Milton surveys the sparse record. In animals the disease is well established: Montgomery in 1906 described three new parasite species from Indian horses and cattle and concluded the human parasite could live in India. In humans, though, Milton could trace only six references across twenty-one years, and most cases were probably infected abroad, such as pilgrims returning from Mecca. He leaves the question of a truly Indian human infection open on thin evidence.
europmc-pmc5238551:
Sumudu P. Leelananda and Steffen Lindert reviewed computational methods in drug discovery in the Beilstein Journal of Organic Chemistry in 2016. Bringing a drug to market takes years and, by a 2014 estimate quoted here, about 2.6 billion dollars, with nine of ten candidate drugs failing in human trials. Computer-aided drug discovery offers a virtual shortcut that can cut both time and cost.

The review covers two families of methods. Structure-based work uses the shape of a target protein: virtual screening of huge libraries, predicting protein structure, and docking, the fitting of candidate molecules into the target. Ligand-based work learns from known active molecules through pharmacophore models, which map the features a drug needs, and QSAR models, which link chemical structure to activity with numbers. The authors collect recent successes and argue such tools are now a routine, valued part of the pipeline in both universities and industry.
europmc-pmc5238751:
Dandan Luo, Kevin A. Carter, Dyego Miranda, and Jonathan F. Lovell reviewed chemophototherapy for solid tumours in Advanced Science in 2017. Near-infrared light passes a short way into tissue, letting doctors aim harmless radiation at a defined target. Light-based treatments, photodynamic therapy and laser heat therapy, are proven in the clinic, yet each alone can leave tumour cells alive.

Chemophototherapy pairs light treatment with chemotherapy drugs. Chemotherapy can kill cells the light missed or stop damaged tumour vessels from regrowing, while light treatment can open tumour vessels so drug-loaded nanoparticles pile up inside. Newer particles join light-sensitive agents and drugs in one package, or release their drug cargo only when lit. Trials in animals and early clinical work show the pairing can wipe out tumours with tight spatial control. The authors call for more clinical testing to settle doses and timing.
europmc-pmc5240851:
B. J. van Meer and nine colleagues measured how the silicone polymer PDMS soaks up small drug molecules in Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications in 2017. PDMS is the standard material for microfluidic cell culture chips, including organs-on-chip, because it is easy to shape. Its flaw is that it absorbs drugs, which can quietly lower the dose cells actually see in a drug test.

The team built an assay that measures what is left of a drug after contact with PDMS, using liquid chromatography, and ran it on four heart drugs. Uptake differed between drugs, grew over time, and was not set by fat solubility alone, contrary to earlier claims. Two commercial fatty coatings changed absorption, as did the presence of living cells in the device. The authors suggest such coatings may help keep drug levels honest in chip-based screening.
europmc-pmc5367551:
Stephen Ross and co-authors tested a mushroom compound for cancer-linked distress in the Journal of Psychopharmacology in 2016.
