Many patients with life-threatening cancer face deep anxiety and depression, which worsen both mind and body outcomes. Past work, old and new, hints that psilocybin, the active part of some mushrooms, can ease that distress. Their trial was strict: neither staff nor patients knew who got what.

Twenty-nine patients took a single mid-size dose of psilocybin or a vitamin stand-in, each with talk therapy. Seven weeks on, before the groups swapped, the psilocybin arm showed fast, large, and lasting drops in anxiety and depression. Despair and hopelessness tied to cancer fell, while spirit and life quality rose. At half a year, most still held the gains. The depth of the felt mystical side of the trip carried much of the gain.
europmc-pmc5407851:
Renata Micha and eight co-authors, for the Nutrition and Chronic Diseases Expert Group, review diet and heart and metabolic disease in a 2017 paper in PLoS ONE. Diet is a major driver of heart disease, stroke, and diabetes, yet the strength of proof for each food and the best intake levels were not well settled. The team judged cause using a classic set of tests, then pooled studies to size each effect.

They found causal links for ten foods and seven nutrients. Fruit, greens, beans, nuts, whole grains, fish, and yogurt guard health, as do fiber and potassium. Red and processed meats, sweet drinks, heavy starch loads, trans fats, and salt do harm. Effects faded with age but rarely differed by sex. Best intake levels mostly matched national figures and major diet guides.
europmc-pmc5420351:
Boycott and co-authors set out a global plan to diagnose every rare genetic disease. Their review appeared in the American Journal of Human Genetics. Rare diseases are uncommon one by one. Together they strike at least one person in fifty. A firm genetic diagnosis ends years of searching for families. It also guides care and family planning. Yet clinics confirm only about half of cases at first pass. The rest need new gene discoveries.

The authors write for the International Rare Diseases Research Consortium. That group formed in 2011 to pool rare disease work worldwide. The review maps the blocks that slow gene discovery. It covers data sharing, disease catalogs, and variant proof. It then offers ways to clear each block. Each new gene found opens a path to diagnosis. Some finds also point to precise treatments. The piece serves as a roadmap for labs, clinics, and funders.
europmc-pmc5434551:
Shafiee and co-authors estimate the worldwide prevalence of sarcopenia in older adults. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in the Journal of Diabetes and Metabolic Disorders. Sarcopenia is age-related loss of muscle mass and function. It brings disability and higher death risk. Single studies reported widely inconsistent rates. Definitions and tools varied across regions. The team searched three databases for population studies. Eligible studies covered healthy adults aged 60 and over.

Thirty-five articles met the criteria. They pooled 58,404 individuals in total. Overall prevalence came to 10 percent in men. Women matched at 10 percent. Non-Asian populations showed higher rates than Asian ones. The gap widened when impedance analysis measured muscle. There it reached 19 versus 10 percent in men. Women showed 20 versus 11 percent. A tenth of healthy elders thus have sarcopenia.
europmc-pmc5452251:
Wang and co-authors review how probiotic bacteria fight oxidative damage in the body. Their review appeared in Nutrients. Oxidative stress tips the balance toward harmful oxygen radicals. Those radicals scar DNA, proteins, and fats. They link to arthritis, diabetes, and heart disease. Synthetic antioxidants face safety doubts. Liver harm and cancer risk shadow two common ones. Natural options draw growing interest.

Probiotics are live microbes taken for health. Certain strains show antioxidant power in dishes and in animals. The effects vary by strain. The review sorts their modes of action. Some boost the body's own defense enzymes. Some cut radical production at the source. Some reshape the gut flora itself. Altered gut flora ties into oxidative stress levels. The authors admit the deep mechanisms stay murky. Their map frames tests for safer food-based antioxidants.
europmc-pmc5504351:
Olivares and co-authors report a cancer metabolism study in Nature Communications. Pancreatic tumors grow inside a dense collagen mesh where food and oxygen run short. How the cancer cells feed there was not fully known. The team suspected the surrounding collagen itself might serve as food. Collagen is rich in the amino acid proline.

The cells take up collagen fragments and break them down, they report. Proline from that breakdown feeds their energy cycle. It helps the cells survive when other fuels are scarce. An enzyme called PRODH1 proved required for tumor growth in mice. The matrix around the tumor thus doubles as a nutrient store.
europmc-pmc5515051:
Johnson and co-authors present a systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. It compares HIV self-testing with standard testing services. Self-testing is private and convenient, reaching people who skip clinics. About 40 percent of HIV infections worldwide stay undiagnosed. The review fed into World Health Organization guidance.

Five randomized trials with 4,145 people, all men, were pooled. Self-testing doubled testing uptake among men, they report. Testing frequency nearly doubled among men who have sex with men. Positive diagnoses roughly doubled as well. No sign of social harm appeared across the trials. The authors urge more work on linking self-testers to care.
europmc-pmc5558651:
Wang and co-authors present a research article in Molecular Cancer. Their subject is a long noncoding RNA called HOXD-AS1 in liver cancer. Such RNAs do not code for proteins, yet they can steer cell behavior. The team found this one raised in tumor tissue.

High levels linked to poor survival and more advanced disease. A protein named STAT3 switches the RNA on. Lowering HOXD-AS1 slowed cancer cell migration and invasion in lab tests. It also cut lung spread in mice. The RNA acts as a sponge for a small RNA, miR-130a-3p. That frees a gene called SOX4 to drive spread. Readers learn how a noncoding RNA can push cancer to new sites.
europmc-pmc5600151:
Palmerston Mendes, Pan, and Torchilin review dendrimers as delivery carriers in Molecules. Dendrimers are polymers that branch like tiny trees. Their size, shape, charge, and solubility can all be tuned. Their surfaces are easy to modify.

Drugs can ride inside the branches or attach to the surface. That helps water-hating drugs dissolve and reach tissue. DNA and RNA bind to the charged outer groups. Extra parts, like folate or antibodies, can steer the carrier toward tumors. The review covers the main dendrimer families in use. It explains how each can carry drugs or genes. It also covers ways to sharpen targeting for cancer therapy. Readers get a full survey of a flexible delivery platform.
europmc-pmc5607351:
Lee and co-authors map support cells in the adult lung in Cell. The lung's lining renews itself with help from nearby mesenchymal cells. Those helpers were poorly defined. Two markers, Lgr5 and Lgr6, were known from stem cells in other tissues.

Lineage tracing, single-cell RNA sequencing, and organoid cultures sorted the helpers out. Lgr6 cells are a slice of the smooth muscle around airways. They steer airway progenitors using Wnt and Fgf10 signals together. Removing them hurt airway repair after injury. Lgr5 cells sit in the air-sac region instead. They push progenitors toward air-sac fates through Wnt alone. Tuning Wnt levels changed what the helpers instructed. Readers get a region-by-region map of lung repair partnerships.
europmc-pmc5614451:
The GBD 2016 Risk Factors Collaborators present a vast risk study in The Lancet. It is a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016. The team sized up 84 risks in all. The risks span habits, the environment, jobs, and body measures. Estimates run from 1990 to 2016, by age, sex, and place.

The work rests on 481 risk-outcome pairs with strong proof of cause. Source data came from trials, cohorts, surveys, censuses, and satellite records. The team asked how many deaths and lost healthy years each risk caused. Smoking and high blood pressure topped the global list. Exposure rose for 30 risks and fell for 31. Body-mass and blood sugar risks rose and need policy focus, the authors say. Gains from risk cuts stayed small next to ageing and growth.
europmc-pmc5649151:
Vaportzis, Clausen, and Gow present a focus group study in Frontiers in Psychology. It explores how older adults view tablet computers. Eighteen adults aged 65 to 76 took part. All were novice tablet users. Three focus groups discussed familiarity, barriers, and attitudes. The feedback also helped refine an intervention protocol.

Barriers included missing guidance, low knowledge, and low confidence. Health issues and cost also held people back. Concerns covered complexity and feelings of inadequacy. Some feared less social contact from screen use. Still, most participants felt eager to learn. Tablets offered easy access to information, they said. Brief hands-on time raised their stated future use. Clear support matters most for adoption, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc5684251:
Sochocka and co-authors present a review in Molecular Neurobiology. It weighs inflammation in the brain as friend or foe. The answer depends on how strongly glial cells activate. Mild activation of microglia and astrocytes tends to protect. Released signals help keep synapses flexible and cells growing. Toll-like receptor activity can spur new neuron growth too.

Strong activation flips the balance toward harm. Cytokine output then runs out of control. That excess speeds up neurodegeneration instead. A key shift involves p53 and NF-kappaB cross-talk. The tumor suppressor and the inflammation regulator sway each other. The authors flag that axis as a treatment target. Tuning toll-like receptor activity is another future route.
europmc-pmc5696751:
Mlinarić and co-authors present a review in Biochemia Medica. It argues for publishing negative research results. Positive findings fill the literature far more than negative ones. That skew is known as publication bias. Skipped results distort later meta-analyses in turn. Doctors, researchers, and policymakers then get misled. Money is also wasted repeating work already done. Human subjects accepted risk expecting shared benefit.

The review defines three kinds of negative results. Only well-run studies with clear null findings truly count. Some evidence disputes that editors alone drive the bias. Positive work is simply cited more often. The authors urge all stakeholders to share both kinds. Researchers carry the largest share of that duty.
europmc-pmc5830451:
Zhu and co-authors build nanoPOTS, a platform for proteomics on tiny cell counts. Protein profiling usually needs thousands of cells. Rare cells and thin tissue slices fall below that bar. The team shrinks every step into nanodroplets.

Processing happens in under 200 nanoliters in one pot. Small volumes cut losses on vessel surfaces. Paired with sensitive instruments, the platform names about 3,000 proteins from 10 cells. Applied to human pancreas slices, it quantified some 2,400 proteins. Samples came from diabetic and control donors. Readers get a way to read proteins where sample is precious.
europmc-pmc5850851:
Sanada and co-authors hunt the sources of the chronic inflammation that shadows aging. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine. The smoldering state, dubbed inflammaging, needs no infection to persist. It raises the odds of heart disease, diabetes, and cancer.

Senescent cells are one fountain, leaking inflammatory signals as they linger. An aging immune system misfires in ways that keep the fire lit. Even clotting factors moonlight as inflammation triggers through their receptors. The inflammation outlasts the stimuli that first provoked it. Clearing senescent cells is floated as one anti-aging strategy.
europmc-pmc5917451:
Maffioletti and co-authors grow three-dimensional human muscle from stem cells. Their article appeared in Cell Reports. They used induced stem cells from patients with muscular dystrophy. Forms included Duchenne, limb-girdle, and congenital types. Cells grew in hydrogels held under tension. That tension aligned the fibres like real muscle.

The lab muscles matched traits of human skeletal muscle, they report. They could be implanted into mice lacking immunity. Disease hallmarks showed up with high fidelity. Models also included vessel cells and motor neurons. All parts came from human stem cells. The platform may aid drug tests and tissue repair.
europmc-pmc5953551:
Petrie, Guzik, and Touyz review diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease as linked ills. Their review was published in the Canadian Journal of Cardiology. High blood pressure is twice as common in people with diabetes. People with high blood pressure often resist insulin as well. Heart and vessel disease is the top cause of death in diabetes. High blood pressure makes that load worse.

The two ills share risk factors and roots, the authors explain. These take in stiff vessel walls and sore, swollen tissue. A shared hormone system, cell rust, and immune stir also play a part. The review takes in sugar-damaged proteins and small gene bits. It ends with drug care now and new vessel guards.
europmc-pmc5956851:
Chae and co-authors review dual blockade of CTLA4 and PD-1 or PD-L1 in cancer immunotherapy. Their review appeared in the Journal for Immunotherapy of Cancer. Checkpoint inhibitors have won many approvals across cancers. Preclinical work hinted that pairs could beat single agents. Early trials showed clear survival gains for the combination. Nivolumab plus ipilimumab gained approval for advanced melanoma.

The review draws lessons from trials in melanoma and lung cancer. It covers non-small cell lung cancer in depth. Dual blockade is now being tested across many tumour types. Trials also pair it with chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation. The authors sketch prospects for wider use.
europmc-pmc5970551:
Harrison and co-authors give a brief introduction to mixed effects modelling and multi-model inference in ecology. Their guide appeared in PeerJ. Linear mixed effects models are now common for biological data. They flexibly handle many data types. Yet ecological data often need complex model structures. Fitting and reading such models is not always simple. Sound use is required for robust biological inference.

The authors overview current methods for applying these models. They flag pitfalls that arise during statistical modelling. Model selection gets special attention throughout. Information theory and multi-model inference are covered in depth. Practical fixes and key references close the guide.
europmc-pmc6011351:
Rossari, Minutolo, and Orciuolo trace the past, present, and future of drugs that block the Bcr-Abl protein. Their review was published in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. These drugs opened the age of aimed therapy. The first one blocked the fused protein that drives a blood cancer. The cancer then learned to resist in more than one way. Newer drugs were made to beat that pushback. Four of them in two waves have since reached the clinic.

Shapes of the protein and trial facts guided the remakes, the authors explain. Fresh drugs now wait in lab tests. The tale of these drugs holds lessons past this one cancer. It shows how to build blockers for other such proteins.
europmc-pmc6054651:
Woolcott and Bergman propose a simpler way to estimate body fat percentage. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Body mass index is widely used for obesity checks. It often misjudges true body fat, though. Scanning methods are accurate but costly and slow.

The team searched hundreds of body measure formulas. Data came from national health surveys in the United States. One formula, called relative fat mass, won out. It needs only height, waist size, and sex. In validation data, it beat BMI for both sexes. It also missed fewer cases of fat-defined obesity. Misclassification fell across three ethnic groups studied. Readers get a cheap clinic-ready alternative to BMI.
europmc-pmc6125951:
Zhang and co-authors present a research article in Journal of Hematology and Oncology on a long non-coding RNA in colorectal cancer. The RNA, called NEAT1, is overproduced in this cancer. How it drives the disease was not well studied. The team set out to trace its role.

They measured NEAT1 in a public dataset and in 71 tumor samples from a Shanghai cancer center. Lab assays showed NEAT1 helps cancer cells grow, move, and invade. It works by binding a protein called DDX5. That pairing switches on the Wnt and beta-catenin pathway, a known growth signal. The work names NEAT1 as a possible target for future treatment.
europmc-pmc6138951:
Vidaurre and co-authors present a methods article in NeuroImage on finding changing brain networks in large datasets. Brain activity shifts moment to moment, at rest and during tasks. Older methods used sliding time windows to track that change. Those windows blur what is really happening.

The team improved a hidden Markov model approach. Brain activity is modeled as a sequence of distinct network states. The advance lets the method handle very large datasets. It works for fMRI and MEG data from thousands of people. The authors link it to big open projects like UK Biobank. They expect scale to bring new insight into brain function.
europmc-pmc6213751:
Chi and co-authors review how nerve cells die in brain diseases. In healthy adults, nerve cell death is rare. In diseases like Alzheimer's, cell loss is a core feature. The review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. It links death paths to known disease proteins.

The authors first outline general cell death pathways. They include apoptosis and necroptosis. They then give evidence for each major disease. Proteins covered include Tau and amyloid-beta. Alpha-synuclein, huntingtin, and TDP-43 also feature. Each protein ties to death in a specific disease. The review shows shared themes across diseases. It also shows where each disease has its own pattern.
europmc-pmc6227251:
Platts-Mills and co-authors reanalysed the causes of childhood diarrhoea. Good care in poor settings needs better cause data. Old estimates missed many pathogens. The team applied precise molecular tests to stored samples. The study appeared in The Lancet Global Health.

Samples came from the MAL-ED cohort study. Children aged 0 to 2 were followed at eight sites. Sites included Dhaka, Vellore, and Bhaktapur. The team retested stools with quantitative methods. They refined estimates of each pathogen's share. They also described clinical traits for each cause. The results give a sharper picture of diarrhoea burden. That picture can guide vaccine and care priorities.
europmc-pmc6262051:
Sui and co-authors studied a compound that triggers an iron linked cell death in colon cancer cells. Their study appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. The death form is called ferroptosis. It builds up harmful oxygen species when iron is present. The compound, RSL3, was tested on three colon cancer cell lines. Effects were tracked over a full day of treatment.

Cells died as oxygen species piled up inside them. A guard enzyme called GPX4 fell as death advanced. Iron handling signals rose at the same time. Adding extra GPX4 back to cells cut the death sharply. Dose and time both shaped the response. The authors argue that ferroptosis is a live option for killing colon cancer cells. That route differs from the classic death pathway most drugs use. It may help where standard drugs fail.
europmc-pmc6265251:
Moss and co-authors built an atlas that reads the tissue origin of DNA floating in blood. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Dying cells shed DNA fragments into the blood. Chemical marks on that DNA differ by tissue. The team mapped those marks across twenty-five human tissues and cell types. A method then unmixes a blood sample into its sources.

In healthy donors, white blood cells gave just over half the floating DNA. Red cell precursors gave about thirty percent. Vessel lining cells and liver cells gave small shares. Patient samples matched known clinical facts in sepsis and transplant cases. Cancer samples pointed to the right organs, even when the source was unknown. The atlas opens a window on tissue death across the whole body. It could sharpen liquid biopsy tests.
europmc-pmc6292351:
Wang and co-authors review the chemistry and healing uses of Scutellaria baicalensis. The review appeared in Pharmaceutical Biology. Its roots form Huang-Qin, a famed traditional Chinese medicine. The plant is listed in Chinese, European, and British pharmacopoeias. The team searched English and Chinese sources from 1973 to 2018.

They catalogue 126 small molecules and six polysaccharides from the plant. The compounds fall into four main structural types. Studies report antiviral, anti-tumor, and anti-bacterial effects. Other reported effects include protection for the liver and the brain. The review also maps key steps in how the plant builds its flavonoids. It serves readers who study plant chemistry, drug action, or herbal care.
europmc-pmc6297351:
Muñoz and co-authors compare the genomes of Candida auris and its close kin. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Candida auris is a fungus that resists many drugs. It has caused outbreaks in hospitals around the world. The team built near-complete genomes for its four main clades. They added three related species from the same group.

Most mating and meiosis genes were still present in these fungi. Each clade carried one of two mating type loci. The genomes held extra copies of transporter and lipase gene families. Such genes can aid drug resistance and harm to hosts. Changes in the gene ERG11 also stood out. Gene activity tests showed which transporters set this group apart. The work maps traits behind a hard-to-treat pathogen.
europmc-pmc6308051:
Feng and co-authors review lactate dehydrogenase A, an enzyme tied to cancer growth. Their review appeared in Cancer Medicine. The enzyme, short-named LDHA, turns pyruvate into lactate. That step keeps a fast sugar-burning path running in cells. Many cancers show far too much LDHA. High levels track with worse, spreading disease.

The review first covers the enzyme's shape, place, and normal job. It then explains how genes and signals switch LDHA on. Later parts trace its role in tumor growth and spread. The authors also weigh LDHA as a drug target. Blocking it could slow the fuel supply cancers rely on. The piece gives cancer researchers a single map of this enzyme. It points to where new treatments might aim.
europmc-pmc6319251:
Halliday and co-authors test stopping heart drugs after recovery from dilated cardiomyopathy. The pilot trial appeared in The Lancet. Patients had regained normal heart function and felt well. Many ask whether lifelong pills are still needed. The trial assigned 51 patients by chance. Half phased out their heart failure medicines. Half kept taking them for six months.

In the withdrawal group, 44 percent relapsed within six months. No one in the continuation group relapsed. Later, most of that group also tried withdrawal. Nine more patients relapsed after stopping. The authors warn that recovery is often not a cure. Stopping treatment carries real risk for these patients. Close monitoring is vital if withdrawal is tried.
europmc-pmc6341551:
Thomas and Radhakrishnan review how tumor and stroma talk in pancreatic cancer. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer. Pancreatic ductal cancer is among the deadliest cancers. Drugs aimed at cancer cell growth have failed often. Attention has shifted to the tissue around the tumor. Stellate cells there multiply and lay down dense matrix.

That fibrous setting helps tumors grow and spread. It also shields them from drugs. The review covers wound-healing programs the tumor exploits. It covers matrix breakdown and a cell-shape shift called EMT. Each process feeds cancer cell behavior. Stromal parts each add to drug resistance in turn. The authors argue therapy must target the whole setting, not cancer cells alone.
europmc-pmc6391951:
Bijelic and co-authors review polyoxometalates as cancer drugs in Angewandte Chemie. These are clusters of metal and oxygen atoms with many shapes and traits. Lab studies show they can slow many tumor types.

Plain clusters also harm healthy cells and bind too widely, which blocks clinical use. Joining them to organic parts or tiny carriers cuts that harm and boosts effect. The review gathers what is known about how they kill cancer cells. Much of that mechanism is still unclear, the authors say. They map the next steps toward safe medical use.
europmc-pmc6401651:
Caulier and co-authors review antimicrobial compounds from Bacillus subtilis bacteria, in Frontiers in Microbiology. These bacteria form tough spores and make many germ-fighting compounds. Industry uses them to preserve food and protect crops.

The review sorts their weapons by how they are built and what they are made of. Groups include ribosomal peptides, non-ribosomal peptides, polyketides, and volatile compounds. Each group hits a distinct range of germs. The authors build a full map of that spectrum. Such a map helps makers pick the right strain for food or farm use.
europmc-pmc6442651:
Dong and co-authors build a radiomic nomogram that flags hidden peritoneal metastasis in advanced gastric cancer before surgery. CT scans routinely miss these deposits, so patients risk late detection or the wrong operation. The study drew 554 patients from four centers, all called negative on CT; laparoscopy later proved 122 positive and 432 negative.

From 266 image features, signatures of the primary tumor and of the nearby peritoneum both predicted hidden spread, along with Lauren type. Their combined nomogram scored an area under the curve of 0.958 in training and stayed between 0.920 and 0.941 across internal and external validation cohorts. Preoperative use could redirect patients to the right first treatment.
europmc-pmc6460051:
Vines and co-authors review gold nanoparticles for photothermal cancer therapy, where particles parked inside a tumor convert light into tumor-killing heat. Gold has served medicine for centuries and shrinks well to the nanoscale, where its surface can carry antibodies or drugs. Its localized surface plasmon resonance lets it absorb chosen wavelengths, including near-infrared that reaches deeper tissue.

Tuning particle size and shape tunes the heating and the photoacoustic signal used for imaging. Particles drift passively into tumors through leaky vessels and can exit through the urinary system. Synthesis routes, including greener biological ones, and targeting strategies fill the middle sections, with clinical translation still ahead.
europmc-pmc6506551:
Kenry, Chen and Liu review pure organic luminophores that glow at room temperature. Their review appeared in Nature Communications. It covers materials that show phosphorescence without any metal in them. Such glow was once thought to belong only to metal complexes. New molecular design has changed that view in recent years.

The authors explain how these molecules cross into long-lived triplet states. They set out design rules for brighter and longer glow. They cover ways to boost the effect, such as co-crystals and host-guest systems. They also cover steps that make the materials work in water for imaging. The review closes with open problems and likely next steps.
europmc-pmc6509751:
Ciofu and Tolker-Nielsen review how Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms escape drug treatment. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. This bacterium causes long lung infections in cystic fibrosis. It also infects wounds, bladders and lungs on breathing machines. Its cells grow in clumps held in a self-made matrix.

The authors split tolerance from resistance. Tolerance has more than one root. The matrix slows drug entry into the clump. Dormant cells and stress responses help cells survive. Resistance, by contrast, comes from gene changes. Long use of high drug doses drives those changes. The review ends with treatment ideas built on these points.
europmc-pmc6579551:
Humby and co-authors show that the joint lining of early rheumatoid arthritis sorts patients into distinct biological types, writing in Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. About 40% of patients fail standard drugs, with no way to tell in advance. The team biopsied the synovium of 144 untreated patients, then repeated sampling six months into therapy.

Three tissue patterns emerged: lympho-myeloid, rich in B cells; diffuse-myeloid, heavy on myeloid cells; and pauci-immune, dominated by stromal cells with few immune cells. Strong myeloid and lymphoid gene signatures tracked with higher disease activity and better drug response. Lymphoid signatures also matched autoantibody status, while bone-eating gene programs predicted joint damage a year later. Pauci-immune patients ran the mildest course — a step toward biopsy-guided treatment choice.
europmc-pmc6594651:
Lee and co-authors present DeepConv-DTI, a deep learning model that predicts drug-target interactions. Their methods paper appears in PLoS Computational Biology. Finding which proteins a drug binds is a key early step in drug discovery. Wet-lab screening is slow and costly. The model runs convolutions over raw protein sequences. It scans short stretches of amino acids for local patterns. Those patterns act as learned features for each target.

The team trained the model on large-scale interaction data. It beat older models built on hand-crafted protein descriptors. It also beat recent deep learning rivals on unseen data. Pooling maps showed the model flags real binding sites. The code is freely posted on GitHub.
europmc-pmc6628851:
Herforth and co-authors review food-based dietary guidelines from around the world. Their article appears in Advances in Nutrition. National guidelines turn diet science into plain advice for the public. They also shape food and health policy in many countries. No full global comparison of their messages had been done.

The authors drew on the FAO repository of national guidelines. Guidelines exist for 90 countries, with current versions dating from 1986 to 2017. Nearly all urge varied diets rich in fruits, vegetables, and legumes. Nearly all tell people to limit sugar, fat, and salt. Advice on dairy, red meat, and nuts varies much more. WHO advice on nuts, whole grains, and healthy fats is often missing. The authors point to sustainability and culture as future frontiers.
europmc-pmc6683051:
Myers, Kokkinos, and Nyelin review physical activity, fitness, and the metabolic syndrome. Their overview appears in Nutrients. The syndrome clusters waist size, lipids, blood pressure, and insulin resistance. Its spread has climbed for decades. Higher fitness tracks lower syndrome risk again and again. Activity improves each part to some degree. Insulin resistance responds especially clearly. Exercise also raises HDL and lowers triglycerides. Blood pressure and weight improve as well.

No single marker returns to normal through exercise. Combined effects still shift outcomes a lot. Exercise therapy is cheap and effective. Yet doctors underuse it next to drugs. The review details how being fit helps. Prevention and treatment both gain from fitness.
europmc-pmc6711451:
Zeidman and co-authors wrote a hands-on guide to group-level brain connectivity analysis. It is the second part of a two-part guide. The method combines Dynamic Causal Modelling with Parametric Empirical Bayes, a way to compare brain circuits across people. A worked example runs through each step in detail.

At the first level, a model is fit to each person's brain scan data. Those results then feed a group model that splits real group effects from random spread. The guide explains the theory and the prior assumptions behind each choice. Readers can test claims about shared and differing connections across a group.
europmc-pmc6723551:
Childs and co-authors introduce a special issue on diet and immune function. A healthy immune system must stay alert for invaders. It must also tell harmful foreign matter from harmless matter such as food. This preface maps how nutrients shape that balancing act across a lifetime.

The issue covers major nutrients, trace nutrients, and the gut microbiome. Single nutrients can act in several ways at once, and too much of some, such as iron, can weaken defenses. Tailored nutrition may help clinics treat patients. It may also help healthy people delay chronic diseases driven by the immune system. The preface frames the studies that follow it.
europmc-pmc6767151:
Schwarzer and co-authors warn that a popular meta-analysis transform can seriously mislead. Analysts often pool single proportions, such as disease prevalence, across studies. The Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transform is a standard tool for that job. Results must then be turned back to the original scale for reading. That step, the authors show, can go badly wrong.

In a case study of five studies, the back-transformed pooled estimate fell below every single study's own result. Such an outcome is clearly off the mark. The authors urge great caution with this transform for single proportions. Mixed models, they suggest, are a more promising route to honest pooled prevalence figures.
europmc-pmc6798851:
Zhang and co-authors review non-coding RNAs and the networks they form. Genomes are transcribed far beyond protein-coding genes. The non-coding RNAs produced were once dismissed as by-products. Sequencing and computing revealed them as key regulators of gene activity. They partner with coding RNAs, other non-coding RNAs, DNA, and proteins.

The review sorts non-coding RNAs into housekeeping and regulatory types. It covers their functions, interactions, and how they are made, translated in rare cases, and modified. Some RNAs act as sponges that soak up microRNAs, freeing target messages. One message tail, from the versican gene, juggles several microRNAs at once. The integrated network view shows non-coding RNAs as central coordinators of cell regulation.
europmc-pmc6813251:
Yang and co-authors review immune cells in pregnancy in Frontiers in Immunology. A fetus carries genes from both parents, so it is partly foreign to the mother. Her immune system must accept it while still fighting germs. That balance plays out where mother and fetus meet, in the lining of the womb.

The review tracks how cell types there change across a healthy pregnancy. Natural killer cells, macrophages, and T cells each shift in number and role. When the mix goes wrong, problems such as pre-eclampsia, early birth, and repeated loss can follow. The authors compare the healthy pattern with these disorders side by side.
europmc-pmc6838751:
Blazevich and Babault untangle two look-alike effects in Frontiers in Physiology. After a hard contraction, muscle can briefly produce more force. One effect, post-activation potentiation, is a true twitch boost tied to a chemical change in the muscle's myosin. It fades fast, with a half-life of about 28 seconds. Coaches, though, chase a later boost in voluntary power, minutes after the effort.

That later effect, the authors argue, is not the same thing and deserves its own name: post-activation performance enhancement. Fatigue fades while other changes linger, opening a short window of gain. The review covers the history and the mechanisms proposed. It also flags how loosely the older term has been used.
europmc-pmc6853651:
McNair and co-authors present a gene-finding tool in Bioinformatics built for viruses that infect bacteria. These viruses, phages, pack their genomes tightly. Genes sit side by side, overlap, or even nest inside longer genes. Tools made for bacterial genomes miss much of that. No tool had been designed for phage genomes at all.

Their program, PHANOTATE, treats the genome as a network of possible paths. Candidate genes are the routes through it, and the tight packing becomes a clue rather than a nuisance. The authors compare its calls with those of adapted tools on test genomes. They argue phage studies need this purpose-built approach as phage research grows.
europmc-pmc6881351:
Perez and De Palma review dendritic cell vaccines in Nature Communications. Dendritic cells collect antigens and present them to T cells, bridging the first, fast arm of immunity and the targeted one. That makes them a natural vehicle for cancer vaccines. So far, though, such vaccines have underdelivered in the clinic. The authors ask how better cell biology could fix that.

They focus on conventional type 1 dendritic cells, the subset best at priming killer T cells. New methods can now grow genuine versions of these cells at scale. Genetic reprogramming offers another route to build them. The review lays out a design blueprint for personalised vaccines built on this subset.
europmc-pmc6907751:
King and co-authors revisit a famous claim about drug development, in PLOS Genetics. Only about 10 percent of candidate drugs entering early trials win approval. A 2015 study concluded that targets backed by human genetic evidence are twice as likely to succeed. Given the flood of new genome studies since, the figure deserved a fresh test.

Using updated pipeline data, the authors confirm the advantage. Drugs whose targets had genetic support were more likely to pass phase II and phase III trials. The edge was clearest when the causal gene behind the genetic signal could be named with confidence. Their models also adjust for properties of the target and the disease, which sharpen the estimate.
europmc-pmc6942051:
McSwiggen and co-authors urge caution over claims that liquid droplets organise the living cell. Their perspective appeared in Genes and Development. Many cell compartments lack membranes. A popular idea says they form by liquid-liquid phase separation, like oil drops in water. The nucleolus is often cited as the model case.

The authors examine the evidence across several cellular processes. Too often, they find, tests cannot separate true phase separation from other ways molecules could cluster. Much work leans on test-tube experiments instead of proof inside living cells. They call for stricter criteria and better designed experiments. Only then, they argue, can the field judge what these condensates actually do for the cell.
europmc-pmc6943051:
Chen and Wang describe major updates to miRDB, an online database that predicts microRNA targets. Their article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. MicroRNAs are small RNAs that act as master regulators, mainly by turning down their target genes. Knowing those targets is key to knowing what each microRNA does.

A sharper prediction algorithm now powers the database. It holds 3.5 million predicted targets, regulated by 7000 microRNAs across five species. A web server lets users run custom predictions on their own sequences. New cell-specific predictions draw on expression profiles from over 1000 cell lines. A fresh query tool also links predictions with Gene Ontology data to guess microRNA functions. All data remain freely accessible online.
europmc-pmc6954251:
Bai and co-authors design a flexible pressure sensor that stays sensitive from a whisper to a heavy load. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Electronic skins need high sensitivity, but added surface textures usually saturate fast, narrowing the useful range. Poor squeezing room is the cause.

Their design uses grooves with undercuts, shaped so squashed surface features can fold inside. That intrafillable structure squeezes far more before flattening out. The sensor reached sensitivity above 220 per kilopascal across a range from 0.08 pascal to 360 kilopascals. It could resolve pressure steps as small as 18 pascals across the full span, and stayed mechanically stable. The authors expect the same trick to widen the range of other sensor types.
europmc-pmc6962351:
Cerqueira and co-authors review how exercise intensity shapes inflammation in the body. Their systematic review appeared in Frontiers in Physiology. Exercise stirs a strong inflammatory response, calling white blood cells into action and raising signal molecules from immune cells and working muscle. Moderate activity seems to help immunity; long, hard effort may weaken it.

The team screened studies in healthy adults aged 18 to 65 and kept 18 articles. White blood cells rose right after intense exercise, but not after moderate work. Inflammatory signals such as IL-6 rose most after hard bouts, followed by calming IL-10. A general inflammation marker, CRP, climbed after both intensities, peaking up to 28 hours later. Muscle damage markers rose only after long, intense sessions.
europmc-pmc7003451:
Liu and co-authors review how probiotic surface parts and products protect the gut wall. Their review appeared in Microbial Cell Factories. Gut microbes strongly shape the intestinal barrier, the single cell layer that keeps gut contents out of body tissue. Friendly bacteria help hold that line.

Helpful strains include Lactobacillus, Bifidobacteria, and newer candidates such as Akkermansia muciniphila. Their surface features, including surface proteins, flagella, pili, and sugar capsules, match receptors on gut cells. Those contacts trigger signals that calm inflammation and block cell suicide, strengthening the barrier. Products the bacteria release work too: proteins, organic acids, indole, vesicles, and bacteria-killing compounds. The authors explain each route in molecular detail. Earlier reviews mixed in pathogens and the immune system; this one stays on probiotics and the barrier itself.
europmc-pmc7026051:
Pratap and co-authors report a cross-study evaluation in NPJ Digital Medicine. Remote health studies run through phone apps can recruit huge numbers fast. Their weak point is retention: most people stop taking part within days. That dropout can bias the data such studies collect.

The team pooled app data from eight remote studies run between 2014 and 2019. Over 100,000 people completed nearly 3.5 million health checks in all. Median retention ranged from 2 to 26 days per study. Referral by a clinician added the most retention time, the authors report. Pay, having the condition under study, and older age also helped. Four patterns of daily app use emerged. Most studies also failed to match United States diversity.
europmc-pmc7055351:
Van Velzen and co-authors pool brain scans to study white matter in depression in Molecular Psychiatry. Changes in white matter microstructure have been tied to major depressive disorder, but earlier studies disagreed, partly through small samples and the illness's variety. The ENIGMA consortium's depression working group ran the largest multi-site analysis to date, harmonising imaging and statistics across centres.

The study compared 1,305 patients and 1,602 healthy controls, aged from 12 to 88, drawn from 20 cohorts worldwide. Adult patients showed subtle but widespread lower fractional anisotropy, a measure of fibre coherence, in 16 of 25 white matter tracts examined. The strongest effects sat in the corpus callosum and corona radiata. Radial diffusivity ran higher across the brain. Differences were driven mainly by patients with recurrent depression and adult onset. The work gives the field effect sizes it can trust, if modest ones.
europmc-pmc7066851:
Zhang and co-authors pattern RNA methylation in stomach cancer in Molecular Cancer. The m6A mark is a chemical tag placed on RNA by a set of regulator proteins. Whether those tagging patterns shape the immune cells inside a tumour was unknown. The team evaluated modification patterns across 1,938 gastric cancer samples using 21 known m6A regulators.

Three distinct patterns emerged. Their immune landscapes matched the three known tumour immune types: inflamed, excluded, and desert. A scoring system, the m6Ascore, quantified each tumour's pattern. Low scores marked inflamed tumours with more mutations and active immunity, and those patients had a 69.4 percent five-year survival. High scores marked stroma-rich tumours where immune cells were locked out, and survival was poorer. Scoring individual tumours also tracked stage, subtype, and genetic variation. The work suggests an RNA-tagging fingerprint could help predict which gastric cancers immunotherapy can reach.
europmc-pmc7081551:
Wei and co-authors review how noncoding RNAs help gastric cancer resist treatment, in Molecular Cancer. Gastric cancer ranks among the most common cancers worldwide, and advanced cases often rely on chemotherapy or targeted drugs. Resistance, present from the start or gained later, causes many treatments to fail.

Three kinds of noncoding RNA get close attention: microRNAs, long noncoding RNAs, and circular RNAs. Each can change how cancer cells respond to chemotherapy agents and targeted drugs. The review sums up the known mechanisms and argues these RNAs could serve as new treatment targets or as markers that predict how a patient will respond.
europmc-pmc7084551:
Yong, Valiyaveettil, and Tang review what is known about harm from microplastics and nanoplastics in mammals, in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Tiny plastic fragments are widespread in the environment. Damage has been well documented in sea animals, but effects in mammals are only now being studied.

People mostly swallow these particles in food or from food packaging, and may also breathe them in. Mouse studies and human cell tests report changes to gut microbes plus cell and metabolic toxicity. Particles seem able to build up in tissues. The authors stress that the long-term effects in humans remain unclear and call for work that pins down the mechanisms.
europmc-pmc7100151:
Taberna and co-authors review the multidisciplinary team approach to head and neck cancer care, in Frontiers in Oncology. These cancers threaten speech, swallowing, and breathing. No single specialist can cover all the needs they create. Care is now led by teams that plan treatment together.

The review sets out the roles of each team member. Surgeons and oncologists sit beside nurses, dietitians, psycho-oncologists, and social workers. Older patients may need onco-geriatricians as well. The authors argue that research teams should join too, to close the gap with daily practice. Readers see how each discipline adds to care at diagnosis, through treatment, and in follow-up. The result is a model for better quality of life, not just longer survival.
europmc-pmc7124951:
Ohannessian, Duong, and Odone call for telemedicine to be built into health systems worldwide for the COVID-19 fight, in JMIR Public Health and Surveillance. By 31 March 2020, more than 720,000 cases had been reported across more than 203 countries. Video consultations had scaled up fast in the United Kingdom and the United States to cut transmission risk.

Most countries still lack rules to authorise, integrate, and pay for telemedicine, even in emergencies, the authors note. Italy did not count it among essential care, while France authorised and reimbursed it at once. The authors update an earlier outbreak framework and urge all parties to fix the gaps, so remote care can serve this and future outbreaks safely.
europmc-pmc7163451:
Chen and co-authors test a two-drug combination against hard-to-treat KRAS mutant colorectal cancer cells, in Theranostics. Mutations in KRAS blunt the antibody drug cetuximab, a mainstay for metastatic colorectal cancer. The team paired cetuximab with beta-elemene, a compound from the Chinese herb Curcumae Rhizoma, hunting for a different killing route.

The pair worked in synergy, with the best effect at 125 micrograms per millilitre of beta-elemene plus 25 of cetuximab. Death was not the usual apoptosis: the cells accumulated iron-driven reactive oxygen, lost their glutathione shield, and showed the protein pattern of ferroptosis, an iron-based death program. The combination also blocked the shape-shifting linked to spread, and slowed tumors in an animal model.
europmc-pmc7226751:
Roehlen and co-authors review the mechanisms of liver fibrosis and the search for treatments. Their article appeared in Cells. Fibrosis, or scarring, follows chronic liver injury from viruses or metabolic disease. It predicts progression and raises the risk of liver cancer. Diseases differ in cause, yet the scarring pattern is shared.

Work over the last decade transformed understanding of that pattern. Removing the cause, such as curing a viral infection, can reverse scarring. But reversal is often too slow to prevent dangerous complications. Advanced fibrosis especially needs direct anti-scarring drugs. None is yet established. The review gathers current concepts of how scar tissue forms and resolves. It sets out where therapy developers are looking next.
europmc-pmc7227451:
Yi and co-authors pinpoint the exact amino acids where the SARS-CoV-2 spike grips its human receptor. Their study appeared in Cellular & Molecular Immunology. The spike's binding domain attaches to ACE2 to start infection. Both this virus and the earlier SARS virus use that route. The team tested which residues in the binding motif matter most.

They checked the same spots against available neutralizing antibodies. Immunizing mice with binding domains from either virus produced strong antibody responses. Responses crossed between the two viruses to a degree. Knowing the key contact points guides vaccine design. It also helps predict whether antibodies will keep working as the virus changes. The study supplies a residue-level map for drug and vaccine work.
europmc-pmc7241451:
El-Sayed Ahmed and co-authors review colistin, an old antibiotic revived against resistant superbugs. Their extended review appeared in Emerging Microbes & Infections. It covers the years 2000 to 2019. Multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria now defeat frontline drug families. Carbapenems and other broad-spectrum agents often fail against them. Few new antibiotics can beat these pathogens.

Colistin, long shelved as too toxic, returned as a last-hope treatment. It is one of only two polymyxins sold for clinical use. The review tracks how bacteria resist even this fallback drug. Efflux pumps that expel the drug are one mechanism found. Resistance genes and their spread receive close attention. The authors weigh colistin's shrinking value against its risks. Their survey maps a front line of the resistance crisis.
europmc-pmc7278251:
Di Renzo and co-authors survey how the COVID-19 lockdown changed eating and daily habits in Italy. Their survey appeared in the Journal of Translational Medicine. Italy imposed strict home confinement early in the pandemic. The questionnaire ran from April 5 to April 24, 2020, and gathered answers from 3533 respondents aged 12 to 86 years, of whom 76.1% were female.

Questions covered diet, including adherence to the Mediterranean diet, plus shopping, smoking, sleep, and physical activity. Many respondents felt they had gained weight during confinement. Reported weight and height let the team track body changes alongside food choices. The study captures how a sudden break in routine reshapes everyday health behavior, information public health planners need when confinement lasts for weeks.
europmc-pmc7384151:
Burgess and co-authors write the standard guidelines for Mendelian randomization in Wellcome Open Research. Mendelian randomization uses inherited gene variants as natural experiments to test whether a risk factor causes a disease. Done badly, it misleads, so the field needed a shared playbook.

Ten sections walk through the whole job: motivation, data sources, choosing variants, aligning data, the main analysis, and checks on the result. Extensions, presentation, and interpretation get their own sections. The audience is double, both researchers writing studies and editors and reviewers judging them. The guidelines are living, updated on feedback and at least every 24 months; this version is the summer 2023 update.
europmc-pmc7415151:
Warrier and co-authors examine autism rates among transgender and gender-diverse people in Nature Communications. Clinic reports had suggested a link, but large community samples were lacking. The team combined five independently recruited datasets totaling 641,860 people, with diagnoses and self-report trait measures.

Compared with cisgender people, transgender and gender-diverse participants had higher rates of autism and of other neurodevelopmental and psychiatric diagnoses. They also scored higher on autistic traits, systemizing, and sensory sensitivity, and lower on empathy measures, whether autistic or not. The authors draw a clinical lesson: services should improve access and tailor mental health care for this group. The paper is descriptive, not causal, and it says so plainly.
europmc-pmc7449951:
Rodríguez-Pérez and Bajorath explain how to interpret machine learning models in drug research. Black-box models limit trust and use in pharmacy work. The SHAP method assigns each feature a share in a model's prediction.

SHAP works with any model, from tree ensembles to deep neural networks. It ranks the features that drive compound class and activity forecasts. The authors test an exact Shapley value method for decision trees. They compare it with the general model-free SHAP approach on potency tasks. New uses include reading deep network models that predict activity on many targets at once. Ensemble regression models for potency also get the SHAP treatment. The work aids clear, checkable model use.
europmc-pmc7486751:
Kang and co-authors trace how IL-6 signaling drives a clotting factor in cytokine release syndrome. This syndrome is a life-threatening surge of inflammation. No targeted immune therapy existed for it.

In patients with sepsis, lung failure syndrome, and burns, IL-6 drove output of inflammatory cytokines and of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, or PAI-1. The signal ran through vessel lining cells by the trans-signaling route. PAI-1 blocks clot breakdown, so its rise links inflammation to clotting risk. Blocking IL-6 signaling with tocilizumab lowered PAI-1 output. It also eased symptoms in severe COVID-19 patients in this work. The authors mark IL-6 blockade as a candidate therapy. The path may serve several hyperinflammatory states at once.
europmc-pmc7575751:
Chen, Yu, Kang and Tang review iron metabolism in ferroptosis. Ferroptosis is a regulated cell death driven by iron. It ends with membrane rupture and release of damage signals.

Iron drives reactive oxygen species in this process. It also drives enzyme activity in fat peroxidation. Control points cover iron uptake, storage and export. Gene and protein controls set how sensitive cells are. Faulty ferroptosis links to cancer and brain diseases. It also links to ischemia-reperfusion injury in tissues. Iron chelators can block ferroptosis from occurring. The review sums up models of iron control in this death pathway. Treatment ideas for iron-linked disorders are highlighted.
europmc-pmc7579351:
Ramón-Arbués and co-authors estimate depression, anxiety and stress among college students. Mental health problems are a major public health issue. Students face study pressure and life changes at once.

The study used the DASS-21 scale for distress. A sample of 1074 college students took part. Depression symptoms appeared in 18.4% of students. Anxiety symptoms appeared in 23.6% of the sample. Stress symptoms were highest at 34.5% overall. Problem internet use linked to all three outcomes. Smoking, insomnia and low self-esteem also linked to them. Age under 21 raised risk across outcomes. The authors urge action to promote student mental health on campus.
europmc-pmc7589951:
Al Bander, Nitert, Mousa and Naderpoor give an overview of gut bacteria and inflammation in the body. Gut bacteria aid food use, immune control and defense against infection in the host. Some bacteria link to signals that can start inflammation in body tissues.

Inflammation sits beneath many long-term conditions that affect whole body health. These include obesity, artery disease, type 2 diabetes and bowel disease in patients. Parts of bacteria can trigger pathways that release signals in tissues. Other bacterial products can calm those pathways in the gut. Short-chain fatty acids are one such calming product made by gut bacteria. Bacteria mixes differ by person due to diet and family traits. That spread may explain why the same disease looks different across patients. It may also explain varied responses to the same treatment across people. The review notes gaps and the promise of probiotic care.
europmc-pmc7794651:
Howe and co-authors explain how manual curation greatly improves genome assemblies. Assemblies underpin much of modern biology. Error-free assemblies remain an unmet goal. Automated pipelines still miss that mark for complex genomes.

Expert review bridges the gap for now. Curators check assemblies and fix errors by hand. This cuts error counts a lot. Lessons from curation feed back into the automated pipelines. The authors describe their method with gEVAL, a genome evaluation browser. They also give advice that works without gEVAL. The goal is wider use of curation across the genomics community.
europmc-pmc7886651:
Tay and co-authors present a review of CD4+ T cells in cancer immunotherapy. Most cancer immunotherapy aims at CD8+ killer T cells. Helper CD4+ cells have stayed in the background. The review argues that this split view no longer fits the evidence.

The authors describe the many roles CD4+ cells play against tumours. These cells can attack tumours directly. They also direct and sustain the wider immune response. The review notes a striking pattern: CD4+ responses often target epitopes drawn from the body's own proteins. That finding raises design questions for new therapies. The authors argue that using the full power of CD4+ cells could improve treatment. Readers get a fresh map of an old paradigm under revision.
europmc-pmc8022551:
Kim and co-authors assess new cancer therapies that target the TGF-β pathway. TGF-β is a signaling cytokine that can either suppress or promote tumors. As a promoter, it speeds growth, invasion, and spread. It also shields tumors from immune attack and feeds drug resistance. That double life makes the pathway a tempting but tricky target.

The review judges antagonists from many drug classes now in trials. Small molecule inhibitors, antibodies, ligand traps, antisense drugs, and vaccines all feature. The authors highlight Vactosertib, a potent receptor kinase inhibitor with a sound safety record. Ligand traps such as Bintrafusp alfa and AVID200 get close attention. The core challenge is blocking the tumor-promoting side only. Biomarkers to pick the right patients remain a pressing need.
europmc-pmc8037451:
Reddy and co-authors compare natural and synthetic biopolymer composite scaffolds for tissue engineering. Scaffolds carry cells and drugs into damaged tissue, where new growth takes hold. Choosing the right polymer decides whether that repair works. Materials may be natural or synthetic, degradable or lasting. Each choice trades strength against friendliness to cells.

The review surveys the main polymers of both families and their composites. It weighs biocompatibility, biodegradability, and mechanical strength for each. Morphology, pore size, and porosity get the same treatment. Fabrication techniques are laid out in tables. A few commercial biopolymers appear as well. The aim is a practical guide for matching scaffold to task. Tissue targets range from small patches to whole organs.
europmc-pmc8043951:
Gerrits and co-authors separate the microglia tied to amyloid from those tied to tau in Alzheimer's disease. Microglia guard the brain and are deeply implicated in the disease. Mouse models show one activated type, but human profiles were unclear. The team sequenced single nuclei from donor brains. Their set held 482,472 nuclei from controls and patients. Some patient brains bore amyloid only, others amyloid plus tau.

Two disease-linked microglia profiles emerged from the data. The AD1 type tracked tissue amyloid load and gathered at plaques. It looked phagocytic and activated. The AD2 type tracked phospho-tau load instead. It grew abundant only where tau pathology was overt. The split matters for therapy design. A drug aimed at one microglia state may miss the other completely.
europmc-pmc8066851:
Speranza and co-authors review dopamine as the neuromodulator behind lasting synaptic change, reward, and movement. Dopamine shapes motor control, mood, and the drive to repeat rewards. It also tunes higher mental functions. When its signaling fails, the fallout is severe. Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia, and addiction all trace back to it.

The review follows dopamine through two forms of synaptic plasticity. Long-term potentiation and long-term depression both bend under its hand. The authors cover these effects across cortical and deep brain areas. Dendritic spines, the tiny seats of synapses, get close attention. There dopamine sits between the motor and cognitive systems. Three diseases anchor the discussion throughout. Parkinson's disease, vascular dementia, and schizophrenia show what broken tuning costs. The picture is of one molecule with many levers.
europmc-pmc8067651:
Wemheuer and co-authors present Tax4Fun2, a tool that predicts what a microbial community does from its 16S rRNA genes. Sequencing those genes names the microbes in a sample. Names alone cannot say what the community can do. Prediction tools fill the gap, but they lean on public genome databases. Those databases often miss the microbes of the ecosystem under study.

Tax4Fun2 improves on PICRUSt and the first Tax4Fun in accuracy tests. Predicted profiles matched metagenome profiles from the same samples closely. Users can add their own habitat-specific genomes to sharpen the fit. The tool also predicts functional gene redundancy. That measure hints at how well a community withstands disturbance. Redundancy scores matched those from simulated communities. The R package runs on modest hardware, with no cluster needed.
europmc-pmc8118651:
Hägg and Jylhävä review how biological aging differs between women and men. Women live longer than men in nearly every country. Molecular clocks also rate women as biologically younger. Yet a paradox haunts the end of life. Women arrive there frailer, with worse health scores. Men keep better physical function in the same years. Many age diseases strike the sexes on different schedules.

The review gathers human studies, backed by animal work. Hallmarks of aging, from telomere wear to cell senescence, get a sex split. Sex chromosomes offer one set of explanations. Hormones supply another, shifting across the life course. Theories of aging are tested against the split. Why longer life pairs with weaker late health stays open. The authors press for sex-aware aging science. Drugs and trials that ignore the split may mislead both sexes.
europmc-pmc8205851:
Mitchell and co-authors test MDMA-assisted therapy for severe post-traumatic stress disorder. Current treatments help many patients only modestly. This phase 3 trial ran at several sites with a strict design.

After a washout from psychiatric drugs, 90 participants were assigned at random. Half received MDMA with therapy, half received placebo with therapy. Care included three preparatory and nine integrative sessions. Many participants also carried depression, dissociation, or past substance use. The trial judged both benefit and safety. Its design set a high bar for a contested treatment. Severe PTSD with common extra conditions was the target group.
europmc-pmc8314151:
Nikolov and co-authors build a deep learning tool that segments head and neck anatomy for radiotherapy. Over half a million people a year face head and neck cancer. Radiotherapy can cure it, but planning is slow.

Experts must outline radiosensitive organs by hand. That delays treatment and varies between operators. Dose errors can follow from shaky outlines. The team trained a 3D U-Net to draw 21 organs at risk. They tested it against expert performance. The aim was expert-level accuracy at machine speed. Such tools could free planners for harder judgements.
europmc-pmc8721651:
Wang and co-authors review the airborne spread of respiratory viruses, with lessons drawn from SARS-CoV-2. For a century, large droplets and touched surfaces were seen as the main routes. Small aerosols that float in air were often downplayed. The pandemic forced a fresh look at that view.

Evidence now shows many respiratory viruses spread through inhaled aerosols. These tiny particles can travel short and long distances in air flows. The authors argue airborne spread may dominate for several viruses, SARS-CoV-2 among them. They trace how infection starts from this route. Better grasp of the route can sharpen control steps such as ventilation and mask use.
europmc-pmc8779751:
Lopes and co-authors review treatments and advances for peripheral nerve injury from a One Health view. Such injuries stem from trauma or medical procedures. They can cause loss of movement and feeling, disability, and nerve pain. The review first details nerve anatomy and the main injury types.

Care options span surgery, drugs, and cell-based therapy. Cells are often paired with tube guides made from biomaterials. Even with many options, full recovery stays hard to reach. The authors stress new therapies for severe lesions. They also cover how to judge nerve regrowth in lab and animal models. Sound models are key to moving gains into human care.
europmc-pmc8822551:
Wilkinson and Gathani set out breast cancer as a worldwide health problem. It is now the most often diagnosed cancer on Earth. Global figures count 2.26 million new cases in 2020. The disease is also the top cause of cancer death in women. Rates rise as countries develop. Survival, though, lags far behind in poorer regions.

The authors trace the gaps to late diagnosis and poor access to care. They describe the World Health Organization's Global Breast Cancer Initiative. Its three pillars are health promotion, timely diagnosis, and full treatment with supportive care. The article gives readers a compact global picture. It shows where the burden falls and what might ease it.
europmc-pmc8998851:
Buonacera and co-authors review the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio as a mirror of immune balance in disease. The ratio comes from a routine blood count. One cell type drives the first, fast immune response. The other carries the slower, targeted response. Their ratio flags the body's inflammatory state. Over the last 10 years, studies of it have boomed. It predicts death in the general public. It also predicts outcomes in sepsis, pneumonia, and cancer.

COVID-19 gave the marker a fresh role. It helped guide admission choices for lung cases. No single cut-off value has won agreement yet. The review explains the biology under the number. It traces how each cell arm shifts in illness. Disease sections follow the marker's record. The authors call it a cheap, sturdy signal. It reflects both inflammation and adaptive strength. Standard cut-offs are the missing piece.
europmc-pmc9007451:
Dickson, Walker, and Gould extend the AMBER lipid force field to cover realistic cell membranes. Force fields are the rule books for atomic simulations. The older lipid set covered only a few fat types. Real membranes mix far more kinds. The new set, Lipid21, adds charged lipids. It adds fats with many double bonds. It adds sphingomyelin, a key raft fat. Head group twist rules were refit. Chain rules were updated as well.

Long test runs checked the new rules against lab data. Fit with measured order values improved. The melting point match for a standard fat improved too. Mixed raft-like membranes were simulated next. Adding more polyunsaturated fat disturbed cholesterol's behavior. The rules follow the AMBER style throughout. They mix freely with protein and drug rule sets. Membrane modelers gain a fuller palette.
europmc-pmc9113351:
Putri and co-authors introduce HTSeq 2.0, a Python toolkit for high-throughput sequencing data. The software counts reads from genes and helps users study expression and other traits. Version 2.0 adds a wider programming interface and a new way to store sparse genomic data. It also adds full Python 3 support.

Upgrades to the htseq-count script suit the rise of single-cell studies. It can now handle many files at once and use several processor cores. New output formats ease import into popular analysis tools. A new script handles data tagged with cell and molecule barcodes. Better docs, tests, and bug fixes round out the release. Users get a free tool built for modern sequencing work.
europmc-pmc9178451:
Jakob and co-authors systematically review what helps or hinders adherence to mobile health apps for chronic diseases. Such apps can support patients and health systems as these diseases grow more common. Yet many users stop using them as intended. The team searched five databases for studies from January 2007 to December 2020.

Of 2,862 articles, 99 met the criteria. Four app traits helped across all health domains. They were personal tailoring, tailored reminders, friendly and stable design, and personal support beside the app. Social and game features also helped in several domains. Average adherence across apps was 56.0% of intended use. The authors urge clearer reporting of intended and actual use in future studies.
europmc-pmc9184651:
Yuan and co-authors map signaling pathways in chronic kidney disease and the therapies that target them. This disease means lasting kidney dysfunction, with nephron loss, inflammation, and scar tissue buildup. Fat toxicity and oxidative stress drive the loss of nephrons. Injured kidney cells then call in immune cells.

The review sorts pathways by the process they drive. Some govern inflammation, like NF-kappaB and the NLRP3 inflammasome. Others switch on scar-forming cells and matrix deposits. For each path, the authors introduce drugs aimed at blocking it. Unifying these paths should advance both lab and clinical work. Readers get an updated map of a slow, common, and deadly disease process.
europmc-pmc9210451:
Reynolds and co-authors show that immune boosting by Omicron infection depends on a person's prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure. Omicron carries many spike mutations and partly escapes neutralizing antibodies. The team studied T and B cell immunity in triple-vaccinated healthcare workers. Their past infection histories differed in known ways.

Immunity to earlier variants grew stronger after three vaccine doses. But responses against Omicron spike itself were smaller. Past Alpha infection left less durable binding antibody against Omicron. Workers first infected during the Omicron wave gained against older variants but responded weakly to Omicron. Past infection with the original strain even erased some cross-reactive gains. History, the authors conclude, shapes each boost.
europmc-pmc9348751:
Tang and co-authors test whether mRNA vaccination builds immune defense inside the airways against SARS-CoV-2. Blood responses after vaccination are strong, but the virus enters through the respiratory tract. The team compared lung wash fluid and blood from vaccinated people and recovered patients. Mouse experiments tested ways to close any gap.

Vaccinated people had far weaker neutralizing antibodies in lung fluid than recovered patients. Their spike-specific B and T cells were missing from lung fluid too. In mice, shots alone gave weak airway protection, above all against Omicron BA.1.1. Adding an airway-delivered adenovirus vaccine built strong local defense. It covered the original virus and the Omicron variant. The authors call for mucosal boosters to block infection at the door.
europmc-pmc9454251:
Lin and co-authors probe how nanoplastics harm mitochondria in human liver and lung cells. Plastic debris is building up across the living world. Tiny plastic particles can reach organs with key metabolic jobs. How they damage cell power plants was not clear.

The team exposed liver L02 cells and lung BEAS-2B cells to 80 nm particles. The particles entered the cells but caused no mass cell death. Under the microscope, mitochondria showed clear damage. Harm signs included excess reactive oxygen species and lost membrane voltage. Breathing of the mitochondria also fell. Effects showed at doses as low as 0.0125 mg/mL. Untargeted metabolomics pointed to mitochondria linked paths as the most hit. Liver cells proved more sensitive than lung cells.
europmc-pmc9519451:
Vassallo and co-authors use a functional selection to find hidden anti-phage defence systems in E. coli. Bacteria and their viruses have fought for ages. Known shields include restriction systems and CRISPR-Cas. Computer screens hunt new shields in defence islands. Such screens may miss systems that sit elsewhere.

The team built a selection that ignores genome context. They screened 71 diverse E. coli strains for defence power. The hunt found 21 conserved defence systems. None had shown up as enriched in defence islands before. Intact prophages and mobile elements proved to be key reservoirs. These elements carry and spread the systems across strains. Hotspots in them held dozens more uncharacterized candidates. The method can map defence systems in other species too.
europmc-pmc9763451:
Guo and co-authors test whether a blood inflammation index tracks diabetic kidney disease. The index blends platelet, neutrophil, and lymphocyte counts. Immune activity is thought to feed type 2 diabetes harm. Kidney disease is the most common fallout of that harm.

The team used national survey data on adults with type 2 diabetes. The sample held 3,937 patients in total for the study. Of those, 1,510 patients met the kidney disease marks. Models that adjusted for other factors kept the link. High index levels went with higher kidney disease odds. The link held across age, sex, and weight subgroups. No tested factor changed the tie in a real way. The authors call the index a cheap screening aid. They say forward looking studies must confirm its worth. The index needs no special lab work beyond blood counts.
fielding-amelia-1751:
Amelia, published in 1751, was Fielding's last novel, and his most serious. It draws on the troubles of his own first marriage and his years as a London magistrate. Many readers rank its heroine among the finest women in early fiction.

Amelia Booth stays loyal to her husband Billy, a charming, weak ex-officer ruined by debt, drink, and prison. Fielding shows the sponging houses, bailiffs, and corrupt courts that ground the poor of London. The tone is tender and angry at once. Amelia sold more slowly than Tom Jones, but later critics, Dickens among them, praised its truth and pathos.
finney-systematic-theology-1851:
Finney's Lectures on Systematic Theology, published in 1851, give the Oberlin evangelist's complete doctrinal system in his own words. Finney taught theology at Oberlin College in Ohio, where his revival preaching had already reshaped American evangelical life. The lectures were his classroom teaching, set down in full.

His system is known as moral-government theology: God rules as a moral governor, and sinners can repent because the will is truly free. Finney argues point by point against the stricter Calvinism in which he had been raised. The book remains the fullest statement of Oberlin theology and of revivalist doctrine.
firmicus-maternus-mathesis-1551: Julius Firmicus Maternus's Mathesis, in this 1551 Latin edition, is the great Roman handbook of astrology. The 4th-century author lays out how the stars were read to foretell a life. It is the fullest surviving guide to how Rome practiced the art.
firmicus-maternus-mathesis-latin-1551:
Julius Firmicus Maternus wrote Rome's fullest handbook of the stars in the fourth century. Mathesis, in the Latin printing of 1551, gives his eight books in their old form. The 1551 edition is a fine Renaissance print of a late Roman work.

Firmicus teaches the whole art of casting a birth chart: planets, houses, lots, and the fates read from them. He mixes hard rules with praise of the star craft and scorn for its frauds. No Latin book of astrology to survive matches its scope. The old print lets readers meet the work as Renaissance scholars did.
five-treatises-of-the-philosophers-stone:
Pinnell brings old alchemy into English in Five Treatises of the Philosopher's Stone, printed in 1652. Henry Pinnell saw the book through the press for the Earl of Pembroke and Montgomery. Two of the treatises are ascribed to Alphonso, king of Portugal, and said to be taken from his own closet. One is by John Sawtre, a monk, and another by Florianus Raudorff, a German philosopher.

A treatise on the names of the stone, by Guglielmo Gratarolo, and the Smaragdine Table close the set. The sampled pages warn the worker about fire: take heed that the fire be not set too soon, lest the matter be made red before its due time. The solution of the body and the congelation of the spirit must be made with a light decoction and a moist putrefaction of forty days. The book is a working manual of the old art.
frus-1861-d151:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 September 1861. The dispatch is document 151 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton's early September report keeps the Paris watch at its steady pace. He had learned the court's moods and could read small signs. Washington drew on that feel when it judged how far French patience with the war might stretch. Feel for a court cannot be taught by cable, and Dayton had it in full. Feel for a court is the one tool no office at home could supply by mail.
frus-1861-d251:
The home office spoke to James Shepherd Pike on 5 September 1861, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 251 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d51:
On 8 June 1861, William H. Seward sent a brief letter to Charles Francis Adams in London. The letter is document 51 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward sent Adams frequent, brief direction through the summer of 1861. Each letter dealt with the point then at hand, from notes to claims. This June note is one stroke in a run of orders that kept London's envoy and Washington's chief in close step despite the slow mails. Brief orders suited Adams, who liked clear tasks and disliked loose talk in state papers. Clear tasks also let Adams answer fast when a point turned hot in talks.
frus-1862-d151:
