From London on 25 September 1862, Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. Adams was the American minister to Britain, and his reports home appear throughout the 1862 Foreign Relations volume; this one is Document 151.

An envoy's report mixed what he had done, what officials had said to him, and what the press and public seemed to think. Seward read these London letters to judge the risk that Britain might back the Confederacy or push for a truce. Reports like this one were the government's eyes in the capital that mattered most. Earl Russell, the British foreign secretary, was the minister Adams dealt with most in London.
frus-1862-d251:
On 3 February 1862 William L. Dayton wrote from Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward, in a report printed as Document 251 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton had served as American minister to France since 1861.

Early February brought the fall of Fort Henry in Tennessee, the first big Union win of the year. Such news mattered in Paris, where bets on the war's length guided French choices. Dayton's reports mixed court talk with press and market reaction, giving Seward the raw material for his replies to the French legation in Washington. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d351:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward closed the year with a letter to Henri Mercier dated 31 December 1861, printed as Document 351 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Mercier was France's minister in Washington.

New Year's Eve 1861 found the Trent crisis settled and French, British, and Spanish troops landing in Mexico. Seward faced a year ahead in which France would test American patience on two fronts. His year-end letter to Mercier is a fitting close to the French file's first chapter: courteous in form, careful in substance. Seward tested what Mercier said against what Dayton reported from Paris, week by week.
frus-1862-d451:
On 17 February 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to John Lothrop Motley at the legation in Vienna. The instruction is Document 451 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed record.

February brought Union victories at Fort Henry and Fort Donelson, and Seward was quick to put such news in his ministers' hands. Motley in Vienna had to counter a court press that often took the Confederacy's side. Orders from Washington gave him the facts and the argument: the rebellion was failing, and foreign backing for it would be wasted. The letter is one move in the paper campaign the Union fought in every European capital that winter.
frus-1862-d51:
From abroad on 24 April 1862, Charles Francis Adams sent Seward his latest account. It stands as Document 51 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d551:
Roest van Limburg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 October 1862. His note is Document 551 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

October brought the Dutch minister a Washington calmer than September's, with Lee back in Virginia and the intervention scare cooling. Van Limburg's note took up the standing business of his legation, which centered on Dutch trade and the treatment of neutral shipping. The Netherlands file in the volume never rises to crisis, and that is its historical value. It records the normal temperature of relations between the Union and a friendly maritime power. It does so in the middle of a civil war.
frus-1862-d651:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this letter to Townsend Harris on 23 July 1861. Harris was the American minister in Japan, the man who had won the 1858 trade treaty with the shogun's court. The letter is document 651 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Seward's letters to his envoys carried orders, news from home, and the line each post was to take. This one went out in the first summer of the Civil War, when Washington had few men and little money to spare for far-off posts. It shows the State Department still steering its Japan mission week by week, even with a war on.
frus-1863p1-d151:
Charles Francis Adams closed his mail day with this third dispatch of 9 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 151 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The third sheet of a set often sent the day's last facts or a name to note for the files. Adams's close of 9 April sits in that place. His April letters, read whole, chart the weeks when Britain first curbed the South's shipbuilding in earnest. This one is the tail of a day's work in that turn, plain in tone and firm in its facts.
frus-1863p1-d251: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 28 July 1863. It is document 251 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d351:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 January 1863. His note is document 351 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Seward kept every note, and the State Department printed the exchange for Congress. Reading Lyons's side shows how the crisis looked from the other desk. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d451:
Secretary of State William H. Seward received a letter dated 7 April 1863 from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d51: Dated 27 October 1862, this untitled paper is document 51 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It sits among the Confederate papers in that part of the volume, near the Mallory and Memminger letters. The evidence gives the date and the spot in the run, but no title, no writer, and no one addressed.
frus-1863p1-d551:
In the flow of wartime mail, Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons wrote to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 5 June 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the early summer of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d651:
On 30 October 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d151: Patrick Hurley, the President's personal representative, wrote to Roosevelt on November 20, 1943, and the report is Document 151 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hurley traveled widely on the president's errands in the Middle East and Asia, and his blunt reports were a known White House taste. The record gives the date and the two men and no subject. The report is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d251:
An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers an informal evening gathering at Cairo on 22 November 1943, for which no minutes were taken or have been found. The time and the names of those present come from the President's Log, and the editors piece the purpose together from three published accounts.

Admiral Leahy records that the Combined Chiefs joined the President's dinner party after the meal. Lord Mountbatten laid out his plans and needs for the Burma campaign assigned to him at Quebec. General Alanbrooke calls the aim a discussion of Mountbatten's plans to prepare for meetings with Chiang Kai-shek. The editors doubt the Chinese party listed in the Log actually attended.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d351:
Harry Hopkins telegraphed Steve Early, the President's secretary, from Tehran on 2 December 1943, fixing the release of the next conference statement. Sent by military channels, the short message looks ahead to the Tehran communiqué and back at the troubled Cairo release.

The Tehran text, Hopkins states, will be released for publication at one in the afternoon, Washington time, and eight in the evening, Moscow time, on 6 December. The details of the release are to follow. He also asks Early to send a report on how the Chinese communiqué was handled. The report should include any breaches of the release date. It should cover any unauthorized early publication of facts about the Cairo or Tehran conferences. Early's suggestions for doing better are asked for as well.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d451:
December 6, 1943 was the closing day of the Second Cairo Conference, and the Combined Chiefs of Staff held a session whose minutes the State Department printed in its Cairo-Tehran volume. The chiefs were the senior American and British officers charged with running the two countries' common war effort. Their Cairo work followed directly from the Tehran meeting with Stalin.

Final-day minutes tend to gather up loose ends: last decisions recorded, reports noted, and conclusions readied for Roosevelt and Churchill before the delegations scattered. For the reader, this record closes the military story of the conference. It shows the machinery of alliance settling its business before the leaders went home.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d51: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on October 21, 1943, the same day he exchanged letters with Hull in Moscow. The message is Document 51 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Running two channels at once, one to his minister and one to his ally, was the president's normal method that autumn. The record names no subject for this letter. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series among the Moscow Conference papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d551:
Marshal Stalin addressed a joint message to President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill on January 29, 1944. Stalin usually wrote to the two leaders separately, so a message to both at once marked business he wanted the whole alliance to hear. It appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

The three-way partnership rested on constant reporting among the capitals, and a joint message from Moscow carried the weight of the partner who was doing most of the fighting that winter. The Red Army's offensives were then driving the Germans back across Ukraine. For readers, the document shows Stalin speaking to the Western leaders together, as Tehran had briefly made them.
frus-1944-quebec-d151:
In Scaf 78, dated September 9, 1944, Eisenhower gave the Combined Chiefs a brief situation report and a full statement of his intentions in France. Northern France and much of Belgium were liberated, his troops had entered Holland, and Seventh Army was about to join the central armies. Against that, German-held Schelde islands would delay using Antwerp's port.

His intention was to press on with all speed, destroy the German armed forces, and occupy Germany's heart. The main effort would breach the Siegfried Line toward the Ruhr, with the Saar as the second thrust. An airborne operation to seize Rhine crossings near Arnhem and Nijmegen awaited only good weather. Capturing the Ruhr and Saar, he argued, would strangle Germany's war industry.
frus-1944-quebec-d251:
Stettinius reported a deadlock, and a possible way through it, to Roosevelt on September 14, 1944. Ambassador Gromyko had received his instructions from Moscow on voting in the proposed Security Council. The Soviet government maintained its insistence on the inviolability of the unanimity of the four great powers. On that point, Gromyko said, there was no possibility of his being authorized to give in.

Working with the British and Russians, Stettinius had devised a compromise formula. In procedures for pacific settlement of disputes, the votes of council members party to a dispute would not be counted. In enforcement action, decisions would require the concurrence of the permanent members, including parties. Gromyko was sounding out his government, and Stettinius asked for the president's views as promptly as possible.
frus-1944-quebec-d51:
Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff prepared a memorandum on September 2, 1944. They worked in Washington. Their mission kept London's military positions current with the American chiefs. Gaps between summits made that work constant. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Ten days before Quebec, staff papers lined up the military questions. Officers framed choices about the final drive into Germany. They also framed the war in Burma and the Pacific. Force sharing between the allies needed decisions too. Missions in Washington did that lining up daily. For readers, the memorandum shows professional preparation behind the conference. Chiefs would later argue the choices their officers framed.
frus-1945-50-intel-d151:
On 9 May 1946 the Fourth Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 151 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

Minutes are the formal record of a meeting: who sat in, what was put on the table, and what the group agreed to do. They rarely give long speeches, but they fix the choices that later memos then carry out. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d251:
A memorandum dated 2 December 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence (Wright). The reader was the Chief of the Interagency Coordinating and Planning Staff, Central Intelligence Agency (Childs). It stands as document 251 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. A new order was taking shape: the National Security Council now met at the top, with the CIA as its intelligence arm.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d351: Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter issued a formal statement on 31 August 1948. It is document 351 in the Foreign Relations volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. A signed statement put the head of the CIA on record in his own name. At the time, an outside team was set to review how the young agency worked.
frus-1945-50-intel-d51:
Harold Smith, the budget director, wrote to President Truman again on 28 November 1945. Smith's letters to the president form one of the volume's strongest threads. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

By late November, Smith was steering the intelligence plan toward its final form. It would be a small central group serving the president and the departments, not a giant new spy agency. His memoranda combined advice on structure with the drafts themselves. Readers who want to know why the outcome of January 1946 looked as it did should read Smith's papers with care. Few officials leave so clear a trail from their desk to a president's signature.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d151:
Relations with the London Poles would be no more than “correct,” Stettinius cabled Harriman on 13 December 1944. His secret and urgent instruction, number 2828, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It sets the line Harriman was to hold in Moscow on Poland.

The present Polish cabinet, Washington judged, could not work out any agreement with the Soviet government. Ambassador Lane would stay in Washington until January, and no meaning was to be read into that. Harriman was to make clear that the United States still recognizes the London government. If it helped, he could add that Washington would not look kindly on Soviet recognition of the Lublin Committee. Should the London cabinet fall, Mikolajczyk might yet form one that backed his own policy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d251:
Harriman arranged a Friday meeting to draw Stalin out on the Pacific war. His report to the President of 11 October 1944, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, describes the plan agreed with Churchill the night before. Presidential approval was still to come.

Stalin and his military men would face Churchill, Brooke, Ismay, Deane, and Harriman. The chief aim is to learn two things. How soon after Germany's collapse will Stalin be ready to act against Japan? And what, in general, can Russia bring to that war? The picture gained would clear the way for the detailed talks between Deane and the Red Army Staff. Those, Harriman insists, should be Soviet-American only, with the British kept informed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d351:
Of this meeting, nothing said survives at all. The editors' note reports that no record of its substance has been found in the files. What is known of the session — its time and who attended — comes from the official trip log alone. The log shows the talks went on after lunch until 3 p.m.

Gaps like this run through the Yalta record, and the volume marks them rather than hiding them. A reader learns where the paper trail ends. Whatever passed between the leaders that afternoon stayed with the men in the room. The note stands as a warning against over-reading the famous record.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d451:
Agreement on Poland leads Eden's report in Bohlen's minutes of the plenary of February 10, 1945. Eden told the leaders the foreign ministers had settled the future government of Poland. Two questions within it he would refer to later. He then read the new formula, with one correction he admitted Molotov had made.

A new situation, the formula begins, has been created by Poland's complete liberation by the Red Army. A Polish provisional government, more broadly based, must follow. The session's list runs on: French participation in Germany's control commission, Yugoslavia, the world body, reparations, and the Dardanelles. Bohlen records the conference reaching its harvest day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d51: From Moscow on 11 January 1945, Harriman sent Roosevelt a report that stands as document 51. It belongs to the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, issued by the Department of State. Written three weeks before Yalta opened, the report helped the president judge what the Soviet leadership might demand, and what it might accept, once talks began.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d151:
Churchill showed Truman his reply to Stalin about the Balkan states in telegram number 83, sent June 10, 1945. The message is document 151 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stalin had written on May 27 that the time had come to restore diplomatic relations with Romania, Bulgaria, and Finland, and perhaps soon with Hungary.

Churchill's quoted reply thanks Stalin for the news. Britain has been weighing its own future relations with those states, he writes, and hopes very shortly to put full proposals before Stalin and the United States government. He hopes the three can then discuss them when they next meet. The exchange touched a sore point: the ex-enemy states of Eastern Europe were falling under Soviet control, and recognition was one lever the West still held.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d251:
A briefing paper set American aims on Soviet support for the Cairo Declaration, in extracts dated June 29, 1945. The paper is document 251 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It formed part of the annexes to the State Department's agenda memorandum for the President.

The minimum objective is to win Soviet adherence to the Cairo Declaration. That would give Moscow's backing to the pledge that Korea in due course shall be free and independent. It would also bar any one power from setting up a friendly government on its own in the territories concerned. The maximum objective goes further: an agreement among the three powers, with China's expected cooperation, to jointly support the measures best suited to grow a strong, democratic, independent Korean nation. The full text appears later in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d351:
German central offices form the third topic in Dunn's extracts of his July 14, 1945 talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan at Potsdam. Cadogan cited a memorandum by Field Marshal Montgomery, approved by the Prime Minister. It urged restoring central German ministries so the Control Council could handle problems that touched Germany as a whole.

Cadogan doubted Berlin could house such agencies. Dunn answered that the United States favored building German central administrative agencies, though under a less imposing title than ministries. The exchange shows both allies groping toward the same need: some German machine, under allied control, to run railways, food, and finance across zone lines.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d451:
MacVeagh's letter to Prime Minister Voulgaris, written at Athens on July 13, 1945, carries the Greek election proposal to the Greek government itself. Under his instructions, he informs the Premier of allied obligations to Greece, the undertakings at Yalta, and Article Nine of the Varkiza Agreement. America and Britain have agreed on a joint step.

If the move is agreeable to the Royal Hellenic Government, the two powers will approach the Soviet Union and France. Their proposal: that the approaching Greek national elections be held under the supervision of the four allies named. Voulgaris returned the letter at once, with his signed agreement written on it that same morning.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d51:
President Truman settled the argument over dates in a top secret reply to Churchill on June 5, 1945. The message is document 51 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, answering Churchill's plea for an earlier Big Three meeting. Only part of the telegram is printed, but its decision is complete.

Truman says that after full consideration, July 15 is the earliest date he can manage. Plans are therefore going ahead for him to travel to the area near Berlin and arrive on that day. Churchill had warned that delay would let Soviet power harden in central Europe, but the President held firm. The exchange fixed the opening date of the Potsdam Conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d551:
A top secret briefing paper on Yugoslavia was drawn up for the Potsdam Conference on July 5, 1945. It is document 551 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers. Its subject is how Marshal Tito had dealt with the Crimea, or Yalta, pledges on his country.

The paper says Tito has not carried out those pledges. A regency and a joint government were set up in March 1945 under the Tito-Subasic deal. But the wartime assembly was never widened as promised, and six new federal states are all run by partisans. It cites seized property, attacks on clergy, and U.S. firms put under state control. It urges the three powers to restate the pledges and offer to consult.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d651:
A top secret briefing paper on the future of the Tangier zone was dated June 29, 1945. It is document 651 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Tangier, in Morocco, had been run under an international statute since 1923.

Spanish forces seized the zone on June 14, 1940, by a one-sided decision of Spain's government. Madrid said the move guarded the zone's neutrality during the war. Spain now wished to regularize the situation, the paper says. France and Britain had invited the U.S. to informal talks in Paris on the zone's future. The first task was to shape a provisional regime for the span after Spanish forces and officials left. A full international conference would later settle a permanent regime.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1051:
Britain's delegation proposed this supply plan for the occupation zones at Potsdam on July 30, 1945. Its general rule is that each zone, Greater Berlin included, should draw supplies from the parts of Germany it drew on before the war, so far as practical.

On food, the Soviet zone may have no surplus for the west until the 1946 harvest. Even so, it should feed itself and all Berlin up to the Control Council's minimum standard. From that harvest on, it should supply Berlin and the west at roughly the old scale. On coal, Polish-run land within the 1937 borders would send five million tons a year west for three years.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1151:
Washington's team tabled this proposal on 29 July 1945, as Potsdam entered its final days. Late papers served a new purpose. The broad choices were made; now the teams fought to turn them into exact, signed language that would hold.

Each American paper in this stretch was a bid to shape the Potsdam Protocol, the summit's official record of its choices. Words fixed there would govern Germany and Europe for years. A proposal of 29 July belongs to that drafting fight. It shows the United States driving to close the summit on terms it could defend at home and abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1251:
Hurley wrote to the President and the Secretary of State on 26 July 1945. The date was heavy with news: Britain's count changed its government that day, and the Allies issued their terms to Japan. Hurley's dispatch from China entered that stream at the top level.

His reports kept China's crisis before the men who could act on it. The republic he dealt with was fraying as victory neared, and his cables said so in his own blunt style. This message is one of his summit-week reports. It shows the China file claiming its share of the leaders' crowded day.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1351:
Norman Armour, the American ambassador in Spain, answered the acting secretary of state on 18 July 1945. Two days earlier, Washington had sent Armour fresh instructions. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

An ambassador's reply shows how guidance from home plays out on the ground. Armour dealt with Franco's Spain, a state the winning powers kept at arm's length while still needing to talk. Read with the instruction that came before it, this cable forms a small pair: order and report, question and answer. Pairs like that are the basic rhythm of the whole Foreign Relations series.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-151:
Cohen's notes for July 31, 1945 capture the Potsdam talks on their last full day. Benjamin Cohen had recorded the sessions since the opening week. His final sets were printed in the second Potsdam volume. The closing hours turned on exact phrases, and Cohen's legal ear was built for them.

In these notes the reader hears the talks winding down. Old arguments return in shorter form. New wording gets tested word by word. Cohen's care lets us watch commitments being nailed down. The pages close his run as one of the most useful witnesses the American side produced.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-51:
Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 21, 1945, record a midday session on basic objectives, strategy, and policy. The top secret extracts are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Potsdam papers. Much of the debate turned on a shipping paragraph in the joint strategy paper.

Admiral Leahy proposed a point of clarity first. Wherever the draft said this war, it should say the war against Japan. General Somervell then read the cargo shipping wording Lord Leathers was expected to propose. He recommended the U.S. chiefs oppose the change, since it ignored shipping problems of concern to the United States alone. Admiral Gardner saw no reason to single shipping out for the objectives statement. Food and petroleum, he noted, were matters of the same nature and might claim a place on equal grounds.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d751:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff addressed the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee on July 17, 1945, in document 751. The committee joined the three services' work with the State Department's. Potsdam's opening day found the chiefs feeding military views into that shared channel. The paper entered the second Potsdam volume.

This channel mattered because Potsdam's choices mixed war and policy. Occupation, surrender terms, and force levels crossed every desk. The chiefs wrote to the one body built to join them. Readers see the American system aligning its parts at the summit's start. The document shows coordination as a daily act, not a slogan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d851:
Major Harold Zink of the Political Division, United States Group, Control Council for Germany, wrote this memorandum on July 16, 1945. Document 851 brings a staff officer's view from inside the occupation. Zink was a scholar of government serving in uniform. His memo joined the second Potsdam volume.

A major's memorandum can carry an expert's weight. Zink knew German administration from study and from the ground. Readers get the occupation analyzed by a man inside it. The document shows the Control Council's own staff thinking about their task on the summit's eve. Their questions would outlast the conference: how to govern a beaten land justly and well.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d951:
Edwin Pauley sent President Truman a staff analysis of Marshal Zhukov's charges on July 29, 1945. Zhukov had accused American and British armies of stripping factories in the Soviet zone. Pauley calls the report a smoke screen. Soviet teams, he writes, were already shipping whole plants to Russia before any reparations plan won approval.

His Committee I, chaired by Robert Sproul of the University of California, found Zhukov's facts largely correct but trivial. Western removals, they say, were mostly war booty and new German technology. Damage came largely from looting by freed slave laborers. Soviet removals, by contrast, took farm gear, sewing machines, and textile machines that were no war potential at all.
frus-1977-80v09Ed2-d51: A short letter from President Carter to President Sadat and Prime Minister Begin, written at Camp David on September 15, 1978, sets the endgame of the summit. It is document 51 in Volume IX of the 1977-1980 series. Carter proposes that the day bring each side's best final offers. The next day would go to drafting. The meeting would close the day after, with a joint press statement. He asks both men to hold public comment until noon on Monday. Mondale delivered the letter by hand.
gao-gaoreports-b-298651:
2B Brokers and 89 other firms protested terms in a U.S. Transportation Command solicitation. The buy merged freight hauling and transport coordination across the United States. It formed part of the Defense Transportation Coordination Initiative. GAO decided B-298651 on November 27, 2006.

The firms called the merged buy too tight a curb on rivalry. They also called it unlawful bundling under the Small Business Act. GAO weighed the agency's stated gains from the merger. It found real cost savings and speed gains in the plan. The merged scope fit the agency's true needs. Such bundling can stand on that proof. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298751:
Philadelphia Produce Market Wholesalers, LLC protested a Defense Commissary Agency award to Four Seasons Produce, Inc. The contract covered fresh fruits and vegetables for resale. The stores sat in the agency's East Region. GAO ruled in B-298751 on December 8, 2006.

The firm said its technical proposal earned more credit than it got. Mere dispute with a score does not prove a flawed review. GAO found the scoring and the best-value call sound. The firm also claimed an unfair edge from a hired ex-agency manager. No proof showed that inside facts were shared. The man had no hand in the current terms. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-309751:
The Borenstein Group, Inc. lost its protest — GAO decision B-309751, dated September 26, 2007. The Army had sought support for a big birthday fete. The fete marks 100 years of the U.S. Army Reserve. The firm fought the choice to scrap the call for offers. The work would have covered planning, staffing, and supply aid.

GAO denied the protest. The Army had a fair basis to scrap the call. Its needs could be met through a deal it held. That path was judged better for the government. The ruling backs an agency's right to scrap a call when a held deal serves it more.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-151:
Telecommunications, GAO-05-151 of February 9, 2005, calls on the Federal Communications Commission to take a firmer hand in its E-rate program. Since 1998, the plan has pledged more than $13 billion to wire schools and libraries for the internet and phone service. Claims of fraud, waste, and abuse by some in the plan have since come to light.

GAO asks how the plan's odd setup shapes FCC control. It asks if clear goals and yardsticks guide the work. It asks if the checks on grants bite. More FCC grip is needed, the title says, to keep aid cash safe and well spent.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-251:
Anthrax Detection, GAO-05-251 of March 31, 2005, grades how labs hunted a germ sent by mail in 2001. Letters laced with anthrax spores went to two senators and news staff that fall. In all, 22 people in four states and Washington, D.C., fell ill. Five died. Mail sites then faced a vast test task: prove rooms were clean.

A clean test is worth trust only if the test method is sound. GAO lists how agencies took samples in mail sites. It weighs the results they got. It asks if the methods were ever proven true. They must be, the title warns, before a clean bill means much.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-351:
International Trade, GAO-05-351 of April 19, 2005, tests claims that some states rig their cash worth for trade gain. A 1988 law makes the Treasury grade each state each year. Eyes fell on China and Japan, whose cash some call too cheap. Their low worth could aid their goods and hurt U.S. makers. Congress told Treasury to tell more in 2004.

Treasury's March 2005 report found no rig in its grades. GAO walks through how those grades are made. It checks if the tales told to Congress meet the law. It asks pros how far China's cash sits below true worth, and what a rise would mean here.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-551:
Radio frequency identification in federal hands is surveyed in GAO report GAO-05-551, released on May 27, 2005. The technology uses tags, readers, and databases to identify and track objects. Falling costs have made wide use plausible for agencies and firms alike. GAO explained how the systems work, listed the main agency efforts, and weighed the standards, legal issues, and security and privacy risks that come with them.

Agencies use the tags for building access and for tracking goods, papers, and gear. Homeland Security, for one, tracks assets, weapons, and flight baggage with them. Many rival sets of standards guide the work, which can hinder systems that must talk to each other. Of 16 agencies asked about legal issues, only one raised any. Its worries touched privacy and the tracking of sensitive papers. GAO flagged deeper risks. Tag data can be read, altered, or used to track a person's movements.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-851:
Passenger rail security is assessed in GAO-05-851, a report dated September 9, 2005. U.S. trains carry more than 11 million passengers each weekday. Two departments share the duty to keep rail safe. GAO checked federal risk studies of the rail system. It listed federal steps to raise security. And it gathered practices from U.S. and foreign rail operators.

GAO found 7 risk studies done and 12 under way in one security office. The transport security agency had not finished its own method for weighing rail risks. It set no timelines to finish. A wider framework for comparing risks across sectors was also unfinished. After the 2004 Madrid rail attacks, emergency directives went to U.S. operators. Officials questioned whether the orders could be met in practice. GAO called for stronger federal leadership to set priorities.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-51:
Tax season means about 130 million returns, refunds, and millions of questions. Report GAO-06-51, issued November 14, 2005, grades the Internal Revenue Service's 2005 filing season. Budget cuts pressed the agency. Its strategy shifted resources from taxpayer service toward enforcement. That shift made quality service harder to provide. GAO compared performance with past years and with 2005 goals.

GAO covered paper and electronic return processing. It also covered telephone service, face-to-face help, and Web site service. It asked whether long-term goals exist to guide trade-offs. The agency improved some services, GAO found. It also summed up the response to Hurricanes Katrina and Rita.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-151:
Big defense firms mentor small disadvantaged firms under a Pentagon program meant to build them up. GAO surveyed the small firms in GAO-07-151, dated January 31, 2007. The Mentor-Protege Program pays mentors to coach the smaller firms. GAO asked former proteges whether the help worked. It also checked the accuracy of the program's yearly reports to Congress. GAO tracked program spending too.

Most of the 48 proteges who replied valued the program, GAO found. About 87 percent said mentor support helped their business grow. Together they credited it with 95 new contracts and about $131 million in added revenue. Still, the yearly reports to Congress rested on shaky data, GAO said. The Pentagon sent its March report before validation checks finished in September. In fiscal year 2004, 40 of 183 active agreements were never reviewed at all. GAO urged the department to validate first and report second.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-351:
The deposit insurer's computer defenses improved, though gaps remain on the books. GAO assessed them in GAO-07-351, a report dated May 18, 2007. The audit supports GAO's review of the insurer's 2006 financial statements. GAO checked fixes for flaws found earlier. It tested controls that guard financial data. Work ran at the insurer's Virginia computer site.

The insurer corrected or eased 21 of 26 old weaknesses, GAO found. That marks substantial progress over the prior review. The remaining issues do not amount to a significant deficiency. That judgment appears in GAO's audit of the insurer's funds. GAO still urges steady management focus. Without it, gains could slip. Financial and sensitive data need lasting protection. The report lists the flaws left open. It also notes where controls now hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-451:
One blueprint for the Pentagon's back-office systems is judged in GAO-07-451, a GAO report of April 16, 2007. GAO first flagged Defense business systems as high risk in 1995. Congress later told the department to build a business enterprise architecture, a map for joining its systems. Version 4.0 came out in September 2006. Defense then issued a plan to spread the map to the services and agencies.

GAO found the plan sound as a concept but thin as a guide. It lacked the detail staff need to act. A prior GAO call for a management plan for the build was still open. GAO repeated that call with fresh detail. Until the plan exists, the odds of a smooth rollout stay low. The report shows why paper strategy alone does not move a vast bureaucracy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-51:
One network for the whole Navy and Marine Corps is the bet behind GAO-07-51, a GAO report dated December 8, 2006. The Navy Marine Corps Intranet is a 10-year, $9.3 billion services deal. A contractor runs the network, software, and gear for a fixed price per seat. The web reaches about 550 sites. GAO reviewed the program on the Comptroller General's authority.

GAO asked four things. It checked whether the program hits its strategic goals. It weighed the contractor's record against service level deals. It asked users whether they are happy with the service. It then traced what is being done to lift satisfaction. Plans and data came from the program office, the contractor, and users at shipyards and air depots. GAO warned that goals meant little without measures tracked and reported to decision makers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-651:
Katrina's toxic legacy gets a full accounting in GAO-07-651, a GAO report dated June 25, 2007. The 2005 storm wrecked over 90,000 square miles. More than 1,600 people died, and over a million fled their homes. Floodwater spread chemicals and hazardous waste across the Gulf Coast. Demolition of ruined homes in New Orleans stirred asbestos dust. The Environmental Protection Agency led the federal environment response.

GAO credits the agency's work under harsh terms, including rescue work that brought 800 New Orleans residents to safety. It then turns to open risks. Many homes still await gutting or demolition. Work by owners is largely unregulated, so asbestos care varies by street. Health messages to the public also drew mixed marks. GAO urges tighter checks on the long tail of the cleanup, since the hazard phase will outlast the headlines by years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-851:
Costs of a new Pentagon personnel system are faulted in GAO-07-851, dated July 16, 2007. The National Security Personnel System reshapes pay and job rules for civilian staff. GAO launched this study on its own authority. It checked whether the Defense Department counted the full cost of the shift. It tracked funds spent or pledged through fiscal year 2006.

A November 2005 estimate put the cost at $158 million for 2005 to 2008. That sum covers the program office and service program shops. It omits other costs the department expects to bear, GAO found. Program staff could not say which costs were left out. Federal standards call for full cost figures to guide choices. GAO urged the department to define all costs and restate the estimate. It also urged a frame to capture every dollar spent. The department generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-251:
Homeland command planning is assessed in GAO report GAO-08-251, issued April 16, 2008. U.S. Northern Command was created 5 years earlier to defend the homeland and aid civil leaders. Planning raids and relief on home soil differs from war planning abroad. Laws and partners at every level shape each move. GAO reviewed the command's plans against joint planning yardsticks.

GAO found progress in the command's plans. Gaps remain in how forces are assigned to it, though. Tracking of readiness also falls short. The review counted the command's planning staff and weighed their training. It also tested how well the command works with other federal agencies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-351:
U.S. and international efforts in Somalia are assessed in GAO report GAO-08-351, dated February 19, 2008. Somalia has had no working central government since 1991. The United States, the largest single donor, has given roughly $362 million in aid since 2001.

GAO found that a shortage of peacekeeping troops and a weak transitional government limited efforts to steady the country. A recent reconciliation round shut out key opposition groups, which then rejected its results. Aid work was curbed by insecurity and poor access, and acute malnutrition rates stayed above the emergency threshold in some areas. GAO recommended a fuller U.S. strategy built with the Departments of State and Defense. Defense partly agreed; State did not directly respond.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-51:
GAO-08-51, a GAO report dated October 31, 2007, covers NASA's Ares I crew launch vehicle. Ares I will carry the Orion crew vehicle as the nation returns humans to the moon. The first crewed flight is planned for 2015, and NASA wants to shrink the gap after the Space Shuttle retires in 2010.

NASA is building its business case on proven technology and on gaining knowledge before big commitments. It tracks many risks closely. Yet gaps remain in requirements, cost, schedule, technology, and design. The shifting Orion design keeps Ares I requirements unsettled. The J-2X upper stage engine runs on a fast schedule out of step with the rest of the project, and funding may fall short. GAO urged NASA to prove a sound case before the July 2008 design review, or delay it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-851:
Ports, airfields, and roads the military counts on must stay ready in a crisis. A Defense Department program exists to guard such key assets. GAO-08-851, dated August 15, 2008, checks how the U.S. Transportation Command picks and ranks its critical transport assets, using a sample of 22 assets.

The command counts whole bases as single assets, rather than naming parts like runways or fuel farms. That blurs the master list and skews spending choices. It also used weakness probes to pick assets, against program guidance. Officials from the homeland defense office flagged the mismatch. GAO told the command to use the set criteria and set a timeline.
gesner-historia-animalium-lib1-1551:
Conrad Gesner, a Swiss doctor and tireless scholar, began his Historiae animalium in 1551 with this first volume. It treats the viviparous quadrupeds, the live-bearing four-footed beasts, mammal by mammal. Scholars call the whole work the founding text of modern zoology.

Gesner names each animal in several languages and reports its habits, uses, and lore. Fine woodcut portraits made the books famous across Europe. He includes tales he doubts alongside facts he trusts, and often says which is which. The scale of the labor still stuns readers. Volume one set the pattern for three centuries of animal books.
glauber-furni-novi-philosophici-1651:
Johann Rudolf Glauber published Furni Novi Philosophici in 1651, a work on new philosophical furnaces. Glauber was a German-Dutch chemist known for Glauber's salt and for skill with furnaces and distillation. Better ovens, he argued, meant better chemical work.

Designs and directions show how to build furnaces and use them to draw spirits, oils, and salts from many materials. Glauber treated wine, metals, plants, and minerals, and he hinted at uses in medicine and trade. He guarded some secrets while printing enough to prove his skill. The book captures a moment when craft knowledge of fire and vessels was becoming modern chemistry.
godey-s-lady-s-book-vol-42-january-1851:
Godey's Lady's Book was the leading American magazine for women of its day, and this is its January 1851 number, opening volume 42. The first pages give a model cottage in the style of Heriot's Hospital in Edinburgh, with plans for porch, dairy, cow-house, and pig-stye. A New Year's Day in France leads the pictures. Fiction, fashion, and household arts fill the issue.

One tale here has a wife defend her patience with a club-loving husband, while her friend vows to rule hers more strictly. Tales, poems, needlework, and advice crowd the pages in the magazine's usual mix. Readers get a full month of what American women of 1851 were offered to read and make. The number is a rich sample of the magazine that shaped taste for a generation.
govdocs-archive_org-SeptuagintBrenton185:
Sir Lancelot C. L. Brenton published his English translation of the Septuagint in London in 1851, through Samuel Bagster and Sons. The Septuagint is the ancient Greek version of the Hebrew Bible, the form of scripture used by the early church.

Brenton's edition includes the Apocrypha alongside the Old Testament books, giving English readers the full Greek canon in one volume. His translation stayed close to the Greek text and became the standard English Septuagint for generations. It is still the version many readers reach for when they want the Greek Bible in English.
gregory-letters-candid-inquirer-1851:
William Gregory systematized animal magnetism in Letters to a Candid Inquirer, printed in 1851. Gregory, a chemist at Edinburgh, wrote the letters as a manual for the open minded. Magnetic sleep, clairvoyance, and mesmeric cure receive ordered treatment. He gathers the evidence claim by claim, with cases in support.

The book became the standard British manual of the subject for mid Victorian readers. Through it, many households first met mesmerism in sober form. Gregory answers doubters while granting the field its share of fraud. His order and calm made the strange seem studyable. The letters preserve how Britain learned mesmerism. They remain a clear window on the practice.
hawthorne-house-of-seven-gables-1851:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The House of the Seven Gables in 1851, his romance of inherited guilt. The tale turns on the Pyncheon curse and a Salem house built on stolen land. Hawthorne called it a romance, free to bend fact toward mood and moral truth in prose.

Colonel Pyncheon seized Matthew Maule's lot and saw him hanged for witchcraft in old Salem days. Maule cursed him from the scaffold, and Pyncheons die strangely for two hundred years after in turn. Hepzibah, a faded gentlewoman, opens a shop in the house while her brother Clifford returns from prison. Young Phoebe's cheer and Holgrave's secret soften the gloom toward a late, guarded hope in love. The book probes how class, guilt, and old wealth decay in a young republic.
hawthorne-snow-image-1851:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Snow-Image, and Other Twice-Told Tales in 1851, a full story collection. The volume holds famed tales like The Great Stone Face and Ethan Brand among its pieces. It gathers his later magazine work into the last tale book of his lifetime in print.

A father shapes a snow child who cannot live in a warm room by the fire. A lime-burner hunts the Unpardonable Sin and finds it in his own cold, watchful heart at last. The Great Stone Face teaches a valley poet to match the profile he reveres on the mountain. Hawthorne mixes whimsy and dread, children and sinners, in tales of rare finish and quiet power here. The collection rounds out the story art that first made his American name.
hawthorne-wonder-book-1851:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys in 1851, his retelling of Greek myths. The book fixed the classical myths in the Anglophone imagination for generations of young readers everywhere. Hawthorne wrote it fast, for money, and it became his most popular book in his lifetime.

Student Eustace Bright tells six myths to children at Tanglewood, in the Berkshire hills of Massachusetts. Perseus slays Medusa, Midas turns his child to gold, and Hercules and Pandora fill the set. Hawthorne softens the myths' cruelty and pagan edge for the nursery without killing their wonder and strangeness. His frame of child listeners keeps the old tales warm, present, and full of questions. The book set the pattern for children's myth retellings in English ever since.
hero-of-alexandria-pneumatica-woodcroft-:
Hero of Alexandria, a Greek engineer of the first century, wrote the Pneumatics on machines moved by air and water. Bennet Woodcroft's English version came out in 1851, in the Taylor Walton and Maberly edition. All 78 sections are here, with the editors' opening matter.

Hero describes siphons, fountains, temple doors that open by fire on an altar, and singing birds worked by water. His aeolipile, a ball spun by jets of steam, is the first known steam engine. The book is the base text for the study of ancient machines. Engineers still rebuild his devices to test how they worked.
hobbes-de-cive-1651:
Thomas Hobbes published De Cive in Latin in 1642, and the English translation of 1651 gives it as Philosophical Rudiments Concerning Government and Society. Three parts treat liberty, dominion, and religion in turn. The book stands between his Elements of Law and the Leviathan of 1651, where his political philosophy reached its famous form.

Hobbes argues that men in nature, without a common power, live in fear and war. Peace requires a sovereign set up by covenant, whose commands are law. Religion, in the third part, must answer to that sovereign within his realm. De Cive states the case more briefly than Leviathan, and scholars prize its clarity.
hume-enquiry-principles-morals-1751:
Hume called An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals, from 1751, his own favorite among his works. Nine sections, two appendices, and a closing Dialogue make up the book. Its question is plain: why do we praise some traits of character and blame others, in every age and land?

Hume's answer is the moral-sense theory in its ripest form. We approve what is useful or agreeable, to ourselves or to others, and sentiment, guided by reason, does the approving. Benevolence, justice, and politeness all fall under his calm survey. The Enquiry reads more smoothly than any other of his books. It remains a founding text of modern moral philosophy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-phineha: Phinehas Abraham was a West Indian merchant born in Jamaica about the start of the nineteenth century. He died on Feb. 19, 1887. He was one of the last survivors of the West Indian merchant body that had added much to the colonies' wealth. In former years he ranked among Jamaica's largest landowners. He served as senior justice of the peace for Trelawny parish and as an agent of Lloyds. He was also the last surviving captain in the Trelawny militia, and an early member of London's Berkeley Street Synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acsady-ignatz-i:
Ignatz Acsády was a Hungarian historian born at Nagy-Károly on September 9, 1845. He studied at Debreczin and Budapest. He began press work in 1869 on a political journal. In 1870 he joined the "Pesti Napló" staff. In 1888 the Hungarian Academy of Sciences made him a corresponding member. His study dealt most with trade and money life in Hungary in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

His books cover state law, the freeing of the Jews, and state funds under Ferdinand I. One prize essay treats Hungary at the retaking of Buda. He also wrote novels and plays. Since 1894 he led the records work of the Hungarian Jewish Literary Society. He wrote two volumes of a national history of Hungary. They cover the years after the battle of Mohacs in 1526 and the reigns of Leopold I and Joseph I.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adon-olam-music:
Adon Olam is a hymn of strict meter in the Jewish rite. Its fine words and smooth verse have given it high place. Sephardic and British flocks sing it at the close of Sabbath and feast day morning rites. Ashkenazic flocks sing it at the close of eve rites as well. Both sing it on the Eve of Atonement. It is also read by the bed of the dying.

For so loved a hymn, the old tunes are few. Just four or five count as handed down. The oldest seems to be a short tune of Spanish birth. A north tune serves the days of repentance. Most song men of the nineteenth century set the hymn in rich parts. That style blocks flock song, and the fault is now seen. A set by Simon W. Waley has become a classic for British Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-b-shila-of-: Aha b. Shila of Kefar Tamrata, also spelled Temarta, was a haggadist of the second amoraic generation, in the third century. The entry preserves one comment of his, on a verse in Esther. Esther says a deed was written in the king's book of chronicles. Aha drew hope for the God-fearing from that line. If mortal chronicles assure rewards for good deeds, he argued, God's own book of remembrance will surely reward the pious.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aksakov-ivan-se:
Ivan Sergyeyevich Aksakov was a Russian Panslavist leader. He was born on October 7, 1823, and died at Moscow on February 8, 1886. He helped found a Moscow circle of Slavophils. They wanted Russia restored to its state before Peter the Great, free of West European ways. That stand set them against all foreign elements in Russia, Jews above all.

Aksakov's paper, the "Den," turned on the Jews over time. In 1862 he fought the entry of Jewish graduates into state service. After the riots of 1881 in South Russia he led the reaction that followed Alexander II's death. He called the attacks on Jews a just revenge, and he backed the May Laws of 1882. In 1883 he charged the Alliance Israelite with a secret world plot, a charge the Alliance answered in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alkan-napoleon-:
Napoleon Alexandre Alkan was a French pianist and composer. He was born in Paris in 1826. He was a brother of Charles Valentin Alkan. Like his brother he entered the music school young. He studied under Adolphe Adam and Pierre Zimmerman. In 1850 he became a teacher of solfeggio there.

He held that post for nearly fifty years. His pupils grew to wide fame. Bizet and Sarasate both studied under him. As a composer he won less fame than his brother. In 1890 he took a second prize from the French Institute. A study on a theme from an opera is his best known work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amalek-amalekit:
Amalek names a wandering nation south of Palestine. Its stock was kin to the Edomites, the entry holds. Amalek was a son of Eliphaz, the first-born of Esau. His mother was Timna, a Horite woman. The Amalekites first met Israel in war. They struck the weak rear of the march at Rephidim.

From then on they stand as foes of Israel. They helped Moab and Midian in later wars. Saul led a march against them in his turn. The entry sifts each verse that names them. It weighs the Kenites, who lived at their side. Arab tales that made them a world power are called false. A named scholar is said to have proved that point.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anah-1451:
Anah is a name borne by three kin in Genesis. One Anah was the mother of a wife of Esau. She was a daughter of Zibeon. One was a son of Seir the Horite. He stood among the chiefs of Edom. One was a son of Zibeon of note. He is famed for a find in the wilds.

That find is given as hot springs in this text. Old versions give the word as mules instead. Jerome lists four senses drawn from Jewish sources. Seas, hot springs, a swift ass, and mules all stand there. The mule sense held the field among Jews. Tale says Anah first bred that beast.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apologists-1651:
Apologists were men of pious zeal who defended the Jewish religion and the Jewish race in writing. Their works, as essays or as dialogues, set Judaism's spirit and doctrines in the proper light. The entry notes that such defense doubled as attack, since it had to expose the weakness of the foes' case.

While the Jewish state stood strong and neighbors kept their reverence, no such defense was needed, the entry argues. Jews lived in harmony with Persians and Greeks in early ages. Need grew when the state decayed, Greek faith in its own gods faded, and the Bible in Greek laid Jewish teaching open to outside attack. The entry then follows the great defenders age by age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arepol-samuel-b:
Samuel ben Isaac ben Yom Tob Arepol was a commentator on the Bible who lived in Safed and Salonica in the sixteenth century. The entry lists six of his books. Imrot Eloah holds homilies on the Pentateuch, and Wa'ad la-Hakamim comments on the prayer-book, both printed at Venice.

Leb Hakam, on Ecclesiastes, came out at Constantinople in 1586. Mizmor le-Todah treats Psalm 119 and the fifteen Songs of Degrees, at Venice in 1576. Sar Shalom, on Canticles, was printed at Safed in 1579. His Agudat Shemuel gathers extracts from his earlier works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aryeh-loeb-ben-:
Aryeh Loeb ben Jacob Joshua, a German Talmudist and author, was born in 1715 and died at Hanover on March 6, 1789. His father wrote the Pene Yehoshua and died as rabbi of Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1755. The son assisted him in youth and taught in his academy about 1745 to 1750. Later he served as rabbi at Skala in Galicia, and from 1761 at Hanover, until his death.

His own work follows the scholastic type of his school. In 1780 he edited the fourth part of his father's book at Furth. To it he added his own notes on the tractate Baba Kamma under the title Pene Aryeh, The Face of the Lion. His son Issachar Berisch, who lived from 1747 to 1807, followed him at Hanover.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenaz-1951:
Ashkenaz names a people in Genesis chapter 10, traced through Gomer to Japheth, the third son of Noah. Jeremiah chapter 51 joins the name with Ararat, Minni, and the Medes as foes of Babylon. Where that people lived is the entry's whole problem. Targum, Talmud, and Midrash match the name to Asia, the Roman province covering Lydia, Phrygia, and Caria.

Other matches crowd in. One Targum gives Adiabene, the district of old Assyria. Medieval Jews, like the writer of Yosippon, read Ashkenaz as the Teutons, and Eusebius had done the same. Saadia took the Slavs as meant, Josephus an unknown people called the Rhegines. Modern scholars since Bochart tie the name to Ascanius, found in Mysia and Phrygia and in a Homeric river.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-astrology-2051:
Astrology, the reading of fate in the stars, came to the Jews from outside. The entry stresses that its very names are foreign, drawn from Greek and Roman use. The Sibylline Books praise Jews for shunning star-gazers. Josephus faults the people on a like point. In fact, the entry says, there were no Jewish astrologers in the Holy Land or in Babylonia, and the art stood condemned.

Yet no one then doubted that the stars held real power. The entry retells the lore: fallen angels taught star-gazing, and Abraham wore a tablet showing every man's fate. God told him, in the Talmud's words, that for Israel there is no planet. Other sayings tie length of life, children, and income to the stars. Lucky and unlucky days close the survey of this popular belief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-australia-2151:
Australia is the island continent between the Indian and Pacific oceans. The entry calls it a land of sunshine for the Jews. Its colonies, raised on British habits, granted full religious freedom once they gained self-rule. Jews who settled there found a welcome and a home. Their numbers stayed small, never much above 15,000 in a population of three and a half millions.

Sydney holds the oldest congregation, in New South Wales. About twenty Jews lived in the colony in 1817. They formed a society to bury their dead, and in 1820 they won their own corner of ground. Later sections follow congregations across the colonies, even a gold-rush synagogue at Coolgardie that was sold to a Masonic body within three years. Jews served as mayors of nearly all the capital cities. Most worked in trade and making goods, and some rose high in sheep and cattle raising.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-badge-11751:
Badge, in this entry, means a mark sewn on Jewish dress so Jews could be told apart from others. The fourth Lateran Council of 1215 made it a general rule of Christendom under Innocent III. The stated aim was to stop unions between Jews and Christians. The entry doubts that aim and calls it largely a pretext. It traces a like rule to Islam and the Pact of Omar in 640.

Most of the entry works country by country. In France the mark was a ring called the wheel, ordered by Saint Louis in 1269 and kept up for centuries, with fines for those found without it. Spain, Italy, and England each get their own shapes, colors, and dates. England used a band from 1222 and later the form of the Tables of the Law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baginsky-adolf-:
Adolf Aron Baginsky was a German doctor and professor of children's diseases at Berlin, born May 22, 1843, at Ratibor in Prussian Silesia. He finished medical study at Berlin in 1866 and worked at a cholera hospital, then in practice at Seehausen and Nordhausen. He returned to Berlin after the Franco-Prussian war. In 1881 he became a privat-docent, and in 1892 an associate professor.

Baginsky gave his career to sick children. With Virchow's help he founded a children's hospital in Berlin in 1890, and he edited the "Archiv für Kinderheilkunde" from 1880. The entry lists his textbooks on school hygiene and on children's diseases, both reprinted often. It also notes his work against anti-Semitism in Berlin and his essay defending the health laws of Moses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-banu-bahdal-245: Banu Baḥdal is named here as a Jewish tribe in Medina that dwelt with the Banu Ḳuraiẓa. The hosted entry is only two sentences long, and it says almost nothing more than that. Even the name is in doubt. The sources, it warns, also give the forms "Ḥadal" and "Ḥandal." No leader, event, date, or fate for the tribe is stated. A single source line, signed with initials, is all the support the note carries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barrocas-mordec: Mordecai Barrocas was a Marano, physician, and poet. In Holland, at an advanced age, he openly returned to Judaism about the year 1605. To celebrate his initiation he composed some tercets in Spanish. The entry adds a darker note from the same circle. Tamar Barrocas, a Marano-Jewess and probably one of his relatives, suffered a martyr's death at the stake in Lisbon on August 3, 1603. She died in company with Diego de la Ascension. Nothing further is recorded here of Barrocas' medical practice or his other writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-bing-isaia:
Isaiah Beer-Bing was a French journalist born at Metz in 1759. He died in Paris on July 21, 1805. At twenty-five he published a French version of Mendelssohn's work on the soul. He also rendered the same work into Hebrew, printed at Berlin in 1786.

In 1788 Beer-Bing won the notice of leading reformers with pamphlets defending the Jews. His open letter answered attacks by a named foe of his people. Family needs later forced him from letters into a post running salt works in eastern France. The entry stresses that he never let Hebrew study lapse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bemidbar-rabbah:
Bemidbar Rabbah is the Midrash commentary on the book of Numbers, first printed at Constantinople in 1512. It is the latest part of the great Rabbah set on the Pentateuch. Rashi and other early writers never cite it, the entry notes.

The work falls into two parts of unlike age. The first, near three quarters of the whole, comments in late style on the opening chapters of Numbers. The second copies another Midrash, the Tanhuma, almost word for word. The entry lists the contents section by section and weighs the small changes between the two texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berenson-bernha: Bernhard Berenson, an art critic and historian, was born at Wilna, in Russia, on June 26, 1865. Educated in America, he finished at Harvard in 1887. For some time he had lived in Italy studying Italian art. He was counted a leading authority on its technique, using Morelli's methods to test who truly painted early works. He wrote for the New York Nation and for French and German reviews. His books treat Lorenzo Lotto, the painters of central Italy, and the study of Italian art.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-sinai:
Leopold Bernstein-Sinaieff was a Russo-French sculptor. He was born at Wilna on November 22, 1868. Most people called him simply Sinaieff. He settled in Paris at fourteen. There he studied sculpture under Dalou. His first shown work was a bust in 1890.

The entry lists busts of Count Waldeck and Rambaud. It also names the violinist Léon Reynier. His noted statue "Ezra Mourning" entered state hands in 1892. A marble version followed in 1897. His works won a medal at the Paris Exhibition of 1900. He joined the Legion of Honor in 1901. When the entry was written, he was carving a bust of Tolstoi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bial-rudolf-325: Rudolf Bial was a violinist, conductor, and composer. He was born at Habelschwerdt, Silesia, in 1834. He died at New York on November 13, 1881. He began in an orchestra at Breslau. Then he toured Australia and Africa. His brother Karl, a pianist, traveled with him. Back in Berlin, Bial directed several theaters. They included Kroll's and the Wallner Theater. His own operettas played at the Wallner. Later he worked in New York as a concert agent. His operettas and dances won wide popularity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bland-maria-the: Maria Theresa Bland was an English actress and singer. She was born in 1769 to Italian-Jewish parents. She died in London on January 15, 1838. At age four she acted at Hughes' Riding School. She returned at Drury Lane in 1786. Success made her leading lady there. Her best early rôle was Antonio in Grétry's opera. In 1790 she married Mr. Bland. Her later parts spanned opera and comedy. Her mind began to fail in 1824. She retired after a benefit that July.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bochim-3451: Bochim is named as a place near Beth-el. That short statement is nearly the whole entry. It cites the Septuagint reading in Judges ii. 1, given as the place of weeping to Beth-el and to all Israel. The entry then offers one cautious note: Bochim may be identical with Beth-el itself. It points readers to Moore on Judges for the point. No people, events, or later history for the place are described.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonviva-or-fren: Bonviva, in French Bonnevie and in Hebrew Ben Isaac, was a French Tosafist. He flourished probably early in the thirteenth century at Château-Thierry. He and his father are named in manuscript Tosafot on the treatise Bezah. The entry thinks Bonnevie is likely another name for Hayyim ben Isaak. Hayyim means life, matching the French name. One legal ruling by him is cited in the Mordecai. No works under his own name are listed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-braun-josef-365: Josef Braun was an Austrian journalist, dramatist, and librettist born at Budapest on May 5, 1840. He trained for medicine at Vienna but quit in 1860 for newspaper work. He edited several Vienna papers and ran a humor paper in 1869 and 1870. In 1871 he founded the Bombe, then sold it to start another comic paper. His plays and libretti include Flotte Bursche of 1861. Carneval in Rom, with music by Johann Strauss, came in 1877. A romance by him ran in his own paper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-broyde-isaac-37:
Isaac Broydé was a Russian Orientalist born at Porozowo, in the government of Grodno, on Feb. 23, 1867. He left for Paris in 1883 and studied at the Sorbonne. He took diplomas from two Paris schools, in 1892 and 1894. From 1890 to 1895 he served as secretary to Joseph Derenbourg.

After Derenbourg died, Broydé helped continue the publication of Saadia's works. He became librarian to the Alliance Israélite Universelle in 1895 and left in 1900. He catalogued Elkan Adler's library in London, then moved to New York. There he joined the editorial staff of the Jewish Encyclopedia. The entry lists his French and Hebrew works on Bahya ibn Pakuda and on the Persian capture of Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bush-lewis-3851: Lewis Bush was an American soldier born in Philadelphia, from a known family of Jewish merchants there. He won a first lieutenant's commission in the Sixth Pennsylvania Battalion on Jan. 9, 1776. That June he became captain of the same unit. In January 1777 he moved to a new continental regiment under Colonel Hartley. He rose to major on March 12, 1777. The entry calls him a brave soldier who served with distinction in many fights. At the battle of Brandywine, on Sept. 11, 1777, he took a fatal wound and died soon after.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carmoly-eliakim:
Eliakim Carmoly, a French scholar, was born at Sulz on August 5, 1802, and died at Frankfort-on-the-Main on Feb. 15, 1875. His birth name was Goschel David Behr. He took the older family name Carmoly while still young. He studied Hebrew and Talmud at Colmar, then studied old Hebrew manuscripts in Paris.

In 1832 Carmoly became rabbi at Brussels for the new Belgian consistory. There he helped the young congregation, chiefly by providing schools for the poor. Reform plans brought strong opposition, and he resigned after seven years. At Frankfort he turned to Jewish literature and to collecting Hebrew books and manuscripts. His long list of works covers biography, travel accounts, Jewish history, and editions of older texts. Critics attacked some of his claims as unreliable, yet the entry credits him with real service to Jewish letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-category-greek-:
Category is a term Aristotle brought into philosophy. It means attribute or predicate. Aristotle held that every word in a proposition falls under one of ten categories. The list runs from substance and quantity to action and passion. Only substance, he taught, has real existence. The rest attach to it and describe its qualities.

The doctrine changed little from Aristotle to Kant, the entry says. Plotinus split the categories into five for the intelligible sphere and five for the sensible world. Jewish thinkers kept Aristotle's list. Saadia used the ten categories to show that none can apply to God. Gabirol and Baḥya also used them. Abraham ibn Daud opened his Emunah Rammah with them. Maimonides refers to them often in his Guide, calling them by the name genus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-charlemont-eliz: Elizabeth Jane Caulfield, countess of Charlemont, was a convert to Judaism. Born on June 21, 1834, she died at Roxborough Castle, in County Tyrone, Ireland, on May 31, 1882. She was the only daughter of the first Lord Athlumney. In December 1856 she married the third earl of Charlemont. Though raised a Christian, she attended synagogue worship often and sought counsel from rabbis. She was a fine linguist and musician, with a gift for recitation used for charities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chorin-choriner:
Aaron Chorin, a Hungarian rabbi, was born at Weisskirchen, Moravia, on Aug. 3, 1766, and died at Arad on Aug. 24, 1844. He studied at Mattersdorf and then at Prague under Ezekiel Landau, where he also learned German. After a failed start in trade, he took the rabbinate at Arad in the spring of 1789 and held it for life.

His first pamphlet, in 1798, argued that the sturgeon could be eaten under Scripture, and the fight over it made his name. Later writings backed German prayers, the organ, and daily temple service, while keeping the Shema in Hebrew. The entry follows his clashes, his recall of one work, and his return to Reform views.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crescas-abiatha: Abiathar ibn Crescas, ha-Kohen, was physician in ordinary to King Juan the Second of Aragon. Abiathar was a skilled oculist and a learned astrologer. In September of 1468 he freed the king, then seventy years old, from a double cataract of the eyes. The cataracts had caused the king's total blindness. Abiathar also preached the memorial sermon at the funeral service held by the Jewish community of Cervera. That service marked the death of the king in January of 1479. One chronicle, the Anales de Aragon, is cited as the source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-custom-hebrew-m:
Custom, in Hebrew minhag, is an old usage or religious practice with no direct Bible base. Long observance has made it as sacred and binding as set law. Custom always precedes law, one rabbinic book says. That holds even for Bible rules. Circumcision and the ban on eating blood may both reach back to patriarchal custom. Other customs came later, or from foreign lands.

Written law never fixed every detail of practice. Tribal and family customs filled the gaps and lived on beside the codes. The article gives case after case: a shoe exchanged to seal a sale, acts of piety by single rabbis taken up by whole communities. Women's customs around Sabbath and festivals close the long survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dalberg-karl-th: Karl Theodor, Baron von Dalberg, was archbishop of Mayence and later Grand Duke of Frankfort. He was born on February 8, 1744, and he died on February 10, 1817. The entry praises him as one of the noblest German princes of his day. He always favored full emancipation of the Jews. Local patricians long blocked him in Frankfort. On December 28, 1811, he decreed full civil rights for the Jews of Frankfort and their descendants. The Jews paid 440,000 florins for the change, and the yearly protection tax ended.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-jacob: Jacob Meir's son David was an Italian astrologer of the fifteenth century and a member of the Kalonymus family. In 1464 he wrote two astrological treatises. The smaller one treated the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter. He dedicated it to King Ferdinand I of Naples, hoping to win religious liberty for his fellow Jews. In 1466 he translated an astronomical work by John of Gmünd from Latin into Hebrew. The king gave him an office, probably that of astrologer. In 1484 he wrote on Averroes for his son.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-del-banco-miria: Miriam Del Banco was an American author born on June 27, 1867, at New Orleans. Her father, Rabbi Max Del Banco, died soon after her birth. She was raised in St. Louis and at Cape Girardeau, where she finished the State Normal School with honors. In 1885 she took a teaching post in Chicago's public schools. Since 1889 she had been assistant principal at the Von Humboldt School. She wrote many poems for the Jewish and general press, and translated works by Kayserling and Alberti.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutz-emmanuel-:
Emmanuel Menahem Deutz was chief rabbi of the Central Consistory of the Jews of France. Born at Coblenz in 1763, he studied at the school in Mayence and then became rabbi in his home town. He sat in the assemblies of 1806 and 1807 that Napoleon called. Under Napoleon's new order he took a seat in the Central Consistory beside David Sinzheim.

From 1822 Deutz was the Consistory's only chief rabbi. He preached in the old school style: though he knew French, he never used it in the pulpit. His last years were darkened by family sorrow, above all his son's desertion of Judaism and unhappy political career. He died on January 31, 1842.
