A drug that restarts cell housekeeping could offer the first real lever against this ataxia.
pmc-13238851:
Douglas Grbic and team linked medical school class makeup to graduates' confidence in working across backgrounds in a 2026 study of 139,681 entering students. The data covered 973 cohorts at 139 American MD-granting schools, with students entering between 2013 and 2020. A combined index measured how much each class varied in gender, race and ethnic mix, and parents' schooling, and graduation surveys supplied the outcome.

Classes with greater internal variation produced graduates who more strongly agreed that their class diversity had sharpened their skills with people from different backgrounds. The link was moderate and survived multilevel modeling checks. The authors frame cohort makeup itself as a teaching input, not just an entry outcome. Diverse classrooms, their evidence suggests, teach something lectures cannot.
pmc-13239751:
Collince Odiwuor Ogolla, Benard Guya, and Apollo O Maima study why blood donation stays low in underserved Kenyan communities in a 2026 survey paper. Safe transfusion depends on regular donors, yet social, economic, and cultural barriers keep many rural residents from giving blood.

Questionnaires in two rural districts compared donors with people who had never given. Those non-donors knew far less about who may give blood and were less sure the process was safe. Lack of awareness was the commonest reason for not donating, followed by fear of pain, cultural or religious objections, and costs such as transport and lost wages. Regression confirmed awareness and beliefs as the strongest predictors.
pmc-13240151:
Xue Liu and colleagues hunt early warning genes for a devastating newborn gut disease in a 2026 computational study. Necrotizing enterocolitis strikes premature babies and kills a fifth to a third of cases, partly because no clear early blood or tissue marker exists to trigger fast treatment.

The team merged five public gene datasets and ran more than a hundred machine learning combinations to find a diagnostic signature. Three genes stood out, one falling and two rising in diseased tissue, with the best model separating cases almost perfectly. Single-cell data, virtual gene knockouts in a computer model, and mouse experiments all backed the trio. Immune cell mixes also shifted in characteristic ways.
pmc-13240451:
Sara G Hamad and colleagues explain a stubborn wheeze in a baby as a rare chest tumour in a 2026 case report. Neuroblastoma is the commonest solid cancer outside the brain in children, yet it usually grows in the abdomen, and chest tumours from the lower spine's nerve chain are particularly unusual.

Their patient, a 10-month-old boy, kept wheezing with a persistent shadow on imaging that ordinary explanations did not fit. The tumour was traced to the sympathetic chain at the lowest thoracic level, far below where chest neuroblastomas normally arise. The authors urge clinicians to place this cancer on the list when an infant's chest mass or lasting wheeze resists the usual diagnoses and treatments.
pmc-13241451:
Gao and colleagues in Shandong reviewed how Sjögren's disease dries and inflames the eye surface. Its dry eye runs harsher and more stubborn than the ordinary kind. The team synthesized recent pathology work across every ocular surface component. Glands, tear film, nerves, and surface cells all feature.

Failing tear glands, vanishing goblet cells, and overly salty tears feed relentless surface inflammation. Corneal nerve damage completes a self-reinforcing cycle of worsening injury. Gao argues these interlocking lesions explain the disease's treatment resistance. The review targets gentler diagnostic criteria and therapies aimed at breaking the cycle.
pmc-13241651:
Tae Hyung Kim and co-authors publish a 2026 reply letter about their ultrasound study of neck lymph nodes in Alzheimer disease. A commenter had questioned how much the node measurements depend on counting method. The reply clarifies which results were calculated per person and which per individual node.

The authors reran key comparisons with a statistical method that accounts for nodes clustered within the same person. The main categorical findings kept their direction and significance after that adjustment. They explain that their composite score summarizes a gradient of node features rather than stacking separate signals. A single-measure model performed nearly as well as the composite. They agree the score is exploratory and needs outside validation.
pmc-13241851:
Connor WJ Bevington and co-authors present a 2026 imaging review of how brain energy use changes with healthy aging. The brain burns large amounts of energy to power thinking, mood, and movement. Combined PET and MRI scanning can now map where that energy comes from across the living brain.

Energy comes mainly from burning glucose with oxygen, an efficient route, while a faster fallback route yields far less per glucose molecule. The balance between these routes shifts across brain regions and across the lifespan. The authors explain how spatial pattern analysis of scans can separate healthy aging from early disease change. Such markers could support earlier detection of neurodegeneration and guide therapies aimed at brain energy pathways.
pmc-13242751:
Lise Lotte Brauckhoff and co-authors publish a 2026 review of patients with stubborn face pain at a national clinic in Bergen, Norway. Records covered ninety-eight consecutive patients assessed by an interdisciplinary team. Diagnoses were later mapped onto the international classification of orofacial pain.

Muscle-based facial pain was the most common diagnosis, followed by nerve pain after injury and persistent unexplained facial pain. Women made up the large majority of patients. Muscle pain patients had the longest pain histories and the most widespread body pain, headaches, and joint complaints. Muscle pain also frequently accompanied injury-related nerve pain. Anxiety and depression scores ran highest in the muscle pain group. The authors support personal, team-based care plans.
pmc-13242851:
Hongyan Song and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study of stress-driven high blood sugar in a severe tick-borne viral disease marked by fever and low platelets. Blood sugar rises under severe infection stress, but its meaning in this disease was unclear. Records for just over a hundred seventy patients were analyzed.

Admission glucose and a stress glucose ratio were higher in patients than in controls. Severe cases and patients who died showed higher values than mild cases and survivors. In survivors, glucose trended down over the stay, while in non-survivors it stayed high or climbed. Glucose levels also tracked with virus amount, organ damage markers, clotting problems, and inflammatory signals. The authors propose glucose measures as simple severity markers.
pmc-13243851:
Yohanna Kusuma and colleagues weigh a hard choice in stroke care for people with active cancer in a 2026 review. A catheter procedure can pull a clot from a blocked brain artery and restore blood flow. Cancer patients were long viewed as poor candidates for the procedure.

Pooled studies show the procedure reopens vessels well in cancer patients, with bleeding rates near those of other patients. Even so, fewer cancer patients regain independence, and more die within 90 days. The review blames the cancer itself and prior frailty more than the procedure. It offers a framework that weighs clinical, ethical, and cost factors for each case.
pmc-13245051:
Ali Mahmoud Ahmed and colleagues present two patients whose inherited small-vessel brain disease was mistaken for multiple sclerosis. Their case report and review appeared in BMC Neurology in 2026. CADASIL, caused by NOTCH3 gene faults, scars the brain's white matter through repeated small strokes. In some patients it produces inflamed, MS-like attacks that send diagnosis down the wrong road for years.

Beyond their two cases, the authors found twelve reports covering nineteen similar patients. Closer image review showed a mushroom shape wedged at that same spot. A scope confirmed both the stuck food and the underlying narrowing below it. Late signs can mislead, so blocked passage deserves care in such children.
pmc-13283951:
Double-shell sulfur hosts that move electrolyte on their own anchor a 2026 battery study by Ziqing Yao and colleagues. Lithium-sulfur cells promise very high energy storage but suffer sulfur shuttling and slow reactions. The host design aims to stop sulfur compounds pooling near catalysts.

Hosts were built from Prussian blue relatives through ion exchange with careful ratios. The shell layout drives fluid movement during charge and discharge cycles. That motion spreads reactants and steadies the sulfur reaction zone. Cycling stability improved for practical cells built with the hosts. A pouch cell at ampere-hour scale reached a high energy density value. Steps toward real-world use are the focus.
pmc-13284551:
Lin Li and colleagues compared resting brain scans in 2026 between two groups of schoolchildren recorded ten years apart. Children's thinking changes fast with age, and the team wanted to see which brain areas shifted. Scans from thirty Changzhou primary schoolers aged seven to twelve, taken in 2008, were matched against thirty similar children scanned in 2017 on the same machine with the same settings. Two measures of resting activity and hub strength were computed.

Some back-of-brain and cerebellar areas showed higher activity in the later group, while memory and frontal areas showed lower values. One visual area gained hub strength, and a parietal area lost it. The authors read the mix as development: some regions working harder, others working more efficiently, across attention, memory, and cognition networks.
pmc-13284751:
Yike Chen and a large team hunted blood proteins in 2026 that track brain amyloid build-up, the defining plaque of Alzheimer's disease. Brain scans and spinal fluid tests confirm amyloid but are costly or invasive, so blood markers matter. The team paired amyloid PET scans with plasma profiling of about seven thousand proteins in 1,429 people across two cohorts.

They found 454 proteins tied to amyloid load, and 54 of those held up across both cohorts. A combined score from those 54 proteins tracked amyloid burden, other disease markers, and clinical severity. Clustering pointed to coordinated groups covering cell signalling, immune activity, and protein housekeeping. The authors position blood profiling as a companion to the leading blood marker and to PET for sorting patients by disease biology.
pmc-13285451:
Hao Li and co-authors chart the burden of appendicitis across Africa from 2010 to 2023, with projections to 2030, in a study published in 2026. Appendicitis is a common surgical emergency, yet continent-wide evidence about its scale had been thin. The team used Global Burden of Disease estimates covering 54 countries.

Case numbers rose steeply, from about 2.45 million new cases in 2010 to about 3.73 million in 2023, mostly because populations grew. Deaths also rose in raw numbers, although death rates adjusted for age fell. Southern and western regions carried heavy nonfatal burdens, while eastern Africa saw the worst death and disability rates. The authors call for faster diagnosis, referral, and emergency surgical care.
pmc-13285651:
A self-feeding loop locks liver cancer growth on, Chunxun Liu and co-authors map in a 2026 study. The protein STRAP runs high in many cancers, yet its liver role was fuzzy. Database, cell, and patient sample checks confirmed high STRAP in liver tumors and a link to poor outlook.

STRAP grabs a brake protein, DKK1, sparing a growth messenger from breakdown and letting it enter the nucleus to switch genes on with a partner. That same partner then binds the STRAP gene switch, making yet more STRAP. Hitting both STRAP and the Wnt path at once crushed tumor growth in tests. The authors back paired targeting as a liver cancer plan.
pmc-13286351:
Pablo González-Suárez and co-authors revisit the gene switches that build leaf breathing pores in a 2026 plant study. Three related factors were thought to work in strict sequence, with SPEECHLESS starting the line and FAMA finishing the pore's guard cells. New hints said the starter lingers late in development, and the team combined gene readouts with targeted switches to test what it still does there.

Both the starter and finisher proved active in late cells, sharing many target genes. Their balance, rather than a clean handoff, set whether guard cells divided again or swelled to final size. Twisting target genes out of their proper timing warped pore shape and function. The revised picture replaces a relay race with two partners whose shifting ratio steers the last steps of pore building.
pmc-13286451:
Yingshan Lin and colleagues test whether a combined nutrition and inflammation score predicts survival in intensive care patients with atrial fibrillation. The 2026 study draws on a large critical care database. The score, first built for lung cancer patients, mixes body mass, blood albumin, and a white cell ratio into one number.

Patients with higher scores died less often within thirty and ninety days, with each step up in score band lowering risk further. The link curved: benefit grew until a middle value, then reversed. The score beat any single nutrition or inflammation marker at forecasting death, and pairing it with a standard organ failure score sharpened accuracy. The authors propose keeping the score in its favorable range.
pmc-13286751:
Alessandro Barbarossa and colleagues compare two ultrasound probes used to guide a heart procedure that seals the left atrial appendage, an alternative for stroke prevention when blood thinners are unsafe. The 2026 single-center study reviews 46 patients treated between 2021 and 2024. A miniature probe can work under light sedation instead of a full breathing tube.

Success rates matched between the standard and miniature probes, with one failure from a sizing problem in the standard group. Complications around the procedure were similar and mild. The miniature probe shortened procedures by roughly twenty minutes and avoided intubation more often, without extra radiation or dye. One-month follow-up showed no added problems. Larger studies are still needed given the small miniature-probe group.
pmc-13287051:
Christer Malm and Michael Svensson review whether meldonium, the drug at the center of famous doping cases, truly improves athletic performance. Their 2026 narrative review examines its chemistry, movement through the body, safety, and the quality of human performance studies. The drug blocks carnitine production, shifting muscles toward burning glucose, which uses oxygen more efficiently.

Despite wide use and a place on the anti-doping prohibited list since 2016, rigorous placebo-controlled trials in healthy athletes are essentially missing. Existing studies carry high bias risk and design flaws. The ban rested on signs that athletes used it hoping to gain an edge, not on proof that it works. Better trials are needed to settle genuine effects and long-term safety, the authors conclude.
pmc-13287151:
Feng Qiu and co-authors examined a growth-related gene called RHEBL1 in mouth cancer during 2026, asking whether two stem-cell factors switch it on. Tissue staining compared healthy, precancerous, and cancer samples, while altered cell lines and mouse work tested what changing the gene does.

RHEBL1 was abundant in tumours, especially near invading edges. Raising its activity helped cells form spheres and produce tumour-like growths in mice, while removing it had the opposite effect. The paired factors Oct4 and Sox2 attached at two places in the gene control region and boosted its activity. The authors link that control route to early tumour growth.
pmc-13287351:
Haitham Jahrami and colleagues translated a six-question scale on problem YouTube use into Arabic in 2026 and checked it with 1,134 young adults from Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Tunisia. The short scale was rendered through forward and back translation, then tested for structure and stability over time.

Answers fitted a single underlying trait well. Scores were steady on repeat testing and lined up with related measures of social media overuse, distress, food addiction scores, and poor sleep. The scale behaved the same across sex and viewing habits. The authors offer it as a screening aid for clinics and surveys in Arabic-speaking settings.
pmc-13287651:
Urszula Hohmann and co-authors filmed living glioblastoma cells in 2026 to see how crowding changes the way this aggressive brain tumour spreads through tissue. Established and patient-derived cell lines were watched at varied densities, and cell division events were tracked against nearby movement.

A division briefly sped up cells up to three cell lengths away. Under a density slope, some lines kept crawling on their own while others moved mainly by growth pressure. Cells that lined up into liquid-crystal-like order kept moving well even when packed tight. The authors suggest that self-ordering may help the tumour keep invading under confinement, a trait that makes it hard to contain.
pmc-13287751:
Zefeng Xu and co-authors report early human testing in 2026 of rovadicitinib, a tablet that blocks two signalling families at once, for myelofibrosis, a severe bone marrow scarring disease. Lab work on patient cells and mice came first. Then 64 patients at nine Chinese centres joined a first-in-human dose study run from late 2018 to late 2020.

Patients had primary disease or disease that grew out of related blood disorders, at medium or high risk. The letter format outlines dose steps and expansion groups rather than full outcome tables. Existing drugs of one family shrink spleens but often fade; the dual blocker aims for deeper control with one pill.
pmc-13288551:
Afeefa Tahira and co-authors survey diabetes app users in Pakistan in 2026. The survey drew 397 patients with type 2 diabetes. Hospitals in four provinces took part. Both public and private sites joined. Models tested what turns trial use into steady use.

Acceptance strongly foretold steady use. Doctor advice fed acceptance a lot. Social image and confidence also fed it. Day to day, satisfaction mattered most. Better sugar reads also helped. Easy access to trusted facts helped too. Fast internet and good clinics aided use. They worked in part through confidence. Local context should shape app design, they say.
pmc-13288951:
Javeria Mansoor and colleagues map active learning in public health schools. Their 2026 scoping review covers case, problem, and team methods. These methods are well studied in clinics. Their use in public health is less clear. Public health work deals with whole groups.

The search found 22 studies in all. Problem-based work led the set. Team work came next. Topics ranged from global health to job health. Six themes ran through the reports. Skill growth and real-world fit stood out. Each method had its own snags. Problem work could overload students. Team work ate student time. Case work needed more staff and funds.
pmc-13289251:
Theresa Farhat headed a 2026 review of learning gains from a rural trauma training program in Nepal. The Rural Emergency Trauma System Strengthening program, called RETSS, began after the 2015 earthquake. Partners included the Nepal Red Cross Society, the Canadian Red Cross, and the Centre for Global Surgery at McGill. A train-the-trainer model aimed to leave local teachers behind.

Program records from 2017 to 2020 covered 1170 health workers trained across 158 government sites in Sindhupalchok and Kavrepalanchok. Most trainees were women, and just over half were aged 18 to 29 at training. Basic life support scores jumped from a median of 9.0 to 22.0 right after training in the data. Repeat testing then tracked how much skill faded over time, a key test for rural readiness.
pmc-13289551:
Caroline Lager and colleagues present a 2026 population study on pain and device-measured activity patterns in older adults in Sweden. Pain often cuts movement, but daily patterns of sitting, stepping, and intensity matter beyond total activity alone. Data came from the SNAC-K aging study in Kungsholmen for 2016 to 2019, with thigh-worn sensors tracking real behavior.

A total of 665 older adults wore the activPAL3 sensor and answered pain questionnaires for analysis. Three activity classes emerged: Active Movers, Balanced Movers, and Sedentary Movers, based on steps, sitting bouts, and activity levels. Stronger pain tied to the sedentary class versus the active class in the full sample. Links clustered in women and in those aged 80 or older.
pmc-13289651:
Hongmei Li and colleagues review a 2026 topic on regulatory T cells along the path from pancreas inflammation to pancreatic cancer. These cells keep immunity in check and limit tissue harm, but in pancreatic cancer they can shield tumors from attack. Acute inflammation, chronic inflammation, and cancer share immune features that shift cell roles over time and place.

In early inflammation the cells protect by calming excess attack, while in tumors they may block useful defense. Simply wiping them out can even speed tumor growth in some settings, the review warns. Differences in cell subtypes, tissue residence, and disease stage decide the net effect. The authors map drug ideas that tune rather than erase these cells.
pmc-13289851:
Pedro Agustin Lovato Gutiérrez and Francisco Molina present a 2026 case of a giant hair mass in the stomach of a 27-year-old woman. Such masses, called trichobezoars, form from swallowed hair and mostly affect young women with mental health conditions. When hair trails into the small bowel, doctors call it Rapunzel syndrome, a rare and dangerous variant needing surgical removal.

She had six months of belly pain, vomiting, weight loss, and inability to keep food down before care. Scoping showed hair filling about 90 percent of the stomach and blocking its outlet, while scans showed stomach stretching that mimicked an artery squeeze syndrome. Open surgery removed the mass whole, recovery went smoothly, and psychiatric review confirmed hair pulling and eating.
pmc-13290151:
Outcomes of a radical operation for advanced pancreatic cancer are reported by Carsten Hansen and co-authors in 2026 from a high-volume center. The procedure removes part or all of the pancreas together with the celiac artery axis, territory once considered untouchable because of ischemia risk.

Data collected prospectively covered 58 patients operated on between 2014 and mid-2025, most after chemotherapy or similar treatment first. Median overall survival reached 28.0 months for patients treated before surgery, yet recurrence-free survival had a median of just 6.0 months, showing how early the cancer tends to return. Leak and ischemia rates were in line with standard pancreas removals. Hansen and colleagues conclude the operation is feasible but demands careful patient selection.
pmc-13290551:
Something in cow's milk calms human immune cells in a dish, and Lili Flad and colleagues name a suspect protein in a 2026 study. Milk's beta-casein comes in A1 and A2 variants, long debated for health effects, and both kinds were already known to slow the growth of stimulated blood immune cells.

The team split each milk type by molecule size and found the heavy fraction did the inhibiting. Protein screening of the cell supernatants singled out TOM1, the only protein markedly raised after exposure to both milks' heavy fractions. Added on its own, TOM1 also curbed the stimulated cells, and marker analysis tied it to interleukin-1β signaling. Flad and colleagues propose TOM1 as an anti-inflammatory mediator hiding in milk.
pmc-13290651:
Md Abdullah Evna Hasan and colleagues hunt drug-resistant Klebsiella in pet birds in Bangladesh, in a 2026 study. Ornamental birds may carry bacteria that shrug off last-line antibiotics. The team collected 112 samples across bird feces, cages, water, feed, shop air, and handlers' hands and noses. Homes and pet shops contributed equally. Lab tests confirmed the bacterium and probed its resistance genes.

Over half the samples, about 53 percent, grew the target bacterium. Shops ran slightly higher than households in positive samples. Most isolates resisted several drug classes, and about eighty percent formed strong biofilms. Resistance to key hospital antibiotics passed sixty percent for two of them. Genes for extended-spectrum and carbapenem resistance were widespread in the isolates. Shop isolates carried extended-spectrum traits far more often than home ones. The authors, reporting a first for Bangladesh, urge One Health action.
pmc-13290851:
Childhood emotional neglect may deepen adult depression partly through body-wide inflammation, Yongqi Ding and colleagues report in a study from 2026. They tested whether a combined blood marker sits on the path between early neglect and how bad depression gets in major depressive disorder.

The study enrolled 236 patients who filled in trauma and mood surveys and gave routine blood tests. Patients with childhood trauma histories showed higher inflammation and worse depression. Among trauma types, neglect predicted depression scores most strongly, and among blood markers the combined index predicted best of all. A mediation analysis assigned about 28% of the neglect-to-severity link to that index. Ding and colleagues stress the design cannot prove cause, but flag inflammation-lowering add-on treatments as worth testing in future trials.
pmc-13291251:
Dogs and owners act much alike across the world. Juliane Bräuer leads a 2026 study testing hunting dogs in five rural societies. Most past work used dogs from rich western homes. That bias left a big gap in knowledge.

Teams worked in Vanuatu, Mongolia, Madagascar, Peru, and Germany. Owners and dogs did six shared social tests. A survey also probed the bond in daily life. Bonds looked strikingly alike across all sites. Small gaps traced back to hunting style. A few gaps split rich and poor settings. Shared roots may matter more than local custom. The bond seems a deep, world-wide human trait.
pmc-13291351:
One kinase does far more than start DNA copying. Lorenzo Galanti and Boris Pfander review this enzyme in a 2026 article. The kinase, called DDK, pairs two protein parts. Its classic job is firing DNA copying starts.

The review views the enzyme from three angles. Timing shows when it acts across the cell cycle. Placement shows where it sits on chromosomes. Targets show what proteins it switches on. New targets guard chromosome splitting and DNA repair. Damage response work also sits on its list. Cancer drugs may exploit this wider role. Genome care, not just copying, is its true brief.
pmc-13291551:
An antibody can turn killer immune cells on pancreas tumors. Ruoxi Xiao leads a 2026 study of KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer. Such tumors shrug off growth signal blockers. The mutant gene keeps growth switched on below the blocker.

Antibodies of one class can still flag tumor cells. Killer cells then destroy the flagged cells directly. The team paired nimotuzumab with added killer cells. Dish, ball culture, and mouse models all showed strong killing. Killer cells woke fully and homed to tumors. Tumor EGFR levels predicted how well it worked. KRAS status did not block the effect. Flag-based killing thus bypasses the mutant switch.
pmc-13292051:
Julia Banaszkiewicz and co-authors review a 2026 topic in cancer therapy: using Clostridiaceae bacteria, which thrive without oxygen, to attack solid tumors. Tumor interiors hold low-oxygen and dead zones that resist standard drugs, yet suit these anaerobic microbes perfectly. The review surveys strains, engineered variants, and combinations with chemotherapy, radiation, and immunotherapy.

Clostridium spores germinate inside tumor tissue while sparing healthy tissue, and their toxins and enzymes can burst cancer cells and wake up immune responses. The strain Clostridium novyi-NT, stripped of virulence factors, produced strong tumor cell killing in studies. Engineered strains can also carry enzymes that switch on prodrugs only at the tumor, cutting body-wide toxicity. The authors see real promise, especially in combined regimens.
pmc-13292551:
Gabriel Caetano de Jesus, Victor Ary Câmara, and Arthur Menino Castilho audit a 2026 twelve-year record of newborn hearing screening across Brazil's states. Federal law has required screening in every maternity hospital since 2010, with national guidance from 2012 targeting coverage above 95 percent in a baby's first month. The study traces how actual coverage evolved as the program matured.

Coverage fell to 26.39 percent nationally in 2023, far below target in the reported figures. The South region led the states at 62.52 percent, and the Federal District reached 83.19 percent that year. Brainstem response testing has grown in both number and share since 2018, suggesting a shift toward the method reserved for at-risk newborns. The authors frame the state-by-state gaps as the central policy problem.
pmc-13292651:
Paula Gerlero, Silvia Vanessa Lourenço, and Marcello Menta Simonsen Nico report a 2026 letter on an unlikely pairing: white sponge nevus inside the mouths of two patients with ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-cleft syndrome. The syndrome, usually driven by TP63 mutations, deforms limbs, skin, and the lip, while the nevus thickens oral mucosa into white, velvety plaques. Fewer than a handful of combined cases exist.

Both patients, treated at the University of São Paulo dermatology service, showed diffuse mucosal thickening reaching tongue and palate, with biopsy features matching the nevus. Symptomatic lesions received liquid nitrogen cryotherapy. Results were excellent in both, and one patient's lesions had not returned after ten years. The authors suspect the overlap is no coincidence, pointing to shared keratin biology, and offer freezing as a practical fix for painful lesions.
pmc-13292851:
Songping Yi and co-authors set out a trial plan, published in 2026, testing mindfulness training for women having frozen embryo transfer. Many patients feel anxiety, low mood, poor sleep, or strain during fertility care, which the trial aims to ease.

Women aged 18 to 45 with mild to moderate distress will be split evenly between mindfulness sessions and basic counseling without mindfulness. The main outcome is the clinical pregnancy rate, with mood, sleep, and stress tracked as well. Enrollment will reach 434 participants across the single center. The team will also test whether calmer minds explain any link to pregnancy.
pmc-13292951:
Akihiro Kojima and colleagues report, in 2026, two cases of hernia through a surgery port hole after robot-assisted prostate removal, plus a new way to prevent them. Such hernias are rare yet serious and need repair surgery.

Both cases arose in 2024 among 73 robot prostate operations at their center, where a 12-mm port had sat. Their fix applies an anti-stick agent at the port site and sews the tough wall layer closed without the inner lining. One later patient treated with the new method stayed hernia-free. The team calls the step simple and safe for all patients.
pmc-13293451:
Donghao Zhang and co-authors build, in a 2026 finance study, a network map of extreme loss risk among Chinese financial firms. Gauging how shocks spread between firms matters for guarding the whole system, yet older models miss joint tail events.

Their method blends factor and pairing models to estimate expected shortfall shared across firms, then checks the model with backtests. The new model cut test rejection rates clearly versus three rival models, with gaps the authors report as large for two of them. The risk network's shape matched real market stress events. Firm and market traits shaped how strongly risk spilled across the network.
pmc-13293651:
Whether a plant compound called morin can block a key energy enzyme in Cryptosporidium parvum is what Mengge Chen and colleagues tested in a 2026 study. The gut parasite causes severe diarrhea in children and people with weak immunity, and good drugs are lacking.

The parasite leans on sugar breakdown for energy, so its aldolase enzyme is a tempting target. The team mapped the enzyme, found it in parasite cells and secretions, and showed morin docks onto it. Morin or immune serum cut sugar uptake, energy levels, and parasite counts in dishes. In infected young mice, morin cut egg shedding by 61.8% and eased gut harm, a drop the authors report.
pmc-13293751:
Jinpeng Yang and colleagues design a smarter way to judge how much nitrogen rice plants hold, in a 2026 agricultural study. Fertilizer decisions depend on plant dry matter and nitrogen uptake, yet field measurements are too sparse to guide whole regions. Their framework first teaches a deep learning model how rice grows, using a crop simulator run across thousands of virtual fields, then fine-tunes it with satellite image sequences and real field data.

The trained model estimated dry matter and nitrogen uptake more accurately than standard machine learning methods. From those estimates it classified nitrogen status with reasonable accuracy and computed how much fertilizer each field still needed. Field trials at seven sites cut nitrogen use noticeably while holding or raising yields. The authors offer the system as decision support for precise, lower-waste fertilization.
pmc-13294051:
Md Jashim Uddin and colleagues probe a protective immune pathway in mouse COVID in a 2026 study. Lung RNA data showed sharp rises in CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11 after infection with mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2, along with their shared receptor CXCR3. Flow checks linked stronger arrival of CXCR3-bearing T cells and other immune cells to milder illness.

Blocking CXCR3 worsened disease, cut T cell entry, and let neutrophils flood in. Removing neutrophils eased that harm, and mice lacking adaptive immunity lost the protection. Transfer of normal CD4 T cells, but not CXCR3-deficient ones, restored defense. The axis appears to guard lungs by holding neutrophil damage in check.
pmc-13294151:
Jehad A. Aldali leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of central line bloodstream infections in Saudi Arabian intensive care units. Lines save lives but can seed severe infections, and local pooled data were scarce. Four databases were searched for studies from January 2015 to November 2025 that reported rates, microbes, or outcomes.

From 2,788 records, 11 studies entered the review and 7 entered the pooling. The combined rate was 3.05 infections per 1,000 line-days, with wide variation by unit type, region, and design. Mixed units ran highest at 3.41 per 1,000 line-days in the reported subgroup. High statistical heterogeneity warns against treating one national figure as uniform.
pmc-13294651:
Andrew Dickman leads a 2026 consensus study on giving intravenous medicines safely in critical care and cancer care. Open questions include which tubing materials to use, when filters are needed, and when light protection matters during storage and infusion. Poor choices can degrade drugs, block access devices, or harm patients.

Eight expert pharmacists rated statements over three Delphi rounds, starting from 181 medicines and finishing with 174 medicines. In all, 1044 storage and administration requirements were judged, and agreement was reached for 697 of them. The resulting guidance gives pharmacists and nurses shared, evidence-informed rules for tubing, filtration, and light protection in routine practice.
pmc-13294851:
Jon García-Ormaza and colleagues study suicidal thoughts and self-injury in early adolescence in a 2026 survey from Spain. Both problems are common at this age and carry serious health risks. Attention difficulties, mood, and trouble managing emotions were examined together rather than separately.

The sample held 1,079 pupils aged about 13 in their first year of secondary school. Roughly one in ten reported suicidal thoughts and about one in six reported self-injury without suicidal intent. Young people with either problem showed more attention difficulties, more negative mood, and far greater trouble regulating emotions, which emerged as the strongest single predictor in the models.
pmc-13294951:
David Alejandro Rodríguez Carvajal and co-authors map where a three-oxide recipe melts into glass, in a 2026 materials study of the cadmium oxide, tellurium dioxide, and germanium dioxide system. Tellurite glasses are prized for optics, with high refractive index and wide transparency, but they can be thermally fragile. The team melted thirty-six compositions at high temperature and quenched them, charting which mixtures formed clear glass and which began to crystallize.

Most mixtures stayed amorphous, though the richest cadmium blends showed early crystal peaks, including one matching a cadmium tellurium oxide phase. Spectroscopy revealed cadmium loosening the tellurite network, reshaping its building units, while germanium adopted mixed coordination. Heating tests placed the glass transition in the mid four hundreds Celsius, with tellurium-rich glasses resisting crystallization up to far higher temperatures. Cadmium encouraged crystal formation, while germanium guarded stability, a trade-off designers of optical glass must balance.
pmc-13295851:
Sofia Rouot and co-authors introduce ProbeST in 2026, free software for designing probes that map gene activity in tissue slices. Commercial probe sets cover only humans and mice, which blocks studies of infection where both host and germ matter.

The team tested their pipeline on preserved mouse gut cells infected with Salmonella, pairing custom germ probes with a standard mouse panel. Both host and bacterial signals were picked up cleanly in place, and host response genes sat near bacterial ones. The authors argue the workflow opens spatial mapping to non-model species and host-pathogen work.
pmc-13297051:
Xuele Xu and co-authors engineer, in 2026, a zirconium-based solid electrolyte for all-solid-state lithium batteries. The base material is cheap but conducts ions sluggishly and reacts at interfaces, so the team dose it with extra lithium, aluminium, oxygen and fluorine together.

Oxygen loosened the structure into a glassy state easing ion flow, aluminium raised lithium content, and fluorine hardened the cathode boundary against side reactions. The tuned material conducted well at room conditions. Cells built with a high-nickel cathode kept most capacity after five hundred cycles. The authors credit the combined doping recipe.
pmc-13297151:
Sergey Taskaev and a large team report the status of the VITA accelerator neutron source for a new form of cancer therapy in a 2026 paper. Boron neutron capture therapy loads tumour cells with boron, then destroys them with a neutron beam. Compact accelerator sources are needed because reactors cannot sit in hospitals.

The facility was checked against current recommendations and met them, the team reports. A gamma-ray spectroscopy method was added to image boron during treatment, and dose-measurement techniques were developed. The group also carried out lithium-based capture therapy for the first time, claiming advantages over the boron version. Reliability and compactness are presented as the source's strengths.
pmc-13297851:
Yoshikazu Ohtaki and colleagues rethink core rules of information theory through a mirror concept called the dual probability distribution, in a 2026 paper. The rules in question include the maximum entropy principle, which picks the least-biased distribution fitting known facts. The dual distribution arises naturally when data are sampled from a multinomial scheme, through a classic lemma of Sanov.

Viewed through the mirror, a key quantity called the Massieu potential becomes a plain distance measure between two dual distributions. Its partner quantity becomes a generating function taken against the dual reference. The correspondence sharpens as samples grow large. The authors expect the mirror view to matter for everyday data analysis, where sampling is the starting point.
pmc-13298851:
For women living with daily urinary leakage, mood may shape sexual wellbeing more than the leakage itself, find Nancy Yang and colleagues in a 2026 analysis of trial data. They studied 240 women aged 45 and older enrolled in a pelvic floor yoga versus conditioning trial, tracking sexual function scores over thirty-six weeks.

Among the 54.7% who were sexually active, more frequent leakage modestly worsened condition-specific sexual scores, as did depression and anxiety symptoms. Among inactive women, depression and weaker physical function tracked with poorer ratings. After adjustment, the type of incontinence, urge or stress, made no difference. The authors argue care should address psychological and physical health alongside bladder symptoms.
pmc-13299551:
Deyin Cao and a large team compare chloroplast genomes of six commercial pluot cultivars to trace their maternal parentage within the plum genus, in a 2026 genomics study. Pluots are plum-apricot hybrids, and their maternal lines were unclear. All six genomes showed the standard circular structure with highly conserved organisation and gene content.

Structural similarity split the group. Three cultivars grouped maternally with one plum species and three with another, resolving four major clades across the genus overall. Hundreds of repeat loci and four highly variable regions were catalogued as candidate markers. The authors offer the first plastome comparison for these cultivars, aiding identification and germplasm evaluation.
pmc-13300051:
Jia He and colleagues build a deep learning framework that reconstructs single-cell spatial profiles from ordinary bulk RNA sequencing, in a 2026 methods study. Bulk data average across mixed cells, hiding the architecture that shapes disease. Their two-stage system first rebuilds faithful single-cell profiles, then places cells onto tissue coordinates using reference and stained-image guidance.

Validation across human tissues showed strong agreement with real spatial data. Applied to fourteen colon cancers, the tool found macrophage hubs at the invasive front forming a belt that keeps killer T cells out of the tumour core. The authors name the macrophage-fibroblast axis as a target for sensitising tumours to immunotherapy.
pmc-13300551:
Assylzhan M. Messova and co-authors systematically review autoimmune thyroid disease after COVID-19 infection in a 2026 paper. Reports since the pandemic link the virus with new or worsening Graves' disease and Hashimoto's thyroiditis, plausibly through immune disruption. Following PRISMA methods, the team searched three databases for studies from 2020 through 2025 and gathered forty-six of them, mostly case reports and series, covering 3,856 patients in total.

Thyroid antibody prevalence ran higher after infection than in controls, at about sixteen percent against eight. New Graves' disease after infection tended to show fiercer hormone excess than non-viral cases. Rare severe events included thyroid storm, myxedema coma, periodic paralysis, and a weakened, enlarged heart muscle. Standard treatments still worked, and the authors advise thyroid testing during post-COVID recovery, especially for women and anyone with lingering fatigue, palpitations, or weight change.
pmc-13300851:
M Jung and co-authors track heart function and a key blood marker after ablation in patients who have both persistent atrial fibrillation and heart failure, in a 2026 retrospective study. The 331 patients were split by pumping strength into reduced, mildly reduced, and preserved groups. Ultrasound measures plus NT-proBNP levels were compared before and long after radiofrequency ablation at one university hospital.

Pumping function improved markedly in the reduced group, climbing from about thirty-three to forty-eight percent, and rose modestly in the middle group, while the preserved group stayed flat. Atrial size shrank significantly in every group, evidence of favorable remodeling. The blood marker fell steeply across all three phenotypes. Right sided pressure measures barely moved. The authors conclude that ablation brings structural and biomarker gains across the heart failure spectrum, even where pumping strength itself cannot improve.
pmc-13301751:
Pulling a child's central line early can be the difference between life and death, Coskun Ekemen and colleagues show in an eighteen-year candidemia cohort from western Turkey. The 2026 study covers 465 bloodstream infection episodes in hospitalized children between 2008 and 2025. Candida parapsilosis caused the largest share of cases, and nearly nine in ten episodes involved a central catheter.

Thirty-day mortality ran at 10.8 percent overall. Among line-linked infections, death claimed 4.8 percent of children whose catheters came out within seventy-two hours, against 13.1 percent without early removal. Keeping the catheter was the strongest independent death predictor in adjusted models, ahead of low platelets, severe neutropenia, and immune suppression.
pmc-13302851:
Teaching a computer model how water moves in cement pores speeds durability work a thousandfold, Chunlong Liu and colleagues report in a 2026 study. Atom-level simulations first traced how pore water spreads through calcium silicate hydrate, the glue of concrete. A graph neural network then learned to link each atom's surroundings to that movement.

The model's guesses matched the slow simulations while running about a thousand times faster. It also handled rougher, many-particle pore shapes it had never seen. The authors sketch a future where these fast pore-level guesses feed bigger models of salt attack, guiding tougher concrete design.
pmc-13303451:
Rukiye Burucu and Tuba Korkmaz Aslan report a 2026 descriptive study of body esteem and sexual life in 103 cancer patients in Turkey. Treatment can change weight, cause swelling, and require catheters, all of which may affect how patients feel about their bodies.

Patients treated in a university oncology unit between November 2022 and January 2023 completed a body esteem scale and a sexual experiences scale. Body esteem scores fell below the scale midpoint, and sexual problem scores sat well above the clinical cut point. Weight loss, swelling, and catheter use shaped body esteem, while sex, body mass index, and cancer stage shaped sexual function.
pmc-13303951:
Francesc Cabré and Marta Cascante survey drug treatment options for cardiovascular disease in a 2026 narrative review. Heart and vessel diseases remain the top global cause of illness and death, and many patients juggle several conditions at once.

Established drugs for high blood pressure, heart failure, rhythm problems, and thickened heart muscle are covered by how they act, proof of benefit, harms, and guideline place. Newer options include gene-silencing drugs for hormone pathways, SGLT2 blockers, vessel-relaxing stimulators, and heart muscle inhibitors. Shared pathways with lung vessel disease receive special attention throughout.
pmc-13304751:
Bo Han, Yue Zhang, and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, cannabidiol as a treatment for diseases of mucosal surfaces, from gut to airways. The cannabis compound calms inflammation and fights microbes without causing intoxication, and the body's own cannabinoid system helps govern mucosal health. Its Achilles heel is physical: oily and poorly water-soluble, it absorbs badly.

The review maps cannabidiol's actions, then surveys its promise across digestive and respiratory mucosal disorders. Delivery routes and engineered carriers receive detailed attention, since getting the compound through mucus and holding it at the diseased site decides success. Safety questions, including liver signals and drug interactions, are weighed alongside the benefits. The authors close with the formulation and clinical challenges still blocking translation.
pmc-13306651:
Jiaqi Fang, Hemin Sun, and Hongquan Li propose in 2026 a way to recognise targets in synthetic aperture radar images by fusing several kinds of features. Radar images suffer speckle noise, distortion, and tangled feature types, which blunt accuracy. Their design starts with preprocessing that suppresses noise and lifts contrast.

A dual-branch network then extracts physical features based on domain knowledge alongside deep learned features. A weighted fusion layer balances the streams according to their variance, cutting redundancy and conflict. Tests on two datasets improved precision, recall, and F1 scores by five to fifteen percent over baselines. Extra checks under stretched conditions supported robustness and speed. The authors argue that keeping physical meaning beside deep features suits radar's special image character.
pmc-13306751:
Juan Arredondo-Valdez and a large team detect hidden salt stress in prickly pear cactus in 2026 using hyperspectral imaging and a three-dimensional neural network. Young cactus pads can look healthy while salt quietly harms them, so ordinary visual indices fail early. Plants faced six salinity levels in controlled experiments.

Cameras captured light from 400 to 1000 nanometres, and seven vegetation indices were folded into the network as an extra dimension. Validation accuracy reached near ninety-nine point seven percent, with perfect precision at the critical high salt levels where action matters most. Confidence maps confirmed reliable readings across the pads. Training took only about eight seconds. The authors propose the setup as an early-warning tool for irrigation decisions in dry regions where salty water is common.
pmc-13307151:
Chinmaya Mutalik tested dye films that both catch and read breath aerosol parts in a 2026 study. Methylcellulose films carrying phenol red were exposed to model aerosols mixing sulfate salt, serum protein and plastic beads across acid to alkaline settings.

Infrared spectra moved in opposite directions for sulfate and protein bands as acidity changed. Their ratio climbed from 0.86 ± 0.01 at pH 4 to 3.56 ± 0.32 at pH 10 in reported values, separating ion and protein shares. Colour shifts from 432 to 556 nm confirmed the dye still answered after capture. The cheap films could suit field kits where breath tests must stay fast and light to carry.
pmc-13307351:
Lei Wang and co-authors propose in 2026 a self repair plan for sensor networks that float on the sea surface and drift with currents and wind. Drift breaks links and bends the backbone of such networks, so fixed round based upkeep often reacts too late.

Their plan fixes faults close to where they occur, through cluster head handover, backbone repair, and member rejoining, and it rebuilds the whole network only when quality stays poor. In tests fed with Taiwan Strait flow and wind data, the full method cut the cluster head break rate to 5.15 percent, well below the rate for the DARCR method.
pmc-13308351:
Gabriele Rigano, Daniela Billi, and Yannick Lara compare in 2026 the genomes of three desert cyanobacteria strains that have flown in space and faced Mars like tests. These Chroococcidiopsis strains dry out for long spans and shrug off harsh rays, which makes them models for life at its limits.

Fresh gap free genome builds let the team spot shared and strain only genes for drying defence, DNA guard work, and repair after harm. Every strain held the gene set for a sun screen pigment called scytonemin, and one strain added a second shield. Such shared tools may explain how the cells revive after wetting, and they hint at survival odds off Earth.
pmc-13308751: Chinasa Odo and co-authors issue a 2026 correction to their protocol paper. That protocol covers a qualitative case study of a symptom based risk tool for suspected head and neck cancer. The item itself is only a brief publishing notice, so it adds no new data or findings. It records that Multimedia Appendix 1, a topic guide for case study interviews, has been swapped for a fresh file. The fixed version has been sent again to the main repositories that hold the work.
pmc-13308851:
Katrina Himpson and co-authors track in 2026 healed sea turtles set free in the Indian Ocean, using satellite tags to learn how they fare and roam. Olive ridley, green, and hawksbill turtles all took part, with young turtles a focus since past tracking work has skipped them most.

Freed turtles lived long past release and moved in ways that matched wild kin of the same kind and age. Monsoon driven currents pushed open sea paths, yet turtles swam hard to hold place or to ride shelf and ridge lines. Rehab thus aids both welfare and science, and wide ranging turtles need joint guard work across sea borders to stay safe.
pmc-13309551:
Jan Maier and co-authors trace carbon movement along the whole Danube River in a 2026 study. Rivers carry carbon from land to air and sea, yet basin-wide seasonal control data stay scarce. Dissolved inorganic carbon, its isotope mix, and water carbon dioxide levels were the core measures.

Five sampling trips covered the main river and its large side streams across seasons. Dissolved carbon made up over 90 percent of total carbon and stayed fairly steady along the river, fed by groundwater and rock weathering upstream. Isotope shifts downstream pointed to steady carbon dioxide loss to the air. The authors confirm the Danube acts as a lasting source of that gas and map where inputs enter.
pmc-13309651:
Abigail Tisler and co-authors describe a newborn with two rare conditions in a 2026 case report. The baby girl had an enlarged clitoris at birth, a sign of excess male-type hormones before birth. Adrenal hormone disease is the usual cause and can threaten life, so hormone treatment began at once while tests ran.

Chromosome testing showed a mosaic pattern matching Turner syndrome, a condition that does not usually cause such genital change. A search for Y chromosome material came back negative, and the newborn adrenal screen was also negative. A later hormone panel showed a raised marker more in line with adrenal disease. The authors present the case as a diagnostic puzzle where both conditions may coexist.
pmc-13310051:
Ming Yang and co-authors screen inflammation proteins in eye fluid from people with severe nearsightedness in a 2026 study. High myopia stretches the eye and raises the risk of sight loss, yet its inflammation signals were little mapped. Fluid taken during cataract surgery offers a direct sample from inside the eye.

Twenty surgical patients were split into a high myopia group of twelve and a control group of eight. A panel measured 92 inflammation proteins in the fluid, and nine proteins ran higher in the high myopia group under strict cutoffs in the analysis. The strongest signals included HGF, CST5, and CCL19. The authors flag these proteins as candidate markers for study in larger groups.
pmc-13311151:
Dorothy Armstrong and colleagues explore safety risks felt by optometrists in Scotland in a 2026 focus group study. Proof on risk in eye care practice is sparse next to other primary care fields, and pandemic era change reshaped roles. Safety was picked as the theme for required national training, so views were gathered first.

Sixteen optometrists from nine health boards joined three online groups in 2021. Six themes covered current risk views, skill gaps, conduct, work setting, future tech risks, and fixes. Peers felt clinical risk is rising with new tech and wider roles. More role training and incident support were urged.
pmc-13311251:
Katarzyna Pogoda and co-authors analyze the 2026 cohort on how HER2 status shifts in breast cancer after drug treatment given before surgery. Such shifts can change which follow-up drugs make sense.

The team compared tumor samples before and after treatment in 736 patients treated from 2019 to 2024. HER2 class changed in 34.2 percent of patients, and drops in HER2 level were more common than rises. New HER2-positive status after treatment was rare. Knowing how often the marker moves helps doctors decide when retesting the leftover tumor is worth doing. That timing question matters for drug choice after surgery.
pmc-13311951:
Shivana Neeta Modi and co-authors present their 2026 London cohort study on what counts as a successful move from child to adult epilepsy services, and whether success improves seizure outcomes.

The study followed patients aged 20 to 24 who had moved from a pediatric service between 2009 and 2023. Success needed four marks: timely start, full preparation, a joint clinic visit, and adult follow-up within six months. Of 59 eligible patients, 72.9 percent met all four in this cohort. Successful movers had over fourfold adjusted odds of better seizure control or staying seizure-free by age twenty.
pmc-13312051:
Juan Yang and co-authors follow, in a 2026 longitudinal study, how symptom groups and quality of life change around surgery in women with cervical cancer. They tracked 183 patients at a hospital in northwestern China from admission through the days after their operations.

Using symptom and quality-of-life questionnaires at three time points, the team found five symptom clusters, covering pain and fatigue, mood, hot flashes and nerve symptoms, digestion, and low energy. Most clusters peaked one to three days after surgery and then eased, while quality of life dipped and only partly recovered. Worse cluster scores went with worse quality of life, which supports watching symptoms as shifting groups rather than one by one.
pmc-13312151:
Caio César Gonçalves Silva and co-authors report a 2026 three-dimensional study of how Le Fort I osteotomy changes the nose and sinus region. This jaw surgery, which frees the upper jaw so it can be repositioned, is widely used to correct midface deformities. Moving the bone also disturbs the walls of the maxillary sinus and nasal cavity.

Comparing scans from before and after surgery, the team found that breaks in the continuity of the sinus walls, nasal cavity, and septum were common after the operation. The lining of the maxillary sinuses thickened more in the postoperative period, while the air volume of both the sinuses and the nasal cavity shrank. The authors suggest watching factors that could upset sinus balance after surgery, since lasting swelling raises the risk of sinusitis.
pmc-13312251:
Jay Olivet and colleagues present a 2026 program evaluation of rapid molecular testing for bloodstream infections caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. This severe infection does best on targeted beta-lactam drugs such as cefazolin. Many patients sit on vancomycin while conventional cultures crawl, and late switches are tied to slower clearance, more failures, and kidney harm.

The study compares care before and after the hospital adopted a blood culture identification panel, run on an automated platform, that names the organism directly from a positive culture. Patients are then ranked by a combined desirability score weighing treatment success, kidney injury, and survival, with secondary measures such as time to optimal therapy and length of stay. The authors set out to learn whether faster identification leads to earlier targeted treatment and better overall outcomes for these patients.
pmc-13312551:
Mohamed Mahmoud Shalaby and Fatma Aboalsoud Taha follow, in a 2026 prospective study, the hearts of newborns born with a left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia around the time of surgical repair. Babies with this defect face lung and circulation trouble, and a small, strained left ventricle often decides how they fare, yet serial heart measurements across the operation were scarce.

Thirty term newborns at a tertiary center had detailed ultrasound heart scans within a day before repair, again two to three days after, and once more at one month. Significant pulmonary hypertension was present before surgery in 70 percent of the babies. After repair, left ventricular dimensions, both raw and size-adjusted, grew significantly at the early and one-month checks, while several measures of pumping function dipped significantly in the early period. The authors chart a heart reshaping itself as circulation normalizes.
pmc-13312851:
Mohamed Taha Mellouki, Zineb Benmassaoud, and Hind Cherrabi report a 2026 case of a hair mass blocking a child's small intestine. Trichobezoars form when swallowed hair accumulates in the digestive tract. They usually sit in the stomach, and usually in children with behavioral disorders. Their patient, a nine-year-old boy, arrived with an acute small bowel obstruction. The trichobezoar was lodged in the terminal ileum, an unusual location that made the diagnosis harder.

Abdominal computed tomography first suggested the mass, and surgery confirmed it. Surgeons removed the hair mass through a small cut in the bowel wall, ten centimeters before the junction with the colon. The authors draw three lessons. Imaging earns its place before surgery. The whole digestive tract should be checked during the operation for further masses. Psychiatric follow-up matters afterward, since untreated hair-eating behavior can bring the condition back.
pmc-13313051:
Ali Ghais and colleagues survey, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, why medical residents in Lebanon order routine inpatient laboratory tests so often. The anonymous web survey went to residents in internal medicine and general surgery at a teaching hospital, asking about their ordering habits, what drives unnecessary testing, and which fixes they would welcome. Sixty-two complete responses came back from 115 invited residents.

Nearly two-thirds, 64.5 percent, admitted ordering routine tests frequently, even though most disagreed with daily testing regardless of need. Chemistry panels and complete blood counts topped the list of tests seen as unnecessary. Habit led the cited drivers at 62.9 percent, followed by poor cost awareness and expected attending preferences. Residents most endorsed short cost-awareness sessions, bundled test pricing, and removing daily options from order sets. Junior residents ordered routinely far more than seniors, which the authors use to argue for stewardship built into training and workflow.
pmc-13314151:
Elmabrok Masaoud and co-authors offer, in a 2026 methods paper, a tour of techniques that rank correlated predictors inside regression models, aimed at animal researchers. When explanatory variables overlap, ordinary coefficients cannot say which one truly drives the outcome. The authors implement five approaches in R software, from Shapley values and relative weights to dominance analysis. They demonstrate them on the abalone data set, where measurements predict the shellfish's age in rings.

Every method agreed on the headline: shell weight was the strongest predictor of ring count. The methods differed in texture, though. One metric blurred the predictors together with wide uncertainty bands, while the Genizi method separated them cleanly. Relative weights, like Genizi, produced narrow bands. Dominance analysis gave the deepest ranking detail at the highest computing cost. The paper serves as a menu, matching each technique's strengths to the questions aquatic and animal data pose.
pmc-13314351:
Fahad Yaseen Taha, Ayman Hani Taha, and Omar Hashim Sheet investigate, in a 2026 study, Staphylococcus aureus hiding in buffalo milk in Iraq's Nineveh governorate. The bacterium is the leading cause of udder inflammation in buffalo, including subclinical cases that cut yield. Sixty subclinical milk samples collected between October and December 2024 underwent culture and biochemical identification. PCR screening followed for seven genes covering identity, methicillin resistance, binding factors, and toxins, with one gene used to build a family tree.

Nine samples, 15 percent of the total, carried the bacterium, with one district reaching 30 percent. Every isolate carried the identity gene and both binding factor genes, while the resistance gene and all three toxin genes were absent, a comparatively benign profile. Five distinct strain sequences were lodged in GenBank, and the tree showed the local strains sharing features with isolates worldwide. The authors map a low-threat pathogen population worth continued watching.
pmc-13315051:
Deepika C Parameswarappa and co-authors update, in a 2026 review, the management of ABCA4 retinopathy, better known as Stargardt disease. It is the most common inherited macular dystrophy, stealing central vision in life when clearance of vitamin A byproducts poisons the retinal pigment layer. No approved therapy alters its course, and care remains supportive, built on low-vision rehabilitation and counseling.

The review surveys how that is beginning to change. The pipeline now attacks the disease at heights. It slows the visual cycle, deploys modified vitamin A that resists toxic clumping, blocks retinol transport, replaces or edits the gene, silences it with antisense drugs, and transplants retinal cells. For end-stage eyes, optogenetic therapy promises independent vision restoration. The authors organize the options by disease stage, discuss which trial endpoints can prove benefit, and argue that combination therapy and matching offer optimism for a condition written off as untreatable.
pmc-13315351:
Tara I. Chang and colleagues weigh, in a 2026 Medicare study, the trade-off between open surgery and catheter procedures for restoring blood flow to the legs of older patients with chronic kidney disease. Surgeons and patients value currencies: days spent at home versus limbs preserved. The team compared 87,446 beneficiaries aged sixty-six and over treated between 2008 and 2017, only 15.3 percent of them surgically, computing days at home and days lost to limb events over the year.

Surgery cost home time at every horizon: about 8.4 fewer days at home by one month and 31.9 fewer by one year than the endovascular route. In exchange, surgery protected limbs, with 17.3 fewer days given up to serious limb events by one year in that comparison. Neither approach wins outright; the numbers describe a values trade. The authors argue these figures, time at home against limb risk, belong in conversations with kidney patients.
pmc-13315451:
Jinmei Gao and colleagues studied in 2026 how high homocysteine in mother mice affects the fertility of their daughters. Mothers fed a high-methionine diet developed the condition, defined by blood homocysteine above 15 micromoles per liter, and the team then checked the ovaries and eggs of female offspring.

Resting follicles switched on too early, driven by stronger signals through proteins including mTOR, AKT, FOXO3a, and RPS6. Mature eggs held fewer mitochondria that worked less well, with more reactive oxygen, more DNA damage, and more spindle faults. Together those changes lowered egg quality and help explain reduced fertility in the offspring.
pmc-13315651:
Mitsutoshi Okuda and colleagues describe, in a 2026 case report with review, a forearm flap that survived its patient's cardiac arrest. An 85-year-old woman had a tumor excised, leaving a defect of 100 by 250 millimeters repaired with a free flap of thigh tissue connected to vessels. Two days after surgery her heart stopped. Ten minutes of resuscitation with adrenaline restored circulation, but a free flap, dependent on a single vessel connection, was the tissue surgeons would expect to lose.

Watched for a month, the flap showed no death or infection, and the patient left for a facility on day fifty-three, her cognition impaired but the reconstruction intact. The authors gathered the comparison set: two cases at their institution and three in the literature, six surviving flaps. Their analysis suggests arrest and resuscitation may not doom a free flap, a reassuring signal for teams weighing how to fight for one.
pmc-13316651:
Yang Zhang and colleagues report 2026 lab work on Staphylococcus aureus, a germ that switches between free floating growth and sticky biofilm life on skin and inside cells. Acid stress is common in those niches, and the team asked how a secretion machine part called EssC shapes the switch.

Deleting the essC gene made biofilms grow thicker and heavier at acid levels near skin, even though fewer bacteria inside stayed alive. The mutant stuck faster, clumped more, and leaked more DNA from self-digested cells, all changes that cement a biofilm. Gene control circuits shifted in step, turning down a biofilm brake and turning up glue making paths. EssC emerges as a quiet governor of survival strategy.
pmc-13316751:
Maureen Norah Nabulime and colleagues offer a 2026 protocol for sorting and testing city solid waste from many sources, so towns can judge energy recovery options on solid data. Waste differs by source, and sloppy sampling ruins the math for digestion or gasification projects.

Called MSW-CAP, the framework standardizes collection, sorting, and lab checks, building on an existing ASTM method. Trials ran on home, grocery, restaurant, and school waste across five United States states. Samples split by moisture level, sending wet waste toward digestion and dry waste toward gasification paths. The shared recipe lets cities compare results fairly and pick recovery routes with fewer surprises.
pmc-13317951:
Helen Kuo and a multi-country team ask, in 2026, whether phone surveys can measure maternal care coverage accurately in Mozambique. During the COVID-19 pandemic, rapid remote measurement became attractive because face-to-face interviews carried risk. Their programme tested two ways of reaching women by mobile phone.

One sample was drawn from an existing national surveillance system, and the other used random digit dialling. Women aged 15 to 49 answered questions about care for recent births during 2022. Estimates were then compared with the national Demographic and Health Survey. Even after adjustment, phone samples gave far higher coverage for antenatal visits, facility delivery and skilled attendants than the benchmark survey. The authors conclude that phone surveys overestimated coverage in this setting.
pmc-13318051:
Mathieu Hénault and co-authors build, in a 2026 yeast study, a unified model of how wrong chromosome counts arise, persist, and sometimes fix themselves. Extra or missing chromosomes cause many birth and tissue disorders, and oddly, a second sorting error can restore balance.

The team measured gain and loss rates for each chromosome in budding yeast, weighed the fitness of each state, and fed the numbers into population models. True back-errors proved too rare to matter for most chromosomes. A few chromosomes that seemed to revert fast instead passed through a brief unstable state, with stuck-together chromosomes breaking and being repaired across divisions, as sequencing and live imaging confirmed. Chromosome-specific routes, they conclude, shape genome change.
pmc-13318251:
Giovanna Spina leads a 2026 retrospective study of total elbow replacement for older patients whose lower arm bone fractures near the elbow could not be rebuilt with plates and screws. Records covered operations done between January 2017 and December 2024.

Thirty-seven patients, averaging 80.4 years old, were followed for a mean of 107 months and assessed for movement, pain, function scores, imaging findings, and complications. Final results showed good elbow motion and function, with a revision rate of 11 percent and implant survival of 94.2 percent at five years in this group. Other health problems did not clearly change outcomes, supporting replacement as a primary option for selected older patients.
pmc-13318551:
Adriano José Pereira and a large team set out a 2026 protocol for TELESCOPE 2, a trial testing whether telemedicine support can shorten stays in intensive care units in Brazil. Earlier work showed remote intensive care is safe and workable, but its effect on patient outcomes is unproven.

Twenty-five units will join in a stepped-wedge design, starting the programme at staggered times in five randomised sequences between January 2024 and January 2026. The package combines daily remote rounds led by intensive care doctors, coordinated input from nurses, physiotherapists, and pharmacists, and a quality and safety programme. Length of intensive care stay is the main measure, backed by death rates, ventilator-free days, readmission, and tube accidents.
pmc-13319651:
Şeyba Sara Mansuroğlu and co-authors compare rinse methods for killing germs deep in tooth roots in a 2026 lab study. Germs that hide in tiny tubes in root walls are a main cause of lasting tooth infection. Five ways to stir rinse fluid were tested for how deep their kill reached into those tubes.

Sixty pulled human teeth with one root canal each were filled with a hardy germ type, then rinsed by needle, soft tip, sound, or pulse methods. Slices at three depths were viewed under a strong scope to measure the kill zone. Pulse rinsing reached deepest at both top and tip ends, while plain needle rinsing reached least. No method cleared germs in full.
pmc-13320351:
Wanyue Li and co-authors study sleep habits and spine curve risk in a 2026 long follow up study from a British health bank. Sideways spine curves can arise in adult life, yet forward looking proof on sleep as a risk factor was near absent. A five part sleep score joined bed time type, sleep length, sleeplessness, snoring, and day sleepiness into one habit grade.

Among 408870 adults free of the curve at the start, 2976 new cases arose over a mean span near sixteen years. Each added healthy sleep trait cut risk by about a tenth in the adjusted counts, and those with all five traits faced far lower risk than those with almost none. The link held across most subgroups, which hints sleep care may aid spine health.
pmc-13320451:
Kamran Dousti and co-authors survey public knowledge of invasive mosquitoes in Saarland, Germany in a 2026 study. The region has no settled tiger mosquito yet but faces rising invasion risk as the insect spreads in Europe and can carry tropical fevers. A public form ran from February to June 2024 through digital and paper routes to gauge awareness, habits, and knowledge.

Of 1064 replies, 623 met the study rules for a close look in the counts reported. More than half knew that clearing still water blocks breeding, yet fewer than one in five did it on a regular basis. Most had heard of the tiger mosquito, but fewer than half tied it to one fever it can carry. Seasonal teaching drives may slow the insect foothold, the team argues.
pmc-13321251:
Ernestina Melicoff, David Moreno McNeill, and Christian Benden look ahead for children's lung transplantation in a 2026 review. The piece opens a special issue on paediatric chest transplantation and covers donor access, graft failure, and how fitness shapes outcomes. Lung transplant is a settled option for a small group of children with severe lung disease.

In the United States, 1511 paediatric lung transplants were reported from 1988 to 2024, and 46.8 percent were for cystic fibrosis, long the leading reason. New cystic fibrosis drugs are reshaping who needs a transplant. The authors argue that donor supply, long term graft health, and frailty checks will decide the field's next gains.
pmc-13322751:
Zengchun Xie and co-authors tune reflected colour in laser written nanocomposites in a 2026 study. Ordered layers of tiny silica particles can produce structural colour without dyes, much like patterns in nature. Direct laser writing was used to arrange the particles in stacked tiers inside a composite material.

By adjusting particle size, particle type, loading, and laser settings, the team widened the reflected colour range across the visible spectrum. Electron microscopy showed the neat, non-packed order survived the writing process, with features below a micron made reliably. Colour measures matched the tuning, and the method produced tiny three dimensional multicolour images, including versions with plasmonic coated particles.
pmc-13322951:
Zrinka Greblo Jurakić and colleagues study team climate and well-being in teen handball, in a 2026 survey of 522 players aged 14 to 17 years. Players rated the motivational climate set by their coaches and completed scales for anxiety, depression, stress and self-esteem.

Teams were seen as more task-focused than ego-focused overall, though boys reported a weaker task climate than girls. A task focus linked to lower anxiety, depression and stress and to higher self-esteem, while an ego focus showed the reverse pattern. Among girls, those coached by men saw a weaker task climate and stronger ego climate than those coached by women. The authors advise coaches to reward effort and learning over comparison.
pmc-13323151:
Angana Mukherjee and co-authors study the transcription factor FOXI3 in prostate cancer that has spread to bone, in a 2026 tissue and cell study. FOXI3 helps normal bone develop, and the team had earlier found it raised in prostate cancer without knowing its role.

Staining of human tumours linked FOXI3 to worse pathology and higher grade, and public gene data showed it markedly raised in bone metastases alongside FGF8. Adding FGF8 lifted FOXI3 in bone-derived cancer cells but not in a brain-derived line. Movement and growth of bone-derived cells depended on FOXI3 in their tests. The authors cast the FGF8-FOXI3 link as a bone-specific driver worth targeting.
pmc-13324151:
James S. Lorriman and team found a third route for the Parkinson-linked kinase PINK1 inside mitochondria. Their 2026 paper revisits a familiar picture. In healthy mitochondria, PINK1 enters the inner membrane, is cut by the protease PARL, and is degraded. In damaged mitochondria it stays on the surface, activates, recruits Parkin, and triggers mitophagy. The team asked whether any PINK1 escapes both fates.

Structural modeling predicted that PINK1's transmembrane domain is plastic, folding as either a helix or a helix-sheet hybrid at the TIM23 import complex. The helical form appears to pass through a ROMO1/Tim17 channel into the matrix, while the hybrid form engages PARL and is cleaved. The authors argue that this shape switch decides PINK1's fate, expanding its role beyond damage sensing toward healthy mitochondrial function with relevance to Parkinson disease.
pmc-13324251:
Ekhlas Qays Al-shawway and Zohre Balak test a two-layer high-entropy ceramic composite, in a 2026 materials study. One layer joins five metal carbides with graphite and silicon additives, while the other forms medium-entropy borides in place from oxides with carbon sources.

Spark plasma sintering pressed the layers at 2,000 degrees Celsius under pressure for ten minutes. The carbide layer densified almost fully, reaching far higher density and hardness than the boride layer in their measures, with hardness near 15 GPa against about 1.2 GPa for the boride side. Grain sizes sat in the hundreds of nanometres for both. Microscopy and diffraction mapped how additives shaped each microstructure.
pmc-13326951:
Si Shen and team mapped brain shape shifts in neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease tied to NOTCH2NLC changes. Their 2026 study scanned 41 patients and 21 healthy controls with two brain map scans. It weighed grey matter size and cortex fold depth, plus shrinkage links to white matter bright spots and brain fluid share. Early tests tied zone brain size to GGC repeat length, years ill, age at onset, and thinking scores.

Shrinkage was wide, most in front cortex, cerebellum, insula, orbital gyrus, front cingulate, amygdala, and temporal pole.
