Longer GGC repeats tied to more shrinkage in striatum, middle cingulate, sense-movement cortex, and cerebellum. An early start tied to shrinkage in thalamus, back brain zones, and cerebellum. Weak thinking tied to shrinkage in front cingulate, upper back cortex, and upper temporal pole. The team argues human-only gene shifts behind human cortex growth may also leave the brain open to decay.
pmc-13327051:
Steve Pambayi and team review inflammatory pseudotumor, a growing known cause of full hip replacement failure. Their 2026 paper tells of a mass that is not cancer and not infection, round a hip implant, which may be cystic, solid, or mixed. At first tied to metal-on-metal joints, it can also come with other types. Risks run to female sex, gene lean, big thigh bone heads, mix-and-match stems, high metal ions, and wear bits.

Pseudotumor wrecks hip replacements by force and swelling, often bringing pain, wobble, or loosening. Finding it leans hard on scans: X-rays, ultrasound, CT, and MRI with metal glare cut-down scans. A mix of scans is key for surgery planning. Care runs from close watch with no signs to new surgery when signs show or grow. The team stresses knowing this scan-spotted snag for swift, better care.
pmc-13327451:
Nikolai Ramadanov and team set benchmark figures for blood loss and transfusion after hip socket bone surgery. Their 2026 systematic review and pooled study hunted PubMed, Embase, Epistemonikos, and CENTRAL through March 30, 2026. It took in forward- and look-back primary studies that logged surgery-time blood care results. Forty-seven studies covering 4,402 patients and 4,767 hips gave data on transfusion rate, units given, surgery-time and total blood loss, hemoglobin fall, and post-surgery hemoglobin.

Pooled maths with random effects joined rates and means, and single-factor pooled regression probed study-level drivers. The pooled figures show heavy blood loss and a real transfusion load after the surgery, giving doctors benchmark values for surgery-time blood care planning. Graded as level III evidence from a review of mostly look-back groups, the work aims to base transfusion hopes and blood-saving plans on measured averages, not stories.
pmc-13327651:
Mingyang Wei and co-authors describe a 2026 case where a slipped upper back disc caused belly pain for years. A 65-year-old woman had right lower abdominal pain for more than five years, worse over the last three months, with back pain and pain down her left leg. Repeated belly, gynecology, and urinary checks found nothing to explain it.

Back scans showed wear at several levels, including a disc slip at L2-3 and narrowing at L4-5. A guided numbing injection at the L2-3 nerve root cut her belly pain score from 7 to 3, naming the level, and keyhole removal of that disc dropped it further to 2. A later fusion at L4-5 eased the leg pain, showing how spine disease can masquerade as abdominal illness.
pmc-13327951:
Kristine Santos and co-authors update a comparison of two pain methods for chest wall surgery in a 2026 meta-analysis. The Nuss procedure fixes sunken chests, and pain control comes from either freezing chest nerves or an epidural catheter. Fifteen studies covering 1,391 patients were pooled, with 823 receiving the freezing method.

Freezing lengthened operations by about 29.1 minutes and raised hospital costs by about 1,655.3 US dollars on the pooled estimates, yet patients left hospital 2.7 days sooner, reported less pain on day three, and used far fewer opioids. Matched and randomized subgroups backed the same pattern, with no clear difference in complications. Recovery gains may justify the higher upfront cost.
pmc-13329751:
Christian Kim and co-authors review breast cancer spread to the eye socket and add four new cases in a 2026 article. Breast cancer is the most common cancer worldwide and the most common source of such spread. The team searched medical reports from 2011 to 2025 for biopsy-proven cases.

Of 220 records screened, 63 articles with 69 cases met the rules in the reported counts. Most patients were women, with an average age of 60 years at eye symptoms. In 43 percent of cases, eye spread was the first sign of breast cancer in those summaries. Double vision and blur were the top complaints. Care varied widely. The authors advise doctors to weigh spread when patients with breast history show eye signs.
pmc-13332451:
Man Wu and colleagues tested a wake-up-and-kill strategy against Epstein-Barr virus linked stomach cancer in a 2026 laboratory study. The virus hides silently in these tumor cells, and forcing it into its active cycle can make the cancer vulnerable to antiviral drugs.

The HDAC inhibitor nanatinostat switched on the virus's early and late genes in two representative cancer cell lines and raised overall histone acetylation across the genome. It also suppressed the growth drivers c-MYC and BCL2, halting the cell cycle and killing tumor cells. Combined with ganciclovir, the pairing showed strong antitumor effect and acceptable safety in cell and animal models. The authors note the same pairing already looked promising in EBV-positive lymphoma trials, and argue stomach cancer of this subtype deserves the same precision approach.
pmc-13332551:
Songbo Xue and colleagues report 2026 surgical outcomes for lateral skull base tumors reaching the craniovertebral junction. These tumors bring varied symptoms and demand plans tailored to each patient's anatomy and to neck stability after removal. The retrospective cohort included twelve patients treated between 2018 and 2024. Most were treated through the infratemporal fossa approach in its A, B, or combined forms, with occipital-cervical fusion when condyle and upper neck removal required it.

Hearing loss, headache, and neck mass were the leading first symptoms. Imaging showed the tumors often involved the temporal bone, the foramen magnum, and the jugular foramen. Eight patients needed staged resections and four had single-stage surgery. The series shows how approach choice and staged planning balance tumor removal against stability at the skull-neck junction. Surgeons gain a small but detailed map of trade-offs in these rare, high-stakes cases.
pmc-13333351:
Ainhoa Andueza and colleagues describe a gene therapy pairing in a 2026 commentary on their Cancer Cell study: radiation first, then a virus that delivers immune-stimulating genes into the tumor. Radiation kills tumor cells and spills their antigens. Yet it switches on immune suppression, so immune attacks rarely follow.

The team found radiation reshapes the viral genome's packaging in tumor cells. It strips methyl marks and adds the mark H3K27ac at the switch, which boosts how much the genes are read. A protein, YY1, binds the DNA after radiation and matters for the boost, since mutating its landing site cut expression. To keep the payload time-limited, they used a switch that answers to interferon, itself raised by radiation. They injected the vector into tumors irradiated, and mouse imaging confirmed it stayed at the target. The authors frame the alliance as a way to reprogram the irradiated tumor.
pmc-13334951:
Joel Mwanga and co-authors studied exclusive breastfeeding and child malnutrition in Mwanza, Tanzania, in a 2026 field study that also studied how health workers teach feeding practices. Malnutrition in its many forms still threatens young children's survival and growth.

Five hundred mothers with children aged 6 to 24 months joined the study, plus 15 healthcare providers. Bayesian logistic regression, run with Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, weighed how exclusive breastfeeding relates to malnutrition measures such as stunting and wasting. Provider interviews and observation cross-checked how feeding education is actually delivered along the maternal care sequence. The joint design links home feeding behavior with the clinic support meant to sustain it, pointing to where teaching can be strengthened.
pmc-13336051:
Mingzhu Zhao and colleagues present 2026 a combined DNA nano-probe for in-nucleus imaging and in situ mapping of OGG1 action. However, due to hard nucleus placement and weak signal output, cell-level imaging has not yet been achieved.

The authors report a nucleus-aimed DNA prism nano-probe designed to beat these limits via a two-part plan. The nano-probe combined an AS1411 aptamer for active nucleus drop-off and a FRET array for signal readout. In living cells, the nano-probe enabled watching of nuclear OGG1 action, showing distinct shifts in base enzyme levels across different cell lines. Also, early tests in lung wash fluid from pneumonia patients suggested its use in clinic settings. It also served as a testbed for drug checks, effectively testing OGG1-aimed drugs.
pmc-13336351:
Raveena Raveena and colleagues present 2026 a general enzyme plan for site-chosen adding of changed genetic building blocks into DNA. Methods for site-chosen adding of changed DNA building blocks remain limited. Standard chem method, the most common approach, suffers from low coupling power, error-prone making, and toxic waste making. Enzyme plans on the other hand operate under mild water settings but are highly context-bound, cannot add multiple changes, or lack broad use.

The authors present a proof-of-concept for a general enzyme plan that uses template-guided enzymes to add changed DNA units at set spots with high trueness. This gives very pure products through built-in error fixing. This plan can be run on DNA readers using SBS tech, opening a path for routine, eco-friendly making of long, site-chosen changed DNA sequences, including gene starts and gene fragments.
pmc-13336451:
Yanyu Su and co-authors mapped drug heteroresistance in the yeast Candida glabrata in a 2026 fungus study. Heteroresistance, where a stubborn subgroup survives drug levels that kill the rest, had rarely been recorded in this species.

From a many-center collection of 156 isolates, 25 percent showed heteroresistance specific to caspofungin and tied to 37-degree growth. Gene activity scans of the survivors under rising drug pressure showed an adaptive program around cell cycle and cell wall integrity, centered on the calcineurin pathway. Blocking calcineurin with drugs or deleting its genes erased the trait. Survivors also spawned descendants with a range of stable resistance, marking heteroresistance as a reservoir. Machine learning on genomes found a known mutation and a new candidate gene loss.
pmc-13336851:
Mahni Fatahi and colleagues decorate a blue light emitter to raise OLED performance in a 2026 study. Efficient, stable blue screens made by solution printing remain hard to achieve. Their strategy adds bulky carbazole donor units at two spots on a known delayed-fluorescence emitter.

The new emitter dissolved better and moved holes better while keeping its blue color. In doped films it reached a light yield of 93% with a tiny energy gap of 0.01 eV and a short delayed lifetime of 2 µs in the reported measures. Printed devices hit a top external quantum efficiency of 29.4% at blue coordinates of (0.145, 0.211) in the study runs. Wider charge spread and faster recycling curbed wasteful collisions.
pmc-13336951:
Sanbao Zhang and co-authors map the sheep rumen microbiome one cell at a time in a 2026 atlas study. Tough microbial walls had blocked fair single-cell profiling of this gut community. A tuned 25 min enzyme lysis method let them profile 60 748 cells across 21 samples, resolving 213 genera and 662 species in the dataset.

Seven cross-species functional clusters emerged, tying lifestyle to metabolic specialty. In heat-tolerant hosts, energy clusters switched on fast, and one species shifted toward sugar-burning in a way that spared nutrition for the host. The atlas gives rumen ecology a reference map and a method for probing how whole communities flex under stress like heat.
pmc-13337251:
Apa Juntavee and colleagues compared fluoride-free toners with a fluoride toothpaste for rebuilding softened tooth enamel, in a 2026 lab study. Sixty human premolar samples were demineralized, split into four groups of 15, and treated twice daily through a week of acid cycling. The toners, BAT-1 and BAT-2, rely on calcium phosphate minerals and antibacterial agents rather than fluoride.

Hardness recovery and remineralization scores varied across groups, with BAT-1 matching the fluoride paste overall. Microscopy favored BAT-1 for preserving enamel structure and driving minerals deeper, and it cut lesion depth the most. The authors present BAT-1 as a promising fluoride-free option for early decay treated without drilling.
pmc-13337451:
Jiaoru Liu, Denise Manahan-Vaughan, and Josué Haubrich compare how mouse strain and age shape reward-guided learning in a 2026 study. Juvenile mice aged 2–3 months and mature mice aged 7–8 months, from CBA/CaOlaHsd and C57BL/6 lines, learned a T-maze where one arm paid rewards first reliably, then with falling odds.

CBA mice chose faster, reached high performance earlier, and held up better as rewards thinned. Aging slowed choices in both lines and bent strategies in strain-specific ways, which reinforcement learning models helped expose. The work warns that age and genetic background jointly script decision behavior, so mouse studies of memory and aging must report and plan for both factors.
pmc-13337651:
Zhiyan Zou heads a 2026 mouse study tracking gut bacteria as Alzheimer's disease develops. Three common transgenic models were followed: APP/PS1, 3xTg, and 5xFAD. The question was whether gut communities change in the same way as each model ages and worsens.

Stool samples collected at 2, 4, 6, and 8 months were read with 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Diversity and community structure shifted over time, but the pattern differed by model. Each strain showed its own set of changing bacterial groups. Those differences matter for anyone using mouse gut findings to reason about human disease, since model choice shapes the result.
pmc-13338851:
Yi-Fen Li and colleagues issued a 2026 correction to a laparoscopy study comparing endometriosis with and without painful periods. Several values in Table 1 were wrong as published. The corrected table is given in full, covering 345 patients with painful periods and 144 without.

Corrections fix the deep nodule shares in the group without painful periods to 50.7 percent without nodules and 49.3 percent with nodules as stated in the notice. The matching p-value becomes 0.047 instead of 0.04 as reported there. Age, hormone, and severity stage rows are also restated, so readers should use the corrected table for any comparison.
pmc-13340151:
Xiaoye Liu and colleagues probed gut microbes in 2026 in diabetic patients with thinking decline after stroke. Thinking decline after stroke gets worse with type 2 diabetes, yet gut microbe and body chemistry links were unclear. Stool samples from 28 diabetic patients with thinking decline and 29 matched controls went through deep gene sequencing and chemical profiling.

Overall diversity held steady, but germ and fungus mix shifted in small, telling ways. Butyrate making germs such as Lachnospira fell, while Butyricimonas virosa rose, and five fungus species including Torulaspora globosa declined. The gut brain signals point to new markers and possible aids for thinking decline after stroke in diabetes.
pmc-13340651:
N. Fagni and colleagues reported an Eagle syndrome case in 2026 where years of face and throat pain finally found a cause. Eagle syndrome is rare, marked by a long styloid bone spur or calcified tendon near the hyoid bone. The patient had suffered dental pain, painful swallowing, temple headaches, neck pain, and trouble swallowing, while routine checks looked normal.

Neck CT showed long, ossified styloid processes on both sides, matching Eagle syndrome. Surgeons removed the ossified segments through both sides of the neck in a minimally invasive approach. Symptoms resolved fully. The case shows how anatomy knowledge plus imaging can end years of unexplained head and neck pain.
pmc-13341451:
How esophageal cancer patients hunt for nutrition advice at home is explored by Xinhui Song and coauthors in their 2026 qualitative study. Semi-structured interviews with 15 patients recovering after surgery at a Guangdong tertiary hospital ran from November 2025 to January 2026.

Four themes emerged: wide-ranging information needs, many different sources, barriers while searching, and patterns in applying what was found. Seeking proved symptom-driven and fragmented, with real difficulty in reaching, understanding, and using guidance. The authors recommend continuous, individualized, family-inclusive nutrition support after discharge instead of one-off advice at the hospital door.
pmc-13341651:
Difficulty naming feelings may carry early trauma into adult emotion trouble, in a 2026 study by Angel Vásquez-Romero and Carlos Miguel Pérez-Lara. The Trujillo project surveyed 108 adults aged 18 to 25 with forms on childhood adversity, alexithymia, and emotion regulation.

Medium levels led across all three measures, in 62%, 56%, and 72% of participants. Mediation analysis found alexithymia clearly linked the trauma and regulation scores, with an indirect effect whose confidence interval ran from 0.04 to 0.31. Helping young adults identify and voice emotions could thus be a practical point of help after early harm.
pmc-13341951:
Konstantinos Prokopidis and co-authors relate testosterone levels to muscle mass and grip strength in middle-aged men, using United States national survey data from 2011 to 2014. Their 2026 study examines 1,001 men aged forty to fifty-nine, split into two age bands, comparing lean soft tissue in the limbs and handgrip strength across hormone levels.

Higher total testosterone was associated with stronger grip, with the link clearest in men aged fifty to fifty-nine, who also had higher odds of being in the stronger group. Men above the deficiency threshold for testosterone had substantially higher odds of greater lean tissue than men with deficiency, and normal-range levels showed a similar but weaker pattern. Linear analyses confirmed a modest lean tissue advantage above deficiency. The authors conclude that non-deficient testosterone in midlife, especially in the fifties, tracks with better muscle mass and strength.
pmc-13342051:
A new workplace wellness questionnaire is validated by Christine E. Garver-Apgar's team in their 2026 psychometric study. The Work and Well-being Inventory separates personal wellness from employer-supported wellness across eight dimensions each, aiming for scores managers can actually read.

Staff (949 people) from four large behavioral health organizations in four states filled in the survey in 2022 or 2023. Factor analysis on split samples backed a final 106-item inventory with 16 separately usable subscales and good internal consistency. Links with established measures matched expected theory. Organizations wanting to track wellness programs get a tool built for that exact purpose.
pmc-13343151:
Mak B Djulbegovic and colleagues built a computer tool in 2026 to rank drug targets for a severe eye disease after retinal detachment repair. The disease, called PVR, has no good drug therapy. A cell shift known as EMT drives it, yet which EMT regulators can be drugged, above all those with floppy disordered parts, was poorly mapped.

The tool screens EMT linked proteins by computer models of shape and disorder, ranking those most open to structure based drug design. No human samples were used in this idea generating study. The ranked list gives drug makers a short, focused set of targets for a blinding eye complication.
pmc-13343851:
Jan V. Henkel and a large team study bacteria clinging to magnetic minerals deep in Baltic Sea mud in 2026. Acetate breakdown below the sulfate-methane boundary seems to run through teamwork fed by electron flow. Conductive minerals such as magnetite may host the partners, so the team pulled magnetic grains straight from the sediment.

Tracer tests confirmed acetate oxidation matched methane formation rates, a signature of syntrophic teamwork. Magnetic particles ran through every layer and hosted communities ruled by relatives of Desulfatiglans, sulfate breathers whose recovered genomes oddly lack sulfate-breathing gear. Instead they may oxidize acetate and dump electrons onto the minerals. Cytochrome-rich ANME-1 archaea shared the grains, though their exact partner role stays open.
pmc-13344251:
Mehreen Zaigham, Ines Nunes, and Bo Jacobsson frame maternal and newborn health for the era after the 2030 development goals in a 2026 commentary. A woman still dies every two minutes from pregnancy or childbirth causes, with 260,000 maternal deaths in 2023 and 2.3 million newborn deaths in 2022, most of them preventable.

Progress toward the Sustainable Development Goal targets has slowed badly, and the global average death ratio sits far above the goal line. The authors introduce the Lancet Commission on Maternal and Newborn Health, launched in 2025, which gathers researchers, clinicians, policymakers, and advocates to set post-2030 priorities. Grounding advice in frontline realities, they argue, matters as much as the evidence itself.
pmc-13345851:
Zhan Tang and co-authors build a forecasting tool for severe childhood shortsightedness from school screening histories in 2026. Single snapshots miss how a child's refraction travels, so the team used repeated Binchuan County screenings from autumn 2023 to autumn 2025 and stacked several classifiers under expert guidance.

The resulting EGS-Net pairs an ensemble of models with a clinical rule override designed to catch risky children other tools miss. Recall reached 0.9533 with precision of 0.9211 on held-out students, beating the false-alarm burden of a near-perfect but sloppier rival. Importance analysis confirmed that trajectory features drive the calls. The system suits mass school screening where missed high-risk children cost the most.
pmc-13346651:
Parviz Ghaderi and colleagues investigated in 2026 how the frontal cortex lets mice use a brief sound cue to shape what a whisker touch means. Flexible behaviour depends on context: the same sensation should trigger a lick for reward in one context and restraint in another, after a delay.

Mice learned a Go or Nogo task in which an auditory cue, a delay, and then a whisker deflection determined whether licking earned reward. Targeted optogenetic silencing showed that whisker secondary motor cortex contributed across all trial phases, while recordings revealed stable context signals in that area and in anterolateral motor cortex. The work pinpoints where context and sensation first merge to guide a choice.
pmc-13346851:
Sunyoung Choi reviews how implant surfaces shape bacterial sticking and biofilm growth, in a short literature review from 2026. The review notes that gum disease around implants starts with film forming on the surface. That tissues around implants lack the ligament found around natural teeth, which raises the risk of colonisation.

Adhesion is traced from loose first contact to firm binding and mature film, with rough surfaces giving bacteria sheltered spots while polished neck areas stay easier to clean. Zirconia tended to draw less bacterial adhesion than titanium in lab reports, though patient factors also matter. Design that limits film is presented as key to long implant life.
pmc-13347151:
Mohammad Reza Shadmand Foumani Moghadam and a large team test links among activity, work, mood, and muscle loss in a registry feasibility study published in 2026. A total of 766 healthy adults gave activity and job histories and took mood scales, with muscle loss judged by European working group rules for sarcopenia.

Past and current activity, sports time, and being in work were each tied to lower odds of muscle loss. Swimming plus some traditional Iranian sports stood out in the reported links. Higher depression, anxiety, and stress scores went the other way, raising odds in the same models. Combined models kept activity and mood as separate signals, supporting a broad registry approach.
pmc-13348051:
Nikkia Zarabian and co-authors told in 2026 of a severe psoriasis flare after tralokinumab therapy for atopic dermatitis. This adverse event is rare and poorly grasped. Tralokinumab blocks interleukin-13. It is approved for moderate to severe eczema in patients aged twelve and up. Trials showed a largely kind safety profile.

The case spells out checks and care for a patient whose skin illness shifted sharply after starting the biologic. It raises asks about how blocking one inflammation path can unmask another. Usual side effects are upper airway infections, eye inflammation, and jab-site reactions. This flare stands out from that list. The report urges clinicians to watch for paradox skin reactions when targeted eczema drugs shift immune balance.
pmc-13348251:
Xintao Wang and colleagues developed in 2026 a flexible artificial lateral line, inspired by the flow-sensing system of fish, to measure underwater velocity vectors from light signals. Fish sense water movement through hair cells along their flanks, giving real-time feedback on the flow field around their bodies.

Their sensor uses a dual-layer inverted cup rocker: flow pushes the rocker, compresses a flexible silicone spring, and changes the light flux reaching photosensitive units in several directions. A deep neural network interprets these signals despite large deformations and nonlinear mechanics in the flexible material. The device could give underwater robots and vehicles a compact, fish-like sense of local flow for navigation and control.
pmc-13349351:
Abolfazl Jokar and co-authors tested in 2026 whether joined vitamin D and A supplements lift outcomes in pneumosepsis, a severe lower lung infection that can kill. Vitamins D and A back immune function. Yet their joined effect in acute lung infection had not been tested in a controlled trial.

Eighty-four patients were split at random into four groups. One got standard care plus both vitamins. One got standard care plus vitamin D alone. One got standard care plus vitamin A alone. One got standard care alone. High single muscle doses were used. Inflammation markers, kidney function, and linked measures were tracked at base line and at 24, 48, and 72 hours. The joined group showed the top gains.
pmc-13349751:
Laura Menchetti and colleagues trial a quality-of-life frame for free-range chickens based on felt experience, in a methods study from 2026. Four slow-growing types were watched over five weeks outdoors, acts were sorted as good or bad feeling signs. A balance score gave the share of good acts among all acts for each type across the full watch.

Good acts outweighed bad acts in every type, with balance scores from 73.7 percent to 92.5 percent and no clear split among types in the reported values. Tricky acts such as sheltering and attacking resisted fixed labels, so the authors urge judging each act by timing, pattern, and setting rather than by name alone.
pmc-13349951:
Wenming Zhang and colleagues evaluated a gentler CT angiography method in 2026 for checking dialysis access in the arm. Patients on haemodialysis often need repeat scans of their fistula or graft, and standard scans bring heavy radiation and dye loads.

One hundred and two patients with suspected access problems were randomly assigned to routine-dose scanning or a low-dose version using less dye and an AI image rebuilding method. Image quality and readings were compared, and 44 patients also had the reference dye test through a catheter. A reliable low-dose option would ease the burden on patients who face these scans again and again.
pmc-13350351:
Han Yajuan and a large team studied abnormal cortisol levels in people living with HIV in a 2026 retrospective analysis of 117 patients seen between 2017 and 2025. Nearly half, 47.9 percent, showed unusually high morning cortisol.

Patients were grouped by low, normal, or high morning cortisol. The low group had longer-standing HIV, higher treatment use, and higher diastolic blood pressure, while the high group carried higher triglycerides. Different antiretroviral regimens were checked for links to the hormone patterns. As people with HIV live longer, hormone and metabolic side effects of lifelong therapy deserve the same attention as virus control itself.
pmc-13350451:
Siyuan Ding and colleagues reviewed surgery through the nose as the sole treatment for early cancer of the nasopharynx in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Four retrospective studies covering 164 operated patients were found.

Most patients, 58 percent, had stage I disease, and two studies reported three and five year survival of 100 percent for that group; pooling all stages gave five-year survival of 90.6 percent. Comparisons in two studies set surgery against modern radiotherapy or open surgery, and quality of life and complications were extracted. Avoiding radiation would spare patients lasting side effects, but the thin, retrospective evidence base limits certainty.
pmc-13352051:
Abhishek Deshpande and co-authors surveyed in 2026 practice shifts in handling Clostridioides difficile infection. The doctors were in the United States. After 2021 rules from gut and infectious disease societies gave conflicting advice, clinicians grew unsure. First-line therapy and gut microbial treatments were the main doubts.

An online survey of 302 doctors ran in early 2023. Gut doctors, infectious disease specialists, and primary care doctors were split evenly. Rule use and views on microbial therapies were asked about. Minimum monthly germ caseloads were needed for inclusion. Hospital and academic doctors knew rules better than independent practice doctors. Only half of gut doctors followed one society's guidance.
pmc-13353351:
Ronak J Mahatme leads a 2026 database study of smoking and clot risk after joint arthroscopy. Smoking drives clotting, inflammation, and heart-lung harm, yet its short-term effect after keyhole joint surgery was ill-defined. Patients having shoulder, hip, or knee arthroscopy in the TriNetX network were matched one-to-one by age, sex, health conditions, and procedure type.

Ninety-day rates of clots, lung embolism, emergency visits, readmission, infection, and wound opening were compared. Among 18,948 shoulder patients, smoking showed no clear link to clot outcomes, with a risk ratio of 1.086 for venous clots. Emergency visits, though, ran higher in smokers, with a risk ratio of 1.627. Joint-specific results guide counselling before elective keyhole surgery.
pmc-13354651:
Edward Willow and co-authors reviewed studies in 2026 on dextromethorphan, a common cough drug sold without a prescription in the United States. At high doses the drug can cause psychedelic-like effects, which has raised interest in it for hard-to-treat mental illness. The review asks what doses cause which effects, and how safe those doses are.

Only eight studies, with 104 people in total, met the review rules. Effects began near 100 mg, while nausea, slow thinking, and trouble moving grew above 200 mg, and stronger visions came at higher doses. The authors say the proof is too thin to set a safe dose range, so larger dose-finding studies are needed.
pmc-13354951: Eran Gefen and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their study of sprinting and surface activity in scorpions. The note fixes how running speed was scaled: speed was split by body length, not by shell length as first stated. It also fixes a count in a figure, raising one species group from 39 to 40 animals. The authors state that the values and findings of the study do not change.
pmc-13355151:
Adnan Ur Rehman and co-authors studied 160 patients with acute pancreatitis in Pakistan in 2026 to see if diabetes made the illness worse. Pancreatitis is a sudden, painful swelling of the pancreas, and it can range from mild to deadly. Patients at a medical college hospital were tracked from April to September 2025 for severity, complications, and death.

About 42 percent of patients had diabetes, and severe illness was about twice as common in that group. Organ failure, dead pancreas tissue, intensive care stays, and death were all higher, and hospital stays were longer by about three days. The authors say spotting diabetic patients early may help improve their care.
pmc-13356551:
Menghan Zhou and co-authors built a glucose-responsive microneedle patch in 2026 to treat diabetic wounds, which often stall in a state of lasting inflammation. The patch carries a plant compound, isoliquiritigenin, tied into a framework that releases it when sugar is high. The needles push the drug deep into skin, past the surface barrier.

In lab tests, the system released drug under high sugar, calmed inflammation, and mopped up harmful oxygen particles by targeting an immune sensor called ZBP1. In diabetic mice, the patch steadied inflammation and drove full-thickness wound healing with new collagen. The authors present it as a promising path for clinic use.
pmc-13358451:
Richard C. Oude Voshaar and Radboud M. Marijnissen wrote a 2026 review on death wishes in older adults. As societies age, more older people say they wish to die, even when they are not ill or depressed. The authors pull together past research to explain where such wishes come from.

They sort the causes into layers: loss of meaning and self, loneliness and feeling like a burden, and wider views on ageing and dependence. Laws on assisted dying form the last layer. The review helps doctors and families hear these wishes with care and not rush to treat them as a sign of mental illness alone.
pmc-13358751:
Vladislav Muldiiarov and co-authors review a rare condition in a 2026 paper: lung hernia, where part of a lung pokes out through a gap in the chest. Once tied mostly to injury, it now shows up more often after surgery, including lung transplant, or after long spells of heavy coughing that spike chest pressure.

The authors searched the medical literature through the end of 2025 and gathered what is known on causes, signs, scans, and treatment. Most of the evidence comes from single case reports and small series. Even so, the review gives doctors a practical guide to spotting this uncommon problem and choosing between watchful care and repair.
pmc-13358851:
Tomoki Makino and co-authors wrote a 2026 reply in a debate over surgery for advanced esophageal cancer. Their earlier paper reported 90 cases where the cancer had grown into nearby organs and surgeons removed those organs along with the esophagus. Two groups of commentators questioned how far such extended surgery should go.

Makino and co-authors stress they do not propose the operation for every such patient. They argue it can be done safely in a carefully chosen few at experienced centers, where drug and radiation treatment leaves stubborn local disease. Their reply sharpens the line between bold surgery that helps and surgery that only harms.
pmc-13359151:
E. Steve Roach wrote a reflective parable on training traditions, issued in 2026, opening with a Vonnegut line about being trapped in the amber of a moment. The essay turns to a beloved eight-year-old convertible, turquoise and white, that idled softly and roared when challenged. For its young owner, the car embodied adventure, independence, and a maturity not yet earned.

Over time the car became a mobile museum of fading youth, its classic design standing against the computer-made sameness of newer models. The parable uses that attachment to explore how training traditions, like old cars, carry memory and identity. Readers gain a short, literary meditation on what is kept, and what is lost, when a wave's symbols age.
pmc-13359551:
Hanwei Zhang and co-authors survey exercise habits among adults with a migration history in Germany in a 2026 study. Staying active protects health, yet little was known about activity levels in this large group. Building and then testing the model on genuinely future data gives a fairer read on whether routine records can stratify liver injury risk before damage shows.
pmc-13402251:
Isabella Pereira Pesenato and a large team report frogs in Bahia, Brazil, carrying two kinds of parasites at once: soft ticks and chigger mites. The hosts were Bokermannohyla frogs caught in Chapada Diamantina National Park, a genus spread across Brazilian habitats with several endangered species. Parasites can weigh on frog survival, and some tick and mite families specialize on this frog group.

Using body shape alone, the team named the ticks as Ornithodoros saraivai, the first record of that species in Bahia State. The mites proved new to science and are described as Hannemania diamantinensis, raising the known Brazilian Hannemania count to eight. Finding both parasites on the same frogs, a pattern called co-parasitism, adds a data point for tracking the health of threatened frog populations.
pmc-13402651:
Takuya Takami and colleagues compare two ways of joining the bowel during keyhole colon surgery: stitching inside the body, or pulling the bowel out through a small cut to join it outside. Their COMMIT analysis drew on a Kyoto multicenter database covering 3213 patients operated between 2018 and 2025, then matched 650 pairs by propensity scores to level the comparison.

Heavy bleeding of 200 milliliters or more struck 2.5 percent of the inside-join group against 4.9 percent of the outside-join group, a gap the authors call significant. Total blood loss, lymph node harvest, and complication rates otherwise ran close, and inside joins tended to take longer, though the time gap flipped by surgical approach in subgroup checks. Margin quality leaned toward the inside method without reaching significance. The authors present inside joining as a way to cut heavier bleeding events.
pmc-13402951:
Daniel M Ripley and Ashleigh Donaldson report, in a commentary, on catch-and-release stress in Greenland sharks, drawing on fieldwork by Yuuki Watanabe and colleagues. Twelve sharks were caught, blood-sampled, fitted with GPS trackers, and released. The question matters because these ancient, slow Arctic sharks increasingly meet fishing gear, and nobody knew how badly capture harms them.

During capture their blood lactate and glucose, markers of exhaustion and stress, ran lower than in many other sharks. Released sharks swam hard for a while, then settled back to normal behavior within about 10 hours, and at least 90 percent survived the 30 days when capture deaths usually strike. Longer hooking did not raise lactate, supporting the idea that a calm, slow life blunts the ordeal. Cool Arctic surface water, near 3 degrees, may help too.
pmc-13403051:
Md Mohiuddin and Md Al Mamun Ahsan write a perspective on autophagy, the cell recycling system, as a double-edged target in cancer therapy. Early in cancer, recycling suppresses tumors. In established tumors it keeps stressed cells alive and blunts chemotherapy. That feeds the resistance that defeats treatment. The balance shifts with tumor stage, which cell groups are present, and the surroundings, which is why simple on-off strategies disappoint.

First-generation blockers such as hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine sensitize some tumors in the lab and have reached trials, but they lack specificity and bring off-target toxicity. The authors spotlight narrower pathways, mitophagy and ER-phagy among them. They argue for precision approaches: selective blockers, markers that warn ahead, and nanoparticle delivery that controls where and when autophagy is touched. Their verdict is promise with discipline.
pmc-13403151:
Stem Cells International retracts a 2021 article that claimed lithium and copper drive bone-forming and vessel-forming coupling in bone marrow stem cells through Wnt and HIF-1 alpha signaling. The retraction was agreed between editor-in-chief Renke Li and publisher John Wiley and Sons. It followed an investigation into image concerns. The probe began when the authors themselves asked to correct figures after repeating experiments.

A PubPeer commenter flagged a staining panel in Figure 6a that closely matched a panel in another group article. The journal probe found more. Corners of Figure 1a echoed Figure 6a. Two Figure 2c panels looked alike, one seemingly a magnification of the other. Near-duplicate staining panels sat within Figure 6a itself. GAPDH blot bands in Figure 4d reappeared flipped in Figure 6c under different stated conditions. With core images compromised, the findings could no longer stand.
pmc-13403551:
Juliana Pineda-Ortega, María Juliana Soto-Chavez, and Ana María Gómez told in 2026 of a young man with type 1 diabetes who grew brain damage usually tied to salt shifts. His blood sugar swung wildly, across a very wide range, and his sodium stayed steady. He also had heart and kidney failure that needed dialysis.

Brain scans showed the pattern of osmotic demyelination, where protective nerve coating breaks down. Other causes were ruled out by the team. They blame sharp sugar swings and unstable body-fluid balance, made worse by dialysis. The case widens the list of triggers doctors should watch for.
pmc-13404251:
Jose Antonio Sanchez Salas and co-authors looked back in 2026 at what shapes bleeding control when people with haemophilia face procedures. Such patients bleed easily around any invasive step, so prep matters a great deal. Their center's records covered 158 procedures in 61 men from 2010 to 2025.

Bleeding response rated good or excellent in about 95.6 percent of procedures overall. Poor or fair response clustered in the heaviest patients, hitting about 27 percent of procedures in men over 100 kilograms. That rate far topped lighter weight bands. Major procedures also trended worse, though less firmly. Weight care before procedures may lift safety, the team suggests.
pmc-13404851:
Theresa Ms Burkard leads a 2026 network study of autoimmune and inflammatory illness after COVID-19 across nine countries. Records come from primary care, hospitals, registries and claims in Europe, the United States and Korea. Follow-up starts on day 91 after infection or a negative test, placing the focus on the post-acute period.

Conditions tracked include POTS, chronic fatigue syndrome conditions, multi-inflammatory syndrome and diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. Patients are followed for up to a year, until an outcome, death or a new infection ends their record. A separate reinfection group shows whether a second infection changes risk. The design uses shared definitions so results can be compared across databases.
pmc-13405451:
Yuan-Lang Brian Chan and colleagues survey glioblastoma care with an Asian focus, in a 2026 review of challenges and future directions. Glioblastoma is among the most feared brain cancers, with high illness and death rates despite rarity. Brain tumour incidence across Asia has risen since 1990 and is expected to keep climbing.

Care quality varies sharply across the region in their account. Centres in Singapore, Japan, South Korea and other wealthy settings offer advanced imaging, awake surgery and combined drug-radiation treatment. Many lower-income countries lack enough trained specialists to match that standard. The review sets out current obstacles and research horizons, framed around closing that regional gap.
pmc-13406951:
Meiqing Yang and co-authors review, in 2026, electrochemical sensors built to find antibiotic leftovers in fish and other aquatic animal foods. Leftover drug traces threaten food safety, so quick, cheap, small-scale tests carry real value for producers and inspectors.

The review covers eight antibiotic families, from fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines to beta-lactams, and sorts sensors into four kinds: direct devices, antibody-based sensors, aptamer-based sensors, and molecularly imprinted versions. Attention goes to how each target behaves electrically, how sensing surfaces are built, how signals get amplified, and how samples are prepared before testing. Stubborn problems remain, notably messy real-world samples and uneven preparation methods, and the authors sketch where development should head next.
pmc-13407951:
Chady Ghnatios and Kazem Fayazbakhsh model, in 2026, why composite tape warps while a robot prints it. Continuous-fibre thermoplastic printing promises strong light parts, yet feedstock deformation during deposition seeds defects and defeats path planning. The team therefore combined experiments with physics-based and learning-based modelling to pin down the drivers.

Residual stress relief, drying, crystallisation, and thermal stress were separated using thermal and mechanical test data. A viscoelastic physics model handled the prepreg mechanics while a stabilised neural differential-equation model captured drying and ordering behaviour. Fitted together, the hybrid reproduced tape conduct well beyond the temperatures it was trained on, a strong sign of validity. Robotic printing trials then validated the model in real printing settings.
pmc-13408051:
Cahit Ucar and co-authors probe, in 2026, a stress-defence protein as an early warning of heart trouble in lupus. People with systemic lupus erythematosus suffer cardiovascular damage long before symptoms. Sestrin-1, an antioxidant guardian protein, was measured in 60 patients and 60 matched healthy controls. It was read alongside heart tracings, heart ultrasound, and neck-artery thickness scans.

Patients carried far less Sestrin-1, about 10 against 17.8 nanograms per millilitre, and their corrected QT interval, an electrical timing measure, ran significantly longer. In adjusted modelling, lower Sestrin-1, a wider left atrium, and longer QT each independently accompanied lupus status, with every unit of Sestrin-1 lowering the odds substantially. The authors propose the protein as a marker of the subclinical cardiovascular alterations accumulating silently in lupus.
pmc-13408151:
Li Wang and co-authors report, in 2026, a phase II trial of a two-in-one immune antibody plus chemotherapy. It targets the hardest-to-treat lung cancer subgroup: advanced non-small-cell tumours with no PD-L1 expression, where immunotherapy usually falters. Cadonilimab blocks PD-1 and CTLA-4 in a single bispecific molecule, and fifty patients received it first-line with chemotherapy.

The headline endpoint was met: 42.1 percent of patients remained progression-free at twelve months, median progression-free survival reached 9.7 months, two-thirds responded, and every patient's disease was at least controlled. Median overall survival had not been reached. Severe treatment side effects hit 52 percent. Blood DNA methylation patterns predicted real responses about five treatment cycles before scans did, and a baseline methylation risk score separated longer from shorter benefit. Controlled trials are warranted.
pmc-13408351:
Andrea Di Pietro and a large Australian team profiled melanoma lymph node samples in 2026 to learn what responding tumours contain that resistant ones lack. T cells that take up residence inside tumours are known guardians against melanoma, yet their part in checkpoint immunotherapy success had not been mapped in full.

Thirty-two samples from untreated, responding, and resistant patients were profiled cell by cell and in place. Responding tumours were rich in resident CD8 and CD4 T cells that had multiplied and switched on killing programmes, while resistant tumours showed exhausted cells stuck in chronic interferon signalling. Only responders held an organised trio of the two resident T-cell types plus a particular dendritic cell. That spatial pattern could become a biomarker for predicting who benefits from treatment.
pmc-13409551:
Jiali Yu and colleagues ask in 2026 whether a trip to the dentist changes what patients do at home afterwards, surveying two hundred forty-six patients at a Guangzhou hospital. Brushing, interdental cleaning, diet, and follow-up attendance were each recorded for the period before and after treatment, and statistical models hunted for what predicts actually adopting prevention.

Twice-daily brushing rose modestly but significantly after treatment. Daily interdental cleaning stayed low at under a quarter of patients, while about three fifths reported changing their diet and just over half kept follow-up appointments. Most demographic traits predicted nothing. The consistent lever was comprehension: patients who understood the preventive advice flossed more, returned more, and followed recommendations more, while merely receiving advice, in whatever format, showed no independent effect. Men brushed adequately less often than women. The message for clinics is to teach until understood, not just to advise.
pmc-13410551:
Sarah Jasat and co-authors update in 2026 a review of what helps or blocks physical activity for people on dialysis. Exercise improves health for these patients, yet few stay active and clinics offer it unevenly. The review uses behavior theory to turn scattered views into a plan for lasting change.

Five databases yielded 17 papers with views from patients and staff. Barriers and supports were mapped onto a standard framework of behavior domains. Patient and staff views lined up closely, and every broad driver of behavior played a part. Training, reshaping clinic settings, teaching, showing examples, and practical support came out as the most workable levers for routine care.
pmc-13410851:
Stephen Olaide Aremu and colleagues survey in 2026 hepatitis B vaccination among adults at a hospital in Nasarawa State, Nigeria. The virus remains a major health threat in sub-Saharan Africa despite a safe vaccine. Adult uptake inside hospital populations was poorly documented, so 1,200 attendees answered a structured questionnaire.

Awareness ran high, and about 94 percent reported at least one vaccine dose. Finishing the full three-dose course was another story: only about 22 percent had done so. Most people said they were willing to complete the course. Cost, poor access to facilities, and fear of side effects topped the barriers named. Knowledge and attitudes scored well overall, which suggests access, not awareness, is the binding problem.
pmc-13410951:
Verena Petzer and co-workers search in 2026 for a simple clue that flags men carrying mutations behind VEXAS, an inflammatory illness described only in 2020. The mutation hides in blood-forming cells and can mimic many diseases, so picking who to test is hard. Oversized red blood cells are a near-constant sign of the syndrome.

The team traced men who had both a blood protein disorder and available marrow samples, narrowing over a thousand cases to 160 for gene testing. They compared mutation rates in men with and without those enlarged red cells. Pairing the size clue with the protein disorder may preselect patients far better than either sign alone, sparing many men an unneeded gene hunt.
pmc-13411151:
Di Zhang and Jing Zhou mine in 2026 a United States side-effect database for safety signals of three drugs used to trigger ovulation in polycystic ovary syndrome. The condition is common, and each drug carries its own risk profile. Knowing those profiles apart can guide personal prescribing.

Of 21,730 reports tied to the condition, letrozole accounted for the vast majority, then tamoxifen, with clomiphene rarely reported. Fatigue surfaced as a shared signal, and tumor progression plus joint pain appeared across all three drugs. Tamoxifen and letrozole reports clustered around tumor-related terms, while clomiphene leaned toward psychiatric and gut events. The authors stress matching drug choice to each patient's risk profile.
pmc-13412151:
Rachel Lean and colleagues followed very preterm children to ages nine and ten in 2026 to test whether thinking skills explain their behavior profile. Children born at or before 30 weeks often show weaker executive function alongside attention, anxiety, and social differences, yet the chain linking birth, brain injury, and behavior stayed unclear.

Among 123 preterm children and 79 full-term controls, preterm birth and high-grade white matter injury both predicted weaker executive function, which in turn tracked with the behavior profile. The paper points early support toward memory, self-control, and flexible thinking as a route to better social and emotional outcomes.
pmc-13413451:
Zlatko Kirovakov, Angel Yordanov, and Vasilena Dimitrova gather in 2026 what is known about pregnancy in women with myasthenia gravis. The disease weakens muscles when nerve signals fail at the muscle door. Pregnancy can stir it up or calm it down, with little warning. Their review searched four large databases for group studies, case sets, and strong case reports. The mixed designs ruled out pooled sums, so the team wove the finds into a story form.

Birth results were most often good when care teams watched closely and tuned treatment to each woman. Flares bunched in pregnancy and just after birth, most in wide-spread disease or weak breathing. Past thymus surgery may lower flare rates and brief weakness in newborns, though data stay thin. Joint care by nerve, birth, sleep-drug, and newborn staff is the core advice.
pmc-13415151:
Irene Zapata-Martínez leads a 2026 systematic review of physical activity in people with celiac disease. Gluten triggers immune damage in this condition, and a gluten free diet is the only proven treatment. The reviewers searched five databases for studies linking activity levels or exercise programs to health outcomes.

Fourteen studies qualified, most of them one-time surveys rather than trials. Higher activity sometimes matched better body composition, calmer inflammation, and stronger quality of life. Findings for metabolism and bone density conflicted across studies, often tied to diet differences. The authors call those findings preliminary and ask for long term trials, especially in children.
pmc-13415551:
Abdulhusein and co-authors test, in 2026, whether curcumin, the compound in turmeric, helps broiler chickens withstand coccidiosis, a gut parasite disease, and whether the oil source matters. Their 42-day trial placed 660 one-day-old male Ross 308 chicks into five treatments with six replicates of 22 birds each, crossing soybean or canola oil diets with curcumin at 0.02 percent, and challenged the birds with mixed Eimeria parasites on day 14.

Among challenged birds, curcumin improved weight gain and feed efficiency, trimmed abdominal fat and relative liver and spleen weights, and raised post-challenge antibody levels. It shifted gene expression protectively, suppressing the inflammatory switch NF-kappaB and interleukin-6 while boosting interleukin-10 and the antioxidant master gene NRF2 in the factorial analysis. Gut counts moved the right way too, with more Lactobacillus and less ileal E. coli. The canola oil plus curcumin group showed the clearest recovery, while canola oil alone gave endpoint-specific effects.
pmc-13415751:
Laure Inçaby and co-authors publish the first complete mitochondrial genome of the Pacific spiny dogfish, in 2026. This small North Pacific shark is taken in commercial and bycatch fisheries. Long read sequencing assembled a circular genome of 16,738 bases holding the standard thirty-seven mitochondrial genes.

Thirteen protein coding genes, twenty-two transfer RNAs, two ribosomal RNAs, and a control region make up the set. Adenine and thymine together form about 61 percent of the sequence. Family tree analysis placed this shark as sister to the Atlantic spiny dogfish with maximum support. Gene change ratios suggest strong purifying selection since the pair split.
pmc-13415851:
Roman Jerala and Duško Lainšček comment in 2026 on a molecular velcro trick for precise genome repair, discussing work by Mu and colleagues. Base editors rewrite single DNA letters without cutting both strands, yet the editors are too large for the adeno-associated virus carriers used in gene therapy. Split editors solve size, provided the halves find each other inside cells.

Programmable coiled coil peptides act as the velcro, pairing the halves on arrival. The split editors worked efficiently in living animals, sometimes beating intact versions. Delivery limits have stalled base editing's clinical path, so a modular self assembling design could widen treatable diseases.
pmc-13416751:
Eisendrath and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare heart event during a hip replacement operation. A 63-year-old man had an elective right total hip replacement, and monitoring later showed his ventricles had stopped contracting for twenty seconds during surgery. This event, called ventricular standstill, means the heart's main pumping chambers pause completely.

This patient stayed asymptomatic, with steady blood pressure before, during, and after the pause. No treatment emergency followed, and the event was found only on the heart monitor record. The authors discuss possible triggers, including a vasovagal response, where a nerve reflex slows the heart, and inflammation linked to surgery and anaesthesia. They note that no earlier case in their search described standstill during an operation. The report adds a data point on how long a pause a stable patient can tolerate.
pmc-13418051:
Ma and colleagues report a 2026 study of a chemical tagging system that restrains sugar burning and bowel cancer growth. Many tumors run aerobic glycolysis, a fast but wasteful way to burn sugar. The team found that an enzyme called UFL1 attaches a small tag, UFM1, to enolase 1, a core sugar-burning enzyme, at two specific sites on the protein.

The tag breaks up enolase pairs and lowers its activity, which cuts the flow of sugar burning. Tumors with active tagging grew more slowly in dishes and in animals. A licensed antibiotic, torezolid, strengthened the tagger's grip on enolase and sharply boosted the standard drug 5-FU in lab models, patient-derived tumor organoids, and grafts, without visible toxicity. The work names a new control point in cancer metabolism and a drug pairing ready for further testing.
pmc-13418251:
Yanli Lin, Marne L White, Jihong Zhang, and Todd S Braver track brain networks during mindfulness training, in a 2026 longitudinal study. Sixteen beginners completed up to 24 lab sessions of two meditation styles: focused attention on one object, and open monitoring of whatever arises. Brain waves and self rated mindfulness quality were collected each session, then modelled as networks over time.

The two styles produced distinct brain and experience networks, supporting their theoretical split. Both shared strong carry over of mindfulness skill between sessions, plus opposing effects of front versus back brain alpha rhythms. One size EEG markers mislead, the authors argue; meaning depends on practice type and stage.
pmc-13420651:
Yasunaga and co-authors describe a surgical technique for controlling blood flow during open repair of a chest-and-abdomen aortic aneurysm. Their patient was a man whose aorta had earlier been treated from inside with a stent graft. Clamping the old graft directly looked difficult. So they used inflatable occlusion balloons to seal the aorta from within.

The patient was a 76-year-old man whose earlier repair had developed a pseudoaneurysm, a contained leak beside the original stent. Guided by X-ray imaging, the team placed balloons into each graft limb through leg artery sheaths. Blood kept flowing to the legs through side branches during the operation. A composite graft bridged the size mismatch, and an inner cuff stopped bleeding at the lower join. He survived without major complications. Scans at 12 months showed no recurrence.
pmc-13421151:
Linn Renman, Lotta Andréen and Sahruh Turkmen report a 2026 study from northern Sweden on how women want to be followed up after surgery for endometrial cancer. They compared newly operated patients who had not yet entered follow-up with patients already attending a standard hospital-based programme.

Ninety patients completed questionnaires about their preferences and quality of life. Newly operated patients showed more varied wishes, with about half favouring doctor-led hospital visits, while more than four in five of the experienced group preferred that format. Quality-of-life scores did not differ clearly between the groups. The findings suggest that follow-up plans may need to adapt as patients gain experience of the programme.
pmc-13421251:
Simona S Ghanem, Tara Al-Barazenji, Rehab Badi and Essam M Abdelalim show in a 2026 study that growing stem-cell-derived liver cells as three-dimensional organoids helps them mature. The team grew liver progenitor cells in flat culture, then either kept them flat or gathered them into organoids for the final maturation stage. Organoid cells expressed higher levels of mature liver markers and performed better, secreting more albumin and producing more urea and stored glycogen. Gene sequencing found 1,266 genes differing between the two formats, pointing to the pathways behind the improvement.
pmc-13421451:
Matteo Montalbano and eight colleagues characterise, in a 2026 study, oesophageal adenocarcinomas that have lost one or both of two chromatin-remodelling proteins, SMARCA2 and SMARCA4. These proteins keep DNA packaging dynamic, and their loss marks aggressive cancers elsewhere, yet the pattern in this cancer was undefined.

They clustered in patients aged 65 and over. They carried MET gene amplification more often, especially after pre-surgery therapy. pmc-13422351:
Lu Peng leads an eleven-author team building, in a 2026 study, a living vaccine against the bacterium behind pig pleuropneumonia, a costly disease of swine worldwide. Starting from a virulent strain, they defanged its three main toxins while keeping them visible to the immune system and deleted a fourth toxin as the tell-tale marker. The strain proved far milder in mice and protected most animals against three different serovars. Pigs tolerated high doses without fever or lung damage, and vaccination protected two thirds to all of the pigs depending on challenge strain.
pmc-13422751:
Pusec and colleagues present in 2026 the case of a patient whose tumor was an IDH-mutant grade 2 astrocytoma, a slow-growing brain tumor. The patient's scans seemed to worsen soon after starting an IDH inhibitor drug, ivosidenib. New bright areas appeared on MRI four months into treatment.

Its growth marker stayed near two percent of cells in samples taken both before and after treatment began. After surgery the patient had radiation and temozolomide chemotherapy and stayed stable for more than 18 months. The case warns that scan changes can mimic true progression.
pmc-13423151:
Nanna Lind, Patricia DeCosta, and Jannet Svensson report translating a United States questionnaire on life with type 1 diabetes into Danish for parents of young children. Mismatches led to small wording and cultural adjustments, including debate over the answer scale and items reflecting United States health care. Face validation with the target group completed the process, yielding a Danish version ready for wider testing.
pmc-13424251:
Alline Gomes Lamenha e Silva and colleagues tracked carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide in 2026 across Brazil's Amazon-Cerrado transition zone using satellite data from December 2018 to August 2024. Planners gain a land-use and transport lens for air-quality policy in fast-changing tropical frontiers and for road planners weighing new corridors.
pmc-13425851:

A speaking valve redirects air through the upper airway, supporting speech and breathing mechanics, and the team tested whether valve use speeds early mobilization. Reports from the trial link valve use with improved respiratory measures during recovery.

Patients using valves also scored higher on the EQ-5D-5L quality-of-life scale in the study highlights. For intensive care teams, the results support fitting valves early as part of getting tracheostomy patients moving sooner. Care teams can fit the valve check in with the daily round, since the gear is small and the steps are few once staff learn the way.
pmc-13425951:
Svärding and colleagues follow in 2026 adults recovering from surgery for a distal radius fracture, a break near the wrist. They ask whether two psychological traits predict lasting hand disability. Disability scores improved greatly over the year, and pain at rest settled, though grip and one bending motion had not fully returned by twelve months. Sense of coherence never predicted disability. pmc-13426351:
Mohammed Ali Qasem Al-Soufi and coauthors surveyed complementary medicine knowledge among health students in Sana'a, Yemen, in a 2026 single-centre cross-sectional study. Complementary and alternative medicine is widely used in Yemen, while formal teaching for future clinicians stays limited. Their questionnaire reached 318 final and pre-final year medical and pharmacy students at the University of Science and Technology, a 53 percent response.

Knowledge, attitude, and practice scores were split at sixty percent of the maximum to define good knowledge and positive attitude. Results show how prepared Yemeni graduates feel to counsel patients who already use traditional and alternative remedies.
pmc-13427751:

The model combines a multi-resolution patch tokenizer, lean self-attention, and a gated feed-forward network. That mix catches small lesions without heavy math. It scored 0.94 accuracy on the Kvasir v1 benchmark and 0.95 on Kvasir v2 in the reported tests. On the highly imbalanced Kvasir-Capsule set it reached 0.97 accuracy, with a matching 0.97 F1-score. pmc-13428151:
Katrin Conen and colleagues surveyed internal medicine residents at McMaster University about training in palliative care, meaning care that eases symptoms and supports people with life-limiting illness. They paired a survey of junior residents with interviews of senior ones to map training gaps.

Only half felt happy with the training they now get, though most felt at ease managing symptoms and talking with patients. Residents felt unsure about local resources and about discussing feeding tubes with patients and families. Senior residents praised hands-on learning but cited weak role models and timetable clashes, and backed required rotations and case-based teaching.
pmc-13428251:
Cibele R. Bonvicino, Maria Julia Cardoso, and Filipe Souza-Gudinho trace, in a 2026 study, the family history of olingos, small tree-dwelling carnivores of Central and northern South America. Populations from the Guiana Shield formed a well-separated branch from those in western Amazonia.

Combined with body differences noted earlier, the authors argue the Guiana Shield animals merit subspecies rank under the name beddardi. Kinkajous caught at the same sites used different local spots, hinting at habitat splits. Field guides and conservation lists for a shy genus get firmer lines.
pmc-13428351:

In epilepsy those identities survived, but three of the four proteins shifted in amount and place, pointing to faulty glutamate clearance and water control. pmc-13428451:

Each standard deviation rise in the visceral version carried a hazard ratio of 1.36, and the roundness version a hazard ratio of 1.32 at baseline. People whose levels stayed high over time faced roughly double the risk, with hazard ratios of 2.28 and 2.01 respectively, and associations were strongest at syndrome stage 2.
pmc-13428551:

pmc-13434151:

pmc-13436551:

pmc-13439951:

pmc-13440051:

pmc-13440451:

pmc-13442851:

pmc-13444251:

pmc-13445651:

pmc-13446351:

pmc-13447351:

pmc-13447451:

pmc-13448051:

pmc-13449651:

pmc-13450551:

pmc-13452151:

pmc-13454651:

pmc-13454951:

pmc-13457451:

pmc-13458251:
