Identifying renal cell types by eye is slow and expert-bound, while general models are too heavy for resource-limited labs. CytoECA-Net uses five stages of depthwise separable convolutions with channel attention and residual links to capture nuclear patterns from fluorescence images.

On the TissueMNIST benchmark of about 236,000 images, accuracy reached 75.56 percent with an area under the curve of 0.9564, using only 1.7 million parameters and 2.43 milliseconds per image. On a kidney histopathology dataset it reached 97.76 percent accuracy, the best among models tested, with attention maps landing on relevant nuclear structures. Labs gain an efficient, interpretable classifier for large-scale kidney tissue work.
pmc-13458351:
Victor Wang and colleagues share the lessons of assembling a large public database to support America's Ending the HIV Epidemic initiative. The initiative targets a 90 percent cut in new infections by 2030. Plenty of datasets exist, but few blend HIV outcomes with social determinants and community context in one place. Their 2026 viewpoint describes stitching 242 variables from 8 public sources across clinic, ZIP code, county, and state geography.

Four decisions, they argue, made the build replicable: bounding the source hunt before construction, and automating data engineering from day one. The other two were fixing a shared data dictionary before entering one variable, and weaving quality control through the whole workflow, not bolting it on. The project took 350 hours; early spot checks found errors in about a third of sampled entries, traced mainly to manual entry. The finished resource sits at Yale's implementation science center, a modest-budget model for other integration teams.
pmc-13458551:
Mirella López-Miguel and colleagues identify Cretaceous predator teeth from Algora, Spain, in a 2026 fossil study. Algora holds the richest haul of Cenomanian backboned-animal remains in south-west Europe, and lone predator dino teeth lead its predator record, yet earlier labels wavered between giant hunters and abelisaurids. Forty lone teeth were analysed with shape checks, multi-factor stats and tree methods.

The work supports an abelisaurid identity, most likely the branch Majungasaurinae, backing that lineage in Europe from the Cenomanian onward in the late chalk age. Teeth alone cannot name a species, but the larger, stricter sample firms up a southern-linked predator presence during a faunal shift between early and late chalk-age Europe. Diggers and experts gain a clearer naming anchor for Algora's predator community.
pmc-13459251:
Bingbing Tuo and co-authors measured how evenly China's price negotiated cancer drugs are spread across its 31 provinces. Since 2016, national negotiations have cut prices and expanded insurance coverage of anticancer medicines, but availability can still depend on local wealth. Their 2026 study collected province level data on which hospitals and pharmacies stock the negotiated drugs. It computed gap indices tied to provincial income and broke those indices down to find what drives them.

Both indices showed pro rich gaps: hospitals scored 0.125 and pharmacies 0.139 on the concentration measure used. Medical insurance spending and inpatient costs together explained much of the hospital side gap, while pharmacist numbers drove the pharmacy side gap. Even within one disease the pattern held, with two breast cancer drugs showing higher gap scores of 0.244 and 0.223. The authors urge targeted supply measures for poorer, remote areas.
pmc-13459451:
Yang Fu and co-authors investigated low platelet counts, called thrombocytopenia, in children with lupus, an autoimmune disease that attacks many organs. Their 2026 study reviewed 236 children diagnosed with childhood onset systemic lupus erythematosus at a Fudan University children's hospital between 2020 and late 2025. The team compared children who had low platelets at diagnosis with those who did not. Blood counts, complement levels, and autoantibody patterns were examined to find what predicts the complication and what it signals clinically.

Low counts appeared in 19.5 percent of the children, forty six of the 236 in the cohort. That group showed more white cell reductions and more frequent positivity for antiphospholipid antibodies, anti-beta2-glycoprotein antibodies, and lupus anticoagulant, all markers tied to clotting problems. Severity subgroups were also analyzed to grade how deep counts fell. Platelet status at diagnosis is a useful flag for a more complicated disease profile, the authors say.
pmc-13460051:
Meng Zhang leads a Beijing team reporting in 2026 on six patients whose hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, an inherited vessel disorder, was complicated by pulmonary hypertension and treated with bevacizumab. Experience with this drug in that rare pairing is scarce. Charts from Beijing Anzhen Hospital between 2021 and 2024 were reviewed, and matched comparison groups with other forms of high lung blood pressure set the context. Five patients completed follow-up after a three-month starter course.

Compared with the other groups, these patients pumped far more blood per minute while their vessels offered unusually little resistance. After that course, every followed patient improved in activity class, hemoglobin, a heart strain marker, and a combined scan measure of right heart performance. Two patients improved despite starting with lower cardiac output.
pmc-13460951:
Shahdad Ahmadi and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a probiotic bacterium taken from camel milk can ease acute inflammatory pain in rats, benchmarking it against acetaminophen. Forty-two male Wistar rats were split into seven groups, including pain controls and three groups fed Lactobacillus plantarum strain NIMBB003 at rising doses. The bacteria were fed for fourteen days before a formalin injection triggered pain in two phases. Blood levels of three inflammatory signals were also measured.

Only the highest dose worked, cutting pain behavior in both phases about as strongly as the painkiller did, while lower doses showed nothing significant. The high dose and acetaminophen each lowered the inflammatory signals IL-1 beta, IL-2, and IL-6. The authors propose the strain as a candidate alternative for inflammatory pain.
pmc-13461351:
Federico Caporaletti and co-authors used an X-ray technique that watches molecular motion at specific length scales to settle how two kinds of movement in supercooled liquids relate. When a liquid is cooled fast enough to skip crystallization, its molecules rattle inside cages of neighbors in a fast secondary process, then escape in the slow process that sets flow. Their 2026 study examined a hydrogen bonded glass former. It found the two processes are not independent: the fast rattling is the prelude to escape.

Before diffusion begins, the mean squared displacement of molecules grows more slowly than linearly, the signature of this constrained rattling in their measurements. The team reads the secondary relaxation as molecules testing the cage walls just before breaking out, linking it directly to the onset of flow. Tying this relaxation to diffusion sharpens predictions for pharmaceutical glasses and other materials that must not crystallize in storage.
pmc-13461851:
Zhichang Liu and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, that the gene PLAU helps head and neck cancer reshape its surroundings and spread. The cancer type starts in flat cells of the mouth, throat, and voice box. A halfway change, called partial epithelial-mesenchymal transition, lets cells loosen from neighbors and move. The team screened changed genes in public data to find drivers of that change.

Twelve candidate genes emerged, and PLAU stood out as tied to the halfway state. PLAU levels tracked closely with two marker proteins of that state in 75 tumor samples. Turning PLAU down slowed growth, invasion, and movement in lab dishes. Survival models named PLAU a sign of worse outlook, and high levels went with spread to neck lymph nodes. The authors conclude PLAU speeds the rebuilding of tissue around the tumor through that change, marking it as a target for blocking spread.
pmc-13462051:
Fukuda, Kobayashi, and Wakashima built in 2026 a scale to measure how Japanese adults explain mental disorders to themselves. People differ in whether they see such illness as medical, moral, psychological, social, or spiritual, and those views shape what help they accept. The team drafted a scale from an older three-style framework, added social and spiritual styles, and tested it in an online survey of 928 adults using five disorder stories.

Fukuda's analysis settled on 24 items in six factors. Two of them, biologising and medicalising, split apart even though they began as one idea, which the authors flag as exploratory. Most subscales held together well and scored stably over time, but the psychologising part was weak inside and needs better items. Scores lined up with related attitude measures as predicted. The authors present the scale as a first tool for mapping lay views of mental illness in Japan.
pmc-13462251:
Baifeng Chen and colleagues reviewed how infected urachal cysts in babies respond to treatment without surgery. A urachal cyst is a leftover pouch near the bladder that can infect; the study covered first-time infections in infants under one year.

The series covered 49 infants treated between 2012 and 2026 with antibiotics alone or antibiotics plus needle drainage. Belly-button signs were the commonest presentation, in about 79.6 percent, and three quarters had formed an abscess. Overall, 79.6 percent of cysts cleared fully without surgery, and only 12.2 percent of infants eventually needed an operation. Younger babies needed drainage more often, Chen notes, and every surgical case declared itself within three months.
pmc-13462551:
Zhiyan Li and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, a lactate-shuttling protein called SLC16A3, also known as MCT4, as a driver and target in liver cancer. Liver cancer remains lethal, with high rates of return, spread, and drug resistance. Tumors rewire their fuel use, and this protein helps dump acid so cancer cells keep burning sugar fast. It runs high in cancers and tracks with aggressive behavior.

The review gathers evidence on how the protein fuels tumor growth, invasion, spread, immune escape, and resistance in liver cancer, and on the signaling routes it touches. High levels mark worse outlook, giving it prognostic value. Blocking it could starve tumors of their metabolism and reopen them to therapy. The authors frame the protein as a window into tumor metabolism and a target. They call for strategies built around it to improve outcomes in liver cancer.
pmc-13463151:
Yixiang Qian and Chenli Zhang review, in a 2026 article, microecological agents, meaning prebiotics, probiotics, and their combined synbiotic forms, as treatments aimed at the gut-kidney axis in kidney disease. Diseased kidneys often come with disturbed gut microbes, a build-up of uremic toxins healthy kidneys would clear, and body-wide inflammation. Feeding helpful microbes or their food may rebalance the gut, seal its barrier, lower toxin entry, and calm inflammation and oxidative stress.

Across chronic kidney disease, trials suggest these agents can slow the slide in kidney function. They may also ease companion problems such as mineral and bone trouble, heart and brain vessel events, and high uric acid. Evidence is patchy: products, doses, and timing differ so much between studies that firm verdicts blur. The authors sort the findings by disease, weigh their uneven quality, and sketch strategies for turning gut-based support into standard kidney care.
pmc-13463551:
Chi and colleagues build a star-shaped carrier that loads boron for a type of cancer care. The care, called boron neutron capture therapy, kills tumour cells with beams once boron sits inside them. Boron-rich units called carboranes hold much boron. Yet they mix poorly with water. The team tied twenty carboranes to one star-shaped chain. The result still mixed well with water. It could dissolve at high strength in water too.

The carrier did not harm head and neck cancer cells in lab tests. A tagged form lit up on PET scans in healthy mice. Blood held the tag well, and the kidneys cleared it. That path sets up later tumour tests.
pmc-13463951:
Xinru Li and colleagues tracked social life and low mood in 2026 among older Chinese adults living with several chronic diseases. Social activity and depression often move together, and the link runs stronger when illness piles up, yet few studies had followed both directions over time. The team used two survey waves covering 1,435 adults aged 60 or more in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study.

Earlier social activity predicted slightly fewer later depressive symptoms, while earlier symptoms predicted clearly less later social activity, a two-way drag. How long people expected to live shaped the first path: among hopeful elders, social activity weighed more against later low mood. Effects were modest but matter for a group prone to withdrawal, backing programs that keep older adults socially connected.
pmc-13464051:
Soares, Barbosa, and Stolf ask whether a host's immune response can change a parasite's strength in this 2026 study. The parasite, Leishmania amazonensis, causes skin disease and lives inside host cells in a form called the amastigote. The team compared parasites taken from normal mice with those from nude mice, a strain that lacks T cells, the immune cells that coordinate attacks on invaders.

Both mouse groups were infected for 13 weeks before parasites were collected from footpad lesions. Parasites from normal mice survived better and multiplied more once cultured. They also infected cells more aggressively, forming larger internal compartments, and caused stronger disease when placed into new hosts. The authors conclude that living under T-cell pressure had, paradoxically, produced hardier and more virulent parasites.
pmc-13464251:
Jeremy Wells and four co-authors report an emergency valve-in-valve rescue for a failed artificial heart valve. An eighty-two-year-old man arrived with chest pain and fluid-filled lungs after earlier bypass surgery, stents, and a catheter-placed aortic valve. Tests showed his placed valve leaking badly backward, flooding his lungs and starving his heart.

Blood pressure support kept him alive while heart scans ruled out fresh artery blockage. With shock deepening, the team threaded a new valve inside the failed one on the spot. The leak stopped at once, and pressure steadied. Emergency valve-in-valve work, the authors show, can rescue patients too unstable for open surgery.
pmc-13464751:
Abdilahi Abdi Ibrahim and three co-authors build a warning model for a rare flare-up after cryptococcal meningitis, a fungal brain infection. The flare, called PIIRS, strikes as the infection clears and the immune system overshoots. The team studied 149 patients, sixty-five who flared and eighty-four who did not.

Three admission facts stood out as independent risk marks: a prior brain shunt, high complement C3 levels, and spinal fluid pressure. Brain scans added texture data from the inflamed zones, over one hundred measured features per patient. Models joining scan texture, flare location, and the C3 blood value forecast flares with high accuracy. Small numbers mean the tool needs wider testing, the authors caution, before clinics can lean on it.
pmc-13465751:
Hays S. Alfawaz and colleagues surveyed mothers in 2026 in Riyadh on infant swaddling and hip health. Tight swaddling that blocks hip bending and spreading can raise the risk of developmental hip dysplasia, yet what mothers know about safe wrapping was poorly mapped in the region. A web survey reached 436 mothers of children aged five or under, scoring hip knowledge and wrapping practice.

Average hip knowledge scored 67%, but correct wrapping knowledge averaged only 46.9%. Higher schooling and advice from health professionals predicted better hip knowledge, as did early hip screening before six months. Family and social media advice clustered with lower scores, so the authors urge routine safe-positioning guidance in well-baby visits to close the gap between knowing about hips and wrapping them safely.
pmc-13466651:
Qiumei Gu and colleagues review eyes with wet macular disease that responded poorly to standard injections and were switched to double doses of the same drug, in a 2026 real-world study. The drugs block a vessel growth factor that drives leaking in the back of the eye. Eyes qualified only after at least three standard injections left active leaking or swelling.

Vision change and retinal anatomy after the switch form the main outcomes, with injection spacing as a secondary measure. Records captured the full treatment history, so the escalation decision reflects real clinic judgment rather than trial rules. Evidence for this doubling strategy has been thin, which is the gap the authors set out to fill.
pmc-13466751:
Linda Ficociello and colleagues compare hospital use between dialysis clinics that monitor blood volume during treatment and matched clinics that do not, in a 2026 study. The monitoring guides how fast fluid is pulled off during hemodialysis, a balancing act central to kidney failure care. Each of 165 high-use clinics was matched with a non-using clinic over the second half of 2022.

Nearly twenty-five thousand patients entered the analysis. Adjusted rates of hospital visits overall and of fluid-related visits ran lower where monitoring was routine, as did days spent in hospital. Monthly clinical measures were tracked as secondary outcomes. Real-world proof for this monitoring has been limited, which the authors aim to supply.
pmc-13466951:
Seal and colleagues ran a double-blind trial in 2026 to test whether bisphenol A, a chemical in many consumer plastics, directly lowers insulin sensitivity in healthy adults. Observational work ties BPA to diabetes, but no human experiment had tested the link. Forty sedentary young adults of normal weight followed a low-BPA diet, then received five days of oral BPA at a set body-weight dose or a placebo. Insulin sensitivity was measured by the clamp method, the field's reference test.

Urine BPA soared in the dosed group, confirming exposure. Body weight and fasting glucose did not differ between groups, yet peripheral insulin sensitivity fell in the BPA group while it rose slightly on placebo, a clear split. The authors present the result as the first experimental human evidence that short BPA exposure can blunt insulin action, a step toward diabetes risk. Call for work on longer and lower exposures.
pmc-13468851:
Marco Meloni and co-authors report in 2026 long-term results for injecting a patient's own blood cells into the legs of people with ischemic diabetic foot ulcers. These patients have no remaining option to restore blood flow. These patients face high risks of major amputation and death. The therapy uses peripheral blood mononuclear cells, gathered from the patient blood and injected along the wound-related artery in two or three cycles spaced three to six weeks apart.

The prospective single-center study enrolled patients between January 2017 and September 2023 and compared cell therapy plus standard care against standard care alone, following both groups to 24 months. No-option status was defined strictly, including failed revascularization and very low oxygen pressure at the wound. Long-term data are what this field lacks, and a two-year comparison tells surgeons and patients whether the cell injections change the amputation trajectory or merely postpone it.
pmc-13469251:
Meng and colleagues review how sensitivity to thyroid hormone, not just hormone levels, relates to bone strength, in 2026 endocrine research on osteoporosis. Thyroid hormone helps regulate bone turnover, and tissues vary in how strongly they respond to it. The review compares standard thyroid blood tests with newer sensitivity indices. These combine several measures into scores for the brain's control center and for peripheral tissues, and weighs their links to bone density at common fracture sites.

Changed sensitivity in central versus peripheral tissues pulled bone mass in distinct directions. The sensitivity indices fluctuated less than single hormone readings and captured the hormone system's balance more fully. Multiple studies tied altered sensitivity to lower density at the spine and femoral neck, the sites most prone to osteoporotic fracture. Yet results across studies were inconsistent, and Meng calls for large randomized trials before any causal claim or clinical use is justified.
pmc-13469751:
Nelke and colleagues in Germany pooled in 2026 the trial proof for new drugs in myasthenia gravis, a muscle weakness ill, to ask whether age blunts their help. The ill now crowds in old age, and its drug shelf has grown past broad immune calm to sharp, aimed forms. The team swept two banks and kept 18 trials with more than eighteen hundred patients. Each trial scored strength on a clinic scale and daily life on a patient scale.

The drugs beat dummy care on both scales in the pool. Yet one scale split by age: in trials with older crowds, the strength gain shrank by a clear step for each ten years of mean age. The drift ran strongest for the newest class, drugs that speed the clear out of attack proteins. Daily life scores showed no age drift at all. The authors urge age splits in trial reads.
pmc-13470151:
Runco and colleagues build a working definition of cachexia in children with cancer in this 2026 United States study. Cachexia means severe loss of weight and muscle along with poor appetite, and adult criteria exist, but no agreed definition covers children. Without one, doctors cannot reliably spot the condition or measure how often it occurs.

The team drafted five candidate definitions from weight and body mass measures, weight loss patterns, and diagnosis codes, then tested them in two large databases covering 2017 to 2021. Among 26,855 patients under 18, estimated rates of cachexia swung widely depending on which definition and cancer type were used. Rates looked low in most groups and were hardest to judge under age two, where numbers were small.
pmc-13470451:
Liana Lachinani tested tumour-blocker miRs in 2026 against the RNA-binding protein Musashi2 in marrow blood cancer cells. Musashi2 drives normal and bad blood growth, and its excess tracks fast disease. The team found miR-143 and miR-199 low in chronic and acute myeloid blood cancer lines, with code-based and lab links to Musashi2 signal RNA.

In K562 cells, boosting either miR cut Musashi2 signal and protein levels and reduced growth and spread, with miR-143 stronger than miR-199a. Bringing back these miRs thus curbs bad ways, though other target genes may add. Clinic blood cancer samples should test whether the pair can serve as gene treatment targets.
pmc-13471151:
Natalia E. Ostruszka and colleagues present a case from 2026. Heart imaging guided the reopening of two fully blocked coronary arteries. Their patient was a fifty three year old man with standard heart risk factors. He also had a past transient ischemic attack and an inflammatory muscle disease. He arrived from another center for stenting of chronic total occlusions in two major heart arteries.

Chronic total occlusions are among the hardest lesions to treat through a catheter. The wire must cross a segment with no open channel at all. The team used cardiac magnetic resonance imaging to plan the intervention. Coronary computed tomography angiography helped as well. The case is reported as a successful procedure. It is offered as an example of how layered imaging can steer complex reopening attempts.
pmc-13471451:
Aisha S Al-Shammari surveys in 2026 how mangrove stands along the Saudi Arabian Gulf coast differ in their setting, chemistry, and genes. Avicennia marina dominates these hypersaline shores, yet how local conditions shape the trees makeup had not been joined up. Four stands near Dammam were compared through field observation, water and soil chemistry, chemical profiling of leaf compounds, and two kinds of genetic markers.

The sites split sharply: three held salty marine type water, while one was more dilute in the water yet highly salty in its sediments. Profiling found twenty seven compounds, with a shared flavonoid rich base under site specific chemical signatures. Genetic markers showed moderate diversity and clear separation between stands. The author recommends managing the stands as distinct local units rather than one uniform resource.
pmc-13471551:
Choe and co-authors report three cats whose severe mouth inflammation sat on one side only, and who were treated by removing teeth from that side alone. Their 2026 case series revisits feline chronic gingivostomatitis, a painful immune-driven disease where full-mouth extraction is the standard answer, in cats with strictly unilateral back-of-mouth lesions.

All three cats reached complete clinical remission after one-sided partial-mouth extraction, the authors report. That outcome compares favorably with published remission rates of 51.8 to 67.3% for standard extractions, though three cases cannot prove a rate. The cats were also tested for feline viruses and Mycoplasma as part of the workup. The team urges lesion-directed surgery for carefully chosen cases, with larger prospective studies to set selection rules.
pmc-13471651:
Adrizain and co-authors tracked how quickly drug-resistant bacteria settle in high-risk newborns in an Indonesian referral hospital, where sepsis is the leading cause of neonatal death. Their 2026 prospective study followed 46 neonates between May and December 2025 with repeated swabs to map when resistant germs arrive.

Carriage of multidrug-resistant germs was the norm: 32 babies, or 69.6% of those in hospital at least 48 hours, carried them. Babies sent in from other hospitals faced the highest risk, with 93.3% carrying them and a relative risk of 1.61 versus babies born in-house. Of 110 bacterial samples, 72.7% were drug-resistant, led by Klebsiella pneumoniae and E. coli, and 38.1% of blood tests in suspected infections came back positive.
pmc-13472851:
Satyan Lakshminrusimha, Clara H Song, and Robin H. Steinhorn call in 2026 for an identity reset in neonatology, the specialty caring for critically ill newborns. The field faces a squeeze. Units for babies drive major revenue for hospitals and pediatrics departments. Yet the individual specialist carries rising patient acuity, heavy documentation, and long hours. A widening pay gap against adult counterparts adds to the strain. The authors name this the neonatology paradox.

Current productivity yardsticks, they argue, misread the work and punish the workforce sustaining it. Their proposals include new staffing models that trim hours and lower productivity expectations. The models also protect life outside work. Should those fixes fail, the essay floats a bolder step: an independent department of neonatal critical care. The piece is part diagnosis of a workforce crisis, part negotiation brief.
pmc-13473251:
Sehnaz Yuksel and seven colleagues published this 2026 study testing simple blood-based scores against a liver scan in people with psoriasis, a skin disease linked with fatty liver disease. The scan method, vibration-controlled transient elastography, measures liver stiffness and fat directly. The authors asked whether cheap formula scores, worked out from routine blood tests and body measures, could spot significant liver scarring and fat just as well.

The team enrolled 113 patients with psoriasis and compared several fibrosis and steatosis scores with the scan results. After scanning, 67 percent of patients had fatty liver disease. The BARD score performed best for significant scarring overall, though its accuracy was modest. In the fatty liver subgroup, the SAFE score did best and ruled out scarring with a negative predictive value of 95 percent. For liver fat itself, the fatty liver index was strongest. Overall, the authors found the scores limited in this group.
pmc-13473751:
Xu and a team in China tried in 2026 a last ditch gut cure for grave ward patients. Their gut germs had beaten all drugs. The cure was a wash of good germs from donor stool. The germ wash, called WMT, is a cleaned form of stool transplant. Their ten patients were all in deep ill health. None had the one gut germ this care is most known for. The team gave 29 washes in all and scored cures and harms.

Half the patients were cured by the wash, and two more got partly well. Three showed no gain in week one. Belly pain and bloat scores fell by a clear mark. Stool tests cleared the germ in three of four patients who had them. Just one brief fever was tied to the wash, and no grave harm. The authors call the way workable.
pmc-13474651:
Song and co-authors tested whether lysolecithin, an emulsifier that helps animals absorb dietary fat, can rescue piglets fed cheaper, nutrient-thinned rations. Their 2026 trial assigned 96 nursery piglets of about 17 kilograms to a normal diet, a low-nutrient diet cut by 2% in energy and 7% in protein. The third group got the lean diet plus 400 milligrams of lysolecithin per kilogram for 28 days.

The supplemented piglets closed the gap: daily gain improved significantly in the first two weeks at p 0.040 in the group comparison, feed efficiency improved at p 0.032 across the trial, and body weight reached levels comparable to the normal-diet group. Fat and energy digestibility rose sharply, blood urea nitrogen and cholesterol fell, and antioxidant enzyme activity climbed in blood and liver, consistent with better nutrient use rather than more eating.
pmc-13474851:
Tae-hun Lee and colleagues report in 2026 a rare joint disease found during redo knee replacement in a 71-year-old man. His first artificial knee had served well for about twenty years before pain and swelling began. Joint fluid draws confirmed blood in the joint three times. Scans blamed loose parts and bone loss beside the implant.

During surgery, surgeons found widespread yellow-brown frond-like growth of the joint lining. Full removal of the lining plus a new implant followed. Lab study named the growth as diffuse pigmented villonodular synovitis, a rare lining overgrowth. Blood-filled swelling after a knee implant deserves this cause on the list.
pmc-13474951:
Walshe and a large team report a scandium-based porous material in this 2026 chemistry study. The material belongs to the metal-organic frameworks, sponge-like crystals built from metal clusters and organic linkers, here fumarate. Scandium versions normally form a different framework type. The team coaxed one into the MIL-53 layout by soaking the usual material in water or solvent mixtures. It was a rare crystal-to-crystal conversion.

Two shapes of the new framework formed depending on the solvent, and unlike their rigid relatives both could breathe, flexing their pores open or shut. Heating the crystals in methanol swapped 40 to 50 percent of their bridging hydroxide groups for bulkier methoxide groups. That change held the pores slightly open, allowing strong nitrogen uptake at low pressure where the original closed form adsorbed almost nothing.
pmc-13478051:
Xue Cai and coauthors published a 2026 systematic review comparing two PET scan tracers in IgG4-related disease, a rare condition where inflammation and scarring attack many organs. One tracer, FDG, lights up active inflammation through sugar use. The newer FAPI tracer targets activated fibroblasts, the cells that lay down scar tissue.

Only three direct comparison studies covering 90 patients met the quality bar for pooling. FAPI found more total lesions, 136 against 78, and gave stronger contrast in organs like the pancreas and salivary glands. FDG performed better in lymph nodes, where inflammation dominates. Tissue checks matched FAPI with scarring and FDG with inflammation, a flip-flop pattern the authors say supports using both scans together. A tracer uptake ratio also predicted relapse risk.
pmc-13478251:
Espinoza-Gutarra and colleagues mined in 2026 a United States health record bank for real world results of targeted pills in acute myeloid leukemia, a fast blood cancer. The pills block one of three flawed gene switches, FLT3, IDH1, or IDH2. Trial results had looked bright, but clinic results were scarce. Their set held 482 adults treated from 2015 to 2023, some with the pill as first care and some after prior care failed.

Time on the pill ran near three and a half months in both groups. Mid survival sat near one year in both, with no clear edge for early use. Adding a second drug class did not lift scores. Younger age, prior stem cell graft, private cover, and a kind risk class each tracked with longer life. The authors call the real world yield poor across the board, and urge fresh plans for this group.
pmc-13479551:
Soo-jin Choi published a 2026 ecological analysis, as sole author, of walking and quality of life across 229 districts in South Korea. Individual studies link walking with better quality of life, but district-level patterns can mislead when age structure differs. Public aggregate data supplied district rates of walking, stronger exercise, depressive symptoms, stress, and a standard quality of life index.

Walking participation correlated positively with district quality of life in simple models. After adjusting for how old each district's population was, that link faded to non-significance, while the models explained far more variation. Stronger exercise showed its own pattern in the adjusted results. The author cautions city policymakers that raw district comparisons mostly reflect demographics, and walking promotion should be judged with age structure in view.
pmc-13479951:
Miriam Umbria and coauthors published a 2026 twelve-year population study of Alzheimer's drug treatment in Catalonia, Spain. A mandatory regional registry tracks every prescription of the main symptom-relief drugs, letting officials check both guideline compliance and costs. Records covered more than 158,000 patients treated from 2012 to 2024.

The treated population grew by about a quarter across the period, reaching nearly 57,000 people in 2024. About eighty-two percent of treatments began at the recommended moderate disease stages, while under nine percent began at mild stages. The pandemic caused a temporary dip in treatment starts, visible in the yearly counts. The authors argue the registry model keeps prescribing appropriate and spending sustainable even as the population ages.
pmc-13480051:
Moutombi-Ditombi and colleagues reviewed records of children hospitalized with malaria in Libreville, Gabon, in 2026 to find which severe cases will need intensive care. Of 3,009 children admitted between January 2021 and July 2022 with confirmed falciparum malaria, 480, or 15.9 percent, met World Health Organization criteria for severe disease. The team studied those 480 children, whose median age was six years, for signs predicting transfer to intensive care.

Deaths were rare at 0.7 percent, but 41 children, or 8.5 percent of the severe group, needed intensive care transfer during their stay. Brain signs dominated the severe picture, with prostration, extreme weakness, in 49.2 percent of children and any neurological feature in 64.2 percent overall. Impaired consciousness raised transfer odds about 15-fold and coma about 53-fold in adjusted models, while stacking more than three severity criteria raised odds about 11-fold.
pmc-13480251:
Yang and Lin map in 2026 the rise of PROTAC drugs in breast cancer from two angles at once, counting the research literature and auditing the clinical trials. PROTACs are molecules that tag a harmful protein for destruction by the cell's own disposal machinery, a route around the drug resistance that defeats ordinary hormone therapy. Their bibliometric arm covered 350 publications, and their trial arm covered 30 registered studies.

Publication output has climbed steeply since 2016, with China and the United States in front, and the estrogen receptor dominates as the target in both labs and clinics. The leading drug, the estrogen receptor degrader ARV-471, has reached phase III trials after doubling progression-free survival versus the standard drug fulvestrant in mutated advanced disease. Median time without worsening was 5.0 months against 2.1 months on fulvestrant, with fatigue and nausea common but manageable, though work outside the hormone-sensitive subtype remains thin.
pmc-13481751:
Noriyuki Watanabe and co-authors present a 2026 gene therapy test in mice bred to mimic ALS, the disease that wastes motor nerves. The team instead injected a virus carrying the caveolin-1 gene into the brain fluid spaces, a simpler route with wider reach.

The gene spread through movement cortex and spinal cord and raised its protein widely. Treated male mice ran better on wheels and showed stronger nerve-to-muscle signals. Motor nerve cells in the neck and lower back wasted less, and the breathing muscle kept more of its nerve contacts. The route still needs safety proof, yet broad reach from one injection marks real progress.
pmc-13481951:
Nong and co-authors pooled the evidence in 2026 on two operations for shoulders that keep dislocating forward, a comparison surgeons argue about when socket bone loss is moderate. One option repairs the torn rim and tucks tendon into the dent behind it, called Bankart repair with remplissage. The repair looked better on pain and function early, the Latarjet better later, a pattern the authors say should shape how surgeons counsel active patients.
pmc-13482551:
Chavda and a large breeding team grade 24 new citrus hybrids in 2026 for nutrition, crossing pummelo with sweet orange and tangerine to create 16 orangelos and 8 tangelos alongside their parents. pmc-13482851:

pmc-13483051:

pmc-13483151:

pmc-13483551:

pmc-13483951:
Teferi and colleagues asked whether sorghum breeders in dry parts of Ethiopia can select winning varieties at one research station instead of testing in every target district. pmc-13485851:
Ren and colleagues wrote a practical guide to target trial emulation, a method for making health database studies mimic the randomized trials they cannot replace. pmc-13486051:

pmc-13486451:

One candidate, NPACT00730, gripped the enzyme's key residues most strongly across methods. Its chalcone scaffold carries known anticancer pedigree across many cell lines. Computer evidence cannot prove a drug, yet a prioritized natural candidate with a clean predicted profile earns laboratory follow-up.
pmc-13486651:

Their 2026 study grouped patients by stroke type and location, measured three cardiac markers twice in the first day, and tracked deaths and major events.

Bleeding strokes showed the highest marker levels, with over half those patients showing raised troponin, a heart injury protein. Among clot strokes, damage involving the insula, a deep brain region tied to heart control, produced the highest readings of all. pmc-13486751:
Jeong-Ah Yoon, Young Ho Seo, and Myoung-Dong Kim report a food science study, published in 2026, on fermenting bread dough with two yeasts instead of one. Alongside standard baker's yeast, they added Wickerhamomyces anomalus strains taken from Korean nuruk, a traditional fermentation starter known for producing fruity aroma compounds.

One strain matched the standard yeast for gas production while giving the highest ethyl acetate levels. The resulting bread matched ordinary bread in volume and texture, though it lost slightly more weight during baking.
pmc-13486851:
Benjamins and colleagues mapped in 2026 non-fatal firearm violence across United States cities using public police dashboards. The team searched for cities with open dashboards reporting police-recorded non-fatal firearm violence, then compared counts, rates, and trends from 2020 to 2025.

pmc-13488151:

Entry requires an objective twenty-four-hour probe study that links acidity and reflux events with symptoms, which narrows the group to babies with acid-driven disease.

pmc-13488251:

Between a fifth and a quarter of participants met the screening cutoff for presumptive post-traumatic stress disorder, depending on the threshold used in the reported scoring. Stress scores tracked with depression, childhood trauma, and distress during attacks. Early symptom onset and emergency visits for attacks also linked with the diagnosis. The authors propose a two-way relationship.
pmc-13490351:
Ziqing Kong and colleagues build a survival prediction chart for young women with early breast cancer lacking the HER2 growth marker in a 2026 modeling study. Young breast cancer tends to behave aggressively, yet tailored tools for this subgroup were lacking. A United States registry supplied 7,863 patients diagnosed from 2010 to 2015 for model building and internal checks, while a Chinese military hospital cohort served as the outside test.

Six factors shaped the final chart, covering tumor grade, hormone receptor status, tissue type, tumor size stage, node stage, and surgery. Accuracy was fair in training and internal sets and somewhat lower in the outside cohort, with wide uncertainty there in the reported figures. Risk groups split cleanly on survival in all sets.
pmc-13491351:
Barry F. Uretsky and colleagues organize care for myocardial bridging by patient presentation in a 2026 review. In this condition, a heart artery, usually the front descending branch, tunnels through heart muscle and gets squeezed with each beat. Long dismissed as harmless, bridging is now tied in some patients to chest pain, heart attack, and rare sudden death. Most cases surface by chance on scans in people without symptoms. Mechanisms of blood starvation, the worth of each test for proving it, and treatment ladders matched to symptom patterns are laid out in sequence. Evidence remains incomplete, so the authors call their pathway a modest guide and stress tailoring to the individual to avoid overtreatment.
pmc-13491451:

Kidney disease weakens the baroreflex, the reflex that steadies blood pressure from beat to beat. The group tested whether one session of isometric handgrip exercise, squeezing against resistance without moving the joint, could sharpen that reflex.

Baroreflex sensitivity rose for at least twenty minutes after handgrip and beat sham at the early checks. Heart rate fell during recovery, and systolic pressure dropped modestly by thirty minutes. pmc-13491851:

Just fourteen percent linked the model's core elements into a full causal chain, even though two thirds described engaging community partners. pmc-13492551:

pmc-13493851:

pmc-13495151:

pmc-13495251:

The model scored high at spotting the condition in balanced test data. A far simpler trend-based model scored nearly as high, which shows the synthetic task mostly rewards spotting steady drift. pmc-13495551:

pmc-13499651:

pmc-13500051:

pmc-13500351:

Support mostly reused cigarette methods, and few staff had product-specific training. The top barriers were felt lack of demand, training, and knowledge, while open answers blamed funding rules that exclude these products. pmc-13500551:
Md. pmc-13500851:

pmc-13501651:

pmc-13501951:

pmc-13502851:

pmc-13503751:

pmc-13504051:

pmc-13507251:

pmc-13507351:

pmc-13508451:

pmc-13508551:

pmc-13509151:

pmc-13510451:

pmc-13512351:

Radical-scavenging power ran high, and bacterial blocking rose with nanozyme dose in the tests reported. The authors aim the dressing at wounds stalled by oxidative stress.
pmc-13513151:
Khosla and colleagues gave in 2026 a historical review of biomarkers, measurable blood signals, for cardiovascular stress. Many stress types, from oxidation and infection to emotional strain, raise heart disease risk through a self-amplifying chain of fat oxidation that makes toxic products. Blood tests can track those toxins and the body's stress responses, and they forecast risk well for whole populations.

Khosla explains why the same panels forecast poorly for single patients. The markers overlap, so they add less fresh signal than they seem to. Their ranking in causing disease is unclear, and other illnesses or acute reactions distort readings. The review walks through the landmark studies behind today's risk prediction practice. Its aim is to guide new combined biomarkers that reflect the many stress types driving risk, rather than one path alone.
pmc-13514951:
Popejoy and colleagues published a 2026 study on what gets doctors to order gene tests for antidepressants. Gene tests can flag patients likely to fare poorly on certain antidepressants. pmc-13515151:

Their pipeline flagged fifty-six key sites. Grouping the enzymes by those sites alone produced three clusters that matched cell experiments better than the family tree did. One outlier virus, EV-A89, stood apart in both the new grouping and the lab, with a shifted protein size tied to three flagged changes.
pmc-13518251:

Single long-range neurons often sit positioned to coordinate several body parts plus internal organs at once.
pmc-13518851:
Shahryar Kashi and Ebrahim Najafi Kani examine in 2026 how solid activator choice shapes a one-part geopolymer mortar made from slag and mullite. Calcium hydroxide and sodium sulfate mixes stayed porous and weak. Mullite additions densified the network further. Pore share, the authors argue, reliably signals how long the mortar lasts.
pmc-13518951:

Patients ranged from no or mild apnea to severe apnea, judged by breathing pauses per hour.

At the start, severe apnea patients showed clearly fewer spindles than the milder groups. pmc-13519851:

pmc-13520151:
Marzia Cettina Severino, Costanza Galli, and Sabina De Rosis build a framework in 2026 for recording what family caregivers go through along palliative care pathways. pmc-13520351:

Much of the cited evidence comes from animal and observational work, so firm clinical advice remains out of reach.

Proposed routes involve defence against oxidative damage, hormone building blocks and membrane flexibility in sperm. Human trial results vary, which the authors stress throughout. pmc-13522051:

pmc-13522451:
Md Mamunur Rashid leads a 2026 breeding study from Bangladesh that aims to combine strong aroma, higher yield, and resistance to rice blast in new hybrid rice lines. Three lines stood out for pairing the best resistance with the highest yield potential, and several others outyielded their parents with moderate resistance. One line gave the strongest aroma score. The authors propose the best lines as parents for further multi-location testing toward a resistant, high-yielding aromatic variety.
pmc-13523151:
Si Ling Soh and co-authors report an exceptionally rare fatty heart tumor in a teenager in a 2026 case report. A thirteen-year-old boy referred for a heart murmur had several masses inside the heart affecting the aortic valve, the wall between the ventricles, and the back wall of the left ventricle. The valve leaked severely and was moderately narrowed.

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a large lobulated mass growing from one aortic leaflet into the outflow path. Surgery removed the masses and replaced the valve with a mechanical one. Tissue examination confirmed a spindle cell lipoma, a benign fatty tumor usually found under the skin. Recovery was smooth with no remaining mass on follow-up scans. A literature review found only two prior adult cases.
pmc-13523351:
Kailun Xu and colleagues develop a laddered training model for breast surgery residents in a 2026 study at a university hospital in China. Twenty residents in their second or third training year were randomly split between stepwise training and conventional training over six months. The stepwise program climbed three levels, from basic biopsy skills through minor procedures to advanced operations, within a competency-based framework.

Residents in the stepwise group matched biopsy tissue results with final pathology far more often and succeeded more often at placing venous access ports. Their supervised breast-conserving operations were also much faster, taking about two hours versus three in the control group. The authors present the laddered model as a scalable, structured path for building surgical competence step by step.
pmc-13524551:
Ziv Harel and colleagues set out a 2026 population-based cohort study from Ontario on blood thinner use for atrial fibrillation in elderly long-term care residents who also have chronic kidney disease. Eligible residents were aged 66 or older, lived in long-term care, had kidney disease by filtration rate or dialysis, and had a validated atrial fibrillation diagnosis. New anticoagulant prescriptions after diagnosis formed the exposure. Outcomes were ischemic stroke, major bleeding, death soon after a bleed, and overall death, analyzed with adjusted time-varying hazard models. Ethics review was waived under Ontario privacy law for this authorized data use.
pmc-13526051:
Robert Tamburri and colleagues present a 2026 benchmarking survey update on how pharmaceutical medical information teams create content and measure performance. These teams answer unsolicited questions from clinicians with evidence-based documents. Practice had shifted since the previous survey in 2018, prompting a fresh check through an industry benchmarking group.

Standard response documents remain mostly traditional written pieces, though question-and-answer formats, infographics, and slides are emerging, and most development is centralized. Fewer companies now set target timelines than in 2018. Artificial intelligence use is early, with three companies active and eighteen exploring, and omnichannel delivery appears at over half of companies.
pmc-13527151:
Jundu Zhang and colleagues introduce, in a 2026 computer vision study, a leaner transformer method for human pose estimation, the task of locating body joints in images. Their method, SPTPose, trims that cost through self-distillation, where a model teaches itself, and token pruning, which discards unneeded image patches.

That balance matters for real-time or mobile deployment, where full transformers are impractical. Source code is published openly. The authors position the design as evidence that careful compression can keep transformer quality while shedding most of its computational weight.
pmc-13527951:
Alexandria Nivelle Mekanna, Kingsley Arua Kalu, and Li Li present a 2026 cross-sectional study of food security in Western Sydney after COVID-19 lockdowns ended. Group discussions blamed rising prices, fear of contamination while shopping, and changed shopping habits for lingering strain months later. The authors call for policies that respond during crises and support recovery afterward, with attention to women.
pmc-13528051:

The authors say the marks are new leads on how early body makeup is set.
pmc-13529051:

Rim contamination rates were nearly identical, around three percent in each group. The double soak did cut germs on the eye surface sharply. pmc-13529151:

pmc-13530251:

pmc-13530651:

Elementary pitchers held their strength through seventy pitches. High schoolers began fading near sixty pitches and lost roughly fifteen percent by one hundred. Faster balls with more spin correlated with greater decline.
pmc-13531751:

The picture gives planners a dynamic map of where pushing helps, where pushback builds, and where small moves may unlock larger change.
pmc-13533051:

pmc-13533851:

A link between high levels and survival was rarely seen across studies. High levels did link to lymph node spread in a share of studies, and one tongue cancer study tied them to worse survival. Readers conclude the protein is not a general marker, though tongue cancer needs more checks.
pmc-13534151:

Foreign patients were younger with shorter disease duration, and yearly screening matched European patients in most areas. Gaps appeared in urine and eye checks, and treatment intensity lagged for some origin groups. Overall care scores were lowest for West African patients in this dataset.
pmc-13534451:

pmc-13536251:

pmc-13536651:

pmc-13536851:

pmc-13538551:

pmc-13540851:

pmc-13540951:

Resistance ran highest against chloramphenicol and cefoxitin. It ran lowest against gentamicin and ciprofloxacin. Five isolates resisted several drug classes at once. pmc-13542251:

pmc-13543351:

pmc-13543451:

pmc-13543551:

pmc-13546551:

pmc-13548551:

pmc-13548651:

pmc-13549951:

pmc-13550451:

Readers get a methods-and-clinic guide to safer cancer drug orders.
pmc-13551751:

pmc-13551851:

pmc-13554051:

pmc-13554151:
Linan Sun leads a seven-author team grading how well counties develop in Henan, a big farming province of China, in a 2026 study. Most past work skipped the county level or gave every place the same scoring weights. Their system uses nineteen measures for 102 counties across 2010 to 2021. A new weighting method lets each county's own pattern set its weights, and links between counties count as well.

Quality rose broadly over the decade, yet strong counties clustered ever tighter near big cities. Weaker counties sat mostly at the province's edges. What drove scores differed sharply by place, from farm and factory roots to land shape. Single factors explained less than pairs acting together. The authors propose tailored paths for each county type.
pmc-13554751:
Kaida Ren leads a large Chinese team setting out a trial of clip-based repair for a leaking tricuspid heart valve in a 2026 protocol. Severe leakage burdens the heart, and drugs ease symptoms without fixing the valve, while open surgery carries high risk. The trial will enrol 236 patients across thirty-five centres. Half receive a catheter clip device, and half receive drug care alone.

Patients must stay symptomatic despite at least a month of drug care and face middling or higher surgical risk. Follow-up runs to five years, with checks at one month, six months, and yearly. The main yardstick at one year blends deaths, valve procedures, hospital stays for heart failure, and health status scores. Results should guide future care for severe leakage.
pmc-13555951:
Faizal Maulana leads a nine-author team charting family ties and chemistry across ten umbrella-plant species from Java and Sumatra in a 2026 study. The genus Heptapleurum holds medicinal promise, yet its family tree stays tangled. The team assembled ten fresh chloroplast genomes plus ribosomal DNA sequences. Chemical profiling named 152 compounds, mostly phenolics and terpenoids.

Two species branched away from the main family group in both gene and chemical trees. Four other species shared nearly identical genomes yet brewed clearly distinct chemistries. Overall, chemical family trees did not match genetic ones. The authors argue genes must rule naming decisions, while chemistry maps useful diversity for conservation and drug hunting in this Sundaland group.
pmc-13558051:
Luigia Trabace and eleven colleagues ran a pilot trial in 2026 of a nutraceutical blend called GeNeurofil in people with mild cognitive impairment. This early stage of decline raises dementia risk and still lacks approved treatments. Earlier animal work suggested the blend protects neurons against amyloid toxicity. The team therefore tested it in 54 patients with mild to moderate impairment. The trial ran six months with a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled design.

Patients kept their usual medicines and took the blend or an identical placebo three times a day. After six months, the treated group improved on global dementia rating, mental state testing, and a depression scale relative to placebo. Blood levels of two damage markers, neurofilament light and phosphorylated tau, also fell. The authors present the results as pilot evidence that justifies a larger, longer trial.
pmc-13558651:
Hao Liu and four colleagues mined the UK Biobank in 2026 for links between psychological distress and disorders of the urinary and genital systems. Earlier work treated distress as one blob and rarely followed people forward in time. With half a million participants, the team scored six validated distress instruments covering mood, anxiety, neuroticism, and bodily symptoms, then related them to eight non-infectious urogenital conditions, both at enrolment and prospectively.

Higher scores on every scale came with more urogenital disease. Bodily symptom scores showed the strongest links, roughly raising the hazard of urgency incontinence, bladder pain syndrome, and pelvic pain by about half. Age, sex, and menopause status modified several associations, with bladder conditions tying closer to distress in women and pelvic floor dysfunction in men. Chronic prostate inflammation showed little prospective link. Mental health screening, the authors suggest, belongs in urology clinics.
pmc-13563951:
Natsumi Toyoda and colleagues report, in a 2026 case study, a 59-year-old Japanese man whose anaplastic meningioma, a high-grade tumor of the membranes around the brain, spread widely outside the skull. He first had numbness on the right side of his face and double vision, and scans showed a mass reaching toward the sinuses and the eye canal.

Microscope work found two cell patterns side by side, one resembling typical meningioma and one poorly formed with sarcoma-like features. Spread through that second element reached twelve organs outside the skull, including lung, bone, and liver, confirmed at autopsy. Such extensive spread is rare, and the report helps pathologists recognize the aggressive form.
pmc-13571351:
Yurie Yoshikado and co-authors report a single difficult heart case from 2026: severe mitral regurgitation, a badly leaking mitral valve, in a patient who could not safely receive heparin. The 59-year-old man developed cardiogenic shock and needed an intra-aortic balloon pump, a device that helps the heart pump blood.

While awaiting surgery, his platelet count fell sharply and antibody testing supported suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, a dangerous immune reaction to heparin. Because bypass surgery requires full heparin treatment, the team instead performed catheter-based edge-to-edge valve repair while giving argatroban, an alternative blood thinner. Two implants reduced the leak from severe to trivial, with no clotting or bleeding problems. The patient recovered quickly, the pump was removed at once, and he was taken off the ventilator early.
pmc-13572351:
Haiyan Dong and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, small engineered binding proteins aimed at E6. This viral protein destroys the guardian protein p53 in cervical cancers driven by human papillomavirus type 18. Candidates were fished from a phage display library and fitted with a tag that carries them inside cells.

The best candidate bound E6 specifically in cancer cells, gathered quickly in mouse tumors, and stayed there for hours. Inside cells it stabilized p53 and switched on death-promoting and braking genes. Pairing it with a sibling molecule against the partner viral protein E7 killed more cancer cells than either alone. The pair strategy offers a targeted route against HPV-driven cervical cancer.
pmc-13572451:
Noemí Tomsen, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 trial of a cooling-flavoured drink that aids swallowing after stroke. Many stroke survivors swallow poorly, which raises the risk of food or fluid entering the airway. The drink holds compounds that trigger a cold sensor in the mouth and throat, which may sharpen the swallow reflex.

Fifty patients with chronic swallowing trouble took part in a crossover trial, so each person tried both the active drink and a plain control in random order. Swallow tests and counts of spontaneous swallows gauged the effect. The active drink raised spontaneous swallow rate by 51.6 percent and cut unsafe swallows by 22 percent. Saliva levels of substance P, a signal tied to swallowing, rose by 15 percent. The plain drink changed none of these measures.
pmc-13572551:
Nuha Desi Anggraeni, with two colleagues, reports on a 2026 study of see-through solar panels on the tropical coast of Indonesia. Panels that pass some light can serve as windows or shades, but heat and damp air test their output. The team asked which weather factors drive their performance and how steady it stays over years.

Ten years of daily weather data, from 2012 to 2022, fed regression models of the performance ratio and energy yield. Three model shapes were compared, from a full set of weather inputs down to a fixed benchmark. Sunlight on the tilted panel and air temperature drove most of the change in output. A lean model with just those two inputs matched the full model closely. Performance ratio estimates sat between 0.78 and 0.80, in line with past tropical values.
pmc-13573451:
Rana A Alamoudi and colleagues compared cleft lip and palate patterns across seven Middle Eastern and Asian countries at two income levels, publishing the cross-sectional study in 2026. Clefts rank among the most common birth anomalies, yet how type and severity vary with national income was unclear. The team classified 836 patients at major cleft referral centres in four high-income and three lower-middle-income countries.

Lower-middle-income countries showed more milder unilateral incomplete lip clefts, while high-income countries presented more severe bilateral complete lip-and-palate cases, and associated anomalies clustered with unilateral complete lip clefts. Income level significantly shifted the odds of palate involvement and of severe versus mild cases. The authors call for joint research on genes, environment, and care access to explain the pattern and guide prevention.
pmc-13574151:
Weitong Su and a large team report a 2026 study of a fat that weakens immune guard cells inside belly fat during obesity. Those guard cells, regulatory T cells, keep metabolism calm in lean tissue. In obesity they falter, and the team asked which food fat flips the switch.

Palmitic acid, a saturated fat, but not its cousin oleic acid, switched on a factor called Crebzf in the guard cells of obese mice. Animals lacking that factor in these cells resisted diet-driven obesity and inflammation, since their guard cells suppressed immune attack better. Moving such cells into mice with no lymphocytes calmed disease more than normal cells did. The factor teams with a partner to blunt Foxp3, the master guard gene. In human fat, the factor ran high where Foxp3 ran low.
pmc-13587551:
Ningning Xia and colleagues map how symptoms cluster in the first week after pancreatic cancer surgery. The operation is among the hardest in cancer care, and patients wake to a crowd of complaints at once. Their 2026 study asked 213 patients on day seven to rate 22 symptoms on a standard inventory. The team then drew a network showing which symptoms travel together and which sit at the web's center.

Seventeen symptoms touched more than three in ten patients. Lost appetite, broken sleep, distress, pain, and fatigue were the most common, and lost appetite, vomiting, and fatigue cut deepest. In the network, vomiting sat at the very center, with distress and sweating close behind, while swelling, fatigue, and irritability bridged between clusters. The authors suggest that easing a central symptom like vomiting might calm several neighbors at once.
pmc-13590251:
Shunsuke Shiota and four colleagues tackle a planning problem for studies that test how well a test finds disease. Such studies must fix their size in advance: too few people gives shaky results, while too many wastes money and burdens patients. Older methods treat key rates, such as how often a test catches disease, as fixed known values. Their method instead uses Bayesian tools, which fold prior belief and doubt into the plan.

Two kinds of prior are used, one for the study design and one for the final read of results. The team works out how often a future study of each size would meet a preset success mark. In their tests, less doubt in the design priors shrank the size needed. A more hopeful read prior did the same, which planners should note with care.
pmc-13593651:
Ana Freifrau von Rotenhan and colleagues tested whether a therapy dog in the dental chair can calm anxious children, measuring heart rate before, during, and after treatment. Sixty children aged five to twelve took part in their 2026 study, half treated with a dog present and half receiving standard care.

Heart rate in the dog group fell by about five beats per minute across the visit. It rose slightly in the control group. The gap between groups was clearest after treatment ended. Blood oxygen stayed steady throughout. Parents often said they felt calmer themselves and saw their children cooperate better with the dog nearby. The authors are careful about one gap: anxiety questionnaires were collected only in the dog group, so claims about felt anxiety rest on weaker ground than the heart rate findings.
pmc-13596751:
Marina Abdelshahid leads an eleven-author study of blood-based inflammation scores in 130 adults who had knee ligament reconstruction, asking whether metabolic syndrome leaves a measurable immune signature after surgery. Six composite indices were computed from routine blood counts taken at least ninety days after the operation, and patients were grouped by whether they met the syndrome's criteria.

Overall, the inflammation indices did not separate the metabolic syndrome group from the rest. The picture changed by sex: women with the syndrome ran significantly higher on four indices than men with it. Higher body mass and blood sugar tracked with one index, while low protective cholesterol tracked with several. Postoperative complications also came with elevated scores. The authors suggest that sex and individual metabolic traits shape post-surgical inflammation more than the syndrome label alone.
pmc-13600051:
Jaka Prevodnik and S. Elizabeth Rácz-Brunner asked if short sleep lifts body-level crossness in college youth. Thirty-four undergrads were split by sleep versus CDC sleep rules and did three thought tasks with cross prompts while heart rate was logged. Folks slept a mean of 7.70 hours, more than the team had guessed.

Heart rate jumped most in a no-win puzzle task, which hints task length, blocked prize, and dashed hopes can stir crossness when sleep is short. The work gives a test model for next work on crossness and near moods, and it splits crossness, a raw nerve to prompts, from rage and fights.
pmc-13603051:
Leticia S. Arroteia and colleagues followed 22 periodontally healthy patients for two years after aesthetic crown lengthening for a gummy smile. Excess gum tissue can make a smile look disharmonious and cause physical and psychological discomfort. Self-esteem and quality of life were measured before surgery, at thirty days, and at two years, alongside crown dimensions and recurrence.

Both measures improved significantly by thirty days, and gains grew further by two years: self-esteem rose from a median of 11 to 14, while oral-health impact scores fell from 19 to 6. Crown length established at thirty days remained stable at two years, with no return of the gummy smile. The procedure offers lasting psychosocial as well as aesthetic benefit, the authors conclude.
pmc-13607251:
Mehmet Melih Yılmaz leads an eleven-author team testing two vitamin supplements as protectors for frozen ram semen. Freezing damages ram sperm badly, and oxidative stress is a chief culprit. Pooled semen was split into four extender groups: plain control, nicotinic acid alone, and two nicotinic-folic acid combinations. After thawing, the team measured motility, membrane and DNA integrity, oxidative markers, and two genes' activity and methylation.

The middle combination, 10 millimolar nicotinic acid with 50 nanomolar folic acid, gave the highest motility numerically at 53.34 percent against the control's 43.44 percent, though that gap missed significance. Its clear wins were the lowest acrosome damage, 36.50 percent against 48.00 percent in controls, and better mitochondrial membrane potential. That combination also changed OGG1 gene expression alongside matching DNA methylation shifts. The authors suggest these supplements, especially paired, improve post-thaw ram semen quality.
pmc-13615051:
Marie Line Chedid and colleagues review in 2026 the non-surgical causes of nasal necrosis. This is the death of skin or soft tissue on the nose. They gather case reports and case series from three databases up to December 2025. Causes span severe infection, immune attacks on small blood vessels, drug harm, cancer, and pressure from medical devices. Surgery is often the first thought, yet some patients are treated without it and guidance for them is thin.

Thirty-nine publications met the team's rules. They pulled out each case's cause, signs, tests, treatment, and outcome, and rated the quality of each report with a standard tool. The result is a map of how this rare, alarming problem shows up when an operation is not the driver, giving clinicians a clearer path for diagnosis and drug-based care.
pmc-13616251:
Jinjin Tong and colleagues build a smart nanoparticle that delivers silymarin, a milk thistle extract that protects the liver, to patients recovering from liver surgery. Plain silymarin absorbs poorly. Their particles are built from a modified chitosan shell and measure 250 to 300 nanometres. They release cargo faster in acid and amid reactive oxygen. Those are exactly the conditions at a healing wound site.

Against standard tests the particles beat free silymarin at mopping up harmful radicals, scoring 92.31 percent on one measure, and they mildly curbed two common bacteria. Blood and cell tests showed good safety. Given by mouth to dogs after liver surgery, the particles shifted gut microbes and their chemical output in directions tied to liver health, underlining the gut-liver partnership in recovery.
pmc-13616751:
Faruk Gazi Ceranoğlu, Mehmet Tuğrul Yılmaz, Duygu Akın Saygın, and Cengiz Kadıyoran report 2026 reference values for six angles of the heel bone. Their group held 540 healthy adults aged 20 to 65. They also test how well those angles guess a person's sex. The heel bone carries walking and balance and is often rebuilt after fractures, so normal angle ranges guide surgery. Measurements came from X-rays of both feet.

Some angles differed between right and left sides, and the compression angle differed between men and women. The standard accuracy test for sex prediction gave a weak separation of the sexes. The verdict follows from that result. These angles make useful clinical references for this population, but poor tools for sexing a skeleton. Local reference data matter, since angles measured elsewhere may not fit Turkish patients.
pmc-13617151:
Rohan A. Phadke and seven colleagues compare the long-term value of two operations for lumbar spinal stenosis, the narrowing of the spinal canal that is the most common reason older adults have spine surgery. One option is minimally invasive tubular decompression through a small tube; the other is traditional open laminectomy. Their computer model followed a simulated group of ten thousand sixty-five-year-olds for ten years from a United States payer viewpoint.

In the base case the minimally invasive route cost over four thousand dollars less per patient while giving slightly more quality-adjusted life years, a rare win on both cost and health. It stayed cost-effective in most simulations at common funding thresholds, helped by fewer complications and a cheaper initial operation. The authors say the result should inform coverage policy rather than dictate it, since some inputs remain uncertain.
pmc-13617351:
Iman Nazari and three colleagues present an automated workflow that computes GenePy scores, a gene-level burden measure for rare disease genomes. Single-variant reading of a genome can miss the combined weight of several mild variants in one gene. GenePy instead folds variant consequence, allele frequency, and zygosity into one score per gene per person. The workflow runs inside the Genomics England research environment.

Built on the Nextflow system and deployed through the Lifebit CloudOS platform, the pipeline is fully containerized, meaning each step carries its own software environment for reproducibility. It harmonizes variant annotation, quality control, and chunked aggregation so burden scores can be computed securely across population-scale cohorts under strict governance rules. The authors say auditable gene-level scoring sharpens the search for diagnosis in unresolved single-gene disorders and feeds statistical prioritization and phenotype matching downstream.
pmc-13618951:
Ioannis Kyvernitakis and seven colleagues track cervical stiffness in pregnant women fitted with a cervical pessary, a silicone ring meant to support a shortening cervix and prevent preterm birth. Eighty-nine women were measured with the Pregnolia system early in the second half of pregnancy and again four weeks later. Thirty had received a pessary for a cervix of twenty-five millimeters or less, and fifty-nine healthy women served as controls.

In controls, median stiffness drifted downward over the four weeks, a change that was nominally significant but faded after statistical correction. In the pessary group, stiffness stayed flat, while cervical length and the uterocervical angle did not change in either group, and birth weights were similar. The authors read this as a potential stabilizing association worth confirming. They stress that studies including untreated women with short cervixes are needed to separate the device's effect from natural variation.
pmc-13619051:
Nyissa A. Walsh and five colleagues review what is known about sex differences in sleep waves, in a 2026 synthesis spanning adults with and without insomnia. Sleep spindles and slow-wave activity shape sleep quality, and insomnia is more prevalent in women. Yet sex effects on these oscillations are poorly mapped. The team searched four databases, appraised bias with two scales, and pooled results where possible.

Forty-three studies qualified, but thirteen, covering six hundred sixty-eight normal sleepers, reported enough for meta-analysis. There, women showed higher spindle density and stronger sigma and delta power than men. Most remaining studies recruited people with insomnia. Their statistics were too incompletely reported to pool, and interactions between sex and diagnosis were sparse. The authors conclude that the female advantage in these sleep rhythms is real among healthy sleepers, while the insomnia side urgently needs better-designed and better-reported studies.
pmc-13619751:
C Van der Meer and three colleagues audited a fracture liaison service at a Johannesburg hospital, a program meant to prevent second fractures in people with fragile bones. They reviewed 247 patients admitted to the orthopedic ward and enrolled between October 2022 and June 2024. Records covered risk factors, test results, treatments given, and how long patients stayed.

Most patients were women between sixty and eighty-nine, and hip fractures dominated the caseload. Calcium and vitamin D reached most patients, yet only about a quarter received the bone-strengthening infusion drug while in hospital. Drug shortages explained most missed doses, and kidney disease ruled out others. Vitamin D insufficiency was common, men smoked and drank far more than women, and many patients had fallen before or showed poor thinking scores. The authors say the service helps but cannot reach full effect while drug supply stays unreliable.
pmc-13620251:
Khaled Skaik led a 2026 systematic review of fibrin-based scaffolds added to meniscal repair, a technique meant to help tears heal in the poorly supplied inner meniscus. Surgeons increasingly preserve the meniscus rather than trim it, yet healing in zones with little blood supply remains uncertain. The team searched three databases through October 2025 and kept fifteen studies covering 438 patients, most with tears in low-supply zones.

Among 252 patients who received a fibrin clot made from their own venous blood, about 77.5 percent healed fully, 12.2 percent partly, and 10.3 percent failed, with complications in 8.2 percent. Other fibrin variants, from bone marrow concentrate or platelet-rich preparations, also improved symptom and function scores. Compared with repair alone, fibrin augmentation healed better and functioned better. Surgeons get encouraging but still low-level evidence, since the review's overall evidence grade was level four.
pmc-13620851:
Hamid Valizadeh, Mehdi Taghinejad-Roudbaneh, and Ruhollah Kianfar worked out how much lysine young Japanese quail chicks actually need, and how that need shifts with the protein level of the feed. The first two weeks after hatching set up a quail's lifetime productivity, yet requirement tables for modern fast-growing strains are thin. Nine hundred chicks were raised on fifteen diets mixing three protein levels with five lysine levels.

Growth, feed use, and carcass traits all responded to both factors, and the two interacted for several measures. A mid-range lysine level gave the best weight and protein efficiency before gains leveled off. Requirement estimates from a linear broken-line model, which finds the point where gains plateau, rose with protein level and fit the data better than a curved model. The authors advise setting lysine as a share that climbs with dietary protein.
pmc-13621351:
Anjusha Prakash and four colleagues tested simple, flexible molecular sensors that grab phosphate-type anions out of water. Phosphates run everything from cell energy to fertilizer, yet their strong love of water makes them hard to catch and measure. Ring-shaped receptors bind well but are painful to make, so the team tried straight-chain sensors armed with charged hydrogen-bond donors of three kinds.

Fluorescence titrations showed the chains bound dihydrogen phosphate most tightly, with a clear pecking order across related anions, including the cell energy carriers ATP and ADP. The sensors also caught glyphosate, the widely used herbicide flagged as a possible carcinogen, at weaker strength. Because each sensor answers slightly differently, arrays of them plus machine learning sorted and measured mixtures with perfect classification in the reported tests. Detection limits reached about one micromole per liter for phosphate.
pmc-13621551:
Aimée Kingsada led a 2026 scoping review of what patients value in digital health tools, from phone apps to telehealth visits, and how researchers measure those values. Adoption depends on fit with patient needs, yet preference studies vary widely in method and focus. The team searched five databases for literature from 2000 to 2026, screening 2,419 records down to 85 studies that met the criteria.

Quantitative studies, just over half the set, mostly used choice-based methods that trade attributes against each other, while qualitative studies traced themes in interviews and open answers. Across studies, patients kept returning to cost, privacy, convenience, and personalization, with preferences shifting by tool type, health condition, and age. Few studies priced features or ranked their relative weight. Designers get a practical steer: build personal, easy, secure, and affordable tools, and test them with the older adults managing chronic illness who need them most.
pmc-13623451:
Patrick Steven Tajanlangit and Sean Michael Tajanlangit published a 2026 review of shared epigenetic mechanisms linking eczema and food allergy. Epigenetics covers chemical marks that switch genes up or down without changing the DNA code.
