The two conditions often appear together in the atopic march, the childhood drift from eczema toward hay fever and asthma, and genetics explains only part of the risk.

The review pulls together studies of DNA methylation, histone changes, and small regulatory RNAs across skin and gut tissue. Recurring marks sit on the genes for two immune signals, IL-4 and IL-13, and on FOXP3, a gene that keeps immune tolerance in place. Silencing of barrier genes in skin and gut lining appears in both diseases. The authors argue that this layer of control lets early skin damage prime the gut to react to foods, and they point to allergy biomarkers and treatments as the payoff.
pmc-13624051:
Iasmin Góes Frossard leads a study of how worker body size shapes the skin, or cuticle, of two leaf-cutting ant species. Colonies of these ants split work among small, medium, and large workers, and small bodies lose water faster through their surface. The cuticle's thickness and its fatty outer layer are its main defence against drying out.

Workers of both species were sorted by head width into the three size classes, and cuticle traits were measured on each. Small workers carried thicker cuticles and a stronger lipid signal than medium and large workers, in both species. The lipid response did not separate the species, but cuticle thickness did: one species ran thicker-skinned at every size. The authors argue that size sets the pattern, while each species' work roles tune it, since small workers tend the fungus gardens indoors and large ones forage and defend outside.
pmc-13625251:
Walid Shaalan and a large team audit how far genetic counseling reaches women treated for ovarian cancer at one center. Counseling and inherited gene testing shape care and family warnings, yet routine uptake stays uneven. The team mailed questionnaires to patients operated on between January 2021 and June 2025, linking answers with clinical records and ranking each reported barrier by how often it appeared.

Of 256 patients reached, 132 replied. Most had heard of counseling, chiefly from hospital doctors. About seven in ten went on to attend counseling and take the gene test. A pathogenic variant turned up in over a quarter of those tested. Counseling use climbed across the study years. Remaining gaps in information and access mark where clinics should push next.
pmc-13626151:
Mingjing Dong and colleagues trace how New Zealand's COVID-19 rules bent the nation's electricity demand. Across nearly three years the country moved from an alert level system to a traffic light framework. The team modeled daily demand from late February 2021 to the end of July 2023. Their time-series model, backed by break tests, tied each policy stage to a change in power use against the expected path.

The lightest alert stage came with a three percent rise in demand. The strictest red light phase came with a drop of about two and a half percent. Most other stages showed no clear effect. Break tests confirmed shifts at two stages, and demand drifted down once rules ended, with daily and weekly rhythms reshaped. Grid planners can borrow the method for the next disruption.
pmc-13626351:
Aaron Koay and colleagues write a satirical opinion piece on how not to write about health equity. Borrowing the mock-manual style of Binyavanga Wainaina's famous essay on writing about Africa, they list the field's lazy habits as if they were advice. Declare that no one should be left behind, they say, without naming who does the leaving, and call people vulnerable populations so that history reads like weather.

Each jab targets a real dodge: calling engineered gaps mere differences, praising research gaps that delay action, and draining words of power and blame. The World Health Organization defines equity as the absence of unfair, avoidable differences, and the authors argue writing should honor that sharpness. Clear language, in their telling, is itself a health intervention.
pmc-13626951:
Torsten H Struck led a 2026 paper on a step-by-step procedure for choosing which species to sequence in large biodiversity genomics projects, where candidates far outnumber funds. Picking species by hand risks bias and trade-offs, so the Biodiversity Genomics Europe project built a three-stage process: exclusion, ranking, and a practical check, tested on test data. The aim was a sound list that still mirrors the diversity of nominated species.

The selected set kept the spread of the nominated pool across species groups, places, and population types while reducing bias. Practical limits and funding shaped the final list more than any other factor, pointing to where investment would most expand reference-genome diversity. Project leaders get a clear method they can repeat. It matches the wider European biodiversity community's priorities, with a frank admission that budgets, not biology alone, still decide much of the outcome.
pmc-13629451:
Javier Barriga-Cuartero and four colleagues built a two-step test for Vibrio harveyi, a bacterium that devastates marine fish farms, which also flags isolates carrying a suspected virulence marker. Published in 2026, the workflow first grows samples briefly in a nutrient broth, then runs a duplex DNA test targeting a species gene and a plasmid gene linked to virulence.

The enrichment step improved detection roughly a thousandfold, reaching very low bacterial levels in fish tissue and water. The assay stayed specific when challenged with close Vibrio relatives and performed on spiked samples plus real material from Mediterranean farms. The authors offer it as a rapid, field-practical screen for surveillance programmes that need to spot dangerous strains early.
pmc-13630551:
Mitchell Dickau and two colleagues ask how much damage from overshooting climate targets can later be undone. They used a mid-complexity Earth system model. Their 2026 study ran 42 paired scenarios. In each, temperatures briefly exceeded a goal and then returned. Matching baselines never overshot at all.

For hard-to-reverse changes, in permafrost and across the oceans, the leftover gap scaled simply. It tracked what the authors call degree-years of overshoot. That is how far temperatures passed the target, times how long they stayed there. This single measure predicted extra permafrost carbon loss. It also predicted ocean heat, oxygen, acidity, and sea level changes. The result gives policymakers a compact yardstick. It measures the lasting cost of brief breaches.
pmc-13634051:
Najarzadeh Torbati and colleagues report a 2026 genetics case of a family whose inherited hearing loss may involve two genes at once. Related parents passed the same gene changes to the proband, the first person studied. One sits in PALM3, a candidate hearing-loss gene, and one in OTOA, a known hearing gene. The team tested what the PALM3 change does to gene messages.

A lab test showed the PALM3 change makes the gene skip a segment, breaking its protein across all known forms. Mice lacking Palm3 show hearing problems, though the hearing organ's structure stays intact. The OTOA change could still explain the loss alone, so a dual diagnosis cannot be ruled out. The case shows how a second gene change can muddy the hunt for new disease genes, and why lab proof matters.
pmc-13639551:
Han surveyed a 2026 national study of exercise non-participation among older South Koreans with disabilities, using the 2024 national sports participation survey for this group. Physical activity supports healthy ageing, yet this population exercises far less than peers without disabilities. The sample held 1,865 adults aged sixty or over who reported no exercise in the prior year.

Lack of motivation was the commonest main barrier at about twenty-seven percent, followed by poor health near twenty-four percent and lack of time. Han found barriers varied significantly across disability types, underlining that non-participation is not one uniform problem. Severe disability lowered the odds of intending to exercise, while employment raised them noticeably. Among those intending to start, outdoor walking was the favourite mode at about fifty-eight percent.
pmc-13640851:
Mohd Fazrin Mohd Rohani and four colleagues present a 2026 case of follicular thyroid cancer spreading to the cavernous sinus, a blood-filled space at the skull base. Such spread is exceedingly rare and signals disease that no longer responds to radioactive iodine.

Their thirty-seven-year-old patient had his thyroid removed and received repeated iodine therapy, yet cancer persisted. Four years later he developed palsies of several eye-moving nerves from a skull-base mass that iodine scans could not detect. Biopsy confirmed the spread. Despite radiation and a targeted drug, he died sixteen months later, showing the poor outlook for this pattern.
pmc-13642051:
Dan Liu led a 2026 engineering paper on a see-through metasurface that hides a target in infrared and microwave bands at once, a multispectral stealth design. Single-band stealth fails against modern sensors that scan visible, infrared, and radar wavelengths together, and most dual-band designs stay opaque or trap heat. The new device stacks an infrared camouflage layer with patterned emissivity against a radar-reduction layer that mixes absorption with scattering, avoiding the heat buildup of pure absorption.

A fabricated sample camouflaged in the infrared range of 3 to 14 micrometers, cut radar cross-section by 10 decibels across 7.5 to 16.5 gigahertz, and transmitted up to 55.3 percent of visible light. That combination suits windows and sensor covers that must stay transparent while hiding heat and radar signatures. Defense engineers get a lightweight, integrated prototype, with scale-up and real-world background matching still to be proven.
pmc-13645551:
Dandan Liu and seven colleagues report a genome-wide study of a gene family in tea plants, focused on one gene that helps the plant bear cold. The family is called aldo-keto reductases, a group of proteins that clear harmful byproducts inside cells. The team mapped forty-eight family genes in the tea genome. They then singled out one cold-responsive gene for closer tests.

The chosen gene switched on strongly in cold conditions and sat in both the cell nucleus and the surrounding cell fluid. Adding it to bacteria, tobacco relatives, and Arabidopsis plants improved cold tolerance in each case. Treated plants showed less cell damage and stronger defense enzyme activity under cold stress. The authors offer the gene as a lead for breeding tea varieties that cope better with cold snaps.
pmc-13646251:
Yujing Liu and three colleagues examine, in a 2026 paper, how random molecular noise changes the routes cells take when switching fate. Biology often pictures cell types as valleys in a landscape, with cells rolling from one valley to another as they develop. Standard math finds the cheapest path between valleys under smooth, deterministic rules. The team instead computed paths when noise rules the small-scale motion inside cells.

For their test systems, the noisy paths strayed substantially from the cheapest deterministic routes. Maps of where transitions actually happen, and of the currents that carry them, differed by noise setting. Simple barrier-crossing pictures missed these shifts. The authors say the result matters wherever models predict how cells change type, from development to reprogramming. Their work gives modelers a way to see noise as a route-shaping force, not mere fuzz on top of a fixed map.
pmc-13647951:
Yiying Shi and twelve colleagues design a long-acting peptide that blocks two brake proteins, PTPN1 and PTPN2, which mute insulin and leptin signaling inside cells. Type 2 diabetes and obesity both grow from resistance to those hormones. Current weekly drugs mostly suppress appetite and can rebound after stopping. The engineered peptide, called Y5, carries a fat tail and a tag that together give it potency, durability in the blood, and a long half-life.

In cells, Y5 restored the signaling chains that insulin and leptin resistance had silenced. Diabetic mice dosed once a week gained lasting blood sugar control with lower circulating insulin, a sign of restored sensitivity. Obese mice lost substantial weight and fat while keeping their normal food intake, a route distinct from appetite drugs. Liver fat improved and tolerance looked good across regimens. The authors present dual brake release as a new strategy worth clinical testing.
pmc-13648351:
Caroline E. Roe and four colleagues compare ways to turn adult mouse brain into a single-cell suspension suitable for mass cytometry, a method that measures dozens of markers per cell. Brain is hard to dissociate because it is densely connected and rich in debris, and different cell types survive the process unevenly.

Mechanical breakup combined with gentle enzymes such as papain or collagenase yielded roughly equal numbers of live cells from white and grey matter. A density-gradient cleanup step, by contrast, destroyed most viable cells and left too few rare cells to analyse. Cytometry identified neurons plus six major non-neuronal populations, and freezing preserved most proportions, giving other laboratories a practical preparation recipe.
pmc-13649451:
Dongze Wang and three colleagues asked if a nerve block near the neck can help people with long-term poor sleep and anxiety cut back on sleep drugs. The block calms a nerve cluster tied to arousal. The team reviewed records from 2022 to 2025 at one centre and matched 80 treated patients with 80 who got routine care.

After one month, 40 percent of the block group hit a set goal for cutting drug burden, against 15 percent under routine care. The gain came mostly from halving drug load; full stops were too few to judge firmly. The authors adjusted for age, sex, and starting burden, and the gap held. They frame this as a real-world lead, not proof.
pmc-13649551:
Alaina P. Vidmar and three colleagues argue in a 2026 paper that weight-loss surgery care should treat the whole household, not just one patient. Obesity runs in families, and risk, habits, and treatment results cluster under one roof. Surgery in one person even shifts the health and habits of partners and children who had no surgery.

Their plan joins child and adult care in one structure, with shared teams, shared visit plans, and home routines built on joint goals. They also call for merged records, joint billing, and cross-team deals to make the model pay its way. Gaps to study next include how far the ripple to untreated kin reaches. The authors frame the home as the true unit of care.
pmc-13651451:
Meera Davuluri and five colleagues report a 44-year-old man whose thyroid cancer returned in an unusual place: a tumor in the cerebellum at the back of the brain. His cancer was an oncocytic, or Hurthle cell, carcinoma, a type that spreads through the bloodstream and often ignores radioactive iodine treatment.

After thyroid removal and radioactive iodine ablation, scans looked clean, yet his tumor marker climbed steadily for eighteen months while iodine scans stayed negative. A glucose-based scan then revealed nodules in both lungs. Around twenty-two months after surgery, dizziness and headache led to imaging that found a cystic and solid mass pressing on the brainstem. Surgeons removed it, and tissue markers confirmed thyroid origin with high-grade features. His symptoms resolved, and radiation to the cavity was recommended. The authors argue a rising marker with silent scans should trigger a hunt for hidden disease, brain imaging included.
pmc-13651551:
Xiaobo Huang and two colleagues design a system that judges college students' mental health vulnerability from very few labeled examples and tracks risk as it evolves. Labeled data are scarce, labeling is costly, privacy is sensitive, and samples skew heavily. Older tools give one static judgment that cannot follow a changing student.

Their grading model borrows meta-learning methods that recognize new categories from a few examples. It assigns risk grades through prototype matching with ordered thresholds. A second method frames monitoring as a sequence of decisions learned by a meta-reinforcement policy. Tests used simulated cohorts rather than real students. Grading accuracy beat a deep classifier by a wide margin at ten examples per grade. The decision policy flagged risk more precisely than its non-meta rival without degenerating into escalation. The authors present the pair as a practical route to earlier screening where labeled data are scarce.
pmc-1636651:
Bedogni, Bellentani, Miglioli, and co-authors create the Fatty Liver Index, a simple score for predicting fatty liver. Fatty liver is the most common liver disease in Western countries, yet confirming it usually needs scans or biopsies. A cheap estimate from routine data could help find cases early.

Using data from the Dionysos Nutrition and Liver Study, the team built and tested their formula. They studied people with and without suspected liver disease in the general population. A simple, accurate score lets doctors flag likely cases and choose who needs closer checks.
pmc-2893951:
Kilkenny, Browne, Cuthill, and co-authors present the ARRIVE guidelines for reporting animal research. ARRIVE stands for Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments. The guidelines aim to improve how bioscience research involving animals is written up and shared.

Clear reporting covers how animals were chosen, housed, and assigned, and how results were analysed. Missing details waste animals and money when other labs cannot repeat a study. Journals and funders adopted ARRIVE as a checklist, making it a lever for more honest, reusable animal research worldwide.  Funders soon pointed grant applicants toward the checklist as expected good practice.
pmc-2973851:
Jombart, Devillard, and Balloux introduce discriminant analysis of principal components, a method for studying populations sorted by their genes. New sequencing tools offered unmatched power to reveal how natural groups are set out in space and time. The same tools produced data so large that analysis became daunting.

Older Bayesian grouping methods struggled with that scale. The new method combines two classic techniques to find and describe groups with ease, without heavy guesses. It lets researchers sort members into groups and see which gene traits separate them, aiding work from wildlife care to outbreak tracing.
pmc-3069751:
Murshudov, Skubak, Lebedev, and co-authors describe REFMAC5, a program for refining macromolecular crystal structures. Refinement is the stage where an atomic model is adjusted to fit diffraction data as closely and honestly as possible. REFMAC5 ships inside the CCP4 program suite.

The program uses different likelihood functions depending on whether the data are amplitudes or intensities, and on the problem at hand. Its components handle restraints that keep chemistry sensible while fitting data. REFMAC5 became a standard refinement engine behind many structures in the public archive.  Most deposited protein structures of its era passed through refinement of this kind.
pmc-4888851:
Selkoe and Hardy revisited the amyloid hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease in 2016, twenty-five years on. The hypothesis holds that disease starts when the brain makes amyloid beta faster than it can clear it away. Debate about it has continued for decades.

The authors argue that new lines of evidence from labs and clinics worldwide support the concept. They present amyloid build-up as a very early, often initiating factor in Alzheimer's. That view guides drug development aimed at clearing or blocking amyloid early. The review is a key statement in the long argument over what causes this common dementia.
pmc-5614451:
The GBD 2016 Risk Factors Collaborators published a comparative risk assessment in 2017. The study assesses, for the whole world, how much people are exposed to each risk and how much disease that exposure causes. The analysis covered a wide set of behavioral, environmental, occupational, and metabolic risks.

With estimates that run from 1990 to 2016, the study can track risk exposure trends over time. Critical exposures such as smoking, air pollution, high blood pressure, and poor diet are ranked by the harm they cause in each country. Tracking whether exposure rises or falls tells policy makers if prevention is working. The results guide where regulation and public health spending pay off most.
pmc-6943051:
Yuhao Chen and Xiaowei Wang described the miRDB database for microRNA targets in 2020. MicroRNAs guide gene silencing by binding target messages. Predicting those targets accurately is essential for understanding what each microRNA does.

miRDB predicts functional targets with a model trained on high-throughput experimental data. Users can search by microRNA or by gene and see ranked candidate pairings. The database covers several species and is freely available online. Wet-lab teams use the rankings to choose which predicted targets are worth testing first. Predictions can also be filtered by tissue, since many microRNA effects appear in only one organ.
pmc-7619551:
Zeina Nehme led a 2026 study identifying claudin-1 as a driver and drug target in cholangiocarcinoma, a rising and aggressive bile duct cancer with poor treatment options. Claudin-1, a tight-junction protein exposed on cell surfaces in liver fibrosis and cancer, was upregulated in cancer cells. It was linked to stemness and cell fate in single-cell and spatial analyses of patient tissues. Gain-of-function experiments in orthotopic mouse models shortened survival and boosted tumor growth, confirming an oncogenic role.

Antibodies against exposed, non-junctional claudin-1 slowed tumor growth across cell-derived and patient-derived mouse models and patient organoids, including tumors with medium or low claudin-1 levels. Treatment also curbed migration, invasion, and spread beyond the liver, by blocking Notch1 and TROP2/STAT3 signaling and reducing stemness and epithelial-mesenchymal transition.
pmc-7794651:
Kerstin Howe and colleagues argued in 2021 that human curation, careful checking by experts, remains essential for producing trustworthy genome assemblies. An assembly is the reconstructed full DNA sequence of an organism, and nearly all of biology builds on its accuracy. Sequencing machines and assembly software keep improving, yet error free assemblies remain out of reach.

The authors describe how expert curators inspect assemblies, spot joins that are wrong, break them, and repair the sequence. They show the scale of improvement this hands-on work delivers. Their case is a reminder that automation alone does not finish a genome, and that skilled human judgment still guards the quality of the reference sequences everyone else relies on.
reichenbach-physico-physiological-resear:
Karl von Reichenbach claimed a new force in his Physico-Physiological Researches, in English from 1851. Reichenbach was a rich chief of the craft of steel and tar. In dark rooms, keen guests told him they saw flames of light stream from gems, magnets, and the hands of men. He calls the force Od, from a god of the north.

He prints tests by the score to back the claim. Sages scoffed, yet seers seized on Od as their physics. The book is the root text of that force lore. Its fame shaped the occult.
rochester-knockings-1851:
Raps in a farm house launch a faith in Rochester Knockings!, a brief tract of 1851. No name stands on the tract. It tells of the Fox girls of Hydesville, near Rochester, whose house raps seemed to reply to asks in code. A dead pedlar, they claimed, spoke from the grave through the knocks on wall and floor.

Crowds flocked to hear the raps in halls. Sages came to test and scoff. The tract is the first print cry of the whole wave. It is the birth note of a world faith.
ruskin-stones-venice-vol-1-1851:
John Ruskin published The Stones of Venice, Volume 1, in 1851, subtitled The Foundations. Ruskin studies Venetian buildings as records of moral and social life. This volume lays out the elements of architecture: walls, roofs, openings, and ornament. He judges each form by truth to nature and to its materials.

Ruskin praises Gothic craft against the machine-made work of his own century. Imperfection, for him, is a sign of free and living labor. The book began his campaign to remake English taste. Architects and reformers took its lessons to heart. It remains a founding text of the Arts and Crafts spirit.
smith-pearl-great-price-1851:
Franklin D. Richards published the first Pearl of Great Price at Liverpool in 1851, a slim pamphlet with lasting weight. He gathered pieces of Joseph Smith's work for British Saints who lacked the American prints and papers. Extracts from the Book of Moses and the Book of Abraham stand at its heart, word for word.

Smith's own history and the Articles of Faith, his crisp list of beliefs, complete the little book for its first readers. What began as a missionary pamphlet grew into one of Mormonism's four standard works in time. The 1851 edition shows that scripture in embryo, before canonization fixed its place in the church.
spencer-social-statics-1851:
Herbert Spencer published Social Statics in 1851, his first statement of a social system. The book sets out the law of equal freedom. Each person, Spencer argues, may do as he wills so long as he does not infringe the equal freedom of others. From that law he derives rights to property, speech, and trade.

He opposes state churches, state education, and state poor relief as breaches of the law. Land ownership receives a radical chapter that he later softened. The book became a bible of classical liberalism in its strictest form. Later Spencer revised some claims, yet the core principle endured. It remains his most quoted early work.
the-american-phrenological-journal-and-r: One legible masthead survives amid heavy garbling. It names The American Phrenological Journal as a repository of science, literature, and general intelligence. The journal declares itself devoted to phrenology, physiology, psychology, education, mechanism, and agriculture. It also backs measures meant, in its words, to reform, elevate, and improve mankind, and it promises many engravings. No year, editor, or article title can be read clearly on the pages present.
the-german-classics-of-the-nineteenth-an: Volume seven of The German Classics is a patrons' edition of 1914. Its front pages name five chief writers. They are Hegel, Bettina von Arnim, Immermann, Gutzkow, and a run of poets. The poets run from Anastasius Grun to Georg Herwegh. Only the front matter is present here. It holds volume heads, title pages, and the start of a list of writers and translators. No poem, tale, or essay text appears in these opening pages. So the works cannot be stated from this front matter alone.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
The fifty-first number of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated October 28, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item reports that General Weyler cannot remain in Cuba. Senor Sagasta, the Spanish Prime Minister, has decided to recall him. General Ramon Blanco is to go out in his stead. The news delighted many who hate Weyler's cruel way of waging the Cuban war.

The paper tells how the matter was arranged. Weyler had sent a despatch saying he would not resign. As commander-in-chief of an army in war, he could not offer to resign in the face of an enemy. A cabinet meeting was held the day after the despatch arrived. It was decided that Weyler must be recalled. Sagasta had said his first act would be the recall, and he kept his word.
the-life-everlasting-a-reality-of-romanc:
Marie Corelli frames her romance with an author prologue on voices in the wilderness, in pages matching the other record of this title held here. Contents list twenty chapters from a heroine opening story to a fairy ship, a magic book, dreams within a dream, and a passage into the light. The prologue cites the Gospels voice in the wilderness.

Corelli observes that such voices have sounded warnings through all history and met indifference. Readers should note this record and its twin share identical opening pages. Her story pursues rebirth, spiritual love, and hidden knowledge beyond ordinary life.
the-long-vacation-pg5251:
Charlotte M. Yonge opens The Long Vacation with a preface addressed to younger readers, asking them to treat the first chapters as a prologue. The book continues the domestic politics of her Mohuns and Underwoods, families elder readers already knew. Yonge admits that continuations are proverbially failures, yet says some characters seem as if they cannot be parted with and must have their after-fates described.

She compares aging writers to painters like Turner, who saw colors in different hues as they grew older. The young write in full sympathy with the young, she argues, while older writers watch from outside, with their affections on the parents and aunts. A companion record holds only this book's contents; this record carries the preface itself.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Childhood, the first part of the Venetian Years in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, comes from the 1894 London edition rendered into English by Arthur Machen, with extra chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. Before Casanova's own preface, the volume prints an essay by Symons on Casanova at Dux. Symons complains that the memoirs have enjoyed the popularity of a bad reputation without justice from serious students.

Symons calls the memoirs perhaps the most valuable document we possess on eighteenth-century society. He ranks them above Gil Blas and Monte Cristo as a record of adventures, escapes, and masquerades. His portrait shows a thinker and fighter in one: scholar, adventurer, gamester, and stirrer in politics. The essay also prints Havelock Ellis's judgment that few books are more delightful. Readers meet Casanova first through his defenders, then through his own account of his childhood and adolescence.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
St. Pancras old church opens volume 19, No. 546, dated May 12, 1832. The humble church stood a little north of London, just over a mile from Holborn Bars. Around it, the parish still kept a village feel, although the city pressed close on every side.

Figures from Mr. Lysons give the parish 2,700 acres, reaching from Islington and Hampstead toward several Holborn parishes. Kentish Town, Camden Town, and Somer's Town all lay inside it as hamlets. Eminent churchmen had held its prebend, a paid post at St. Paul's Cathedral, among them Lancelot Andrewes, Archdeacon Paley, and William Beloe, known for translating Herodotus. Growth of the district fills the account that follows.

The Lowther Arcade leads volume 19, No. 541, dated April 7, 1832. The covered shopping passage cut through a newly finished triangle of buildings in the Strand, its main front called West Strand. It ran at an angle toward the back of St. Martin's Church.

Inside, large pilasters divide the arcade into domed compartments, each lit from above by a big domed skylight. It was wider and taller than the Burlington Arcade, though shorter. The builder, Mr. Herbert, gave the shops a uniform Grecian front in the Corinthian order, carried on slim iron columns hidden behind the shop windows. At night, gas lamps in vase-shaped ground-glass shades lit the passage from both sides.
the-winds-of-the-world-pg6751:
Talbot Mundy's Winds of the World appears again in this record, and its opening matches the other library copy: Yasmini's Song first, then the Punjab field-day of chapter one. That shared opening is stated plainly, since the two records duplicate each other. This copy's preserved pages run a little further, into the portrait of Risaldar-Major Ranjoor Singh before the third squadron.

Ranjoor Singh sits his charger like a big bronze statue, proud of a right spur shining despite the mud. A rumour says he wears solid silver spurs in bed. Bending hurts him, though, after long days in the saddle: an Afghan bullet near his ribs was stitched over too hastily in a Himalayan gully, and it still burns after hard exercise. Mundy's imperial soldier carries the coming war in his body.
tob-10051:
Genesis stands first in the Old Testament, in the King James Version's 1611 English, with Moses named in the catalog as its traditional author. God forms the world and humankind, Adam and Eve fall, and Cain kills his brother Abel. Noah rides out the flood that wipes the slate nearly clean.

After the flood and the scattering at Babel, attention narrows to one family. Abraham receives the promise of a great nation, and his line carries the story through Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph into Egypt. These founding stories of Judaism and Christianity are told here in the stately wording generations of English readers knew by heart.
tob-13151:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton published The Coming Race in 1871, sending a fictional explorer deep underground into a hollow earth. There rules the Vril-ya, a superior race wielding vril, a psychic energy that powers their utopia and their weapons alike. The narrator tours their cities as guest, student, and eventually a problem to be solved.

Part satire of Victorian society, part prophecy of energy weapons and a master race, the novel coined a word that haunted occultists for decades. Some later readers took vril literally, which Bulwer-Lytton may not have intended. The book stands as science fiction before the genre had a name, and as a warning dressed as a wonder tale.
tob-4151:
Al-Ghazali, the great theologian of Islam, wrote the Alchemy of Happiness in Persian as a short form of his Revival of the Religious Sciences. Claud Field translated it into English in 1910. Ghazali treats the soul as a kingdom to be ruled: its diseases are pride, envy, and greed, and its cure is disciplined worship.

Self-knowledge opens the book, since a person who does not know his own soul cannot know God. Marriage, food, and friendship all receive a physician's calm advice. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. The little work remains Ghazali at his most pastoral.
tob-4185-78851:
Plutarch's table talk, political counsel, and words of comfort fill much of volume three in Goodwin's Moralia. Friends at dinner debate questions large and small, from why leaves change color to what music suits a feast. The talk shows philosophy as good company.

Other essays advise rulers, console the grieving, and discuss the training of children. Plutarch moves easily between the state and the nursery. His range explains why later ages kept copying him when other essayists vanished. Goodwin's middle volume gives the fullest taste of that range, in steady Victorian prose that lets the Greek shine through.
un-ga-res-a-69-51:
The illicit trade in small arms fuels wars far from any factory, and Resolution A/69/51, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, renews the world plan against it. The text recalls the vote of the year before, and the first of the chain, passed on Christmas Eve 2001. At its heart stands the Programme of Action of 2001, the world deal to bar, fight, and wipe out the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons.

Full work on that plan is pressed as a must. So is work on its twin, the world tracing tool of 2005, which lets states mark arms and track the illicit ones fast and with trust. States had pledged themselves to both plans at past review meetings, and the vote holds them to it.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/51 of the General Assembly is the annual review of work against the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons. It stresses full implementation of the 2001 Programme of Action and the International Tracing Instrument. It endorses the report of the Fifth Biennial Meeting of States held in June 2014. It fixes the follow-up calendar: an open-ended meeting of governmental experts in New York on 1–5 June 2015, and a third review conference in 2018. States are urged to report nationally, control brokering, and match assistance needs with resources.
un-sc-res-1351:
UNDOF, the observer force on the Golan Heights, won a routine renewal in May 2001. On 30 May 2001 the Security Council extended its mandate for six months. The term ran until 30 November 2001. The Secretary-General had reported on the force earlier that month. The Council restated its standard terms without change.

The parties again had to carry out resolution 338 right away. That text from 1973 called for a ceasefire and peace talks. The Secretary-General owed a report when the term closed. It would describe events and steps taken toward 338. These six-month renewals had kept a thin blue line between Israel and Syria since 1974.
un-sc-res-1451: Filed in the official record under number 1451, this Council resolution is catalogued with a 2002 date. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1551:
Bosnia and Herzegovina was taken up by the Security Council in Resolution 1551, adopted on 9 July 2004. NATO planned to end its stabilization force, SFOR, by the end of 2004. The European Union would launch its own mission, with troops, from December 2004. Refugee returns still lay at the heart of lasting peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps SFOR running for six more months under one command. Member states may take all necessary measures to enforce the peace deal and defend the force. The existing status rules will cover the new European mission while it builds up. Local leaders bear the main duty for carrying out the Dayton deal, including handing suspects to the war crimes tribunal.
un-sc-res-1651:
Sudan's wars frame this short decision of 21 December 2005. The Council backed the African Union peace talks at Abuja on Darfur. It also backed full use of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement for the south. At the same time it deplored the violence and atrocities in Darfur. Earlier resolutions had placed sanctions on Sudan and set up a panel of experts to track them.

Here the Council extends that panel's mandate until 29 March 2006. The panel must report before its term ends. Its report goes through the sanctions committee. It covers how the arms and travel measures are working in practice.
un-sc-res-1751: Resolution 1751, from 2007, records a Security Council decision in the official wording held by English Wikisource. The document's structure is disciplined: what the members recalled, what they noted, and then what they decided, in numbered steps. Preserving that structure is preserving the decision, which is the work this entry does for later readers in this collection.
un-sc-res-1851:
Members of the Council adopted Resolution 1851 on Piracy off Somalia on 16 December 2008. Pirate attacks had grown bolder in the past six months. The tanker Sirius Star had been seized far off the coast of Kenya. Somalia's weak government could not police its own waters or try captured pirates.

The text lets states working with that government take all needed steps inside Somalia against piracy. The power runs for twelve months from an earlier vote that month. It backs deals that place law officers from regional states aboard foreign warships. Those shiprider deals help put captured pirates on trial instead of setting them free.
un-sc-res-251: Israel held a military parade in Jerusalem on 2 May 1968, and the Security Council answered the same day. In resolution 250 (1968), adopted on 27 April, the Council had unanimously decided against the parade. The Secretary-General reported on 26 April and again on 2 May. The Council deeply deplored that Israel went ahead in disregard of that unanimous decision. The whole text is this single act of censure, with no further order attached.
un-sc-res-351:
Security Council Resolution 351, adopted on June 10, 1974, recommended Bangladesh for membership in the United Nations. Bangladesh had broken from Pakistan in 1971 after a war marked by mass killing and a vast flight of refugees. Its first bid for a seat had met a Chinese veto in 1972, cast in support of Pakistan; by 1974 the path had cleared.

Pakistan itself had come to accept Bangladesh, and the Assembly seated the new state that September. The resolution is short and formal, yet it closed one of the sorest disputes left from the partition of British India. Bangladesh took its place as one of the world's most populous nations.
un-sc-res-451:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed in June 1979 with talks in view. On 15 June 1979 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 December. The parties had agreed the force should stay. Cyprus's government said the island's conditions still required it. The Secretary-General's May report guided the decision. A ten-point agreement had just set terms for new intercommunal talks.

The parties had to pursue those talks without delay. The Council wanted them steady and aimed at results. The Secretary-General kept his good offices mission. He owed a report by 30 November 1979. China did not take part in the vote. The renewal was routine in form, but the talks it backed soon stalled again.
un-sc-res-51:
Kashmir's fate was still being fought over in the spring of 1948. On 3 June 1948 the Security Council returned to the dispute between India and Pakistan. It restated its three earlier Kashmir resolutions of that year. A United Nations commission for the two countries already existed. Resolution 47 had given that commission its main duties. Those duties centered on ending the fight and arranging a free vote.

The Council now directs the commission to travel to the disputed areas without delay. The work set by resolution 47 comes first. The commission must also study points raised by Pakistan's foreign minister. It would report on those points when it judged the time right. The vote passed with three abstentions.
un-sc-res-651:
The observer group watching the Iran-Iraq cease-fire received a new term on 29 March 1990. The group, called UNIIMOG, had been set up in 1988. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 22 March, covered its work. The settlement plan of Resolution 598, from 1987, still had not been carried out in full. Resolution 651 records the renewal.

The Council called once again on the parties to carry out Resolution 598 at once. That text had set the terms for ending the Iran-Iraq war. UNIIMOG's mandate was extended for six more months, until 30 September 1990. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the steps taken toward the 1987 settlement. The observers stayed on the border line while the peace they guarded remained unfinished.
un-sc-res-751:
Somalia's collapse brought the first United Nations operation there in April 1992. On 24 April 1992 the Security Council established the United Nations Operation in Somalia. Fighting factions had signed a ceasefire in Mogadishu on 3 March. Letters of agreement followed in other towns. The Secretary-General reported on the plan days before the vote.

The Council first sent fifty observers to watch the Mogadishu ceasefire. It also agreed in principle to a security force under the Secretary-General's special representative. That force would guard relief work as aid groups faced a famine. The mission, UNOSOM, was the start of a much larger involvement. Its limits soon showed as the country slid further into war.
un-sc-res-951: United Nations Security Council Resolution 951, adopted on 21 October 1994, is a brief procedural text about the International Court of Justice. A Russian judge of the court, who had served since 1985, died on 28 September 1994. His seat stood open for a term that ran until February 1997. The Council sets 26 January 1995 as the day to elect his replacement. The Council and the General Assembly, at its forty-ninth session, vote on that day.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The Golan watch gained its usual six months in the spring of 2001. On 30 May, the Council adopted Resolution 1351 without dissent. The Secretary-General's report on the observer force had come in that month. The force, UNDOF, keeps Israel and Syria apart along the truce line. It has done so since 1974.

The text calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 at once. That 1973 order pairs a truce with peace talks. The mandate then runs to 30 November 2001. A report from the Secretary-General is due at the end. It must cover events in the area and steps toward Resolution 338. The chain of such renewals has never broken.

The Golan Heights observer force is renewed once more on 17 December 2002. UNDOF stays in place for six months, until 30 June 2003, watching the separation between Israeli and Syrian forces. The Council called on the parties to carry out its resolution 338 of 1973 without delay. It also asked the Secretary-General to report at the end of the period on developments and on steps taken toward that goal.

Chad's seat was handled in the same busy sitting as its neighbors' bids. On 23 August 1960, the Council adopted Resolution 151 without dissent. The Republic of Chad had claimed freedom from France twelve days before. It was one of a string of French African lands reaching self-rule that summer.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Chad. Chad was seated the next month. The landlocked state added its vote to a reshaped Assembly. Seventeen new members joined in that one 1960 session. Most of them were African. Their bloc gave the body's debates a new center of weight.

Bosnia's stabilization force is extended one last time by Resolution 1551, adopted unanimously on 9 July 2004. NATO had decided at its Istanbul summit to end its SFOR operation by the end of 2004. The European Union planned to launch its own mission from December 2004, with a military component. The Peace Agreement's civilian side still depended on the High Representative.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes SFOR to continue for a further planned six months under unified command. It may use all necessary measures to enforce Annex 1-A of the Peace Agreement and control Bosnia's airspace. It welcomes the handover path to the EU mission and decides the existing status-of-forces agreements will apply provisionally to the EU force from its build-up. The parties are reminded that full cooperation with the Yugoslavia tribunal, including surrendering indictees, is part of their duty to implement the peace.

Darfur's sanctions watchers gained three more months in late 2005. On 21 December, the Council adopted Resolution 1651. It acted under Chapter VII. Peace talks on Sudan ran in Abuja, Nigeria, at the time. The new peace deal for the south had just taken hold. Atrocities in Darfur, though, had not stopped.

The text extends the Panel of Experts until 29 March 2006. The panel was built under Resolution 1591. Its job is to police the Darfur arms ban and targeted sanctions. It must report before its term ends. It also sends advice on how the measures are working. Panels like this one built the proof trail for later sanctions steps.

One further month is granted to MONUC, the United Nations mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on 13 April 2007. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council kept the mission at the strength set by its earlier resolutions until 15 May 2007. The bridge extension held the operation steady while a longer renewal for the post-transition period was prepared.

Piracy off Somalia takes a new turn in Resolution 1851, adopted on 16 December 2008. Attacks had grown more daring in six months, reaching a hijacked supertanker 500 nautical miles off Kenya. Somalia's Transitional Federal Government could not patrol its waters or prosecute pirates, and captured pirates were often released for lack of courts. The EU operation Atalanta and NATO were already responding at sea.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council lets cooperating states and regional groups take all necessary measures on Somali territory for twelve months from Resolution 1846 to suppress piracy at sea. They may act with the Transitional Government's notice and consent. It backs 'shiprider' deals so regional officers can sail with foreign navies and bring suspects home for trial. It calls for a contact mechanism and a regional coordination centre, and notes that rising ransoms and the unenforced arms embargo were fuelling piracy's growth.

Four days before a tense election run-off in Côte d'Ivoire, the Council lent troops across a border. On 24 November 2010, it adopted Resolution 1951 under Chapter VII. The Secretary-General had warned that the UN mission in Côte d'Ivoire needed backup. The mission next door in Liberia, UNMIL, still had its own job to do.

The text lets the Secretary-General shift troops from Liberia for no more than four weeks. The package caps help at three infantry companies. It adds an air unit with two utility helicopters. Such lending between missions let the UN surge guards around a risky vote. No new force had to be built from scratch.

A military parade in Jerusalem provoked Resolution 251, adopted unanimously on 2 May 1968. Israel held the parade that day, marking twenty years since its founding, through a city divided since the 1967 war. Days earlier the Council had unanimously decided, in resolution 250, against such a display.

The resolution does one thing: it deeply deplores Israel's holding of the parade in disregard of that unanimous decision. There are no demands or deadlines, which makes the text a pure statement of institutional protest. It still matters as an early sign of how the status of Jerusalem would test the Council's authority, since a member state had openly ignored a direct and unanimous call.

Bangladesh joins the United Nations in the record of Resolution 351, adopted without a vote on 10 June 1974. Bangladesh had applied to join, and the Council had weighed the young state's request. The South Asian country had fought its way out of Pakistan in 1971, but its UN entry waited while recognition politics, including a Chinese veto in 1972, blocked the path.

The resolution recommends that the General Assembly admit Bangladesh to membership. That recommendation cleared the way for the Assembly to seat Bangladesh later in 1974. The two-line text is a reminder that admission is often the end of a long diplomatic struggle rather than the beginning of one.

Fresh hope for Cyprus talks bloomed in May 1979. Chiefs of both halves of the isle met in Nicosia on 18 and 19 May. They set a ten-point plan to restart talks. The UN force, UNFICYP, had kept the peace since 1964. Its host state agreed it should stay. Resolution 451 passed on 15 June 1979 by fourteen votes to none. China sat the vote out.

The force stayed to 15 December 1979. Both sides were urged to seize the ten points. Talks had to be steady, kept up, and aimed at real fruit. No drift would do. The chief's good offices would run on. A report on the work was due by 30 November. The chief's Cyprus report of 31 May had set the stage for the vote.

Kashmir's UN panel was told to get moving in this text of 1948. On 3 June, the Council adopted Resolution 51. Eight members voted yes and none voted no. China and the two Soviet republics held back. Fighting between India and Pakistan over Kashmir ground on. Earlier texts had set up a UN panel for the dispute. Resolution 47 had sketched a vote-based path as well.

The text restates those earlier steps. It directs the panel to head to the disputed areas without delay. The duties from Resolution 47 come first in its work. The panel must also study the extra matters raised by Pakistan's foreign minister. Reports go back to the Council as the panel sees fit. Its mission failed within a year.

Observers on the Iran-Iraq border gained six more months in 1990. On 29 March, the Council adopted Resolution 651. The observer group had watched the truce line since the 1988 halt to the eight-year war. The peace text behind it, Resolution 598, was still not carried out. Neither side had fully complied with its terms.

The text calls once more on both parties to act on Resolution 598 at once. It extends the observer mandate to 30 September 1990. A report from the Secretary-General is due at the end of that stretch. The quiet renewals ended the next year. The observers were then withdrawn for good.

Fifty observers were the seed of the UN's Somalia effort in 1992. On 24 April, the Council adopted Resolution 751 without dissent. Ceasefire deals had been signed in Mogadishu that March. They covered UN watch over the truce. They also set fair ways to share relief aid. Suffering across the stateless land stayed vast all the same.

The text sets up a United Nations Operation in Somalia under the Council's own charge. It backs the Secretary-General's work in the country. He must send fifty observers to the capital at once. Their job is to watch the ceasefire hold. That small mission, UNOSOM I, grew within a year into a vast relief effort. Famine and faction war swamped its first design.

Resolution 951, adopted on 21 October 1994, is a short procedural text on the International Court of Justice. The Council notes the death of Judge Nikolai Konstantinovitch Tarassov on 28 September 1994, which left a vacancy on the Court for the remainder of his term. Under Article 14 of the Court's Statute, the election date is fixed by the Council. It decides the election will take place on 26 January 1995, at a meeting of the Security Council and at a meeting of the General Assembly during its forty-ninth session.
un-un-res-fifth-report-of-the-secretary-:
By 2000 the small observer effort in Sierra Leone had grown into a full peacekeeping mission, UNAMSIL, and this fifth report of the Secretary-General, document S/2000/751, tracks its work. The mission had just survived a grave crisis. Rebels had seized hundreds of UN troops as hostages that spring.

The report reviews the rescue of the mission, the state of the ceasefire, and plans to disarm rebel fighters. It also weighs the force's size and the risks ahead. Council members used reports like this one to decide how much backing the mission would get.
vaughan-lumen-de-lumine-1651:
Thomas Vaughan, writing as Eugenius Philalethes, published Lumen de Lumine in London in 1651. Its subtitle promises a new magical light thrown upon the world. Vaughan wrote at the height of the Interregnum's occult ferment, when civil war had loosened every certainty in England, religion included.

The book is the foundational text of the English Rosicrucian revival. Vaughan mixes natural philosophy, alchemy, and theology in a prose of fire and riddling. He presents magic as a sacred science of nature's hidden light. His twin brother Henry the poet shared the family's mystical bent. Lumen de Lumine made Philalethes the leading English voice of the new occult learning.
zoist-vol-09-1851:
March 1851 to January 1852 is the span of The Zoist's ninth volume. The Great Exhibition year finds Elliotson still editing his journal of mesmerism. Painless operations, trance cures, and clairvoyant sittings fill the reports. Cerebral physiology articles continue the journal's scientific frame.

Spiritualism, newly landed from America, competes for the same public wonder. Elliotson's pages treat the older mesmeric gospel as the true key. The thirteen volume set preserves the English movement from 1843 to 1856. Volume nine shows its ninth year of stubborn print. Few fringe sciences left so full a record. The detail here is dense and direct.
